name: Missouri Independent
title: Melanie Stinnett and Betsy Fogle square off in competitive Missouri Senate race in Springfield
description: SPRINGFIELD — Melanie Stinnett and Betsy Fogle have more in common than their political affiliations might suggest. Both came to politics after careers helping Missourians navigate a complicated healthcare system. Both have made improving access to services for people with disabilities a priority. And both worked this year to restore proposed cuts to funding[...]
text:
Democratic state Rep. Betsy Fogle, Libertarian nominee Cecil Ince and Republican state Rep. Melanie Stinnett are running to replace term-limited Republican state Sen. Lincoln Hough in state Senate District 30, which is almost entirely enclosed by the boundaries of Springfield (photos submitted and by Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).SPRINGFIELD — Melanie Stinnett and Betsy Fogle have more in common than their political affiliations might suggest.
Both came to politics after careers helping Missourians navigate a complicated healthcare system. Both have made improving access to services for people with disabilities a priority. And both worked this year to restore proposed cuts to funding that helps people with disabilities stay in their homes and communities.
But the two state representatives are now competing for a Springfield-based Missouri Senate seat that Democrats haven’t won in 80 years.
Stinnett, a Republican, and Fogle, a Democrat, are vying to replace term-limited Republican state Sen. Lincoln Hough in the 30th District. Libertarian Cecil Ince is also on the ballot.
The contest comes at an unusual political moment. Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected two Republican-backed constitutional amendments in August, including one that would have made it harder for citizens to change the state constitution and another aimed at eliminating the state income tax.
Whether that dissatisfaction will extend to Republican candidates in November remains uncertain. But Democrats hope it creates an opening in Springfield, where a victory would bring them one seat closer to breaking the GOP’s two-thirds supermajority in the Missouri Senate.
The key differences between Stinnett and Fogle were on display during competing events on a warm September evening in Springfield.
About a dozen protesters gathered outside Phoenix Home Care & Hospice, carrying hand-lettered signs criticizing Stinnett’s records. Inside, Stinnett was hosting a panel discussion on healthcare access.
At the press conference outside, held by the Will of the People PAC — which has endorsed Fogle — speakers drew a connection between high healthcare costs and Stinnett’s support for Amendment 5, which would have given lawmakers five years to introduce new sales taxes or raise existing sales tax rates to replace income tax revenues. Fogle opposed Amendment 5, describing it as a cost of living increase for constituents.
Melanie Donnell speaks at a press conference held by Will of the People PAC outside of Phoenix Home Care & Hospice on Sept. 22 (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Melanie Donnell, a kindergarten teacher from Springfield, told those gathered about her family’s medical costs: $10,000 a year, with insurance, to treat her rheumatoid arthritis and her daughter’s cystic fibrosis. If Amendment 5 had passed, Donnell said, those expenses might have risen even higher.
“It’s already so hard to afford the care our families need,” she said. “Why would Melanie Stinnett and Mike Kehoe want to make it even harder?”
Barriers to healthcare were no less prominent in discussions inside, but no one mentioned the state tax code as the problem or solution.
One panelist, Rachel Adams, a speech language pathologist in Ozark, said it’s become so expensive for her clinic to provide insurance to employees that it has switched to a direct care model, which bypasses insurance companies by directly paying providers a flat fee for primary care.
“The whole business is now paying for our employees to have direct primary care access,” Adams said. “It’s more affordable. They’re getting more out of their doctors.”
 A Democratic opening?

Both parties have invested heavily in the race, and Stinnett and Fogle are neck and neck in fundraising. 
As of Sept. 3, Stinnett’s campaign had raised $559,709, while Fogle’s campaign had raised $554,056. With less than a month to go before the election, Stinnett has more cash on hand than Fogle — $480,225 compared to $341,799. But Fogle has outspent Stinnett, including on ads.  
Though Stinnett’s campaign has slightly outraised Fogle’s, the independent PAC supporting Fogle has raised more than one supporting Stinnett. Forward PAC, which supports Fogle, had raised $423,973 with $401,187 on hand as of Sept. 2, while Heart of SGF, supporting Stinnett, had raised $369,250 with $341,863 on hand as of Sept. 3.
Democrats also saw an encouraging sign in August’s primary turnout. That included state Senate District 30, where Fogle netted 14,417 votes and Stinnett got 12,494 votes. Both candidates were running unopposed in the primaries. 
Cecil Ince, running as a Libertarian in the district, won 265 votes. 
And state GOP leaders have expressed concern that November ballot measures will bring out Democratic and independent voters in the kind of numbers that defeated Amendments 4 and 5 in August. 
Amendment 4 lost 80-20 statewide and 81-19 in Greene County, while Amendment 5 lost 83-17 statewide and 84-16 in Greene County. 
November ballot measures include Amendment 6, which would require an 80% threshold for lawmakers to overturn voter-approved legislation and prohibit lawmakers from weakening the initiative petition process.
Dan Ponder, a professor of political science at Drury University, said voter turnout might be higher than expected for an election with only one statewide race, for auditor. But he cautioned that while opposition to Amendments 4 and 5 might have increased turnout for Fogle in August, that might not be enough to help Democrats in the 30th District.
“Clearly, in a Republican area, with both of those things going down with over 80% of the vote, there’s obviously quite a few Republicans who are going to vote Republican, or people who voted for a Republican but also voted against these (measures),” Ponder said.
Fogle told The Independent she supports Amendment 6, saying she would “welcome a generational shift of power away from elected officials and back into the hands of the people who sent us there.”
Stinnett told The Independent that while she thinks the 80% threshold in Amendment 6 is too high, she would support strengthening voters’ voice by putting a moratorium on legislative changes to voter-approved measures in the first few years after their passage.
“Whether we pass as law as legislators or people pass things in a citizen-led initiative, there can always be unintended consequences that weren’t foreseen,” Stinnett said. “…So I think that is the legislature’s role: to really review current statute, review things that are currently in place and ensure that it’s really providing the best outcomes for the state as a whole.”
Ince called Amendment 6 a “wolf in sheep’s clothing,” saying it “bypasses the rule of law and institutes majority rule” and that the initiative petition process should remain in its current form.
 Different paths to Jefferson City

Fogle started her career at Jordan Valley Community Health Center, where she helped low-income patients navigate state government to gain access to services. 
“My job was to address all the non-clinical needs of my patients,” Fogle told The Independent. “So I did Medicaid applications, food stamps, helped with transportation, childcare — all of the things state government plays a role in.”
Fogle recalled working with a patient who struggled with substance use. When the patient became pregnant, Fogle said, she did everything she could to prepare to be a mom.
“I helped her apply for Medicaid,” Fogle said. “She got clean. She would come in every single day to see me and check in and make sure she was holding herself accountable.”
But the patient delivered her baby before Missouri expanded Medicaid coverage for postpartum mothers from 60 days to a year in 2023, and she relapsed and died shortly after giving birth.
“That was a shocking reality of how policy passed in Jefferson City or policy not passed in Jefferson City directly impacts the lives of people back home that we care about,” Fogle said.
“In that moment,” Fogle added, “I just thought, ‘Man, people just deserve better.’”
Fogle, who has served on the House Budget Committee since 2021 and was ranking Democrat on the committee in 2025 and 2026, said her priority has been “passing a fiscally responsible budget that makes the right investments in our state.”
Committee members from both parties this year worked to restore $80.7 million in cuts proposed by Kehoe to Medicaid services that help people with disabilities live safely in their homes and participate in their communities.
Fogle said that while “it was an honor” to work to reinstate that funding, the state is likely to continue facing cuts to Medicaid, as well as education.
“I would imagine we’ll see an intent from the majority party to cut services there, and it would be disingenuous for me not to tie that directly to revenue,” Fogle said. “You have to have dollars to pay your bills.”
Stinnett also worked to restore the proposed disability services funding, though she pursued a different approach.
She sponsored a measure that would have put proceeds from a proposed annual $250 fee levied on video lottery machines toward the services, but the video lottery bill ultimately did not pass.
Stinnett, a licensed speech pathologist and chair of the House Health and Mental Health Committee, told The Independent she started doing legislative advocacy in 2016 because she noticed coverage gaps while working in her practice, which she founded in 2014.
Alongside the Columbia-based group of moms who formed the nonprofit Missouri Disability Empowerment, Stinnett advocated for a 2019 law requiring commercial insurance companies to cover services such as speech and occupational therapies for children with developmental or physical disabilities. An existing mandate had only included children diagnosed with autism.
Rep. Melanie Stinnett discusses healthcare access with Rachel Adams, a speech pathologist from Ozark, and Susan Hinck, an advanced practice gerontological specialist from Springfield, during a panel on Sept. 22 (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Stinnett said her experience interacting with insurance companies helped her work alongside lawmakers to draft the legislation. It’s part of what convinced her to run for the Missouri House, and she was first elected in 2022.
“Over the years, it really became apparent to me…that the things I had done in my life leading up to that point had prepared me with the skill set and knowledge base to really impact positive change,” Stinnett said.
Stinnett said one of her proudest achievements was her work on 2023 legislation that expanded Medicaid eligibility through Missouri’s Ticket to Work program for people with disabilities who are employed.
Stinnett said the legislation allows people with disabilities to access services that are difficult to find outside of Medicaid, such as personal care assistance.
“What that does for individuals with disabilities in our community is open up an opportunity for them to work and contribute something productive in their community, find ways to thrive with whatever skill set or things that they love in their work,” Stinnett said.
Unlike Stinnett and Fogle, Ince’s political involvement began outside the two major parties.
Ince, who has worked as an actor, told The Independent he first heard about the Libertarian Party in 2000 from former Springfield City Councilman Doug Burlison, who was petitioning at the time to put the party’s presidential candidate, Harry Browne, on the ballot in Missouri.
Since then, Ince has run for various public offices but hasn’t been elected. He netted 4.6% of the vote in Missouri’s 2016 Libertarian presidential primary. 
“A lot of people see things in black and white,” Ince said. “They don’t realize that there are other options or other approaches to problems, issues and situations that really need to be discussed rather than just A or B.”
 Party lines

Although Stinnett and Fogle have found common ground on disability services, their legislative records reveal differences that have become central to the campaign.
Will of the People, the PAC that hosted the press conference criticizing Stinnett’s record on Amendment 5, has targeted Stinnett and other Republicans for supporting efforts to reverse voter-approved measures.
Stinnett voted for measures overturning the abortion rights amendment and paid sick leave initiative approved by voters in 2024.  
But Stinnett broke with her party in May, by voting to return a budget bill to conference because it relied partly on uncertain lottery revenues to fund schools. She was one of 16 Republicans to do so. That effort failed.
Ponder said that even though the hill Democrats have to climb in the district is “flatter than has been the case” in the past, it’s “a very competitive seat.”
“Who knows how it’s going to come out?” Ponder said. “I wouldn’t want to bet on the outcome.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: America at its best has an ever-expanding circle of ‘we,’ Tony Award winner writes
description: Supporters of LGBT rights protest on the street in front of the U.S. Supreme Court, wave their placards as they were arrested Tuesday, Oct. 8, 2019, in Washington. The Supreme Court is set to hear arguments in its first cases on LGBT rights since the retirement of Justice Anthony Kennedy. Kennedy was a voice for gay rights while his successor, Brett Kavanaug[...]
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.   

There may be no more powerful word in the American experiment than the simple, one-syllable pronoun we.  
It is the first word of the United States Constitution: “We the People of the United States….” Before government is described, before powers are delegated, before rights are protected, before any ethnicity is proclaimed, there is an act of collective imagination. The Constitution begins not with a king, a ruler or an army, but with a people. It assumes that a nation can be built upon a shared identity rather than shared blood, tribe, language or religion.  
Yet the genius — and the burden — of that first word is that it has never been fully settled.  
Who exactly is “we”?  
America’s story has been, in many respects, the ongoing argument over that single word.  
The Declaration of Independence had already planted the nation’s moral seed 11 years earlier by proclaiming that “all men are created equal” and endowed with unalienable rights. Those words represented humanity at its highest aspirations. Yet at the very moment those ideals were proclaimed, slavery remained woven into the fabric of the colonies. Women possessed few political rights. Indigenous nations were excluded from the American body politic. Property ownership determined participation. The ideals were universal; however, their application was painfully selective.  
From its beginning, then, America possessed a remarkable duality.  
It was simultaneously the most radical declaration of human equality the world had ever seen and a nation unable to extend that equality to everyone living within its borders.  
This contradiction has often been described as hypocrisy. There is truth in that. But there is something even more complicated at work. America was founded not as a completed achievement but as an unfinished proposition. Its founding documents established an aspiration far larger than the society that first produced them. In doing so, they created a permanent moral tension between who Americans were and who they claimed they could become.  
The word we became both promise and challenge that every generation has inherited by fate or design.  
The Civil War was, at its heart, a violent disagreement over who belonged within the American “we.” Abraham Lincoln understood this profoundly. At Gettysburg, he turned not to the Constitution but to the Declaration’s promise that all are created equal, asking whether any nation conceived upon such principles could long endure. The war was fought not merely over territory or economics but over whether the nation’s definition of “we” would forever exclude millions because of race.  
The Declaration of Independence is on display at the National Archives, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
The abolition of slavery answered one question while opening countless others.  
The Reconstruction Amendments expanded citizenship. Yet segregation emerged. The Constitution said “we,” but Jim Crow screamed “not you!”  
Women organized, marched and demanded that the nation’s opening word finally include them politically. Native Americans fought for recognition as citizens within a country built upon lands that had once been theirs. Immigrants arriving from every continent sought not simply opportunity but admission into the American story itself. Labor movements insisted that economic dignity belonged inside the definition of citizenship. The Civil Rights Movement challenged a nation that celebrated liberty abroad while denying equal treatment at home.  
Again and again, the question remained remarkably consistent.  
Who belongs inside the word, the ostensible protected circle of the word, we?  
Every expansion of American democracy has been an attempt to answer that question more generously than the generation before.  
Yet, the struggle has never ended.  
Today the debates have changed their vocabulary but not their substance. Immigration, voting rights, religious liberty, LGBTQ rights, racial justice, economic inequality, disability rights, artificial intelligence, DEI, citizenship and even access to education all circle back to the same foundational question. Whose interests matter? Whose voices count? Whose future deserves protection? In other words, who belongs within “We the People”?  
Perhaps this perpetual disagreement frustrates us because we imagine unity as agreement. It is not.   
Perhaps America’s founders, knowingly or not, created something different?  
The Constitution does not define “we” with mathematical precision. It does not provide an exhaustive list of who to include. Instead, it establishes a framework through which each generation must wrestle with its own conscience. Accordingly, the ambiguity is not simply a flaw, it can also be understood as a source of extraordinary resilience.  
Because the meaning of “we” has never been frozen, America has repeatedly found ways to enlarge it.  
The nation’s greatest leaders have understood this instinctively.  
Frederick Douglass challenged America not to abandon its founding ideals but to fulfill them. Susan B. Anthony and Sojourner Truth insisted women already belonged inside the Constitution’s promise. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke of the Declaration and Constitution as a promissory note yet to be fully redeemed. Labor leaders argued that farmworkers belonged within the circle of American dignity. Barack Obama said “. . . yes WE can.” Countless others — known and unknown — have devoted their lives not to replacing America’s founding principles but to widening the embrace of the word that begins them.  
They understood that patriotism is not blind acceptance of who “we” have been. Patriotism is faithful commitment to who “we” might yet become.  
This is America’s paradox.  
The same nation capable of exclusion has also possessed an unmatched capacity for self-correction. The same Constitution once interpreted to tolerate slavery eventually became the instrument used to dismantle segregation. The same democracy that denied voting rights eventually expanded them. The same institutions that once excluded have often become vehicles for inclusion.  
Progress has never been automatic. Every enlargement of “we” required courage, sacrifice, protest, persuasion, legislation, litigation and often blood. History moves because ordinary people refuse to accept that yesterday’s definition must become tomorrow’s destiny.  
That may be the true genius of the American experiment. Our shared history necessitates a collective approach to a shared destiny defined by common ground.  
Unlike nations built primarily upon ethnicity or ancestry, America has always rested upon an idea. Ideas are powerful precisely because they can grow. They invite interpretation. They demand renewal. They challenge every generation to ask whether its practices are worthy of its principles.  
The Constitution begins with “We the People” not because the authors believed they had already perfected that community, but because they dared to imagine one. In this framing, we are all essential sparks in a grand design. The work of democracy has always been to make that imagination more real.  
Perhaps the ultimate measure of America’s greatness will never be whether it has perfectly embodied its ideals. No nation has done so. Rather, its greatness lies in whether it continues to possess the humility to ask who has been left outside the circle and the courage to bring them in.  
The first word of the Constitution remains unfinished.  
Every election, every courtroom, every classroom, every place of worship, every neighborhood, every act of citizenship quietly asks us to complete its sentence.  
“We” is not merely a description.  
It is an invitation.  
It calls every generation to widen the circle just enough that someone who once stood outside can finally say, without hesitation, qualification or presupposition, “We the People” includes me.  

B.K. Fulton is an author, Tony Award-winning Broadway producer, former CEO of Verizon’s Mid-Atlantic region and producer of films and documentaries, including PBS’ “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel With A Cause.” He is a board member for The Joan Trumpauer Mulholland Foundation, an organization dedicated to civil rights education. Joan Trumpauer Mulholland participated in the 1961 Freedom Rides to Jackson and attended Tougaloo College. Through this foundation, Fulton helps support micro-scholarships and educational programs for HBCU students, including those in Mississippi. Fulton lives in Richmond, Virginia.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Which CT towns are the most walkable?
description: Compared to other cities and towns around the U.S., several CT municipalities were more walkable than most, according to 2025 data.
text:
When people think about Connecticut, bustling city life might not be the first thing that comes to mind. But compared to other cities and towns around the country, several Connecticut municipalities are more walkable than most, according an analysis published by City Health Dashboard.
In the analysis, which used 2025 data, walkability was scored on a scale of 1 to 100, with 100 being the most walkable. On average, U.S. cities included in the data scored 40.5 points.
Walkability promotes both physical and social activity, according to experts. 
Hartford, New Haven and Bridgeport were Connecticut’s most walkable cities in 2025, all scoring more than 70 on the walkability scale. The analysis placed them into a category of “very walkable.” That stands in contrast to most American downs and cities:  In those that scored the average, 40.5, most errands require a car.
Still, the ease of completing errands without a car varies greatly within Connecticut’s top three most walkable municipalities. 
Downtown Hartford is much more walkable than the neighborhoods further afield. Some areas require a car or some form of transportation, the analysis found, while others do not.
And while some towns in the state have greater walkability than the national average, they may not be considered walkable. Any city or town with a score under 50 is considered “car-dependent.” In Connecticut, only six towns are not car dependent, though walkability varies within them.
According to the Environmental Protection Agency walkability index, which is measured differently, Connecticut is a more walkable state than many. On a scale of 1-20, the state scored a 10. Nationally, the average score was 8.9, according to an analysis of the 2021 EPA data by hearthmap.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Eversource CEO tells industry conference he expects Healey to turn down the ‘volume’ on utility criticism post-election
description: Nolan’s comments that Healey will tone down her rhetoric after the election stand in stark contrast to Healey’s pitch to voters that Massachusetts will take on utility profits and go to bat for ratepayers.
text:
AS GOV. MAURA HEALEY has sought to tackle soaring energy costs in an election year defined by cost-of-living issues — and increasingly attacked the utility companies for “greed” and corporate profits at the expense of ratepayers — the top executive at the state’s largest electric and gas company doesn’t sound too concerned with the rhetoric coming from the corner office. 
Joe Nolan, who has served as CEO of Eversource since 2021, said during an industry conference on September 30 that he had a friendly chat with Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll a week prior. 
“It’s only 37 more days to go” until the election, Nolan recalled telling the duo, according to a transcript of his remarks acquired by CommonWealth Beacon.  
“We have good relations with all of them,” Nolan continued, referring to the governors of Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire, the states in which Eversource operates. “As much as you might hear them maybe take a whack or a knock at us or me or at certain things, I will tell you if I had $1 for every time they say, ‘Hey, nothing personal, Joe. You know you’re our friend.’ But they have to do that. Obviously, they’re getting attacked, utility issues are front and center. Rates are front and center. But all that noise in 37 days, you’re going to see the volume is going to go right down and you won’t hear much of that.” 
And the harsh rhetoric from Healey, who is seeking reelection, also hasn’t blunted Nolan’s financial support for her.  
A week earlier, on September 21, right around the time he said he spoke with Healey and Driscoll, Nolan donated $1,000 – the annual legal maximum – to each of their campaigns, according to records from the Office of Campaign and Political Finance.  
Between September 10 and October 6, 14 Eversource executives donated to Healey’s campaign, adding a total of $4,500 to her campaign coffers. The same number of Eversource executives gave Driscoll $4,875 in roughly that same timeframe. Those donating include the president of the company’s gas distribution business, the vice president of transmission, the chief financial officer, attorneys, and lobbyists.  
By contrast, Healey’s GOP challenger Mike Minogue only received two donations from Eversource employees during the months of September and October – neither of which are from Nolan – totaling $150. 
About a week after Nolan’s conversation with Healey and the day after his remarks at the industry event, the governor fired off a letter to the Trump administration asking them to move faster to approve a small gas pipeline expansion proposal. Healey had already publicly thrown her support behind the project, but the letter represented a concrete step to advocate for federal approvals and a rare attempt from the Democratic governor to appeal to the Trump administration on a fossil fuel project. 
Healey previously touted her opposition to gas pipeline expansions in Massachusetts during her time as attorney general.   
This past January, state regulators approved contracts for Eversource to purchase that gas, a step that gives the pipeline company some assurance that their investment in the expansion will be recouped. In her letter to the Trump administration, Healey estimated the project would save 600,000 customers about $40 million per year over 10 years. 
William Hinkle, an Eversource spokesperson, said the company’s leadership consistently takes “any available opportunity to emphasize the need for bringing more energy supply – including natural gas – into New England.”  
“We are also supportive of Governor Healey and have been for a long time,” Hinkle said. “We also respect our elected officials too much to believe that political donations can sway them from acting in what they believe is in the best interests of their constituents – whether from Eversource leadership, anti-utility advocates or business leaders in other industries.” 
There is nothing illegal about Healey accepting political contributions from Nolan, who has donated $1,000 to her nine out of the last 11 years, or the governor meeting with the chief executive of a utility company, or writing a letter to express a policy position that happens to align with Eversource’s.  
But Nolan’s comments that Healey will tone down her rhetoric after the election stand in stark contrast to Healey’s pitch to voters that Massachusetts will take on utility profits and go to bat for ratepayers. They also speak to the delicate balance for the governor, given the significant influence the utilities have over energy affordability and the ability to meet ambitious climate targets. 
The Healey campaign didn’t immediately provide a comment on the record.
Costas Panagopoulos, professor of political science at Northeastern University, noted the timeline of events doesn’t mean that there was a quid pro quo.  
“It’s not unusual for CEOs, like any other individual, to decide to support politicians in the heat of an election cycle, especially when they know that they’ll be doing business with them and when their prospects for victory look promising,” he said.  
Healey, who has criticized utilities like Eversource and National Grid for “repeatedly forcing ratepayers to pay even more” while earning record profits for investors, is confronting a complicated energy landscape featuring looming climate commitments, soaring prices, and rising demand. That confluence is also colliding with a war in Iran that has sent oil prices spiking — Healey has now proposed temporarily suspending the state’s gas tax and plans to offer additional heating relief this winter as a result — and the Trump administration’s crackdown on offshore wind. 
Healey has emphasized an “all of the above” approach to energy issues to boost supply, including natural gas, and lower costs. Her recent letter to the Trump administration on the pipeline expansion, which is planned to be placed in service in 2028, angered environmentalists who worry she is capitulating on the aggressive climate commitments that Healey herself championed when she campaigned for governor in 2022. 
With energy affordability the top concern for households in Massachusetts, the governor has been hunting for ways to cut costs, even as recent polling shows that most voters blame President Trump and the utilities for the high prices. 
“I don’t know anyone who has actually been taking the governor’s threats seriously,” said Vick Mohanka, director of the Massachusetts Sierra Club chapter. “Now, it’s clear Eversource doesn’t either.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: New Alaska sea sponge species fuel debate over fishery practices
description: The vast and largely unexplored seafloor off Alaska’s coastline produces occasional startling discoveries. The latest concerns the sponges that line the bottom of the ocean and contribute to an ecosystem that supports some of the nation’s biggest seafood harvests. Scientists have now identified nine previously unknown species of sea sponges that dwell there,[...]
text:
Deep-sea sponges and other invertebrates collected duriing a bottom trawl survey in Alaska are seen in a basked. (Photo provided by NOAA Fisheries)The vast and largely unexplored seafloor off Alaska’s coastline produces occasional startling discoveries.
The latest concerns the sponges that line the bottom of the ocean and contribute to an ecosystem that supports some of the nation’s biggest seafood harvests.
Scientists have now identified nine previously unknown species of sea sponges that dwell there, including one that represents an entire genus that was previously unknown.
The discoveries are the product of a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration program to better understand Alaska’s sponge and coral gardens, underwater zones about which knowledge is in only the early stages.
 

A sharpchin rockfish internally incubates its eggs while sheltering within a sponge on the seafloor off Alaska. Sponges provide important habitat for Alaska’s fish populations. (Photo provided by NOAA Fisheries)
 

	“Alaska really has these major knowledge gaps, and we regularly are uncovering either undescribed species, which was the case here, or some of these rarely identified species that are really vital for seafloor habitats,” said Sean Rooney, a NOAA Fisheries biologist who was part of the team identifying the sponge species.
Rooney, who is part of the NOAA Fisheries team that conducts routine trawl surveys that gather information needed to set commercial seafood harvests in federal waters, doubled up in recent years to collect sponge samples as well.
Sponges are simple animals but important to the complex ocean ecosystem. They build seafloor structures, filter seawater and are used by fish as nurseries and sheltered areas to protect themselves against predators. They even have chemical compounds that could be developed into important medicines for people.
The sponge discoveries also highlight the importance of seafloor protections, an issue of concern in fishery management.
“They’re the backbone of a healthy ocean. They provide essential habitat for fish as nurseries and protective grounds from predators,” said Cooper Freeman, Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity. “If we want fish to continue to be abundant, they need habitat, and sponges provide that habitat.”
The newly identified species, which include the species now named Polycapus rubrum that is in a new-to-science genus and another species related to sponges previously found only in the tropics – bring the total number of known Alaska sponge species to 232, according to NOAA Fisheries.
Of the nine newly identified species, seven were found in the central and Western Aleutians, two were found exclusively in the Gulf of Alaska and some were found in both areas, Rooney said. They were found at depths between 50 meters and 500 meters, thriving in a rich ecosystem undisturbed by surface wave action, he said.
The discoveries are detailed in studies published in the journal Zootaxa: four in one study, and five in another study.
 

A microscopic image shows the structure of a newly discovered species now named Desmacella alaskensis. Scientists were able to identify the new species by studying the spicules, the tiny structural elements within sponges. (Photo provided by NOAA Fisheries)
 

	The discoveries came from sponges collected during trawl surveys conducted between 1997 and 2022, according to the published studies.
The lag between collection and identification shows how long it takes to figure out sponge species.
“Sponges don’t have eyes, fins or limbs, you know, like so many of the other critters, so we really have to use microscopic examination of some of these internal frameworks,” Rooney said. “What sponges have are these glass-like building blocks called spicules.”
The work that resulted in the new identifications used both examination of the spicules and DNA testing, he said.
The species in the newly identified genus has spicules that are “almost like claw-shaped and rod-shaped building blocks” that had not been seen before in that particular group, Rooney said. They were also arrayed in a pattern that “had never been observed before in sponge science,” he said. “The structure of the spicules is why we ended up calling it a new genus.”
The name, Polycapus rubrum, describes both the multiple layers of silica that create a material almost like fiberglass and the sponge’s red color, Rooney said.
The sponge species that the scientists were surprised to find so far north was also given an appropriate scientific name: Julavis borealis.
There was little knowledge about Alaska’s sponge and coral gardens until the early 2000s. At that point, NOAA Fisheries started a scientific program that documented some of the world’s most diverse cold-water sponge and coral gardens.
 

A microscopic image shows the structural elements of the newly discovered sponge species called Polycapus rubrum. The sponge represents a new-to-science sponge genus. (Photo provided by NOAA Fisheries)
 

	About 61% of the Alaska seafloor has never been mapped using high-resolution sonar technology, Rooney said. In comparison, 56% of U.S. waters have been mapped using modern standards, he said.
“So Alaska lags far behind,” he said. The vast size of Alaska’s ocean territory, rough weather conditions and seasonal sea ice make exploration particularly challenging.
Sonar mapping, if it occurs, gives only partial information, he said. “It gives you information on the depth contours, but not really the animals that are living there,” he said.
Fishery practices
The discovery of the new sponge species adds fuel to a heated debate over commercial trawling and the effects that seafood harvesting method has on the marine environment.
Most of the Aleutian region is off-limits to bottom trawling, a harvest practice that uses large nets to sweep the lowest depths of the sea. That is thanks to action taken in 2006 to protect the coral and sponge gardens there. But a small portion of the territory does remain open to bottom trawling.
Most of the Gulf of Alaska, in contrast, is open to bottom trawling, though there are some established coral-protection and seamount-protection zones.
There are efforts to end bottom trawling in the Gulf, including a campaign mounted by the environmental group Oceana that cites sponges and corals.
For several years, Oceana has tried to convince federal regulators to impose bottom-trawling bans in the Gulf of Alaska similar to those in place for most of the waters off the U.S. West Coast. Oceana also sued NOAA Fisheries in 2024 in an attempt to compel those closures, but the organization lost the case.
 

Large sponges seen in the water off the Aleutian Islands create variable habitat on the seafloor, which promotes biodiversity. (Photo provided by NOAA Fisheries)
 

	The effort to close most of the Gulf to bottom trawling has continued with a proposal presented to the North Pacific Fishery Management Council Meeting, said Lauren Hynes, a marine scientist who is Oceana’s North Pacific campaign manager.
“We are still pushing them on it,” she said.
From the U.S. Arctic to Southern California, only the Gulf of Alaska lacks what she called a “frozen footprint” for bottom trawling. So even if trawl gear is not affecting sea sponges and corals now, it might in the future, thanks to climate change, she said.
“As we’re starting to get all of these warming events, especially in the Gulf of Alaska, especially in recent years, we’re seeing fish species shipped into areas that they’ve never been found in before, or less likely to be found in,” she said. And, as has been already observed in the Bering Sea, the fishing fleets “will follow these fish into places they haven’t fished before historically,” she said.
Beyond bottom trawling, there are concerns among environmentalists and sectors of the fishing industry about damage to seafloor habitat from midwater trawling.
Midwater trawling is an important harvest practice in the waters off Alaska. Alaska pollock, the nation’s top-volume commercial seafood species, is harvested through that midwater trawling, also known as pelagic trawling.
Midwater trawling is not supposed to occur at the seafloor level. But recent studies show that midwater trawl gear often touches the seafloor, putting the habitat there at risk, as well as occasionally crushing juvenile crab.
Hynes said official bycatch reports show that the trawl fleets are affecting sponges and corals. From 2005 to 2025, the bottom trawl fleet reported 8.8 million pounds of sponges and 1.1 million pounds of corals pulled up as bycatch, she said. The pelagic trawl fleet had sponge and coral bycatch during the period, though much smaller volumes: 9,408 pounds of sponges and 82,580 pounds of corals, according to the statistics.
The North Pacific Fishery Management Council, currently holding its October meeting in Anchorage, devoted much of its June meeting to the issue of midwater trawl gear making contact with the ocean floor. The council declined to take regulatory action at that meeting. Instead, the council directed its staff to assess options for preventing such contact from happening. The findings are expected to be presented next year in May, according to the council’s posted meeting outlook.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont general election ballots mailed later than expected
description:
Following “technical problems,” all ballots were mailed by Oct. 7, according to the Secretary of State. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont general election ballots mailed later than expected.
text:
Official ballots sent out by mail to voters for the 2026 general election in Vermont. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger
Some Vermonters can expect their general election ballots a week late this year due to manufacturing problems, according to Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas. 
“We’ve never had a scenario like this,” she said.
Election ballots were mailed to all registered Vermont voters on Wednesday, a week after the deadline mandated by Vermont’s universal mail-in ballot law. The delay came as a result of “technical problems” at the printing press in the last week of September, Copeland Hanzas said. 
Copeland Hanzas said that Vermonters can expect to receive their ballots by mid-October. 
An announcement by the Secretary of State’s office Wednesday recommends that voters mail completed ballots to their town clerk by Oct. 20. Voters can also return ballots in person or to the clerk via a secure drop box. 
Amid delays and mishaps in mail delivery across the state, some Vermonters have expressed concern that they had yet to receive ballots, according to Putney Town Clerk Jonathan Johnson.
“I get between five and 10 calls a day, you know, asking where the ballots are,” he said. “People are pretty aware that the ballots were supposed to be mailed and are a little frustrated that they don’t have their ballots already.”
At least people are paying attention, Copeland Hanzas said. 
“And certainly with all of the rhetoric that we’re hearing out of the Oval Office, they are rightfully anxious and concerned about the potential for interference,” she said. “But all indications that we have are that this election will proceed as expected.”
Vermont first piloted universal mail-in voting for the 2020 presidential election to mitigate the spread of Covid-19. That year saw record turnout, and approximately 75% of registered voters submitted ballots by mail. Seven other states and Washington D.C. use universal vote by mail. 
Throughout the state, Copeland Hanzas said typically about two-thirds of election ballots come in by mail. In Putney, the 2024 presidential election saw twice as many voters mailing in ballots than voting in person, Johnson said. 
Despite frustration, Johnson said, voters in Putney are understanding of delays.
“Interest in this election is really high,” he said.
In a follow-up email Thursday afternoon, Johnson wrote that ballots had gone out for delivery that afternoon. Within three hours, he said he had received nearly a dozen ballots. 
Voters can track their ballot’s delivery online. The general election takes place on Nov. 3.

title: Polk County Jail to launch education and training initiative with DMACC as partner
description: The Polk County Sheriff’s Department is bringing a national initiative to the county jail aimed at providing incarcerated people with the resources and education to strengthen their first steps back into their communities. text:
DMACC has partnered with the Polk County Jail to bring education and training back to inmates through a new initiative. (Stock photo via Getty Images)The Polk County Sheriff’s Department is bringing a national initiative to the county jail aimed at providing incarcerated people with the resources and education to strengthen their first steps back into their communities.
Inmate Growth Naturally and Intentionally Through Education, or I.G.N.I.T.E., will provide those detained in the Polk County Jail who volunteer for the program with their own technology to access training and education, help from others and incentives for participation. Community partners in Des Moines Area Community College and other organizations hope to be able to expand the program even further, Polk County Sheriff’s Office and DMACC officials said.
Polk County Sheriff Kevin Schneider announced the program in September after he and others visited Flint, Michigan, where I.G.N.I.T.E. first started, said Polk County Sheriff’s Office Public Information Officer Sgt. Brittany Worrall.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I think the sheriff said it best,” Worrall said. “His goal is to help our folks … who are incarcerated be successful. The sheriff is really proud of the work that we’re going to be able to offer to individuals, so they can join back into the community more successful, proud of what they’ve done, and hopefully that will impact them and change lives.”
According to a communication sent by Schneider to community organizations, businesses and residents of Polk County,  I.G.N.I.T.E. has been implemented in more than 40 jails in 18 states across the U.S., with Polk County’s being the first in Iowa. Washington County Jail launched its own I.G.N.I.T.E. program just one day after Polk County announced its own on Sept. 21.
Schneider said in the message that “independent research” from Harvard University, Brown University and the University of Michigan showed that one month of participation in  I.G.N.I.T.E. lowers weekly misconduct numbers by 25%, “meaningfully lowers recidivism” and within one year generates “more than $7,000 in social cost savings per participant.”
In Polk County, where 90% of incarcerated people return to the community, the message stated this program will help taxpayers while ensuring people leave jail better educated and prepared for work, leading to fewer repeat offenses.
Both of the 64-person I.G.N.I.T.E. pods, split between men and women, will begin their work through the initiative Oct. 12, Worrall said. Part of the program is providing incentives to inmates to motivate them, such as providing different decor and snacks.
“Each individual will have access to their own tablet; they’ll also have earbuds, so then they can concentrate on the coursework,” Worrall said. “We also will have a two-hour block that everyone will be doing coursework at the same time, so then if there’s any type of facilitation of questions through the coursework, then we’ll have staff kind of ready to go for that too with programs and such.”
All Polk County Jail inmates will still have access to 586 courses through Edovo, an online learning platform for incarcerated people, Worrall said, with the dedicated technology and incentives setting I.G.N.I.T.E. apart, as well as potential offerings from community partners like DMACC.
Before the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020, the Ankeny-based community college primarily offered High School Equivalency Test and life skills courses to Polk County Jail inmates, said Jessica Frederickson, executive director of higher education in prison and adult education and literacy at DMACC. Federal funding cuts to adult education have kept DMACC from bringing these courses back, though she said the county has reached out about it in the past.
With the introduction of I.G.N.I.T.E., Frederickson said the county would like to see these classes return to the jail, with the addition of education in digital and financial literacy and courses leading to “short-term, stackable credentials.”
DMACC has applied for a Bureau of Justice Assistance grant that, if received, would allow the community college and county to start its original programming again, bring in the new training, hold graduation and completion celebrations and hire an “inside/outside navigator” to work with students before and after their incarceration ends.
“Polk County is very supportive of trying to help us in any way that they can to help us secure funding, and so I appreciate that part of it,” Frederickson said. “And it’s a really integral part of DMACC’s community mission to help all of the citizens reintegrate and to be successful when they come back to the community.”

title: Veteran public official running as nonpartisan shakes up Clark County Commission race
description: A strong nonpartisan candidate with backing from one of the state’s most prominent unions is putting a twist in the race to represent Clark County Commission District F. The District F race features Democrat Minja Yan, a progressive political newcomer; Republican Heidi Kasama, a current state Assembly member; and independent candidate Becky Harris, a former[...]
text:
Minja Yan, Becky Harris, Heidi Kasama. (Candidate photos)A strong nonpartisan candidate with backing from one of the state’s most prominent unions is putting a twist in the race to represent Clark County Commission District F.
The District F race features Democrat Minja Yan, a progressive political newcomer; Republican Heidi Kasama, a current state Assembly member; and independent candidate Becky Harris, a former Republican state legislator known for being the first woman to chair the Nevada Gaming Control Board.
While third-party and independent candidates are not uncommon in county commission races, most are not as politically experienced or pose as big of a potential threat as Harris. And most don’t secure  high-profile endorsements.
Harris has been endorsed by the Culinary union, known nationally for its grassroots organizing, usually for Democrats. She has also been endorsed by the Las Vegas Review-Journal, Hispanics in Politics, Ironworkers Local 433, and former state legislators from both political parties.
Regarding her decision to run as a nonpartisan, Harris told KTNV that she has “always been an independent thinker.”
She continued, “I’ve always executed my own judgment. I have always been a good voice for my community, and being a nonpartisan really is what I am and represents me the best.”
Harris was elected to the Nevada State Senate in 2014 and represented the district in two legislative sessions before resigning in January 2018 to serve as chair of the Nevada Gaming Control Board. Her time there was marked by the sexual misconduct allegations that led to the downfall of casino titan Steve Wynn, the legalization of marijuana, and the expansion of sports wagering.
Yan, the Democrat running in District F, works in commercial real estate and specializes in urban and infield redevelopment and community revitalization. According to her website, she has experience working on public transit issues through various public committees. She also serves on the board of The Mob Museum.
Last year, she gave a TEDx Talk in Las Vegas on redeveloping Chinatowns across the United States.
Yan is endorsed by SEIU Local 1107, Teamsters Nevada, Make The Road Action Nevada, and the Sierra Club Toiyabe Chapter. 
Yan emerged victorious in a crowded Democratic primary, besting six others, including Minddie Lloyd, a Republican-turned-Democrat backed by outgoing District F incumbent Commissioner Justin Jones, and Lenna Hovanessian, a community advocate who’d been endorsed by U.S. Rep. Dina Titus.
Kasama, the Republican running in District F, also faced a competitive primary but defeated private equity firm CEO Albert Mack in the primary.
Kasama has represented Nevada State Assembly District 2 since 2020. With the endorsement of Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, she explored a run for Nevada’s 3rd Congressional District in 2024 but opted to run for re-election in the Assembly instead. During her time in the Legislature, she focused on ethics reform and sponsored a bill that put an end to a predatory title scheme.
She has the backing of  Lombardo, the Las Vegas Police Protective Association, the Board of REALTORS® PAC, and at least two chambers of commerce.
Because campaign finance reports are collected quarterly, fundraising and expense totals are currently available only through the end of June.
Kasama reported having nearly $444,000 on hand as of July 1. Her top contributors during the second quarter include South Point Hotel and Casino, Western Elite, and the Lombardo-affiliated Nevada Way PAC.
Harris reported having $139,000 on hand as of July 1. Her top contributors this year include Penta Building Group, M Resort-operator Penn Entertainment, and esports betting company Oddin.gg.
Yan, who promised not to accept donations from corporations or their PACs, reported having just under $4,000 on hand as of July 1. She’d received $87,000 in donations and in-kind contributions during the first half of the year but spent most of it. Her top contributors were Clark County Commissioner Tick Segerblom’s campaign and Maryland state legislator Chao Wu’s campaign.
If Kasama or Harris wins, they will change the political makeup of the Clark County Commission. The seven-member commission currently has just one Republican, April Becker, who was elected in 2024. The others are Democrats.
 What about the other districts?

In addition to District F, two other Clark County Commission seats are up this election cycle. Both feature incumbents expected to easily retain their seats.
In District E, Democratic Commissioner Tick Segerblom faces Republican Manny Hess. Segerblom, a longtime politician representing a heavily blue area, won his last two commission races by 15.7 and 25.2 percentage points.
In District G, Democratic Commissioner Jim Gibson, also a longtime politician, won his last two elections by 9.2 and 13.8 percentage points. He faces Republican Jonathan Maxham this year.

name: Nevada Current
title: Land use, luxury developers, and Lake Tahoe’s future are on the ballot
description: Yosemite made headlines and raised concerns among legislators when word got out that a private Nevada-based developer has been lobbying the current administration to intervene with a ‘public-private’ ask: a park land transfer that would enable construction of a private road connection to the famed national park. This occurred as Yosemite battled problems wit[...]
text:
"Luxury developers are rushing to exploit nature with no opposition from leaders in either political party." (Photo courtesy Pamela Mahoney Tsigdinos)Yosemite made headlines and raised concerns among legislators when word got out that a private Nevada-based developer has been lobbying the current administration to intervene with a ‘public-private’ ask: a park land transfer that would enable construction of a private road connection to the famed national park. This occurred as Yosemite battled problems with visitation safety, overcrowding, vehicle congestion, and ongoing wildfire challenges.
Lake Tahoe, another iconic Sierra Nevada jewel, is under equally tremendous visitor strain and wildfire pressure. Encompassing two states and five counties, Lake Tahoe faces even greater development threats without a commensurate level of concern by the Nevada (or California) candidates who will exercise control over the Lake Tahoe basin. This matters because:

Of the nearly 56,000 people who call Tahoe home nearly 16,000 live on the Nevada side. 
Greater Reno-Tahoe’s permanent population is more than 550,000; adding in commuter regions like Carson City and Douglas and Lyon counties pushes the number closer to 650,000. 
According to the Reno-Sparks Convention and Visitors Authority, 57% of the 3.9 million overnight visitors to Reno in 2025 traveled up to visit Lake Tahoe during their trip, with Washoe Tahoe’s north shore (including Sand Harbor State Park) the most highly impacted.
A 2021 analysis of Tahoe visitation projected the 15+ million annual visitors will increase by 25% by 2035.

Who looks out for Tahoe’s public safety and land management?
The Nevada governor chairs the board that oversees administration of the Nevada Department of Transportation (including the dangerously overburdened evacuation corridors SR-28 and US-50). The governor also appoints a representative to the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency (TRPA) Governing Board as well as appoints the Director of the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR), another TRPA board member. DCNR’s director appoints the State Forester Firewarden to head the Nevada Division of Forestry, which together oversee Nevada’s thousands of acres around Lake Tahoe. Further, the governor has broad emergency powers. The top executive has authority to formally declare a state of emergency or disaster, often necessary during increasingly severe wildfire seasons, major blizzards, or infrastructure failures across the state.
The Nevada Secretary of State, meanwhile, holds a permanent voting seat on the TRPA Governing Board, whereas the state’s Lieutenant Governor serves as Chair of the Nevada Commission on Tourism (Travel Nevada). The commission sets the direction for recreation infrastructure grants and state tourism marketing that affect Tahoe traffic and visitation. The Nevada Attorney General serves as legal counsel for Nevada state agencies (NDOT, DCNR, State Lands) operating in the Tahoe Basin. 
Then there’s Nevada’s Congressional District 2, which encompasses 100 percent of Nevada’s Tahoe Basin across Washoe and Douglas counties as well as the consolidated municipality of Carson City. Through the current, but retiring, CD2 representative’s pivotal seats on congressional committees, this office holds great influence over millions in federal appropriations under the Lake Tahoe Restoration Act and exercises oversight of the U.S. Forest Service’s Lake Tahoe Basin Management Unit’s (LTBMU), particularly regarding wildfire mitigation and forest health funding. LTBMU’s public land, some 156,000 acres, is managed as a single interdependent administrative unit. About one-third of its acreage is in Nevada.
Nevada’s Legislative Committee for the Review and Oversight of TRPA and Marlette Lake exercises formal legislative oversight over TRPA operations, regulations, and state funding. Like each of the elected offices noted above, all but one of the committee’s current members are on the ballot this year.
Public lands in corporate hands
State and local leaders in Nevada (and California), to date, have mirrored the transactions-focused administration in the White House and the first family. This summer saw a bipartisan embrace of “public-private” exploitation at this year’s bi-state Tahoe Summit at Nevada’s Sand Harbor State Park. Nevada Democratic U.S. Sen. Jacky Rosen, who emceed the annual event, made a little noticed Freudian slip that set the stage for the event. 
While attempting to acknowledge the federal and state tax-payer-funded TRPA, Rosen inadvertently asked the developer-funded Tahoe Fund to stand. (The fund’s key members were, after all, prominently seated in front.) The senator’s faux pas wasn’t entirely off base since this powerful private entity is a major force behind the now captured TRPA, once a leading conservation and environmental agency formed to look out for the lake’s unique environment. 
The Tahoe Fund’s board is stacked with multinational resort and real-estate investors and a who’s who of hospitality and private equity interests who stand to gain by furthering Tahoe development. Operating as a private matching-grant powerhouse, the fund plays a central role in paving over, trail-ifying, and luxurifying the once-pristine Tahoe shores to cater to high-net worth visitors. Their reach now extends to the region’s forests. Through a sawmill project (covered by Bloomberg), the fund has helped legitimize commercial timber extraction in the basin. While marketed as a climate-adaption triumph, this is an example of how private capital directs public land management, allowing developers to manage the forest to protect their nearby resort investments.  
You could almost hear echoes of Ivanka Trump’s infamous quote about developing an unspoiled natural landscape “to realize its potential.”
Not to be outdone, Nevada’s senior U.S. senator, Catherine Cortez-Masto, took her plaudits a step further, “We can’t celebrate the 30th anniversary of this summit without acknowledging the public-private partnerships that have been essential to our work. That’s what Team Tahoe is all about.”
Inconveniently for the politicians, the Bug and Stallion fires in nearby Reno raged during the Tahoe Summit, shining an unwelcome spotlight on Reno-Tahoe’s increasingly dangerous roadways and strained infrastructure amid the push for greater development and tourism amenities. Despite the many speeches and photo ops, there was no discussion about out-of-date evacuation plans, one of which notably fails to account for the many thousands of tourists crowding Nevada’s shores. Also absent was any mention of air, soil, and water pollution. Total silence, too, on the overwhelming public opposition to the TRPA allowing controversial chemicals like glyphosate around Tahoe. 
What’s bad for Yosemite is good for Lake Tahoe? 
Amid this cozy ‘private-public’ milieu, luxury developers are rushing to exploit nature with no opposition from leaders in either political party. The same Yosemite-adjacent developer seeking a shortcut through the national park is also actively working to create a cruise ship-sized development in Placer Tahoe Kings Beach on a narrow two-lane road adjoining Nevada and overlooking north Lake Tahoe. Incidentally, this Tahoe development sits on a heavily trafficked road, which is also the main evacuation route for the many thousands who visit or live around the lake. 
An infamous blighted property in Crystal Bay, Nevada, which has gone through multiple luxury developer misfires, is back in the spotlight. Utah-based developers are seeking a five-year extension to control four public roadways. In November, the developers will ask Washoe County to abandon its interest in 60,291 square feet of public right-of-way as part of a massive rework of the formerly TRPA approved Waldorf Astoria.  
Meanwhile, at the southern end of Nevada’s Tahoe east shore another luxury developer has rights to remove several hundred trees (some estimated to be between 120 and 130 years old) and convert nine acres of habitat for local wildlife into what has been promoted on social media as a year-round luxury resort and event center. The developer also advertised the “developed campsite” or “glamping” property as a “shovel-ready”’ joint venture opportunity with all entitlements. 
Local opposition continues to raise concerns about the project’s many misrepresentations, land use, wildfire evacuation concerns, pending environmental damage, and added congestion in an already heavily visited area.
The commercialization and exploitation of nature isn’t new. We can trace the systemic displacement of native people, despoiled land, and rapacious destruction of ecosystems over centuries. 
Developers first re-imagined the TRPA and helped alter its focus to suit their needs in the early 2000s. In 2010 the agency laid off scientists to make room for economically minded staff members who prioritize rewriting strict ordinances and codes to favor developers and greenlight once unthinkable incursions into environmentally sensitive areas. Rather than hire more scientists, the agency’s latest addition is a celebrated “storyteller.” 
TRPA’s executive director, an award-winning PR pro herself, needs a top spin-doctor for a new development-driven lobbying effort: an update to the once sacrosanct Santini-Burton Act. Passed in 1980, it allowed the U.S. Forest Service to acquire thousands of acres of environmentally sensitive areas to protect Lake Tahoe. As if suffering from amnesia, both Nevada senators and their California counterparts have forgotten that the original Act decades ago was to ensure this land would not be controlled by private developers. 
Land set aside by the Santini-Burton Act currently serves as critical safety buffers in the Tahoe basin — providing defensible space, emergency staging capacity, and protection against the cascading risks of high-density land use, explained one resident who wrote about the proposed updates to the Act. She noted that legislators must not turn the original intent of land use conservation on its head. “Modernization must not become a euphemism for dismantling its core purposes. A law designed to stop development pressure should not be repurposed to manage it.”
Cruise-ship model: Extraction tourism
The fight to ensure more natural lands don’t fall under the control of corporate hospitality interests is practically a full-time occupation for volunteer grassroots groups within the Tahoe basin. 
Douglas Tahoe resident Elisabeth Lernhardt at a recent Nevada legislative meeting described Tahoe as the latest in “extraction-style tourism” and likened it to the cruise-ship industry: “The same interests own the ships, the ports, the shops, and the restaurants. The profits leave; the costs stay behind.”
Near Washoe County’s Tahoe watershed, local resident Steve Dolan with Friends of Third Creek has been actively involved in meadow restoration projects. He’s also monitoring the return of native beavers aiding in the repopulation of habitat attractive to the once over-fished Lahontan Cutthroat Trout. His latest concern is a determined push by tourism interests to disrupt the restoration work to make way for a new parking lot to accommodate visitors in the winter months.
“There’s a limit to what this beautiful emerald of the Sierra can accommodate,” he said. “There’s just a limit.”
Nevada officials owe their constituents some answers about Lake Tahoe’s future. One thing is for certain: the “story-telling” to justify all the development will continue.

title: Attorney passed over by judicial selection panel faces hearing master in election
description: Attorney Kristine Brewer, who came in first in June in the primary race for Clark County Family Court Department S, is not responding to questions about the Nevada Judicial Selection Commission subsequently passing on appointing her, the sole applicant, to the seat.  Brewer garnered just under 48% of the vote in the three-way primary, with […]
text:
Kristina Brewer, Randall Forman. (Candidate photos)Attorney Kristine Brewer, who came in first in June in the primary race for Clark County Family Court Department S, is not responding to questions about the Nevada Judicial Selection Commission subsequently passing on appointing her, the sole applicant, to the seat. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]Brewer garnered just under 48% of the vote in the three-way primary, with Hearing Master Randall Forman coming in second with 39%. 
A month later, Judge Vincent Ochoa announced he was retiring early, creating an immediate vacancy in Department S. 
The Nevada Commission on Judicial Selection announced in late July it was declining her application, leaving the seat vacant until voters decide in November. 
“Following its consideration of the applicant, the Commission declined to forward the candidate to Governor Joe Lombardo for appointment,” says a statement posted in July on the commission’s website. 
The move is unusual, as the governor routinely appoints candidates to the bench who are on the ballot at the time of their appointment. In June 2024, Lombardo appointed Tina Talim to the bench. She was elected to the post in November. 
The Nevada Constitution requires that the governor, presented with recommendations from the commission, fill a judicial vacancy within 30 days. However, the commission is not required to submit recommendations in the event there are no suitable applicants. 
It’s unknown why the panel declined to appoint Brewer. 
Federal bankruptcy court records indicate Brewer and her husband, Robert Blau, filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in November of 2025, citing assets ranging from $50,000 to $100,000, and liabilities between $100,000 and $500,000. 
Brewer, who spoke with the Current before the primary election, has not responded since. Her campaign consultant, Steve Sanson of Veterans in Politics, also did not respond to requests for comment. 
Forman says he considered applying for the appointment but decided against it, knowing that if he won but lost the election, he’d have to reapply as a hearing master. 
“That’s a pretty big risk to me,” he told the Current. “I like having a job, so I decided not to put in for that appointment.”
Department S hears divorce and child custody cases. 
Forman, who earned his law degree from UNLV’s Boyd Law School, spent 15 years in private practice, and has been a hearing master for five years, hearing juvenile delinquency cases and issuing domestic violence protective orders. 
This is Forman’s second run for the bench. He lost in the primary race for Dept. Z in 2020.  
He is endorsed by Culinary Local 226, SEIU Nevada, the Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, Laborers Local 870 and other labor organizations.
As of July, he’d raised just under $19,000 and had $5,000 in the bank.
Brewer received her law degree from Thomas Jefferson School of Law in San Diego.  She currently works for Leavitt Family Law Group. She says she’s practiced almost exclusively in family law since 2004. 
This is her third run for Family Court. She lost in the 2014 primary, and in a 2022 special election.  In addition to her 2026 application for appointment to the bench, she applied unsuccessfully in 2023. 
Brewer’s website lists endorsements from half a dozen individuals, including Nevada System of Higher Education Regent Patrick Boylan, who is known for making anti-transgender remarks. 
According to Our Nevada Judges, a website that tracks judges and judicial candidates, Brewer is also endorsed by Veterans in Politics, which is run by her campaign consultant Sanson. 
As of July, Brewer had raised roughly $19,000, including a personal loan of $11,000, and spent $24,000.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: In debate, Utah Rep. Kennedy says he’s ‘just getting started’ while Dem calls him a ‘lap dog’
description: Rep. Mike Kennedy defended his first term in Congress as Democratic challenger sought to cast him as a “lap dog” to the Trump administration.
text:
Candidates for Utah’s 4th Congressional District Democrat Jonny Larsen, left, and Republican Mike Kennedy participate in a debate at Snow College in Ephraim on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)Republican Rep. Mike Kennedy defended his first term in Congress Thursday as his Democratic challenger cast the race for Utah’s 4th Congressional District as a choice between a “blue dog” or a “lap dog” to the Trump administration. 
Kennedy and Democrat Jonny Larsen met on the debate stage at Snow College in rural Sanpete County, sparring over issues including the Iran War, public lands and immigration enforcement. The debate was hosted by the Utah Debate Commission, moderated by Doug Wilks with the Deseret News and broadcast by PBS Utah.
The candidates are vying to represent a newly drawn, mostly rural and heavily Republican district covering the entirety of Tooele, Juab, Millard, Sanpete and Sevier counties, along with portions of southern Salt Lake and western Utah counties.



Kennedy, now representing Utah’s current 3rd House District under the state’s previous congressional boundaries, said he’s“just getting started making Washington smaller and Utah stronger.” 
Larsen pitched himself as a moderate Democrat focused on issues of fiscal responsibility and national security.
“We should be working on the 90% of issues that we all agree on instead of fighting over the 10% that we don’t,” Larsen said in his closing statement. “So I’d like to ask you: ‘Would you like a ‘blue dog’ or a lap dog to this administration?”
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

Kennedy didn’t directly respond to the characterization, focusing his closing remarks on Utah’s pioneer history and saying, “We have the opportunity to work together to build a brighter future here in this state.He told reporters after the debate that he’s worked with Democrats on eight bills he’s sponsored that have won approval from the U.S. House. 
“Every one of them is a collaborative effort with my Democrat colleagues,” Kennedy said. 
When asked during the debate about the cost of gas, Larsen condemned the Iran War, saying “we absolutely need to end this illegal war to bring order back” and drive down fuel prices. 
He criticized Kennedy for voting repeatedly against a war powers resolution that would stop the president from continuing military action without the approval of Congress. 
“As a veteran myself, who did two tours in combat, I understand that cost, and that price that we pay with American blood.”
Candidates for Utah’s 4th Congressional District Democrat Jonny Larsen, left, and Republican Mike Kennedy participate in a debate at Snow College in Ephraim on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)
Kennedy said he’s proud of President Donald Trump’s actions against Iran. 
 “They have to be dealt with. And I recognize that there’s pain in the short run, but there will be significant gain in the long run,” Kennedy said. He added that “to tie the president’s hands in the middle of a national security crisis is not the right thing for us to do.” 
Kennedy said he sponsored legislation that could help drive down gas prices called the License to Drill Act, which seeks to extend federal oil and gas permitting fees.

When it comes to efforts to sell or transfer public land into private hands, Kennedy said, “there is an opportunity for us to use those lands in a responsible fashion.” He said he’s in favor of allowing a community with small tracts of land that are federally controlled to use those parcels for developing homes. 
Larsen disagreed, saying he’s concerned about mining, drilling, and effects of those projects on groundwater in rural areas. 
“Let’s not ruin the water supply that we are so desperately in need of right now, and protect our public lands for our indigenous people and tribes who absolutely deserve that,” Larsen said. 
He called U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s operations “very sinister.”
“Recently, within this own county, there was a turkey farm that was raided,” Larsen said, referring to reports that ICE officers detained people at a turkey processing plant in Moroni. “Families were separated. How can we do that and still say we have family values?” 
Kennedy said the first focus of federal immigration enforcement should be criminals and as a result of Trump’s policies at the U.S. border, “our citizens are safer. The second thing is we need to make legal immigration easier, and I’m dedicated to that.” 
While answering a question about energy during the debate, Larsen stopped speaking and said he lost his train of thought. He declined to finish his answer in that moment but returned to the topic later in the debate, calling the lapse a “brain fart.” 
Libertarian Taylor Wright and unaffiliated candidate Steven Burt are also competing for the 4th Congressional District, but they didn’t qualify for the debate stage based on a poll commissioned by the Utah Debate Commission.
Election Day is Nov. 3.
