text:
Ball State University President Geoffrey Mearns addresses the Higher Education Commission on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Commission for Higher Education’s plan to restore performance funding for the state’s seven public colleges and universities is premature, Ball State University President Geoffrey Mearns told the commission Thursday.
Outcomes-based performance funding accounts for a small portion of Indiana’s higher education budget, using a formula to reward colleges for positive outcomes like on-time degree completion.
Lawmakers zeroed out performance funding in the last budget amidst a dire financial forecast, which later proved false.
The two-year budget cut higher education funding by about 6% from fiscal year 2025.
Now, with state reserves projected to reach $5.2 billion next July, the commission plans to present a simpler version of the formula to the State Budget Committee next month in a bid to restore performance funding in the state’s next two-year budget.
The new version prioritizes affordability, accessibility, on-time degree completion and alignment with industry needs.
Mearns questioned whether there’s enough time to win over lawmakers, whom he said may not realize appropriations to Ball State are roughly the same today as 20 years ago, or that tuition has not outpaced inflation.
He said the state ranks 46th in the nation for higher education funding, which should be a higher priority.
“I think we improve our chances of increasing our investment in higher education if we keep our requests simple,” he said.
The commission met Thursday to hear capital project and line item requests universities intend to present to the State Budget Committee for the next budget.
The current fiscal year budget had no money for construction.
Thursday’s meeting acted as a practice round for college presidents as they prepare to meet with lawmakers, giving the commission an opportunity to share feedback.
Jenner said she anticipates a “very, very tough session.”
Purdue University President Mitch Daniels speaks to the Higher Education Commission on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Mackenzi Klemann/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Talks between Jenner and university presidents about how to overcome the narrative that a college degree is not worth pursuing led back to outcomes, she said.
“I think it will be helpful for our General Assembly to see, because it’s not just — it’s an investment, but it’s also outcomes that we’re getting for Hoosier students,” Jenner said.
University presidents touted those outcomes in their presentations Thursday, boasting of tuition freezes, improvements in on-time degree completion, collaboration with industry and retention of graduates who still live in Indiana.
They previewed line item and capital project requests like the $54 million biomedical research laboratory and applied engineering center the University of Southern Indiana wants to build, and an $88 million Ball State project that would transform the library into a “21st Century learning commons.”
All of Indiana’s public colleges and universities agreed to freeze tuition for a second consecutive year in 2026.
Tuition rates at Purdue University haven’t changed since 2012, a feat President Mitch Daniels said has saved families a collective $2.5 billion in 14 years.
Sixty-seven percent of Purdue students graduate debt-free, with in-state tuition still below $10,000, he said. Students who wish to graduate early can choose from 59 majors that can be completed in three years.
The cheapest tuition in the state is at Ivy Tech Community College, which charges $5,154 a year.
President Martin Pollio said the community college system introduced summer flex credits and transparent textbook pricing to keep costs low for students — 88% of whom leave with no college debt.
“We’re in an era of crippling debt all across this nation for college students, especially college students who leave with no credentials,” he said. “That is setting them up for a life of failure. Four out of five of our students leave with no debt whatsoever, and we get them the credentials.”
Pollio said he will ask lawmakers for a new $13 million line item to pay for deferred maintenance to roofs, HVAC, electrical and plumbing systems, with Ivy Tech investing $98 million of its own money.
Ivy Tech is seeking another $84.5 million to replace outdated facilities on the Terre Haute campus and $78 million toward its Evansville campus.
Daniels intends to ask for $100 million in capital projects funds for a proposed 13-floor health science and engineering hub at Purdue, with plans for offices, classrooms, wellness, retail, dining and student housing in the same facility.
Indiana University will ask for $663 million in capital projects, as well as a new $1.3 million line item to be matched by the school to support its entrepreneurial lab.
Other anticipated capital project requests include:

$40 million for facilities renewal, consolidation and infrastructure projects at Vincennes University
$47 million for renovation of Indiana State University’s Holmstedt Hall and decommission of Root Hall
$88 million for artificial intelligence, new technology and infrastructure updates at Ball State University’s Bracken Learning Commons
and $90 million for a new building for the growing Miller College of Business at Ball State, presented as an alternative if the first request is denied.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Months after session, weeks before election, Republicans propose repeal of data center tax break
description: A group of four legislative Republicans, including two who aren’t running for reelection, announced this week proposed legislation that would repeal the sales tax exemption for data centers that was included in the 2023-25 budget.  The biennial budget signed into law in July 2023 exempts data center developers from paying sales and use taxes for […]
text:
Attendees at a Feb. 12 protest called for a pause on data center construction in Wisconsin. (Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)A group of four legislative Republicans, including two who aren’t running for reelection, announced this week proposed legislation that would repeal the sales tax exemption for data centers that was included in the 2023-25 budget. 
The biennial budget signed into law in July 2023 exempts data center developers from paying sales and use taxes for the “sale of property and equipment to construct, renovate or operate data centers.” An analysis conducted by the Legislative Fiscal Bureau in March found that the provision has saved developers in the state $1.5 billion. 
The co-sponsorship memo for the proposed bill states that it was authored by Sen. Andre Jacque (R-New Franken) and Reps. Lindee Brill (R-Sheboygan Falls), Dean Kaufert (R-Neenah) and Shae Sortwell (R-Two Rivers). Kaufert and Jacque are both retiring from the Legislature. 
The memo points to the significant public opposition to data centers from the public as the inspiration for the bill. 
“The tax code should not be used to effectuate crony capitalism,” the memo states. 
But Democratic leaders say the proposed legislation is a “stunt” because at this point in the calendar, no legislation is going anywhere. For a bill to even get assigned a number and given a public hearing, a special session of the Legislature would need to be called, according to the Legislative Reference Bureau. 
The Republicans who have signed onto the bill say they’ve done so to start a debate about data centers that can be picked up when the new Legislature takes office in January. Brill told WisPolitics.com that it’s “important to start the conversation on this topic.”
For more than a year, data centers have been one of the most prominent political conversations in the state and across the country. President Donald Trump has frequently spoken about his support for artificial intelligence — which he’s decreed should be renamed “super intelligence” — and argued that communities that reject data centers will “end up being backwards and poor.”
In Wisconsin, lawmakers from both parties introduced bills during the last session to regulate the development of hyperscale data centers. 
A proposal from Sen. Jodi Habush Sinykin (D-Whitefish Bay) and Rep. Angela Stroud (D-Ashland) and supported by most of the Democratic caucus would have required data centers to report to the state on their energy usage, incentivized the development of renewable energy to power the data centers and require the use of union labor. The bill received a public hearing but did not move forward
A separate proposal from Republicans that passed the Assembly but not the Senate was authored by Rep. Shannon Zimmerman (R-River Falls) and Sen. Romaine Quinn (R-Birchwood). Zimmerman has been criticized in his reelection effort for his work as an executive for AI companies. 
The Republican bill would have made data centers pay for their own power development and required any renewable energy facilities built to power the data centers to be located on site — a provision that opponents said would have discouraged any solar or wind projects from actually happening.
Data centers have also played a significant role in the race for governor. Republican Tom Tiffany has tried to paint Democrat David Crowley as being pro-data center.  
Crowley’s data center policies largely match the provisions in the previously introduced Democratic bill. Tiffany has said he supports additional regulations on data center developments but has also tied his opposition to the projects with his broader distaste for renewable energy, which he says takes up too much farmland in the state. 
Prior to data centers becoming so broadly despised by the voting public, however, Republicans introduced a number of bills that would have encouraged their construction in Wisconsin. 
The sales tax exemption that was ultimately included in the budget was first introduced as a piece of standalone legislation in June 2023 by more than a dozen Republicans. 
“As we move ever more into a world driven by technology, these facilities will be necessary to provide the storage and processing power required to service societal demands,” Zimmerman said in his testimony at the bill’s June 8, 2023, hearing. “Construction of these facilities require hundreds if not thousands of tradespeople. Once complete, they rely on a highly skilled and highly paid workforce.” 
“Beyond the nuts and bolts of the policy and projects to follow, I have a personally [sic] affinity for the industry as I’ve been a tech entrepreneur for the last 30 years,” he continued. “Putting Wisconsin up for consideration when the site selectors are reviewing potential locations would be a step in the right direction.” 
In April of 2025, a group of Republican lawmakers introduced another pro-data center bill that would have loosened restrictions on their inclusion in local tax increment districts. These districts are a financing tool used by local governments that divert property taxes paid within that area away from the municipal general fund and direct the money toward infrastructure improvements within the district. Critics of TIDs argue they divert public money to pay for private development costs. 
Under current law, the value of property within a community’s TIDs cannot be more than 12% of all the taxable property in the city. The proposed bill would have exempted data centers from the 12% rule. The measure never made it to the floor of either chamber.
“[The sales tax exemption] is already bearing fruit,” Rep. Mark Born (R-Beaver Dam) said at the bill’s April 30, 2025 hearing. “Two enormous data centers are under construction already in Wisconsin (including one in the district that I represent); more are being planned. All of these projects far exceed the minimum capital investment required to qualify for the tax exemption, and it seems that the demand for these facilities in our nation and in our region will only increase with time.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Acton discusses plans for small business during Bexley campaign stop
description: Dr. Amy Acton promised to “give a voice” to Ohio’s small business community during a Tuesday visit to Fox’s Bagel and Deli in Bexley. The Democratic candidate for governor described several ideas including loans to help new businesses get off the ground, and suggested her plans to bring down household costs could help boost foot-traffic. […]
text:
Democratic candidate for governor, Amy Acton, speaking with Scott Bast, left, and Jeremy Fox. (Photo by Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal)Dr. Amy Acton promised to “give a voice” to Ohio’s small business community during a Tuesday visit to Fox’s Bagel and Deli in Bexley.
The Democratic candidate for governor described several ideas including loans to help new businesses get off the ground, and suggested her plans to bring down household costs could help boost foot-traffic.
“It is very tight out here,” she said. “There’s no more breathing room. Everyone’s doing everything right, but it’s very tight right now.”
“I think the biggest thing I can do is give a voice to small business,” she went on. “So I intend to do that. It is the future of Ohio, and I’m excited about the future.”
After a quick tour, Acton picked up a baker’s dozen, and sat down to talk with Fox’s owner, Jeremy Fox, and Scott Bast who runs Scotty’s Café a few doors down. They described how restaurant owners are at the mercy of a wide array of rising costs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“It just feels like as of late, it’s been more and more, and the pressure is building and building, and it’s energy, it’s gas, it’s utilities, it’s everything,” Fox said.
Bast explained his most recent electric bill more than doubled.
“It was $1,500. It’s $3,400 now,” he said. “Which for one month — my rent is that much. It’s just insane what’s going on.”
A large share of Bast’s business is catering for weddings, and that puts him in a bind when he’s quoting prices for couples a year ahead of time.
“I can’t call them two weeks before the wedding and say, ‘Well, the economy’s changed. I’ve got to raise your prices,’” Bast said.
Fox said juggling costs boils down to managing sacrifices. You can’t cut much from labor or food costs, he said, so you’re left carving up benefits that would improve your employees’ quality of life.
Fox said they reimburse a portion of health insurance costs for full-time employees and he’s proud they can offer paid time off.
But for him?
“I’m on my wife’s plan,” Fox said. “Really, when you look at restaurant profitability, owner insurance? That’s a luxury.”
Democratic candidate for governor, Amy Acton ordering bagels at Fox’s Bagel and Deli. (Photo by Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal)
Acton’s agenda
Bast suggested Acton come up with some kind of small business council within her office to “talk about issues for small businesses, not big corporations.” Acton quickly committed to that.
“We’re going to be convening small businesses coming in the door as part of a look at all of our business sector alongside JobsOhio,” Acton said. “But we want to spend a little more attention to entrepreneurs, small businesses, and legacy city small businesses, like you’re mentioning.”
She’s also hoping to replicate workforce training initiatives she’s seen in Indiana and Colorado.
“We do a lot right on workforce,” Acton said, “but there’s a lot more we could be doing, that’s what I’ve heard from businesses.”
To help entrepreneurs get businesses started, Acton is considering loan programs.
“I think about you starting out with your food truck,” she said to Fox, “and the kind of capital you needed at the beginning, and we’re particularly also focusing on minority-led businesses as well.”
Acton has proposed what she’s calling a Working Families Tax Cut, geared toward lower income families with kids.
The proposal includes an earned income tax credit and a child tax credit of $1,000 for kids six and under, and $500 for those seven to 18. She told Fox and Bast that could help their employees and customers alike.
“What we’re finding is we need some immediate relief for cash flow for people who are just working,” Acton said, “and healthcare costs are the number one cost we’re hearing about.”
She expressed concern about lack of healthcare coverage and said she’d try leveraging the state’s purchasing power to negotiate lower premiums.
“We’re doing a lot around trying to get health insurance premiums down,” she said. “We’re going to try to negotiate using the state’s power for small businesses because I’m worried about you guys not having an alternative.”
Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy (speaking) flanked by his running mate and Senate President Rob McColley shortly after lawmakers approved a 90-day tax holiday. (Photo by Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal)
Ramaswamy’s endorsement
The Ohio Capital Journal asked Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign about his plans for small business but got no response.
Ramaswamy has gotten the endorsement of Ohio’s chapter of the National Federation of Independent Business, which represents 21,000 small and independent businesses.
“Our members were looking for a candidate who understands the challenges facing small businesses and has a vision to unlock Ohio’s full potential,” NFIB Ohio State Director Jared Weiser said in August. “They found that in Vivek Ramaswamy.”
In a press release announcing the endorsement, Ramaswamy called small businesses “the backbone of towns and cities across Ohio.” Despite years of unified Republican leadership in Ohio, he insisted they’re “getting squeezed by government overgrowth.”
“They were unfairly penalized by the disastrous COVID lockdowns that my opponent pushed on them,” Ramaswamy said. “I’ll stand with hardworking Ohioans and entrepreneurs who work, hire, build, and take risks — not the bureaucrats standing in their way. We’ll get government off the backs of small businesses so they can grow here and help Ohio families get ahead.”
Asked about Ramaswamy earning NFIB’s endorsement, Acton campaign spokeswoman Virginia Schaus said Ramaswamy’s plans for drastic tax cuts will wind up raising costs elsewhere.
“While Vivek Ramaswamy’s tax scam would raise costs for Ohio families and hurt small businesses,” she said, “as governor, Dr. Acton will be laser-focused on lowering costs.”

title: Ohio’s chronic absenteeism rate is dropping, but is more than 10% higher than pre-pandemic rates
description: Ohio’s chronic absenteeism rate has been trending downward in recent years, but still remains higher than it was pre-pandemic.  The statewide chronic absenteeism rate — missing 10% or more of school hours for any reason — was 23.7% for the 2025-26 school year, according to the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce.  Ohio’s chronic absenteeism […]
text:
School buses lined up.(Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline.)Ohio’s chronic absenteeism rate has been trending downward in recent years, but still remains higher than it was pre-pandemic. 
The statewide chronic absenteeism rate — missing 10% or more of school hours for any reason — was 23.7% for the 2025-26 school year, according to the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce. 
Ohio’s chronic absenteeism rate in recent years, according to ODEW: 

2024-25 — 24.9%
2023-24 — 25.6% 
2022-23 — 26.8%
2021-22 — 30.2% 
2020-21 — 24% 
2019-20 — 11.2% 
2018-19 — 16.7% 
2017-18 — 16%

“The incremental improvements are less and less,” said Arya Ansari, faculty associate at Ohio State University’s Crane Center for Early Childhood Research and Policy.
“We don’t want to settle. We don’t want this curve to completely flatten. We want to continue to improve.” 
He hopes the state’s chronic absenteeism rate can drop back down to pre-pandemic levels in the next five to ten years.
“It’s not going to be next year,” Ansari said. “It’s not going to be the following year. So I think it’s a more moderate to longer-term outlook. … There’s not a single solution that’s going to move the needle to where we were pre-COVID.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Students who are chronically absent do less well academically, socially, and behaviorally, Ansari said. 
A school day missed is equivalent to 2.5 days of lost math learning and 1.5 days of lost language and literacy learning, according to a 2022 report from the Crane Center. 
“Not every day is created equal, and a lot of learning happens while kids are in the classroom academically,” Ansari said. 
“Unfortunately it’s not as if kids just miss a day and that’s it. Kids miss considerably more than that.”
There is often a snowball effect when it comes to chronic absenteeism, he said. 
“It’s hard to get students to catch up,” Ansari said. 
A lot has to go right for a student to show up to school. 
“Underlying a lot of these barriers is poverty, which contributes to things like housing instability, food insecurity, physical and mental health of the child and of the family,” Ansari said. 
“School hours don’t necessarily map onto families who work evening shifts or multiple jobs.”
These Ohio school districts had the highest chronic absenteeism rates in Ohio for the 2025-26 school year, according to ODEW: 

Garfield Heights City Schools (Cuyahoga County) — 61.9% 
Youngstown City Schools (Mahoning County) — 56.7% 
Lorain City Schools (Lorain County) —  56.5%
Cleveland Municipal Schools (Cuyahoga County) — 54.2% 
East Cleveland City Schools (Cuyahoga County) — 54.2%
North College Hill City Schools (Hamilton County) — 54% 
Columbus City Schools (Franklin County) — 53.8% 
Mt. Healthy City Schools (Hamilton County) — 53.1% 
Lockland Local Schools (Hamilton County)  — 50.1% 
New Miami Local Schools (Butler County) — 44.7%

Columbus City Schools Superintendent Angela Chapman “believes reducing absenteeism is one of the best ways to improve student education and scores on tests, report cards and graduation,” district spokesperson Michael Brown said in an email. 
“Even a few days of missed school can hold a student back from their learning journey, from the first days of kindergarten through graduation.” 
Columbus City Schools, the state’s largest district with about 45,000 students, saw a slight increase in chronic absenteeism during the 2025-26 school year, up from 52.6% in 2024-25. The district’s chronic absenteeism rate was 65% during the 2021-22 school year. 
Prior to COVID-19, the district had a 32.7% chronic absenteeism rate for the 2019-20 school year. 
Stay in the Game! Attendance Network works with more than 200 school districts to improve school attendance. It is managed by Battelle Education and was founded in 2019 by the Cleveland Browns Foundation, ODEW, and Harvard’s Proving Ground.
“Students who have never been chronically absent are about three and a half times more likely to be able to read on grade level at the end of the third grade,” said Janet Walton, network director for the Stay in the Game! Attendance Network. 
There was a shift in the value of school attendance during the COVID-19 pandemic, Walton said. 
“It’s about helping (school districts) to identify student groups who are maybe struggling with chronic absenteeism, and then try to find out what the root cause is there, and really intentionally planning some interventions that address that,” she said.
“We’re seeing decreases, and we’re really pleased about that. But I think we know now we are in this for the long haul.”

title: Ohio has reached a turning point on the death penalty
description: On Sept. 30, Tennessee’s execution of Christa Pike failed after two lethal injections, which has resulted in Gov. Bill Lee suspending Tennessee’s remaining scheduled executions for 2026 and ordering an independent review. For Ohio, this failed execution adds urgency to the debate over whether changing execution methods can address the broader concerns about[...]
text:
A view of the death chamber from the witness room at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility shows an electric chair and gurney. (Photo by Mike Simons/Getty Images)On Sept. 30, Tennessee’s execution of Christa Pike failed after two lethal injections, which has resulted in Gov. Bill Lee suspending Tennessee’s remaining scheduled executions for 2026 and ordering an independent review. 
For Ohio, this failed execution adds urgency to the debate over whether changing execution methods can address the broader concerns about capital punishment or whether the state should abolish it altogether. 
Recently, Gov. Mike DeWine has called on lawmakers to repeal the death penalty, more than four decades after helping write the law that reinstated it in 1981. 
After working within the system as a legislator, attorney general, and governor, DeWine now says capital punishment no longer serves its intended purpose, and recent events in Tennessee have pushed the issue to the forefront. 
His reversal places a basic question before the Ohio General Assembly: Does the death penalty make the state safer?
The evidence concerning deterrence remains unsettled. 
In 2012, the National Research Council concluded that existing studies could not establish whether capital punishment increases, decreases, or has no effect on homicide rates, and as a result, advised policymakers not to use that research when judging the deterrent value of the death penalty. 
DeWine has similarly said he no longer believes Ohio’s experience supports the deterrence argument that once shaped his position.
Ohio has not conducted an execution since July 2018. Since that time, the state has struggled to obtain lethal-injection drugs without risking access to medications used throughout its prison system. 
Ohio House Bill 36 would add nitrogen hypoxia as an execution method. In contrast, some other states, such as South Carolina, have considered or adopted firing squads. 
Supporters view alternative methods as a way to carry out lawful sentences. At the same time, opponents contend that each substitute creates additional legal, logistical, and ethical disputes without addressing broader concerns about capital punishment.
Cost is another part of the debate, as capital cases generally involve specialized representation, separate sentencing proceedings, automatic review, and extended appeals. 
Studies consistently show that the death penalty is significantly more expensive than life imprisonment, with recent estimates around the country ranging from 2.5 to 5 times the cost. 
While this does not establish Ohio’s current costs, it does illustrate why lawmakers examining capital punishment often compare its expenses with life-without-parole cases and competing public-safety investments.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Application of the death penalty also varies by jurisdiction, as county prosecutors decide whether to pursue capital charges, and counties differ in their caseloads, resources, and charging practices. 
Researchers and legal organizations have also examined whether race, geography and access to experienced representation affect capital-case outcomes. 
Any assessment of Ohio’s system therefore requires state-specific information on where death sentences originate, how often capital charges are sought, and whether similarly situated cases receive comparable treatment.
Wrongful convictions add another consideration, as DNA testing, witness recantations, newly discovered evidence, forensic reviews, and findings of official misconduct have overturned convictions around the country. 
Post-conviction review can sometimes correct an erroneous prison sentence, although it cannot restore years of confinement, and an execution of someone later found to be innocent is irreversible. 
Supporters of capital punishment respond that extensive appellate review is designed to identify errors before a sentence is carried out; critics, however, question whether any human system can eliminate that risk.
When it comes to the victims’ families, they also do not speak with one voice. Some believe an execution is necessary for accountability and justice after an especially serious murder. 
Others oppose capital punishment or prefer a final sentence that avoids decades of hearings, appeals, and renewed public attention. 
DeWine cited the prolonged effect of capital litigation on victims’ families when explaining his changed position. These differing experiences complicate broad claims that either an execution or a life sentence necessarily provides closure.
To address this dilemma, life imprisonment without parole can be a principal alternative for several reasons, as it permanently incapacitates a person convicted of aggravated murder while eliminating the possibility of an execution. 
Death-penalty supporters argue that certain crimes warrant a punishment beyond incarceration and that juries should retain that option. In contrast, opponents argue that life without parole provides public protection and severe accountability without the costs and risks unique to capital punishment.
The debate is now tied to specific legislative choices as bipartisan repeal proposals are pending in the General Assembly, including Ohio Senate Bill 133. 
Former Republican Gov. Bob Taft and former Democratic Gov. Ted Strickland have opposed capital punishment, demonstrating that the issue does not divide neatly along party lines. 
At the same time, other Ohio officials and prosecutors continue to support retaining the law or establishing a workable execution method.
Ohio lawmakers must evaluate the system the state actually operates: one with lawful death sentences but no executions since 2018, recurring disputes over execution methods, and cases that can remain unresolved for decades. 
Their decision requires weighing deterrence, accountability, cost, consistency, innocence, victims’ experiences, and available alternatives. 
Whatever course they choose will define how Ohio balances punishment, public safety, and confidence in its justice system for years after the current debate ends.

 Catching Our Eye

• Assault on Ohio public schools. The Elyria Chronicle-Telegram’s Owen MacMillan reports, “’We are under assault,’ Advocates say Ohio school funding being actively undercut.”
As districts across the county pursue funding levies next month, and those across the state face mounting financial pressures, a group of parents, educators and advocates gathered to discuss the state of school funding in Ohio and its future.
A panel of policy experts, educators and parents argued at the event that Ohio’s school funding shortfall was not the result of overpaid administrators or local fiscal irresponsibility, but of an active choice by the state legislature to underfund public schools.
• Get the Flock out? WOSU’s Katie Geniusz reports, “Meet the central Ohio residents who want to ‘DeFlock’ their neighborhoods.”
On June 13, the DeFlock chapter of Upper Arlington held its first meeting. It would be the first DeFlock group in central Ohio. Six people showed up, including the group’s two founders, Paul Shannon and Christian Gabis. The organization aims to have Flock cameras removed from the community.
Now, Shannon and Gabis believe the group may have outgrown the 75-seat Friend’s Theater at the Tremont Branch of Upper Arlington Public Library.
• Ohio swing counties. Ideastream’s Matthew Richmond reports, “Ohio’s statewide races could depend on a few counties, Brown’s return to the ballot and Trump.”
This year’s election is similar to 2018 — it’s a midterm election, halfway through President Donald Trump’s term and the president’s approval ratings are low.
And Sherrod Brown’s presence on the ballot may serve to drive up support for other Democrats, like gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, said David Cohen, director of the Applied Politics Program at University of Akron…
The election may come down to who shows up to the polls in a few counties, said Cohen, including Ottawa, Trumbull and Mahoning Counties.
• Vance’s laughable definition of ‘socialism.’ Cleveland.com’s Howard Koplowitz reports, “‘Our VP really is an idiot’: Vance hammered for ‘laughably dishonest’ definition of socialism.”
“So, I don’t know what the term means anymore. I think in reality, what it actually means in the American context is that you want to replace American workers with foreign workers, and you want boys to play in girls’ sports,” the vice president continued. “That’s what united the socialists that I see running across the United States of America today.”
Trump administration critics and political observers both mocked Vance and accused the vice president of being fully aware of the proper definition of socialism.
The primary definition, according to Merriam-Webster, is “any of various egalitarian economic and political theories or movements advocating collective or governmental ownership and administration of the means of production and distribution of goods.”
Vance’s definition “is so laughably dishonest,” said Reason reporter Billy Binion. “The Trump administration would like to change the definition of socialism because it’s engaging in it and has bought stakes in dozens of private companies. JD Vance is practically a woke progressive at this point.”

title: Union files new charges that St. Mary’s Hospital, Dean Medical have violated labor laws
description: The union representing nurses at St. Mary’s Hospital in Madison and Dean Medical Group outpatient clinics in Dane County has escalated charges that the two healthcare providers are violating federal labor laws after employees voted overwhelmingly for union representation. SEIU Wisconsin filed unfair labor practice charges this week with the National Labor Re[...]
text:
The union SEIU Wisconsin Nurses has filed new charges against St. Mary’s Hospital in Madison, part of SSM Health. as well as SSM's Dean Medical Group clinics, accusing the employers of violating federal labor laws. (Wisconsin Examiner photo)The union representing nurses at St. Mary’s Hospital in Madison and Dean Medical Group outpatient clinics in Dane County has escalated charges that the two healthcare providers are violating federal labor laws after employees voted overwhelmingly for union representation.
SEIU Wisconsin filed unfair labor practice charges this week with the National Labor Relations Board against St. Mary’s and against Dean. Both organizations are part of SSM Health, a Catholic nonprofit health system based in St. Louis.
A 71% majority of nurses at Dean’s 10 clinics voted for union representation in September, three months after nurses at St. Mary’s Hospital voted for union representation with an 89% majority in June. Altogether the two groups of nurses total nearly 1,200 people.
To date, SSM has declined to bargain with the hospital nurses’ union, citing pending challenges to the June election. Earlier in September the union charged the hospital management with failing to bargain in violation of federal law.
The newest charge against the hospital alleges a nurse was fired in August in retaliation for supporting the union.
The new charges against Dean allege that the medical group discriminated against union supporters in prohibiting union-related materials from work areas and barring employees from displaying union insignia and other items supporting the union; engaged in surveillance of employees; held captive audience meetings with threats of discipline or firing for people who didn’t attend; and threatened employees with “negative changes to terms and conditions of employment” if employees voted in the union.
Those charges follow previous charges filed with the NLRB, including one against Dean in September for firing a nurse and a string of charges against St. Mary’s earlier in September, including the failure-to-bargain allegation.
“We are doing this so we can have a voice,” said Dean nurse Michelle Camilleri in a phone interview Thursday. “My colleagues and I want to provide a certain standard of care for our patients. We want to be able to care for them in a way so they can get the highest level of care as we can give.”
She said nurses who voted for unionization were responding to policies and practices that were making it “difficult to provide that standard of care” for patients and have driven some nurses to leave SSM.
“We would like to see SSM come to the table,” Camilleri said.
In a statement Thursday, SSM denied violating federal labor laws. “There has been no unlawful conduct. We respect and value all of our employees,” the statement said.
The statement called the allegations “another ongoing attempt to distract us” from the health system’s mission.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Three days in a CT psych unit with a foster teen
description: Mental health ED boarding is more than simply dehumanizing. The experience is tantamount to solitary confinement.
text:
Emily (not her real name) was 16 when I went to see her in the psychiatric wing of the ER at a Connecticut hospital. Emily was in foster care and I was assigned to be her advocate through the volunteer organization Connecticut CASA. I arrived to find her in a room with no windows, only bare beige walls, glass that looked into the nurses’ station, an armchair, and a fuzzy, small TV embedded in the ceiling. 
Emily was normally very charming and expressive. There she looked hollow, as if her humanity had been drained out of her.

Larissa Pitts

Emily had been cleared to leave hours before by the examining physicians. But she remained in that room for a total of three days as a result of a practice called “ED boarding.” In other states, child protection agencies house children who are waiting on homes in their offices. Connecticut no longer allows this, as child advocates have argued this practice is dehumanizing. Mental health ED boarding is more than simply dehumanizing; the experience is tantamount to solitary confinement.
Like many foster children, Emily’s history of abuse and neglect meant she often reacted explosively when angry. When her tantrums were especially destructive, the Department of Children and Families would send her to the hospital for psychiatric evaluation. Emily estimates that she was sent to the ER for psychiatric care 15 times over the course of her life. The ER physicians determined it was medically necessary for her to be there only once. Sometimes she was left in the ER for hours. 
Other times, she was left there for days. Emily’s story is in no way unique. A 2024 study found that within one year of entering foster care, 24% of foster children had been sent to a mental health emergency department. A 2026 study determined that children with experience in foster care spent an average of 24% more time in a mental health ED than other children, and were twice as likely to be physically or pharmacologically restrained.
 The ER’s psych unit is no place for any child. It was eerily quiet, except when a new patient was brought in screaming. I was allowed to bring nothing that could help us pass the time. While nurses came in periodically to check Emily’s vitals, they did not speak to her except at my prompting. It was hard to tell the passage of time without sunlight. After long nights alone, Emily was desperate for human connection by the time I arrived each morning. As much as I enjoyed spending time with Emily, forcing myself to stay in that place was hard to manage even as an adult. I felt relief when I got to return to the real world each night, a world with colors, a variety of activities to stimulate my mind, and human contact. I was the only one who visited Emily. Otherwise, she was alone. 
 Prison policy reformers have long spoken of the damage solitary confinement inflicts upon adults. According to the   Prison Policy Initiative  , human beings experience “social pain” when deprived of human interaction for prolonged periods of time. Half of the inmates who commit suicide are those who have experienced solitary confinement.   Connecticut state law   prohibits the use of solitary confinement for child detainees, as they are   more psychologically vulnerable to its effects  . 
 Prolonged social isolation took its toll on Emily, too. She was so desperate to leave the hospital that she willingly took the first foster placement offered: a home where the family’s teenage biological son had snuck into her room at night to ask for sexual favors. She had never reported the incidents to DCF for fear of not being believed. Refusing this placement would have meant languishing in that room for hours or even days longer. That seemed more intolerable to Emily than sexual harassment.  
I call upon state legislators and DCF to prevent future foster children from experiencing the trauma inflicted upon Emily. Deescalation procedures should be systematically implemented in order to prevent unnecessary mental health ED visits. Restrictions should also be placed on ED boarding in order to eliminate prolonged social isolation. 
Our state’s most vulnerable children need attention and support, not solitary confinement.
Larissa Pitts lives in Southington.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota US House challengers advocate for change
description: Three challengers for North Dakota’s U.S. House seat listed their priorities during a debate Thursday on Prairie Public while criticizing the Republican incumbent for not participating. Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer and independent candidates Helene Neville and Charles Tuttle made their case to voters and showed their differences on the i[...]
text:
Prairie Public News Director Dave Thompson moderates a debate with North Dakota U.S. House candidates Trygve Hammer (D), Helene Neville (I), and Charles Tuttle (I) on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Rick Gion/Prairie Public)Three challengers for North Dakota’s U.S. House seat listed their priorities during a debate Thursday on Prairie Public while criticizing the Republican incumbent for not participating.
Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer and independent candidates Helene Neville and Charles Tuttle made their case to voters and showed their differences on the issues.

Watch the full debate

Republican incumbent Rep. Julie Fedorchak did not participate. In a statement, Fedorchak said she agreed to a one-hour debate with Hammer, but withdrew after Prairie Public added two candidates and planned to extend the debate to 90 minutes.
When Neville and Tuttle became qualified U.S. House candidates, Prairie Public added them to the already-scheduled debate because the station invites all candidates on the ballot, regardless of party, CEO John Harris said in a statement.
Hammer, who is challenging Fedorchak for a second time, said he brought up concerns about data centers and expanding executive authority two years ago on the same debate stage.
“I’m running again this time because all of the problems we discussed here two years ago have only gotten worse,” Hammer said. “We need to bring down prices. We need to make life easier and better for everyday North Dakotans, not just for big donors and corporations.”
Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer poses before a debate hosted by Prairie Public on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Rick Gion/Prairie Public)
Hammer said the debate surrounding data centers reflects the distrust people have involving technology companies, corporations and billionaires. He said he wants more transparency measures, which he believes would help stop developers from “rolling over” small towns and individuals.
“We need regulation, and Congress needs to act to ensure that the AI economy does not hurt regular working people,” Hammer said.
Neville said data centers should have remediation plans for their sites if there becomes a time when those facilities are abandoned for the next technology.
Tuttle said data centers will likely be obsolete in five to 10 years.
“No one seems to have a plan for longevity for any of this stuff,” he said.
Tuttle said he also worries the increased use of AI and data would lead to increased surveillance by the government.
Priorities
Hammer said one of his priorities, if elected, would be to push for an anti-gerrymandering bill.
“That would show Congress getting something done for the people, not themselves and would be popular across the entire political spectrum,” he said.
Hammer said he would not be a rubber stamp for President Donald Trump, political donors or even his own Democratic Party.
As a member of Congress, Tuttle said he would make the Department of Government Efficiency cuts permanent.
“We’ve got fraud, it seems like, everywhere,” Tuttle said. He added he supports Trump and wants to see his policies moved through Congress and into federal law.
“We need the Republicans in Congress to get behind it and get these bills passed,” he said.
Neville said she’s an independent because she is “for the people, not politics.”
Independent U.S. House candidate Helene Neville poses before a debate hosted by Prairie Public on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Rick Gion/Prairie Public)
Her top priority if elected to the U.S. House would be to help enact age and term limits for members of Congress, she said.
“There is no way that a 94-year-old senator from Iowa … has any relevancy on what’s going on today,” Neville said. “The people first campaign is just to help everybody that needs a helping hand.”
Political leanings
Tuttle told viewers he is the only Republican running the U.S. House race, as an independent. He criticized Fedorchak for not seeking the Republican endorsement at the state convention. No other Republican incumbents sought the party’s endorsement this year either.
Hammer said Fedorchak has been ineffective as a member of the majority party in Congress and would be more ineffectual as a member of the minority. 
He added a U.S. House member needs to listen and hear all sides of different issues from people of all walks of life.
“We need someone in Congress who will do that. Go and listen to the people,” Hammer said.
Neville emphasized that she is an independent and not a Democrat. She sought the Democratic-NPL endorsement, losing to Hammer.
“I’m right down the middle,” she said. “As a nurse in ER, you don’t get to ask the patient, ‘Are you a Democrat or a Republican?’ You just serve them compassion, love and whatever it takes to heal them.”
Tuttle referenced COVID-19 several times, questioning why people are still getting the vaccine and calling the pandemic “a hoax,” among other claims. 
Independent U.S. House candidate Charles Tuttle poses before a debate hosted by Prairie Public on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Rick Gion/Prairie Public)
Neville, a nurse, said she worked in hospitals during the pandemic and many people died before the vaccine was made available.
“I disagree,” she said about Tuttle’s comments. 
Hammer and Tuttle differed on the effect the Iran war has had on oil prices.
Tuttle said Iran was a threat and its nuclear program needed to be “taken out.” He criticized oil companies for high prices. 
“I’m sick of hearing these people saying, ‘It’s a world market,’” Tuttle said. “We need to get these oil companies to stop gouging our oil prices.”
Hammer said the price of oil went up with the start of the war, and he believes Congress needs to take back its authority and end the war.
Prairie Public News Director Dave Thompson moderated the debate.
Fedorchak and Hammer are scheduled to participate in a debate hosted by the Forum Communications Plain Talk podcast that will be released at 4 p.m. Oct. 14.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Hammer, of Minot, lost two previous attempts seeking a statewide office. In 2024, he lost to Fedorchak in the U.S. House race with 30% of voter support. He also lost a bid to join the Public Service Commission in 2022. 
Tuttle, of Bismarck, is a frequent political candidate who most recently lost in the June primary for North Dakota superintendent of public instruction. He also lost a run for secretary of state in 2022, superintendent of public instruction in 2020 and U.S. House in 2018.
Neville, of Jamestown, has not sought elected office before this year. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Michigan Advance
title: El-Sayed, Rogers trade barbs, accusations during first televised U.S. Senate debate
description: GRAND RAPIDS — After months of circling each other on the campaign trail, former Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed met face-to-face on Thursday for the first debate of the cycle in Michigan’s competitive U.S. Senate race. Hosted by WOOD-TV 8, the forum covered a wide range of […]
text:
Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers, right, speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed, at WOOD-TV, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)GRAND RAPIDS — After months of circling each other on the campaign trail, former Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed met face-to-face on Thursday for the first debate of the cycle in Michigan’s competitive U.S. Senate race.
Hosted by WOOD-TV 8, the forum covered a wide range of issues including healthcare, housing, tariffs, ending the war in Iran, support for Israel and mass surveillance, giving El-Sayed and Rogers a chance to further draw contrast between their respective campaigns.
That said, the debate quickly devolved into a series of personal attacks with each candidate digging deep into their respective campaign bags to hit each other on their records, their wealth, who is funding their campaigns, and the decisions they’ve made on the campaign trail.
At the top of the hour, moderator Rick Albin asked the candidates about the price of gas, and if they would support suspending the gas tax. 
El-Sayed noted that the Iran war was driving much of the high prices that Americans are dealing with. Rogers also said he believed the nation needed a pause on the gas tax given the lack of resources going through the Strait of Hormuz. El-Sayed agreed that if the war didn’t stop now, the Iranian regime would choke out the strait entirely.
From there, the attacks began, and grew in intensity as the debate carried on. Albin worked hard to reign both in, but struggled to control the tenor of the debate as Rogers and El-Sayed repeatedly and forcefully pushed back on each other’s statements and tried to score political points.
Rogers opened his attacks by saying that El-Sayed’s healthcare and economic policies would raise prices nationwide, particularly in Michigan.
“We can’t afford Abdul,” Rogers said.
Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers, makes a point during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed, at WOOD-TV, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)
In a question on whether he believed the federal government should enact price controls, El-Sayed said it was worth considering. The Democrat then noted his belief that Rogers had a direct line to Trump and had the ability to potentially persuade the president to end the war, but hadn’t because he didn’t want to face his wrath.
Rogers punched back by saying that El-Sayed was not who he says he is, adding that he was “the best con man” he’s ever seen.
El-Sayed countered by saying that Rogers had nothing to run on and a record of tying himself to Trump.
“It’s about whether you can see your doctor, and whether you can trust your next U.S. Senator,” El-Sayed said. “You’re running because Donald Trump called him and asked him to run.”
Rogers said he was running because of high prices and job losses over the past decade, spanning two presidential administrations. He also accused El-Sayed of not wanting to talk about how he would pay for this key campaign planks, such as Medicare for All, because he didn’t have that part of the plan worked out.
Before Albin could move to the next question, El-Sayed interjected to note that the loss of jobs and hikes on prices in goods over the last 30 years was due to Rogers’ support of the North American Free Trade Agreement.
“You did that man,” El-Sayed said. “That was your policy.”
Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed, talks during a televised debate with Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers at WOOD-TV, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)
Albin questioned Rogers about his changing position on Canadian tariffs, noting that Rogers has shifted his stance throughout the campaign on Trump’s trade war with Canada. 
Early in the campaign, Rogers praised Trump’s efforts on encouraging businesses to stay on American soil through tariffs on other nations, including some U.S. allies like Canada. That later changed to Rogers saying that he supported those that created investments and that some of those tariffs were too high, and that he would encourage the administration to bring some of them down.
Now, with the race winding down, Rogers has released advertising saying that the Canadian trade war was causing harm to Michigan and that it needed to end now.
Rogers said on Thursday that he wants to see a deal down with Canada and that it did need to end.
“I have made those phone calls this week to take care of that,” Rogers said.
He then immediately went back to attacking El-Sayed, saying again that he “wants to raise the cost of everything you touch.”
El-Sayed was asked if there was a Trump tariff policy that he would keep, and noted that the UAW has advocated for smart tariffs tied to industrial policies that would “make sense, or be used to protect our own market.” He then called Trump’s tariffs “hamfisted.”
El-Sayed said Rogers was flip-flopping on the tariffs because his polls were lagging.
“Be serious, my guy,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers said El-Sayed wanted to fight every tariff, but he used an anecdote that manufactures he talks to have said they were able to add shifts because of Trump’s trade tactics.
Rogers accused El-Sayed of receiving corporate money, despite El-Sayed’s statements that he had rejected such contributions. Rogers also alleged that El-Sayed received support from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, financier George Soros and the Muslim Brotherhood.
Telecom industry gave Mike Rogers nearly $100K while he pushed to deepen government data sharing

El-Sayed criticized Rogers’ work with telecommunications companies after his time in Congress, including Telefónica, which El-Sayed linked to surveillance practices in Venezuela.
The candidates also argued over their wealth, with Rogers saying El-Sayed was a millionaire who owned luxury property in Dubai. El-Sayed responded that Rogers had a “McMansion” in Florida that he took off the market because he knew he was going to lose. El-Sayed also accused Rogers of having two yachts in Florida, which Rogers denied.

@michiganadvance Michigan Advance Senior Reporter Ben Solis asked both @Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers whether their debate was instructive for voters. Two very different answers. #MISEN ♬ original sound – Michigan Advance


This pattern continued through questions on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, AI data centers, and on the Iran war more directly.
The exchange grew so heated that Albin called a commercial break. It was reported that Rogers and El-Sayed continued to fight off camera about Rogers’ Florida home. When asked after the debate about that exchange, El-Sayed claimed Rogers told him he was planning to rent the home instead of going back to live there. Rogers did not address that exchange in a scrum following the debate. A request for comment on the off-camera exchange from the Rogers campaign was not returned at the time of publication. A comment will be added to this story once it is received.
The debate became more focused on policy during the second half. 
On the actions of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement officers, Rogers said that one thing he would have done differently if he had control of ICE were the raids seen so publicly across the U.S. He said that his time in the FBI taught him that raids of that nature should be quick, decisive, and without public fanfare. He admitted that ICE agents could have made adjustments and said that they had after incidents like what happened earlier this year in Minnesota — where two civilians were shot and killed by immigration officers.
That said, Rogers noted that murders were down in the U.S. and that it was because he believed ICE was first and foremost targeting murderers for deportations.
El-Sayed said that he does want to abolish ICE, but agreed that someone convicted of murder deserved to be deported. However, he said the nation didn’t have to do that by also violating the U.S. Constitution in pursuit of those goals.
“ICE is not about enforcement … they killed two people,” El-Sayed said. “We have to obey our constitution.”
On Iran, El-Sayed accused Rogers of being a ‘cheerleader’ for war throughout his congressional career.
“When you have an international problem, he’s got a war for that,” El-Sayed said, noting that could be dangerous as the U.S. has so many foreign entanglements.
Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers, right, speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed, at WOOD-TV, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)
Rogers said El-Sayed refused to condemn the Iranian regime and its Revolutionary Guard at a recent campaign stop, and accused him of not being able to condemn the Temple Israel attack earlier this year. 
El-Sayed said that was false, and that Rogers was wrong to say that he hadn’t.
The debate again turned personal in the second half, when both candidates brought up each other’s family members — with Rogers suggesting that El-Sayed’s birth mother had connections to organizations that funded terrorism, and El-Sayed kicking back to ask what his mother did. Rogers said his mother worked for a chamber of commerce.
After the debate, Michigan Advance asked both candidates whether the personal attacks had allowed voters to hear the substantive discussion of issues they needed to make a decision before the Nov. 3 election.
“Even his top staff have said he is a manufactured candidate,” Rogers told the Advance. “He tells one group one thing and two hours later another group completely something different.”
El-Sayed said he wished that they did have a better chance to do so, because it was important to him in the campaign to run on the issues. El-Sayed has told the Advance in the past that he doesn’t like the mudslinging, nor the horserace fascination people have with politics.
“He wanted to make this about everything except the policy,” El-Sayed said.
Both candidates are set to participate in a final debate Oct. 21, hosted by WXYZ-TV.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Debate over energy costs highlights how differently Jackson and Collins approach governing
description: During the second U.S. Senate debate on Thursday, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson continued his criticism of Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins for not doing enough to oppose President Donald Trump’s power, while the incumbent touted her behind-the-scenes efforts to alleviate harm caused by the administration.  That was most acute during the WMTW debate amid[...]
text:
Democratic nominee Troy Jackson (left) and Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Susan Collins (right) met for the second time on the debate stage on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photos by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)During the second U.S. Senate debate on Thursday, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson continued his criticism of Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins for not doing enough to oppose President Donald Trump’s power, while the incumbent touted her behind-the-scenes efforts to alleviate harm caused by the administration. 
That was most acute during the WMTW debate amid discussion of energy costs, specifically soaring heating oil prices, an issue of grave concern to many Mainers as winter approaches. 
Speaking over each other until the last breath, the candidates continued their sparring from the first debate on Tuesday over corruption and blaming one another for Mainers’ struggles. 
The second debate also highlighted their disagreement over term limits — both for U.S. Congress and the Supreme Court — and agreement on changes to make Social Security solvent. 
Energy costs
Heating oil prices have hit record highs in Maine. The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program helps certain homeowners and renters with energy costs, but many working families do not qualify and still struggle to pay their bills. 
Both candidates said they would support an expansion of LIHEAP. Collins also suggested expanding the weatherization program, which provides free home energy improvements to eligible low-income homeowners. 
The senator also said the country needs to become energy independent, which Jackson later echoed. However, he brought the issue back to the Iran War as the main culprit.   
“What she doesn’t want to talk about is this is a crisis that was started by her and Donald Trump,” Jackson said. 
Jackson said Collins voted five times against ending the war with Iran. Collins said she voted nine times to end the war. Both are correct. 
Collins initially opposed early war powers resolutions, saying the War Powers Act gives deference for the president to wage wars for 60 days. She then began to support ending the war after the conflict hit 60 days. 
At one point, Jackson alleged that Collins and her husband were profiting off of the Iran War. 
“That is absolutely outrageous,” Collins said, “and you owe me an apology.”
In first debate, Collins and Jackson blame each other for Mainers’ struggles

According to Collins’ 2025 financial disclosure, her husband owns stock in two defense contractors for the U.S. military, Boeing and RTX. Her spokesperson previously told Maine Maine Morning Star that her husband’s investments are managed by a third-party adviser and that no individual stocks have been bought or sold from his account in more than three years.
Meanwhile, the senator touted her current behind-the-scenes efforts to address energy costs, saying she expects her conversations with Trump administration officials will result in getting LIHEAP funding released early, as soon as next week, and releasing all of the oil in the Northeast Home Heating Reserve, which is intended for a crisis.
“It’s great that she might be able to get some fuel released. That’s awesome,” Jackson said. “But look, the 100 million gallons that she’s talking about, the average in the United States is anywhere from 20.5 to 23.6 million barrels a day.”
(Actual consumer demand sits at the lower end of that spectrum.)
As the moderator turned to Jackson’s record as former president of the Maine Senate, he was asked about his 2019 vote to expand Maine’s Net Energy Billing program, which was designed to encourage renewable energy projects by offering customers credits to offset their power bills. 
“It did cost more than it should have,” Jackson said, “but we reformed it twice.”
Jackson also pointed to the volatility of natural gas prices as a significant cost driver. 
Term limits
Both candidates were asked if they support term limits in Congress. Jackson said yes. Collins said no. “That’s what you have elections for,” she added.
When Collins first ran for U.S. Senate in 1996, she said she would only serve two terms. She is now seeking a sixth. The moderator asked what changed her mind.
Collins pointed to the outsized federal earmarks she has secured for the state in recent years.  
“What I’ve learned is how much more effective I could be as the seventh ranked person in the Senate versus 99th,” Collins said. 
Both candidates were also asked if they support term limits for the U.S. Supreme Court. Again, Jackson said yes, and Collins said no.
Social Security 
Discussion of Social Security offered a moment of agreement on Thursday. 
Maine has the oldest median age in the country. Both candidates were asked what changes they would support to keep the Social Security Retirement Trust Fund solvent. The fund is projected to be depleted in 2032, after which the program could pay only 78% of scheduled benefits. 
“We need to remove the cap so that wealthy people pay in at the same rate as working class people,” Jackson said. 
Collins said she agreed that people who make more should pay higher rates for Social Security taxes. 
She added, “I believe that we should create a commission of independent financial experts to give us advice on what should be done.”
Corruption
Accusations of corruption have become a focal point of the Senate race. They served as the first line of questioning during Thursday’s debate, though yielded repeat answers from both parties.   
Collins continued to deny her alleged involvement in a pay-for-play scheme as first reported by ProPublica. When asked what she would say to voters who believe the report raises legitimate questions about whether campaign donors receive special access or influence, Collins responded, “Well, they don’t.”
Jackson was asked about Washington Post reporting that he helped lead a PAC, the Maine Senate Democratic Leadership, that accepted money from corporations while he was president of the Maine Senate.  
Jackson said a group made the decisions about who to take money from and where it should go, not solely him. 
“When we took money from a company, it (meant) nothing that we were actually going to support a bill or get a contract,” he added, referring back to the alleged pay-for-play scheme involving Collins. 
Jackson and Collins also continued to disagree over how much Collins bucks the president. 
Jackson continued to say Collins votes with Trump 96% of the time, which is derived from a CQ Roll Call analysis from the first seven months of Trump’s second term. Meanwhile, Collins said her general party unity score is lower. 
Between the start of Trump’s second term and when senators left Washington for the campaign recess, CQ’s latest analysis has her voting in line with the president 92% of the time. Over Trump’s first and second term so far, CQ’s analysis has the senator supporting his position 90% of the time.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: On ICE, tribal rights, data centers, Charles is outlier in gubernatorial field
description: On a wide range of issues from immigration enforcement to tribal sovereignty, reproductive rights to data centers, Republican Bobby Charles was the clear outlier in the second gubernatorial debate Thursday evening. Hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and News Center Maine in front of a live audience in Bangor, the three candidates reiterated […[...]
text:
Gubernatorial candidates Bobby Charles, Hannah Pingree and Rick Bennett at their second debate in Bangor on Oct. 8, 2026. (Screenshot courtesy of Maine Public)On a wide range of issues from immigration enforcement to tribal sovereignty, reproductive rights to data centers, Republican Bobby Charles was the clear outlier in the second gubernatorial debate Thursday evening.
Hosted by the Portland Press Herald, Maine Public and News Center Maine in front of a live audience in Bangor, the three candidates reiterated some of their stances on housing, affordability and taxes, but were also asked to weigh in on social issues that have often put the state at odds with President Donald Trump’s administration.
Independent Rick Bennett and Democrat Hannah Pingree generally agreed on the need to protect Mainers from the impact of the Trump administration’s cuts to reproductive healthcare funding, aggressive immigration enforcement and tariffs that have resulted in rising costs. Charles, although selectively critical of Canadian tariffs, largely supported federal policies, instead repeatedly blaming what he called the “Mills-Pingree” administration, in reference to Pingree’s work under Gov. Janet Mills, for the range of challenges facing Mainers.
Unlike the first debate, Bennett did not criticize Charles’ positions even when they differed vastly from his own. 
All three candidates were asked about the fatal July shooting of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford as well as federal immigration enforcement that has incited fear among immigrant communities, with the vast majority of people targeted being legally present and without criminal records. 
Charles blamed the shooting on a Maine law that had not yet taken  effect for  a lapse in communication between local and federal law enforcement, and said he would repeal the new law if elected.
“I would argue that Biddeford probably wouldn’t have happened if the sanctuary state law didn’t exist here, because the comms … were sidelined,” he said. “The comms between local and state and feds would have been clear.”
Emergency calls made in the minutes after immigration agents fatally shot Durán Guerrero demonstrated a lack of communication between federal and local authorities, according to records obtained by Maine Morning Star. Federal agents only notified local law enforcement of the fatal shooting after it happened by calling the dispatch center.
Charles also said that he supported legal immigration, and said body cameras should have been worn by agents in Biddeford, but did not explain what actions he would take as governor to address heightened immigration enforcement.
Despite vow of bipartisanship, gubernatorial candidates spar in first televised debate

In contrast, Pingree and Bennett strongly criticized the Trump administration’s actions. Bennett said immigrants contribute to the state and help make it culturally rich, and criticized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement  agents targeting people based on skin color.
“I’m deeply disturbed by ICE’s presence, by the fear and harm that they actually create,” he said.
“And I’m increasingly concerned by the politicization of federal law enforcement to accomplish ends that politicians in Washington want to inflict.”
Pingree said she wants to see ICE out of Maine, which the governor has limited power to accomplish. She was also the only candidate to support taking legal action against federal agents. 
“I would work with other governors across this country and attorneys general to hold ICE accountable for their unlawful actions across this country and here in the state of Maine,” she said. 
“We will also protect people as they’re going to school, in courthouses, in hospitals. We need to do everything possible to keep people safe.”
The American Civil Liberties Union has identified Maine as one of a handful of states with laws on the books that can hold federal officers accountable. Several Maine residents, including some who were detained and later released by ICE, have used these laws to sue the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
Tribal sovereignty
Pingree and Bennett were also aligned in their support for fully restoring tribal sovereignty. Bennett referenced his record in the Legislature where he voted for bills that Mills ultimately vetoed. Pingree has frequently pointed to tribal sovereignty as the key difference between her and the current governor, which she reiterated on Thursday. She added that she expects to be endorsed by four tribal chiefs on Friday.
“I have made it a priority in my first 100 days in office, and I would work in collaboration with the tribal governments to ensure that we have a much better relationship,” she said.
“This is an issue that matters deeply to Maine people. I’ve heard about it since the beginning of my campaign, and I’m ready to get it done.”
Charles did not say whether he would support restoring sovereignty.
“The way it works in Maine is different from the way it works around the rest of the country, and I remember the original treaty,” he said. “So, the short answer is, a governor listens to the people, and that is what I will do.”
Data centers 
Charles, who has laid out a plan to lower energy costs and disagreed with Trump on certain environmental issues, said he is “agnostic” on data centers.
“I am very concerned in general about both the environment and energy, but at the end of the day, what’s good for Mainers is what I will support,” he said in response to a question about banning data centers.
Bennett and Pingree said they both supported the temporary moratorium that the Maine Legislature narrowly passed but Mills vetoed.
“I think there’s a lot of impacts that we don’t know about: noise, water usage, special effects even locally on electric rates,” Bennett said. “And so we need to go in with our eyes open.”
Pingree said she would “enact a moratorium on data center development until we have the strongest laws in the country to protect our ratepayers, to protect our environment, to ensure that communities have a say,”
“ I’ve heard loud and clear: that is what Maine people want.”
