name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Lindsay James, Joe Mitchell argue tariffs, taxes during 2nd District debate
description: Democrat Lindsay James and Republican Joe Mitchell talked tariffs and tax policy during their second debate of the 2026 election season Thursday as they compete to represent Iowa’s 2nd District in the U.S. House. The “Iowa Press” debate saw the two candidate face off for a second time on the debate stage as they compete […]
text:
Candidates for Iowa's 2nd Congressional District, Lindsay James and Joe Mitchell, take questions during a debate on Oct. 8, 2026, at Iowa PBS in Johnston. (Pool photo by Cody Scanlan/The Des Moines Register)Democrat Lindsay James and Republican Joe Mitchell talked tariffs and tax policy during their second debate of the 2026 election season Thursday as they compete to represent Iowa’s 2nd District in the U.S. House.
The “Iowa Press” debate saw the two candidate face off for a second time on the debate stage as they compete to fill the seat left by U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running as the GOP nominee for U.S. Senate. Their first debate was hosted Oct. 1 by Iowa’s News Now, where the candidates discussed issues including immigration, healthcare and data centers.
James, who represents Dubuque in the Iowa House, voted Oct. 2 in favor of a law providing nearly $1.4 billion in tax incentives for a $15 billion steel mill project planned in southeast Iowa. Lawmakers reconvened for a special session Friday to approve the measure after President Donald Trump’s announcement of the project by Mesabi Metallics.
Several Democrats — alongside some Republicans — voted against the measure, saying providing tax incentives for the company through changes to the Major Economic Growth Attraction (MEGA) program could cause the state budget problems in the future as it faces a $1.4 billion deficit, in part driven by recent income tax cuts.
James told “Iowa Press” moderators she voted for the measure because it will provide needed economic opportunities for Iowans.
“I’m hearing across the district that folks are making impossible choices because of the cost of living crisis that we are facing right now,” James said. “This crisis is because of policies directly related to what’s coming from Washington right now. The One Big, Beautiful Bill — which I would argue is only beautiful for billionaires — the war in Iran, and tariffs to name a few. These are driving up costs, and folks are really, really struggling. So when it comes to thinking about this district in particular, and this state, I’m all about lowering costs for hard-working families here in the state, but also making sure that they have economic opportunities. This is one of those economic opportunities for good-paying jobs.”
While James criticized measures like Republicans’ 2025 tax and spending law that made major tax cuts and cuts to programs like Medicaid as well as the president’s trade policies, Trump and Republicans have argued his administration’s tariff policies were the driving force for bringing the steel mill project to Iowa.
“Everyone’s building their plant here because they don’t want to pay tariffs,” Trump said. “It’s really not that complicated. A lot of people say they don’t understand it, but they do. They just don’t like to give us credit.”
James said she disagreed with this argument, saying tariffs are “driving jobs overseas.” She pointed to manufacturers like John Deere and Whirlpool, which have shifted some jobs from Iowa to Mexico in recent years.
“I stood with those workers on the picket line as they watched their jobs disappear to Mexico, all because of these impulsive and chaotic tariffs that are driving up costs and causing folks to make these impossible choices,” James said. “I would argue that these are the very policies that my opponent supports.”
Mitchell, who previously served in the Iowa Legislature, said he “absolutely” would have voted in favor of the tax incentive package if he was still a state lawmaker. He also argued it was “hypocritical” for James to say she supported the project while opposing Trump’s trade policies, which he said “directly impacted bringing that project to Iowa specifically.”
“This will be the largest economic development project in the state’s history, $15 billion invested right into eastern Iowa,” Mitchell said. “… And also, John Deere right now is adding jobs back in our district because of the president’s fair trade policies. And so, this is something I do champion, because we want to bring American jobs back to Americans. We went to reshore manufacturing jobs. We went to grow domestic manufacturing. And you can see right here, what a great example of the president bringing the steel mill right here to Iowa.”
Mitchell referenced a September announcement by John Deere, where the company stated it planned to bring “more than 375 employees back to work across its Quad Cities factory operations,” alongside bringing back or hiring more than 800 employees in Iowa and Illinois in 2026.
Mitchell and James also sparred during the debate as they countered one another’s claims about their campaign. James said, “my opponent has used my 16-year-old daughter in an attack ad against me” that was posted on social media, stating, “her face was blurred, but she was clearly identifiable.” Mitchell denied the claim and said James was lying, countering with, “you used a family photo of mine, too,” which James denied.
When Mitchell said his opponent “has not seen a tax hike she does not like,” James said his comment was “absolutely misleading.” Mitchell said his statement was made in reference to her votes against GOP-led measures cutting Iowa income tax rates and a 2026 property tax law as a state legislator. He also brought up her opposition to the OBBB Act, which he said included “no tax on Social Security, no tax on tips, no tax on overtime.”
“I support no tax on Social Security, I support no tax on tips,” James said. “You are being misleading and mischaracterizing. I’m against putting billions and trillions of dollars of tax relief to the ultra-wealthy and big corporations. That’s very clear.”
There are two other candidates in the race — independent Dave Bushaw and Libertarian Rick Stewart. Bushaw and Stewart did not meet the qualification requirements to make it on the Iowa’s News Now or “Iowa Press” debate stages.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Collins, Ossoff trade personal insults during Georgia’s first U.S. Senate debate
description: Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Congressman Mike Collins came out swinging on the debate stage Thursday night, discussing topics like the economy, healthcare and data centers in between brutal insults ahead of the November election. During an hour-long debate hosted by Atlanta News First and Atlanta-based Gray Media, Ossoff, who is facing his[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff (left) and Congressman Mike Collins participate in a debate Thursday at the Atlanta News First studio in Doraville. Photo credit: Atlanta News First/WANFDemocratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Congressman Mike Collins came out swinging on the debate stage Thursday night, discussing topics like the economy, healthcare and data centers in between brutal insults ahead of the November election.
During an hour-long debate hosted by Atlanta News First and Atlanta-based Gray Media, Ossoff, who is facing his first re-election challenge since taking office in 2021, repeatedly hammered Collins over President Donald Trump’s tariffs, the war in Iran and a series of racist and antisemitic statements made by associates.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff participated in a debate Thursday at the Atlanta News First studio in Doraville. Photo credit: Atlanta News First/WANF
“Mike Collins has brought dishonor to our state through his personal bigotry and his widely documented ties to white nationalists, and he sold out Georgia in his pathetic, childlike devotion to Donald Trump, voting for the tariffs that have sent groceries soaring, voting for the healthcare cuts that have doubled your insurance premiums and voting for the war that sent diesel to its record high,” Ossoff said.
Collins, who has represented Georgia’s 10th Congressional District in the northeastern part of the state since 2023, sought to paint Ossoff as “a trust fund kid who’s never had a job in his life” and criticised him for what he characterized as not preventing a government shutdown last year and policies he called weak on the border.
“He wanted to keep the borders wide open so that we had fentanyl coming across this border,” Collins said. “No one has ever asked or held Jon Ossoff accountable for any of his votes or the reasons why. I had to write a bill to fight these synthetic drugs because he left that border open and allowed this stuff to just funnel into our country, killing these young people.”
Ossoff is the only incumbent Democratic senator up for reelection in a state Trump won in 2024, and heading into this election cycle, Republicans viewed Georgia as a good opportunity to pick up a seat and protect their Senate majority against potential losses elsewhere.
Congressman Mike Collins participated in a debate Thursday at the Atlanta News First studio in Doraville. Photo credit: Atlanta News First/WANF
But Ossoff has maintained a steady advantage in polls and prognosticators like Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball have shifted their predictions to favor an Ossoff win. And as polling has shifted against Republicans nationwide, some in the GOP have called for resources to be moved from Georgia to other states where it could make a bigger difference. The Collins campaign denies this, pointing to million dollar-plus ad buys from Senate Republicans.
Thursday’s debate represented the candidates’ first time facing each other on the debate stage. They are set to meet again Tuesday for the Atlanta Press Club Loudermilk-Young Debate Series. Early voting also begins Tuesday.
The economy
During Thursday’s debate, the candidates were asked a series of questions by Gray Media journalists from around Georgia.
On questions of affordability, Ossoff said that if Democrats control the Senate, they will work to repeal Trump’s tariffs and end the war in Iran, which he blames for high gasoline prices.
“These tariffs are crushing our state, and we’ll repeal those tariffs, and I’d like to hear the congressman explain why he voted for them over and over and over again,” Ossoff said. “It costs more today than at any time in American history to stock your fridge, to fill up your truck, to power your home.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Collins said Trump is keeping more money in Americans’ pockets through tax cuts and defended tariffs as working to create a level playing field with nations like China.
He put the blame for rising prices on the economic policies of former President Joe Biden.
“That Bidenomics, that Green New Deal that my opponent voted for, that’s where all this inflation came from,” Collins said. “We’ve got to continue to get back to energy independence. First thing that the Biden administration and my opponent and the Democrats did was kill the Keystone Pipeline. That alone would’ve helped keep this energy cost down.”
Healthcare
Ossoff said Democrats would work to lower healthcare costs by reversing Medicaid cuts established through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff (left) and Congressman Mike Collins participate in a debate Thursday at the Atlanta News First studio in Doraville. Photo credit: Atlanta News First/WANF
“Mike Collins and Donald Trump passed the biggest Medicaid cut in history,” Ossoff said. “A hospital in Mike Collins’ own district had to shut down its labor and delivery unit, citing those Medicaid cuts. How can a sitting congressman vote to shut down a labor and delivery unit in his own district? Delivering mothers in Mike Collins’ district now have to drive an hour to get to a labor and delivery unit while they’re in labor, when we already have a maternal mortality crisis.”
Collins said the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s rural health program added $218 million as a first-year allocation to Georgia’s rural hospitals and said the culprit for rising healthcare costs is the Affordable Care Act, which was signed into law in 2010.
“The problem started way back under Obamacare, the Affordable Care Act, y’all,” he said. “I was in the private sector then. I remember that first year, my insurance going up 62%. And from that day forward, I saw our rural hospitals start to close or swap over to swing beds because they couldn’t handle the mandates that were being pushed on them. When you let the federal government take over healthcare, which is what, at the end of the day, Jon Ossoff wants to do to you, then this is what you get.”
Election security
When asked about election policy, Ossoff sought to paint Collins as an election denier 
“Georgia has voter ID, and that’s good,” Ossoff said. “Mike Collins and Donald Trump, they’re still obsessed with overturning the 2020 election. Mike Collins still believes the 2020 election was stolen. Mike Collins has supported Donald Trump’s effort to overturn the election, and he wants to give your tax dollars to the violent thugs and criminals who sacked the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6th.”
Collins has previously said he believes the 2020 election was stolen but did not address the attack from the debate stage. 
Collins criticized Ossoff for not supporting the SAVE Act, which would require that people provide proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote and show a photo ID before casting a ballot, among other provisions. The measure, which is a priority for Trump, has stalled in the Senate. 
And he attempted to paint Ossoff as a hypocrite for requiring rally attendees to show their IDs.
“We live in the best country in the world, and, and there’s no reason that we shouldn’t have the most secure elections in the world,” Collins said. “There’s no reason that you shouldn’t have to show an ID to go in and vote. My goodness, Jon Ossoff requires you to show an ID to show up at his rally, but he doesn’t think you need to do that to go vote.”
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff (left) and Congressman Mike Collins shake hands at a debate Thursday at the Atlanta News First studio in Doraville. Photo credit: Atlanta News First/WANF

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Trump is the elephant in the room during first Healey-Minogue debate
description: Voters in the deep-blue state are sometimes open to a gesture toward bipartisanship through a Republican governor that could, at least in theory, square off against a Democratic supermajority in the Legislature. But Minogue’s odds look long.
text:
AS THE TWO Massachusetts gubernatorial candidates sparred in their first debate Thursday, GOP mega-donor and former Abiomed executive Mike Minogue tried to make the back-and-forth a referendum on the Bay State’s top executive during a cost-of-living crisis.  
Gov. Maura Healey had a simpler plan: tie both her Republican challenger and the economic pain residents are feeling to President Donald Trump, a politically toxic figure to most Massachusetts voters. 
“People can’t afford gas. They can’t afford rent. They can’t afford food. They can’t afford clothes,” Healey shot at Minogue during the debate hosted by WBZ. “And this is all because of, in so many ways, Donald Trump — your guy — his failure to manage the economy.”  
Minogue, taking swings at the state’s slow rate of permitting new housing and its expensive health care, never once said the president’s name.  
“You keep blaming somebody in DC, and we know who it is,” he said. “I am Mike Minogue. I am a father. I am a husband. I am a combat veteran. I am a person who ran a business. I’m in the communities for nonprofits.” He said Healey was “name-calling me.”  
“You know what I have? I have a plan to lower costs and grow jobs,” Minogue said. 
Massachusetts’s politics are rarely friendly to Republicans seeking statewide office, with the notable exception being the corner office. Voters in the deep-blue state are sometimes open to a gesture toward bipartisanship through a Republican governor that could, at least in theory, square off against a Democratic supermajority in the Legislature. 
But Minogue’s odds look long. In late September, just 32 percent of voters said they would back Minogue, trailing Healey at 54 percent in a CommonWealth Beacon/MassINC Polling Group survey. To many, even Republicans, Minogue was still a relatively unknown quantity. About 28 percent of Republicans and Democrats said they were undecided on how they felt about Minogue.  
They are not uncertain about the leader of his party. Trump’s favorability among Bay State Republicans and those who lean Republican is strong — just over 70 percent. But for the rest of the state, the president is deep underwater, with just 4 percent of those leaning Democratic and 12 percent of independents reporting favorable views.  
Healey hammered the connection. Minogue, she pointed out repeatedly, donated $1 million toward Trump and other Republican causes in 2024. 
When Minogue took aim at the cost of housing, pledging to ease permitting and back away from enforcing the MBTA Communities housing law through the courts, Healey pointed to persistently high inflation and tariffs on construction materials because of the White House.  
Minogue said he would opt into a federal scholarship tax credit that he said could bring in $1.7 billion in grants. Healey countered that a tax credit is “not an education plan” and that the program in question was included in the “One Big Beautiful Bill” law that included more than $1 trillion in health care spending cuts. Trump also dismantled the US Department of Education, she noted. 
A first-time candidate largely self-funding his campaign in the staggeringly expensive gubernatorial race, Minogue refused to debate his Republican primary opponent, Brian Shortsleeve. For his face-off with Healey, Minogue brought a tone alternating between combative and conciliatory.  
He took swings at the controversial Springfield courthouse project, which has become a flashpoint over political connections and is estimated to cost $2 billion between construction and rent over at least 40 years. 
“Giving political insiders $2 billion to build a courthouse in Springfield is not integrity. It was a broken process,” Minogue said. Healey defended the courthouse project as saving taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars and creating thousands of jobs. 
The courthouse, one of the most high-profile controversies of the moment in part because losing bidders have launched a PR blitz criticizing the Healey administration, was not Minogue’s only line of attack. 
He brought up a Healey staffer who was accused of trafficking cocaine and erroneously paid $31,438 after he was fired. He suggested that the state should pay taxpayers back for the nearly $500,000 settlement to an employee who said Phil Eng, Healey’s hand-picked MBTA general manager, pulled her hair during a work-related event two years ago. 
Healey, in response, laid into Minogue for “questioning my integrity.”  
“People can fault me for a lot of things that I did, Mike,” the former attorney general said. “But I can tell you this: I was working every day for them. I prosecuted fraud. I prosecuted corruption. I went after scam artists. I held big companies accountable. I’ve done that throughout my career.” 
Minogue thanked her for that work. The candidates then spent minutes going back and forth over whether Healey supported last cycle’s ballot question to audit the Legislature — she did, but hasn’t weighed in on whether it was constitutional or if she will veto legislation that might look to circumvent the audit. 
The debate glanced past one of the most searing pain points for consumers: energy costs. Healey made brief reference to her recent executive order aimed at heating cost relief as the winter looms. Minogue has pledged to cut state-mandated climate utility fees and suspend the 24-cents-a-gallon tax on gas and diesel “until prices stabilize.” Healey rolled out her own two-month gas tax holiday proposal just days later, after legislative leaders publicly scorned the idea. 
Conservatives have long decried the Bay State’s reputation as “Taxachusetts,” and Minogue said he intends to lower eight different tax categories if made governor. Though Healey did not mention her own gas tax proposal, Minogue did.  
“You called for it,” he said, just before the debate cut to a commercial break. “Why has the Legislature ignored you?” 
When she wasn’t reminding viewers about Trump, Healey leaned on her record, highlighting housing accomplishments like signing a sweeping bond bill two years ago, cutting permitting times, and allowing small accessory dwelling units by right statewide. On education, she pointed to her administration’s initiatives like free community college and said Beacon Hill must revisit local school funding formulas. 
She and Minogue offered contrasting views of the state’s economic health.  
“Massachusetts is a good place to live if you can afford it,” Healey said. She noted that it has one of the fastest-growing GDPs in the country and has a strong bond rating, and has attracted expanding companies like Whoop, Gillette, and AstraZeneca.  
Minogue painted a more dire picture, accusing Healey of poor budget management and a failure to direct her attention toward state priorities.  
“I am focused on Massachusetts. I am focused on helping,” he said. “It really doesn’t matter who the president is. We are last in Massachusetts, so you own that. We’re last in jobs. We’re most expensive — health care, electricity, education, child care — that’s been the result of your four years.” 
Minogue claimed Healey was more focused on blaming Trump than advocating for the state, saying he would try to take down the political temperature and work with whoever happens to be in office, which may be a Democrat in two years. 
Healey’s constant rejoinder? The most helpful thing her opponent could do is call the president and say, “Cut it out.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Debate underlines deep divisions on what WA voters should do about income tax
description: An enclave of Washington’s wealthy provided a backdrop Thursday for a saucy debate on the merits and dangers of a ballot measure to erase the state’s controversial new income tax on millionaires. Brian Heywood, the hedge fund manager behind Initiative 645, and House Minority Leader Drew Stokesbary, R-Auburn, argued onstage at the Meydenbauer Center in […]
text:
Brian Heywood, leader of Let's Go Washington, speaks at a press conference in Tumwater, Wash. on July 2, 2026 before the group turned in signatures for Initiative 645.  (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)An enclave of Washington’s wealthy provided a backdrop Thursday for a saucy debate on the merits and dangers of a ballot measure to erase the state’s controversial new income tax on millionaires.
Brian Heywood, the hedge fund manager behind Initiative 645, and House Minority Leader Drew Stokesbary, R-Auburn, argued onstage at the Meydenbauer Center in Bellevue that the tax is unnecessary, will drive some wealthy innovators to other states and, eventually, will be levied on people earning far less than a million dollars a year.
“It’s easy to demonize the millionaires, but they provide an important role in our community. We want capital to come here and to invest in things. It’s that growth that is fueling all the great and wonderful things,” in the state, Stokesbary told hundreds of people attending the Eastside Leadership Conference hosted by the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce.
Joining them for a nearly hourlong forum were two supporters of the tax, Sen. Manka Dhingra, D-Redmond, the deputy Senate majority leader, and Soleil Boyd, executive director of the Children’s Alliance.
They defended the income tax as a necessary stride toward fixing a regressive system in which those who make the least expend a greater percentage of their earnings on taxes than the state’s wealthiest. 
Washington, by joining 41 other states with this in their tax code, is better able to deliver services and programs to a growing population, Dhingra said.
“Nice things cost money, and you cannot continue to provide all the things we love, the quality of life that we love, with the most regressive tax structure in the country,” she said. “The math does not work. That’s what 41 other states have figured out.” 
Heywood disagreed. “If the funding is not happening, it’s not because of something that happens with the repeal of an income tax,” he said. It’s because of spending decisions made by legislators, said the leader of the political committee, Let’s Go Washington.
Hours later, former Congresswoman Jaime Herrera Beutler, a supporter of the initiative, was set to debate April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, an opponent, on KING 5
What is the fight about
The income tax is a 9.9% tax on individual and household wage income above $1 million a year. The amount of income subject to tax is based on adjusted gross income reported on federal income tax returns. 
The tax was created by Senate Bill 6346, which the Legislature passed in March. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2028. The first dollars will start to arrive in 2029. The state’s chief economist estimates the income tax will generate $3.5 billion from 25,000 filers in its first year.
Only a few paragraphs in the 110-page piece of legislation actually concern the income tax. Most of the text deals with how the money will be spent.
For example, the new law eliminates sales tax on diapers, personal hygiene products like soap and toothpaste, and some over-the-counter drugs. It also will repeal sales and use taxes for retail services except advertising services and expand a tax credit program for lower-income families. All this happens in 2029 and the costs are to be covered from income tax collections.
A “yes” vote will repeal the income tax while preserving these other changes. A “no” vote will uphold the tax. Ballots go out by the end of next week for the Nov. 3 election.
Fears and loathing
The potential for the threshold to drop below $1 million is an ongoing flashpoint.
Pro-initiative forces have argued throughout the campaign that Democratic lawmakers will eventually levy the tax on households earning far less than $1 million because they will need the money. “Everybody knows it’s coming to that,” Heywood said.
In recent days, they’ve stepped up their assertions that it will decline to the point where retirees will see their pensions taxed.
Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, has vowed to veto any bill that would reduce the threshold. Democratic legislative leaders insist they have no plans to do so.
“I do not see a scenario when that threshold gets lower,” Dhingra said, adding that she would expect Heywood to run an initiative to stop it.
A few minutes later, Heywood asked those attending to raise their hand if they thought the threshold would stay at a million dollars, or higher. None did. 

“Not one single person believes the income tax is going to stay at a million dollars,” he said.
His side got a little validation recently when Shoreline Rep. Cindy Ryu, a progressive Democrat running for a Senate seat, said she could see it reset at $250,000.
“We have candidates and we have electeds. Each one has their own opinion on how they want to improve the lives of people, but the law itself has an inflator built in” to rise with inflation, Dhingra said.
A fear of the unknown underpins arguments from the other side as well.
Opponents of the initiative forecast near ruination of the state’s social safety net and its ability to care for the most in need should those tax collections not materialize. The situation is already challenging with federal support for Medicaid and a host of social services getting cut and this would make it worse.
“More people will die. More children will not have access to high quality care or education. More families will pay more of their income while prices go up and without any relief from our state,” said Boyd, of the Children’s Alliance. The initiative “is absolutely going in the wrong direction, and the reasoning behind it benefits very few people and harms pretty much everybody else.”
Heywood delivered a sharp rebuttal.
“This is the sort of the trope that gets trotted out all the time: We’re going to spend this for the children, and if you don’t spend the money on the children, if you don’t go for this tax, people are actually going to die for a tax that doesn’t even exist yet,” he said.
Washington has been a successful state and has been the launch pad for successful companies like Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon, without an income tax, and can continue to do so, he said.
Washington voters have been asked 11 times over nearly a century to approve personal or corporate income taxes. The first vote, in 1932, was successful. But a 5-4 state Supreme Court decision in 1933 struck the measure down. Later measures failed, most recently in 2010 when the income thresholds were $200,000 for individuals and $400,000 for joint filers.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: President Trump tells Minnesota to ‘fight back’ against Somali immigrants
description: President Donald Trump posted a new fulmination against Somali immigrants on his social media platform Thursday, using violent rhetoric. “The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State. The people of Minnesota must fight back,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. He […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an event at the White House on Aug. 6, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)President Donald Trump posted a new fulmination against Somali immigrants on his social media platform Thursday, using violent rhetoric.
“The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State. The people of Minnesota must fight back,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
He told Minnesotans the federal government was prepared to “come to your rescue,” calling on Gov. Tim Walz and Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey to “immediately ask for Federal help — and leave the rest to us!”

Walz addressed the post in a fundraising email from Small Town PAC, calling it an “unhinged social media tirade” meant to distract from high prices and the war with Iran.
“To our Somali neighbors: You are valued. You belong here. And we’re going to stand with you,” Walz wrote.
Trump called Walz, without evidence, “an incompetent thief.” Walz released his tax returns during his two runs for governor and run for vice president, and they showed he has few assets outside public employee pensions. Trump’s personal wealth, by contrast, has ballooned since becoming president.
Trump’s post echoes his speech to supporters on Jan. 6 before they violently stormed the Capitol in an attempt to stop the certification of the 2020 election results. He told them: “We fight like hell. And if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country anymore.”
Trump’s missive comes amid a spate of criminal cases involving Somali American residents: the ongoing fraud crisis in safety-net programs that has led to scores of convictions of Somali Americans, a string of shootings in the Twin Cities suburbs connected to gangs of Somali American youth, and, on Wednesday, the announcement of federal charges against a Somali American teenager, who is alleged to have plotted a terrorist attack on the Mall of America.
Somali Americans have faced hostility from the president since his first-term ban on immigrants from majority-Muslim countries, but it has intensified over the past year. At a cabinet meeting in December, Trump called Somalis “garbage” and said he wants them to “go back to where they came from.” More than 80% of Somali Minnesotans are American citizens and roughly 40% were born here.
Trump, citing fraud, launched the incursion of some 3,000 federal immigration agents to Minnesota that led to the killing of two Americans.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Cory Booker, Justin Murphy split on Iran war, economy during US Senate debate
description: U.S. Senate candidates Cory Booker (D) and Justin Murphy (R) split sharply on the Iran war, the economy, and other issues during a debate Thursday.
text:
Sen. Cory Booker (D), top, is seeking reelection in November against Republican challenger Justin Murphy. (Booker photo by Danielle Richards/Murphy photo by Anne-Marie Caruso)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]Democratic Sen. Cory Booker and Republican challenger Justin Murphy met Thursday evening for a cordial debate that revealed two candidates with sharply diverging views on the Iran war and the economy.
Murphy, an attorney, endorsed President Donald Trump’s decision to wage war on Iran, citing the risk of Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon and the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps’ repression and support of terrorism in the region.
“The president is right to do this, folks. We cannot continue to do this. We have to stop and think if Iran obtained a nuclear weapon — what an unbelievable, unmitigated disaster that would be. They will use it if they obtain one,” Murphy said. “We are right to do what we’re doing. Stay the course.”
Trump should put his “cowboy hat on and get out there and kick some ass and get this done,” he added.
Booker, whose cash advantage over his challenger is best measured in magnitudes, said he would push to end the war, and that military force should be reserved as a last resort used only after diplomacy fails.
The Iranian lockdown of the Strait of Hormuz prompted by the invasion aggravated the cost-of-living crisis, Booker said, likening the invasion to the nation’s past lengthy and costly engagements in the Middle East.
“This is the kind of yahoo cowboy foreign policy that has mired us in Middle Eastern war after Middle Eastern war. With false bravado, we are saying we’re just going to go in there and kick ass,” Booker said. “You know what that’s done to the treasury of our country? $8 trillion spent in foreign wars in the Middle East, and none of them have ended well.”
Booker is seeking his third full term in the U.S. Senate next month. Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term.
The candidates also clashed about the U.S. economy.
The Iran war and Trump’s tariffs have foisted thousands of dollars in new costs on New Jerseyans, Booker said.
“Costs across the board have gone up, as I said, between $4,000 and $5,000 for the average family, but for other families, they see their healthcare costs go up and skyrocket. For those small businesses that rely on costs being down for fuel, they’re paying higher and higher prices,” Booker said.
Justin Murphy (R) is hoping to oust Sen. Cory Booker (D) next month. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Murphy, a U.S. Navy veteran, praised Trump’s handling of the economy, noting our poverty rate declined to 10.2% last year, the lowest level since the Census Bureau began tracking the statistic in 1959. The declines also brought child poverty to historic lows.
“I’m proud that the Republican Party is worried about the next generation of Americans, to know that they will have the American dream — expanding economy, a manufacturing resurgence, falling interest rates,” Murphy said. “We have the highest median household income now in American history and the lowest poverty rate and the lowest child poverty rate in our country’s history.”
The nation had about 41,000 fewer manufacturing jobs last month than in December 2024, according to Federal Reserve data, which in September unanimously raised interest rates for the first time in three years and signaled more rate hikes were likely before the end of the year.
Both candidates said they want new limits on tech giants who’ve seen their influence balloon amid the artificial intelligence race and broad adoption of social media.
Murphy said he wants to limit the private companies’ ability to control speech on their platforms, calling it a First Amendment issue. He also objected to term limits, arguing elections are a sufficient check.
“You should never have term limits. I oppose them because the American people are the term limit,” Murphy said.
Neither candidate pledged to back their own party’s current Senate leadership. Both said they would discuss the matter with other members if elected.
Sen. Cory Booker (D) is seeking his third full term in the U.S. Senate next month. (Photo by Amanda Brown/New Jersey Monitor)
In an unusual turn, the debate hosted by the New Jersey Globe at Rider University saw both candidates largely eschew attacks on the other in favor of stating their political beliefs, though Veronica Fernandez, an independent candidate who failed to meet debate qualification thresholds, made a brief outburst from the audience before police escorted her out.
At the debate’s outset, Murphy acknowledged the long odds he faces on the path to win the U.S. Senate. New Jersey has not elected a Republican to the upper chamber since 1972, and this year’s political environment is viewed broadly as unfavorable to Republicans.
The two candidates fully agreed on one thing: Murphy has the better hair.
“I’ll stipulate at the beginning: I’m jealous of his hair,” Booke said at the debate’s outset.
“Let’s get this out of the way now: No hair jokes tonight. I’ve got to put up with enough of them,” Murphy said.
The night saw about half a dozen hair jokes overall.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont faces criticism over ‘cozy’ relationship with Eversource CEO
description: CEO Joe Nolan's comments to investors, and published texts between the two leaders, have undercut the governor's tough stance on the utility.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont’s relationship with top utility officials has attracted growing scrutiny this week as he nears the final stretch of a reelection campaign in which the cost of energy has taken center stage.
In campaign ads blanketing prime-time television, Lamont has touted his administration’s efforts to lower electricity bills by hundreds of dollars a year and enact “tough reforms to take on Eversource,” the state’s largest utility. In May, he publicly lambasted Eversource chief executive Joe Nolan’s eight-figure salary in response to the utility’s request for a new rate hike starting next year.
But Lamont’s message has been undercut in recent days by comments Nolan made to a group of investors downplaying criticisms from politicians and describing his relationship with New England governors, including Lamont, as friendly. 
Then on Thursday, CT Insider published text messages between Lamont and Nolan in which the latter repeatedly urged the governor to “intervene” in the company’s dispute with Connecticut regulators over $1 billion in unpaid storm costs.
Lamont’s opponent in the governor’s race, state Sen. Ryan Fazio, R-Greenwich, siezed on those comments and accused the governor of having a “cozy” relationship with Eversource’s CEO.
Fazio stopped short of accusing Lamont of wrongdoing. However, he noted that in the same call with investors, Nolan said Eversource’s financial outlook had been buoyed by the resolution of the storm costs issue and the recent sale of its water utility, Aquarion, for $2.4 billion — both of which required approval from the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, whose members were appointed by Lamont.
“It’s not just the text messages which were overly familiar,” Fazio said. “It was also Nolan bragging to his investors that he’s friends with Lamont, and that the [governor’s] criticism of the company is just kind of insincere and campaign related, and that [Nolan] has been very happy with the resolution of both storm costs and the sale of Aquarion, both which required the active support the active support from the governor to to happen.”
In an interview with The Connecticut Mirror, Lamont defended his contacts with utility officials as part of the job of governor and said that he never felt compelled to act on their behalf. 
He also chalked up Nolan’s comments last week to investors as “telling them what they want to hear.”
“I have a civil relationship with people, that’s what I do, and that includes, you know, leaders of the utilities,” Lamont said. “That does not mean we compromise fighting for our consumers every day.”
Lamont also said his administration has taken effective steps to rein in utility costs with bipartisan regulatory reforms and investments in nuclear and renewable energy sources. Connecticut’s electric rates fell by more than 10% over the last year, and the state now has better rates per kilowatt hour than its neighbors.
“Every single governor in the United States of America has to have a constructive relationship with the utilities that serve customers, who are also taxpayers,” said Max Reiss, a spokesman for Eversource. 
Reiss declined to make Nolan available for an interview Thursday to clarify the CEO’s remarks. 
‘Please Intervene’
For the last several years, Eversource has been engaged in a protracted dispute with PURA regarding its efforts to collect nearly $1 billion in costs the company says it spent responding to a series of “catastrophic” storms between 2018 and 2023. Last June, the company suffered a credit rating downgrade, based in part on what analysts described as a poor regulatory environment and delays in recovering storm costs.
That same month, Nolan reached out to Lamont with an urgent plea, according to copies of text messages published by CT Insider. 
“please don’t leave town until we have a deal on storms. pressure is extraordinary with downgrades,” from credit rating agencies, Nolan’s text read.  
CT Mirror sought access through the state’s Freedom of Information Act to those messages, as well as other communications between Lamont and Eversource officials on Thursday. The governor’s office has yet to turn over the records.
There was no indication in the text messages published by CT Insider that Lamont took any actions bowing to the pressure from Nolan to intervene in the storm costs case. In his response to Nolan, Lamont wrote that he had spoken with Consumer Counsel Claire Coleman — who leads the state agency responsible for representing utility customers before PURA — and had been told that her office was waiting on “a few documents” and “very serious proposal” from Eversource.
Coleman’s office never reached a settlement with Eversource in the storm costs case. 
Instead, the case ended up going before PURA which issued its final decision this July allowing Eversource to recover $861 million in deferred storm costs — more than 90% of the company’s request — but rejecting the company’s request to collect nearly $400 million in interest on those costs. (Coleman’s office was among those who objected to the request.)
In an interview Thursday, Coleman said that she had conversations with the governor’s office, the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection and Eversource throughout the years-long debate over storm costs. She said she felt her views, and the independence of her office, were respected throughout those talks.
“I never felt in any of those conversations that I was being pressured to do something that was against the interests of customers,” Coleman said. 
In the string of text messages published Thursday, Nolan then went one step further, offering to “hire Jonny,” a reference to former Lamont chief of staff Jonathan Dach, to “bang this out.”
Dach was part of Lamont’s team that worked on energy policy, specifically a wide-ranging set of utility reforms, Senate Bill 4, that the governor signed into law that summer. The bill included a provision allowing Eversource to securitize its storm costs through long-term borrowing, in order to lessen the bill impact on customers. Fazio, who is the ranking Republican on the Energy and Technology Committee, was also a negotiator on the bill, which he ultimately supported.
Nolan’s idea was to have Dach — who left state government that June amid scrutiny into his misuse of a state vehicle — work as a “independent mediator” to come up with a binding resolution for the storm costs dispute, according to Reiss. While the position would have been funded by Eversource, it would have been outside the company, Reiss said. In any event, Dach never applied for or received a formal offer for the position.
“During early discussions surrounding a settlement of storm costs, the concept of an independent mediator was raised and Jonny Dach, an attorney with policy and energy expertise, was considered as an option,” Reiss said in a statement. “In the end, this path did not materialize.”
In February, Dach joined the staff at Concourse, a tech startup in New York City that builds software for government agencies. 
“I appreciate Gov. Lamont and Joe Nolan’s confidence that I could successfully mediate discussions between Eversource and the state parties, like OCC and DEEP, to any potential settlement,” Dach said in a statement Thursday. “But we never seriously discussed the role described in those text messages.”
Dach would not have been the first former official in Lamont’s office to go to work for Eversource. Reiss, the company spokesman, previously served as Lamont’s communications director. Jonathan Harris and Leslie O’Brien, who both work in government affairs for Eversource, also worked as aides to Lamont. 
State ethics rules prohibit former executive branch employees from representing anyone other than the state in any matter in which they “participated personally and substantially while in state service.” The rules also include a “cooling off period” that bars ex-employees from lobbying directly with their former agency for at least one year after leaving state service.
Lamont said Thursday that he was not involved in any discussions about hiring Dach as a mediator in the storm costs dispute. He added that he was not surprised that companies like Eversource hire his former staffers and said those prior relationships do not impact his decision making.
“I don’t think there’s anything nefarious about that,” Lamont said. “You tend to hire people who used to be in government who have a lot of relationships.”
But Tom Swan, the executive director of the Connecticut Citizen Action Group, said that the text messages and Eversource’s repeated hiring of former administration officials raises ethical concerns. Earlier this year, Swan wrote an op-ed calling for a complete ban on the “revolving door” of legislators and executive branch employees going to work for utilities and PURA.
“What I think was the most appalling is the fact that the company is so arrogant and so used to just hiring political insiders to get their way that Nolan would put that type of a question on the table,” Swan said.
‘Nothing personal’
The release of text messages between Nolan and Lamont came on the heels of another controversy involving remarks the Eversource CEO delivered to a group of investors on Sept. 30.
During his presentation, Nolan was asked to opine on the upcoming gubernatorial races in Connecticut, Massachusetts and New Hampshire — the three states where Eversource operates — and what they mean for the company’s outlook.
Nolan began by saying he had little doubt that the incumbents in each of those races would win by large margins. He went on to say that Eversource has good relationships with “all of them” and that their occassional public criticisms were driven by political necessity. 
“If had $1 for every time they’d say, “Hey, nothing personal, Joe, you know you’re our friend,'” Nolan said. “But they have to do that. Obviously, they’re getting attacked, utility issues are front and center, rates are front and center. But all that noise, in 37 days, you’re going to see the volume is going to go right down, and you won’t you won’t hear much of that.”
Lamont said Thursday that while he and Nolan have “grudging respect” for one another, the company’s actions tell a different story than the one presented by Nolan.
“You think Eversource thinks we’ve been too easy on them?” Lamont said. “I mean, anybody really think that? I think we’ve been tougher on utilities and held them accountable — performance-based regulation and pushing back — and that’s one of the reasons they were very reluctant to bring a [storm costs case to PURA] in the first place.”
Nolan made another remark later in the call that drew an outcry from Democrats and Republicans alike.
Asked about the company’s plans to invest money in Connecticut, Nolan said the company “shut the faucet off” in the state due to its dispute over storm costs. “Until we get paid the storm costs, we weren’t going to put another dime down there,” he said.
That sentiment wasn’t new.
In 2024, Nolan announced that Eversource would be cutting $500 million worth of investments in Connecticut over the subsequent five years due to delays in the storm costs case and other conflicts that the utility was having with then-PURA Chair Marissa Gillett, who had been appointed by Lamont. Those disputes culminated in a series of lawsuits and Gillett’s resignation late last year.
Since then, Lamont has appointed four new commissioners to PURA, who Nolan expressed optimism about working with during next year’s rate case. “Everybody in the space is a professional,” he said.
Reiss said Thursday that Nolan’s remarks to investors were being cast in a negative light due to the upcoming election.
“In a political season, it is more important than ever to get the story right, and the story Joe Nolan is telling about Connecticut to Wall Street is that the environment for investment is improving every day in Connecticut, which is important for customers, policymakers, and communities across the state,” Reiss said in a statement. “Investors turned their back on Connecticut for years, and now Joe is providing the update for investors that things have improved.”
Fazio said Nolan’s remarks were sign Eversource is getting what it wants from the Lamont administration, specifically with regard to policies such as the rollout of advanced metering technology and the Aquarion sale Fazio and other Republican lawmakers opposed. (Fazio, who voted to to confirm each of Lamont’s most recent nominees to PURA, said it is “too early to judge,” their performance.)
In his interview with CT Mirror Thursday, Lamont also said Fazio was playing up the controversy for political gain. “He was a ranking member on [the] Energy and Technology [Committee], he knew all the players,” Lamont said.
Fazio said he has never met Nolan or spoken to him by phone. He said he has met with other Eversource executives, as well as United Illuminating President Frank Reynolds.
“We don’t text or anything like that,” Fazio said. “Sometimes with many companies, I meet with them in my capacity as a state senator, but don’t have a close relationship at all with them.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland fines developer for more Gunpowder tributary pollution
description: Months after reaching a record settlement over mud pollution from a Harford County housing project, state environmental regulators have fined the developer another $24,000 for continuing to foul a Gunpowder River tributary.
text:
Riverkeeper Theaux Le Gardeur records water quality measurements for a pond off Days Cove along Maryland’s Gunpowder River. (Photo by Timothy B. Wheeler/Chesapeake Bay Journal)By Timothy B. Wheeler
The Chesapeake Bay Journal
Months after reaching a record settlement over mud pollution from a Harford County housing project, state environmental regulators have fined the developer another $24,000 for continuing to foul a Gunpowder River tributary.
The Maryland Department of the Environment levied penalties of $6,000 each for four occasions this past spring and summer when inspectors found that sediment from the Ridgely’s Reserve development had washed offsite into local streams.
On May 19, MDE announced that Texas-based homebuilder DR Horton, its development subsidiary Forestar USA Real Estate Group and a Pennsylvania building contractor agreed to pay $4.1 million to settle a lawsuit brought by the state and the nonprofit Gunpowder Riverkeeper.
That deal came in answer to more than four years of complaints from area residents about chronic muddy runoff from the 121-acre housing development in Joppa. Almost whenever rain fell, Foster Branch and the tidal Gunpowder basin turned murky shades of orange and brown. The lower Gunpowder lost much of its underwater grasses, critical habitat for fish and crabs.
The $2 million civil penalty in the settlement was the largest ever in Maryland for runoff pollution from a construction site, according to MDE. The other $2.1 million paid by the developers is to be used for “community-driven” remediation projects to restore aquatic habitat in Foster Branch and the Gunpowder.
Under the terms of the court-approved consent decree, the companies agreed to pay penalties ranging from $1,000 to $6,000 for any future violations of their permits to build 388 homes at Ridgely’s Reserve.
Maryland reaches $4.1M settlement with homebuilder in sediment pollution case

In a Sept. 10 letter, MDE wrote that state and county inspectors found  sediment and erosion control violations in late May, July and August. MDE assessed the latest penalties against Forestar alone, though, and just for illegal discharges of sediment into the streams feeding into Foster Branch.
Forestar did not respond to an emailed request for comment.
MDE’s inspection reports list other violations, including instances of eroding soil, exposed soil vulnerable to washing off in a rainstorm, and improperly installed “silt fences’’ meant to keep mud from running off the site.
Aimena Lipscomb, an MDE spokesperson, acknowledged that the inspection reports documented other permit violations. But she said the consent decree signed by the developers gave them seven days to correct those violations before penalties would apply.
“MDE has no evidence that those violations remained uncorrected for more than 7 days,” she said by email.
The decree specified that Forestar would have to pay $6,000, though, for each day of unlawful sediment discharges to Foster Branch or the Gunpowder. MDE did not conduct daily inspections, so that might explain why each discharge identified yielded only one $6,000 penalty.
But in at least one case, MDE had documentary evidence that mud from an illegal discharge was either continuing or not immediately cleaned up. Forestar wrote to MDE that it had “mucked out” the sediment-clogged stream bed two days after MDE’s inspection and again six days after the cited violation. The MDE spokesperson did not respond to a request to explain its reasoning in that case.
Theaux Le Gardeur, the Gunpowder Riverkeeper said he and the group’s lawyer want to meet with MDE officials to understand their rationale for not imposing more penalties.
Meanwhile, he and some area residents suggested Harford County could and should do more to crack down on any continuing problems at the development. The county did levy a total of $45,000 fines from 2023 until January 2026 and then got the developer to agree to even more stringent runoff controls than previously required.
Through the summer, county inspectors visited the construction site weekly and after heavy storms. They issued a series of stop-work orders and “correction notices” for multiple infractions, many of them similar to those cited by MDE. The county has since begun making daily inspections, according to a recent county report shared with residents. A county spokesman said in August that based on violations found then, officials were considering revoking permits.
Le Gardeur contended that the settlement does not preclude Harford from levying its own fines and penalties. While penalties assessed by the state go into a statewide clean water fund, he suggested that any fines the county collects could help pay for closer monitoring of the development and for restoring Foster Branch and the impacted habitat of the lower Gunpowder.
“I am concerned about the cumulative impacts on the environment and community of the site being out of compliance for over 4 1/2 years,” he said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland’s energy affordability crisis is a crisis of leadership
description: Maryland lawmakers are learning how hard it is to control utility rates, writes Randy Altschuler, who says they should instead focus on increasing power generation in the state, and insist that funds intended for energy programs be spent on energy programs.
text:
If they want to rein in utility rates, writes Randy Altschuler, Maryland leaders should focus on increasing power generation in the state, and insist that funds intended for energy programs be spent on energy programs. (Photo illustration by Danielle E. Gaines/Stock.adobe.com images from esbobeldijk, martin33, and vasanth)A recent Maryland Matters article on rising utility rates included an important acknowledgment from Annapolis: Despite passage of the Utility RELIEF Act earlier this year, lawmakers know their “work is still not done.”
Maryland cannot control every force pushing energy prices higher: global conflicts, regional energy markets, growing demand, transmission costs and other factors all play a role. That makes it even more important for state leaders to address the costs and policies they can control. Unfortunately, they are making matters worse and as a result Marylanders now pay the third-highest residential electricity prices in the nation.
Maryland needs more affordable, reliable electricity generation. For years, state leaders have increased renewable-energy requirements without creating the business or regulatory environment that would enable Maryland suppliers to meet those needs. As a result, residential electricity prices increased nearly 40% between January 2023 and June 2026, one of the largest increases nationally and the highest among our neighboring states.
One of the clearest warning signs that Maryland’s existing policy is out of balance can be found in a little-known state fund called the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, or SEIF.
Maryland requires electricity suppliers to obtain increasing amounts of qualifying renewable energy. When there are not enough qualifying renewable energy credits available to satisfy those requirements, suppliers have to make Alternative Compliance Payments (ACPs) instead. The cost for those ACPs flow directly down to the Maryland ratepayer through increased electricity rates.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




These compliance payments go into SEIF, which was created to support energy efficiency, renewable energy generation and relief for Maryland ratepayers. Since it was created in 2008, SEIF payments have skyrocketed: In 2022, they totaled $86.6 million, and two years later, they had more than quadrupled to $362.3 million. State budget officials estimate another $336.9 million in both fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027.
Nobody would look at a compliance cost quadrupling in two years and conclude everything is working as intended.
It is a warning light on the dashboard.
In fact, the Department of Legislative Services says these payments are expected to remain elevated unless additional qualifying renewable capacity comes online to meet Maryland’s renewable requirements.
Despite the warnings, Annapolis continues to fail to address the underlying issues. To make matters even worse, they are using the SEIF funds to provide what state budget analysts themselves describe as “budget relief.” Over the last two years, more than $500 million has been diverted from SEIF to fund budget deficits, not renewable energy or ratepayer relief.
What has happened to the SEIF illustrates the underlying problem – the lack of a coherent, realistic and affordable energy policy.
We deserve better and it begins with two straightforward principles.
First, we need to move aggressively to increase affordable and reliable power generation here in Maryland. That means a truly all-of-the-above strategy that recognizes the role of renewables, and other technologies capable of providing the electricity Maryland needs. Requirements to use renewables should mirror the amount of additional renewable energy that is coming online.
Second, the money generated through energy policies should remain focused on solving Maryland’s energy problems. If ratepayers ultimately bear the costs created by these programs, those resources should be used to increase in-state power generation, improve reliability and reduce the burden on ratepayers, not provide a convenient source of money for leaders in Annapolis to use for unrelated state spending.
As the founder of my own company, I learned that if costs keep rising and your strategy doesn’t produce the intended result, you have to quickly change course.
Maryland cannot control global energy markets or every decision made by regional grid operators. But Annapolis can control Maryland’s energy mandates and Maryland’s energy policies.
That is where leadership begins.
Marylanders need leaders willing to solve our affordability crisis by confronting the costs we can control, increasing affordable and reliable energy supply, and putting ratepayers first.
Until then, Maryland’s energy affordability crisis will remain exactly what it is: a crisis of leadership.
