name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Today summit centers on learning in the classroom and on the job
description: Panelists discuss literacy during the "All In On Mississippi" summit at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Local and national changemakers joined Mississippi Today staff in Jackson to examine how to best build on Mississippi’s gains in education and workforce development.
The discussions were part of Mississippi Today’s “All In On Mississippi” summit, which commemorated the publication’s 10-year anniversary. The event attracted hundreds of attendees to the state’s capital to learn more from the people behind the headlines.
Mississippi miracle? More like marathon
The state’s upward climb from the bottom of the nation when it came to fourth and eighth grade reading proficiency emerged after years of work. Beyond introducing more phonics-based instruction into classrooms, the state’s recent educational outcomes also leaned into accountability.
Rachel Canter, the founder and former executive director of Mississippi First, said many states only want to implement the “feel-good” aspects of Mississippi’s literacy plan, such as training teachers on phonics-based instruction, while doing less to hold districts accountable for poor outcomes for students.
“Change starts with honesty,” Canter,  who now directs policy for the Reinventing America’s Schools project at the Progressive Policy Institute, told a crowd at the Two Mississippi Museums. “But we all have to take responsibility for our role in the system when the system is broken. And what Mississippi did right is think about that whole agenda.”
Rachel Canter, director of education policy for the Reinventing America’s Schools project at PPI, discusses literacy in Mississippi during the “All In On Mississippi” summit at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
A large part of that agenda was outlined in the Literacy Based Promotion Act, a 2013 state law that mandated that third graders who do not pass the state reading test must be held back. The act also mandated early screenings for students to identify reading challenges. The Legislature also agreed to pay for literacy coaches to train teachers on more phonics-based instruction. 
As a high school teacher in Mississippi in the early 2000s, Kymyona Burk, a policy analyst at ExcelinEd, said she noticed students were nearing graduation with gaps in their reading ability. She realized that socially promoting students set them up for failure. 
Kymyona Burk, senior policy fellow at ExcelinEd, discusses literacy in Mississippi during the “All In On Mississippi” summit at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Burk later led the Literacy Based Promotion Act’s implementation as state literacy director in the Mississippi Department of Education. She found part of her job required changing the way local district employees perceived the department. In her own experience as a teacher, state employee visits were not welcome. 
“There are so many who are not a fan of the top-down approach, but that is what we had to do in Mississippi to get everyone rolling in the right direction,” said Burk. “I think now we’ve met in the middle, and we understand what we need to do as partners to get things done.”
Expanding apprenticeships to keep opportunities in Mississippi
A challenge for Mississippi is losing the investment in early education when graduates move out of state for jobs. Between 2010 and 2024, roughly 80,000 more residents left the state than moved in, continuing what many experts have labeled a brain drain. 
At 55%, Mississippi consistently records one of the lowest workforce participation rates in the country. But state-sponsored training programs have been growing, and will play a vital role in the future of economic development, speakers said during a panel on apprenticeship programs. 
In August, Gov. Tate Reeves appointed Daniel “Deano” Harrison to direct the Mississippi Office Of Apprenticeship. Reeves has said he created the office with the long-term goal of doubling the number of apprenticeships statewide to about 7,000. 
Daniel “Deano” Harrison, director of ApprenticeshipMS, discusses apprenticeship programs during the “All In On Mississippi” summit at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
At the summit, an audience member asked Harrison if the office would launch an apprenticeship pipeline for youths coming out of juvenile detention. Harrison said no population is off-limits. 
“We need to go into every nook and cranny and grab anybody we can,” he said. 
The state’s first medical apprenticeship program started at Singing River Hospital System on the Gulf Coast. Stephanie Utesch, the system’s human resources operations director, helps run what she called an “earn-while-you-learn” campus in Ocean Springs that has graduated over 600 apprentices since it launched. 
The program started small. In 2021, Utesch recalled during the panel, she walked into an empty clinic and said: “Where’s the chairs? Where’s the tables?”
Stephanie Utesch, human resources operations director for Singing River Health System, discusses apprenticeship programs during the “All In On Mississippi” summit at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Since then, the program has grown and many of its students have thrived, Utesch said. She recalled a single mother caring for her mother and daughter while apprenticing. The single mother is on track to become a licensed practical nurse with no debt, Utesch said. Another registered nurse who is nearing retirement but doesn’t want to give up work has been taking coding classes through the program, Utesch said. Her goal is to switch to a remote schedule, she said, giving her greater flexibility while still working. 
Singing River’s apprenticeship program is a success story, Harrison said, and he encouraged employers statewide to consider starting their own programs. 
“When Mississippians leave Mississippi, we do great things,” Harrison said. “But let’s give them the opportunity to do great things in Mississippi.”
These conversations about educational outcomes and expanding apprenticeship programs folded into a broader discussion about the economic wellbeing of Mississippi during the “All In on Mississippi” summit, an event hosted by Mississippi Today featuring conversations about the forces shaping Mississippi’s future. The summit event is the second of a two-day event celebrating Mississippi Today’s first decade of reporting.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland People’s Counsel will have to compete to keep his job
description: Maryland People's Counsel David Lapp, the state’s ratepayer advocate in utility regulatory cases, will have to reapply for his job after Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown posted the position. Brown says it's nothing personal just the recommended process.
text:
Maryland People's Counsel David Lapp speaks at a news conference in February 2025 alongside Attorney General Anthony Brown. (Photo courtesy the Office of Baltimore City Council President Zeke Cohen)Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown is considering new candidates for the role of people’s counsel — the state’s top advocate for ratepayers in regulatory proceedings concerning utility companies.
The current People’s Counsel, David Lapp, who has served in the role since early 2021, says he wants to stay in the role, after his initial five-year term concluded in June.
But the attorney general’s office, which appoints the people’s counsel, posted a job opening on its website nonetheless. In a statement, a spokesperson for Brown said it’s nothing personal — and Lapp will be considered for reappointment.
“This practice should not be viewed as a reflection on David Lapp’s performance. Rather, it is a fair and equitable process that allows for the broadest possible pool of qualified candidates,” said Jennifer Donelan, a spokesperson for Brown, in a statement.
During his tenure, Lapp has been an outspoken voice, often criticizing utility companies for what he considers overspending on gas and electric infrastructure, which has driven up ratepayer bills.
Lapp, who is an attorney, has long expressed concerns about excessive extensions and upgrades to the state’s natural gas pipelines, which he believes could become sunk costs and burden an increasingly small pool of customers as the state looks toward electrification. He has been staunchly opposed to Maryland consumers paying the cost of any electricity infrastructure build-out needed for hyperscale data centers.
Six years ago, Maryland changed how some electric rates are set. It went poorly, officials say.

In a statement, Lapp wrote that “it has been an honor and privilege to serve Maryland’s residential utility customers as People’s Counsel. I am applying for the position, and it would be an honor and privilege to continue serving in the role.”
Maryland law allows Lapp, who was appointed by former Attorney General Brian Frosh, to stay in his role after the expiration of his five-year term “until a successor is appointed and qualifies.” A competitive reappointment process isn’t required. And Lapp’s predecessor held the job for 14 years before her retirement.
But Brown “fill[s] the vast majority of positions through open, competitive recruitment,” Donelan wrote. The job posting closes Oct. 13.
“This is Attorney General Brown’s first opportunity to consider this important appointment and he owes it to the people of Maryland to recommend to the Senate the best qualified person for the Office of People’s Counsel,” Donelan wrote.
Before his time as People’s Counsel, Lapp was an assistant Maryland attorney general from 2004 to 2020. During that time, he was chief counsel of the office’s tobacco enforcement unit, which litigated against tobacco companies and managed the large multistate settlement that resulted. He also later served as deputy counsel to the Maryland Department of Health.
If he is reappointed by Brown, Lapp will have to be confirmed by the Senate — where he has faced some sharp words recently from Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City), who took issue with a transmission project in his district and the OPC’s handling of a legal loophole affecting the project.
But Lapp has the backing of House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and  Anne Arundel) and a large group of House Democrats. More than 70 delegates signed a letter to Brown in “strong support” of Lapp continuing in the role.
“Not only has Mr. Lapp increased the workload of the Office on behalf of utility customers, he has transformed the Office from a largely reactive agency to one that now routinely initiates matters before regulatory agencies,” reads the letter.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The letter states that Lapp’s office has had more success before regulatory bodies as well. In fiscal year 2025, the office participated in 226 cases and achieved 149 favorable decisions, compared to 200 cases and 94 favorable decisions in fiscal year 2020, before he arrived. That’s an increase in the success rate from 47% to 66%.
Utility companies have publicly sparred with Lapp’s office at times. After Lapp’s office filed a petition calling for an expanded investigation into Baltimore Gas & Electric’s safety inspections, after an inspector was found to be falsifying reports, for example, a BGE spokesperson criticized Lapp.
“OPC, in yet another in a long line of bombastic press releases meant to support its relentless effort to eliminate customers’ ability to use natural gas, is trying to improperly sway the determination of the public utility law judge overseeing this matter,” a BGE spokesman told Baltimore television station Fox45 in March.
In the past, Brown has supported Lapp on the issue of gas pipeline spending. In December 2024, the two co-wrote a Baltimore Sun editorial, in which they called for reforms to Maryland’s STRIDE law, which lets gas utilities recover the costs of pipeline improvements in advance of performing the work. The two appeared together during a February 2025 news conference on the issue.
Del. Marc Korman (D-Montgomery), who chairs the House Environment and Transportation Committee, was a leading signatory on the letter supporting Lapp.
“I appreciate that the AG has to run this process,” Korman said. “I hope that as part of that process, he sees what a great job David Lapp is doing, and chooses to reappoint him.”
Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery), who also signed the delegates’ letter, said she has spent “countless hours” with Lapp and his staff, including nights and weekends, poring over energy policy to try to make improvements that help ratepayers.
She praised Lapp’s work not only interrogating rate increase requests at Maryland’s Public Service Commission, but challenging the underlying policies at the regional grid level that are “rigged against everyday people.”



Quotation







I appreciate that the AG (attorney general) has to run this process. I hope that as part of that process, he sees what a great job David Lapp is doing, and chooses to reappoint him.


– Del. Marc Korman (D-Montgomery), one of more than 70 House members who signed a letter urging Lapp's reappointment


“In my mind, there’s so many levels at which the work he’s doing is helping Maryland ratepayers at the short term, medium term, long term,” Charkoudian said. “When you start to comprehend the fullness of it, you’re like: ‘Wow, we are so lucky in Maryland.'”
She commended Lapp for his work on the extension for Maryland coal plant Brandon Shores. Lapp argued that the plant’s owner was over-inflating the costs it would take to keep the plant running, which consumers must bear. But he also fought the fact that the power the coal plant was not counted in a critical energy auction, driving up costs for consumers across the region by an estimated $5 billion. After Lapp’s advocacy, the regional grid operator changed the policy. He also made a filing urging regulators to return the $5 billion to consumers.
“PJM was like: ‘These are the rules. Too bad.’ And he was like: ‘Let me fight the rules,'” Charkoudian said.
Consumer advocacy group Maryland PIRG highlighted Lapp’s role in winning a significant $1.1 million civil penalty against Washington Gas for customer service issues. That came in 2022, following a 2021 complaint from the Office of People’s Counsel.
“In his time as People’s Counsel, David Lapp has been a powerful and effective voice for energy customers working to stop wasteful utility spending and anti-consumer decisions that drive up our bill,” wrote Maryland PIRG senior adviser Emily Scarr. “He is recognized as an effective consumer advocate not only in Maryland, but nationwide.”
But during the most recent legislative session, Ferguson blamed Lapp for not drawing enough attention to a legal loophole involving underground transmission lines.
Maryland officials say changes to electric grid governance aren’t enough

But Lapp’s office had repeatedly raised the issue starting as soon as 2023, including in news releases and filings to state and federal regulators — highlighted the fact that, because the projects receive fewer layers of review, costs could soar.
At the time, Ferguson was speaking out against an underground power line proposed for his district, in the historic Otterbein neighborhood. It was planned to route power to Baltimore Peninsula, even amid flagging development there.
Local projects like the one proposed for Otterbein are considered “supplemental transmission projects,” and officials at the regional transmission grid, PJM Interconnection, don’t conduct competitive bids — unlike with larger regional transmission projects.
Instead, the utilities select the projects and PJM conducts a “do no harm” review. Their cost-effectiveness can only really be challenged at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission — after the projects are built.
In addition, Maryland regulators only conducted site reviews for overhead transmission lines, further reducing the scrutiny they receive. With key support from Ferguson, the state legislature passed a measure bringing underground lines before Maryland regulators for a siting review for the very first time.
“Frankly, I’m incredibly disappointed in the Office of People’s Counsel, who is charged with protecting ratepayers,” Ferguson said in February. “How this has not been flagged in the past is really unbelievable to me.”
In March, Lapp’s office released a detailed study it had commissioned in 2025, which determined that the costs of supplemental projects were rapidly increasing. The report indicated Maryland customers paid $2.8 billion for supplemental transmission from 2010 to 2030 — and could pay an estimated $2.2 billion more between 2031 and 2035.
“These local projects have been a high priority of our office, and we are encouraged that the legislature is giving it specific attention,” Lapp wrote in a March letter to committee leaders in the General Assembly, citing his years of advocacy work on the issue.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Revenue Department clarifies local sales tax distribution responsibility
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska Department of Revenue has confirmed it is the entity responsible for administering state and local sales taxes under state law as a state senator alleges wrongdoing by Lincoln city officials. The state agency made the clarification Thursday in response to questions from the Nebraska Examiner. Local taxes are determined by some municipa[...]
text:
Nebraska Tax Commissioner Jim Kamm, who leads the Nebraska Department of Revenue, at an inaugural public roundtable of Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen's cabinet. April 20, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Department of Revenue has confirmed it is the entity responsible for administering state and local sales taxes under state law as a state senator alleges wrongdoing by Lincoln city officials.
The state agency made the clarification Thursday in response to questions from the Nebraska Examiner. Local taxes are determined by some municipalities and a couple of counties, up to 2 cents per dollar. State sales taxes are set by the Legislature, currently at a 5.5-cent rate.
“Retailers collect and remit city sales tax to the DOR,” the statement read. “The DOR in turn remits the sales tax to the city minus any applicable refunds. The DOR does not itself collect sales and use taxes. It is the responsibility of the retailer to collect the appropriate tax.”
State senator accuses Lincoln of improperly taxing non-city residents, demands refunds

State Sen. Beau Ballard of Lincoln blasted Lincoln officials this week after he said constituents alerted him that they were being taxed 7.25% for purchases made outside city limits but within a 3-mile zoning buffer around Lincoln. He said that included deliveries and services at their homes. Lincoln’s sales tax rate is 1.75%. 
Ballard said the city should refund any improperly assessed local taxes.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, who lives in the “extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction” around Lincoln, wrote on social media Wednesday: “I have heard/seen this. Very bad for the city to be collecting sales taxes from ETJ citizens. Taxation without representation!”
University of Nebraska College of Law professor Anthony Schutz responded to Hilgers and said it could be intermediaries out of line. Hilgers agreed.
“You are right — lots of mechanics involved in collecting and remitting taxes — so hard to pin any blame without knowing more,” Hilgers wrote. “That said, no matter the mechanism, the city is getting (at least some?) amount of $$ to which it is not legally entitled.”
Both Ballard and Hilgers are supporters of a 2026 ballot measure to allow residents in the 3-mile buffer zone to vote in city elections. Ballot Question 6 is on Lincoln’s Nov. 3 ballot.
The seven-member Lincoln City Council. Top row, from left, Sändra Washington, Justin P. Carlson, Tom Beckius and James Michael Bowers. Bottom row, from left, Tom Duden (vice chair), Brodey Weber (chair) and Bennie Shobe. (Photo courtesy of City of Lincoln)
Lincoln City Council Chair Brodey Weber, who lives in the legislative district that Ballard and previously Hilgers represented, said Wednesday it was “unfortunate” Ballard didn’t reach out to the city before issuing a news release accusing the city of malfeasance. Ballard announced he would seek 2027 legislation forcing Lincoln to issue refunds plus interest. He said he was also considering imposing an additional penalty for any delay.
Weber said Ballard made “no attempt” to work with the city and didn’t detail supposed evidence.
“If there is any evidence, I strongly encourage him (Ballard) to present it to the Nebraska Department of Revenue as well as to the city so any potential issue has the opportunity to be rectified immediately,” Weber wrote.
“With there being no collaborative approach, I fear that this is a hyper-partisan attempt to advocate for a political campaign that seeks to let non-Lincoln citizens, who do not pay city property taxes, vote in our Lincoln city elections.”
Weber ran against Hilgers for Legislative District 21 in 2020. Hilgers was elected attorney general in 2022, and Ballard was appointed to the seat in 2023. He previously worked for Hilgers while he was in the Legislature. Weber was elected to the City Council in 2023.
Ballard said Thursday night he stands by his frustrations with the city and argued that Weber is “more than happy in accepting this windfall.”
“I understand that. That’s his prerogative,” Ballard told the Examiner. “Willing to have a conversation with Brodey, I’ve known him for a long time, and a collaborative approach, I think, is good to try to put more money back in Nebraskans’ pockets that was, again, wrongfully taken from them.”



The Revenue Department said if a customer learns they have overpaid any state or local sales and use tax, they can file a Claim for Refund of Sales and Use Tax, Form 7.
The agency said retailers can use the department’s Nebfile system to file their sales tax returns (Form 10) to report gross Nebraska sales and turn in required taxes. But the department said it does not maintain the actual details of each individual sale that makes its way to a tax return, documents Ballard argued would help determine refunds over 20 years.
Between January 2006 and July 2026, the Department of Revenue returned $1.72 billion in local sales tax revenue to Lincoln, according to data from the department. In the past year, the city has received $132 million in sales tax revenue, an average of $11 million each month.
Businesses can use free tools to assist them in determining the appropriate tax to charge Nebraska customers based on the location of the sale, the department said. Sales made in person, at a store, are taxed based on the location of the business, but sales shipped to a customer are based on the location the item is shipped to.
The department’s suggested tools are:

Sales and Use Tax Rates and Boundary Files, available for download.
Sales Tax Rate Finder, for retailers to determine the appropriate jurisdiction and tax rate.

Ballard said he understands the department might not have the documentation but that the issue needs to be corrected going forward. He said he has heard from more Nebraskans since Wednesday who have faced similar problems. He said Nebraskans are busy with work, raising families and getting dinner on the table and don’t want to fill out a form for a refund.
“I think the state and the city have a responsibility to get it right on the first time and not wrongfully take this money from hardworking Nebraskans,” Ballard said.
Said the agency: “The DOR is willing to work with local city officials or state senators to review and discuss the process of collecting and remitting state and local sales and (use) taxes.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Father of slain 22-year-old pledges to ‘do anything’ to strengthen criminal record keeping
description: Steve Federico continues to push for changes to federal law around criminal record keeping following his daughter's May 3, 2025, murder in SC.
text:
A photo of Logan Federico displayed during a Columbia Police Department press conference May 5, 2025. (Photo courtesy of Columbia Police Department)Seventeen months after his daughter’s murder, Steve Federico said Thursday his “passion now” is a federal law on criminal record keeping that could prevent similar tragedies.
His daughter, Logan Federico, was killed May 3, 2025, in a downtown Columbia home while visiting friends at the University of South Carolina.
Alexander Dickey, 31, is accused of fatally shooting the 22-year-old after breaking into the house where she was staying.
Steve Federico, of Waxhaw, North Carolina, argues it was failures of South Carolina’s court system that contributed to his daughter’s death.
Father of slain 22-year-old wants federal prosecutors to handle daughter’s murder case

“This was preventable,” he said Thursday during a public roundtable meeting in Charleston with federal and local officials.
If there hadn’t been record-keeping mistakes and plea deals that led to lighter sentencing, Federico said, the man accused of killing his daughter likely would have still been in prison for past convictions.
“He shouldn’t have been on the streets,” he said to a gathering that included U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, South Carolina’s U.S. attorney, Bryan Stirling; Lowcountry sheriffs and police chiefs.
“Because of this, I’m not a girl dad anymore, and that’s not fair to me,” Federico said through tears.
Logan’s Law
In May, near the one-year anniversary of her death, U.S. Rep. Russell Fry of South Carolina’s 7th District and the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham introduced matching bills in their chambers dubbed “Logan’s Law.”
After the senator died in July, his appointed replacement, Sen. Darline Graham, signed on to her brother’s bill. On the House side, 5th District Rep. Ralph Norman is the only co-sponsor among South Carolina’s delegation. He’ll leave office in January.
Neither bill has received a hearing and both chambers are on recess until Nov. 9, after the midterm elections. The legislation almost certainly will need to be reintroduced next year.
The proposal would create a national database accessible to the general public of people convicted of crimes considered violent.
Convictions qualify for the database if they involve physical violence or the threat of physical violence, and the sentence is at least 180 days in prison.
States that don’t participate would risk losing federal funding from the U.S. Department of Justice.
Steve Federico speaks with law enforcement and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche at an event in North Charleston, Tuesday, Oct. 8, 2026, nearly a year and a half after his daughter’s murder in Columbia. (Screenshot from U.S. Department of Justice livestream)
“This is my passion now. I will do anything I have to do to get this law passed,” Federico said.
“I’m not going to save one more life; I’m going to save thousands,” he added.
Blanche also pledged his support for the bill. And Graham, if elected to a full term, promised to take up her brother’s mantle, calling Logan’s Law her “new passion.”
Fry said the bill will likely receive bipartisan support.
“This is not a red or blue issue,” he said.
Ongoing case
As for Dickey, his case is still ongoing.
According to police, Dickey killed the 22-year-old amid a multi-day crime spree that began with him stealing a car in Richland County and ended with his arrest after he broke into a Lexington County home and set it on fire.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Dickey remains in jail without bond after his indictment June 25, 2025, on 12 charges, including murder, burglary and possession of a weapon during a violent crime, according to Richland County court records.
He also faces 23 charges in Lexington County, including arson, burglary, larceny and banking crimes, according to court records.
The charges involve a stolen gun and the use of credit cards stolen from Logan Federico.
“He didn’t kill our daughter for a debit card,” her father said. “She was the only one awake that could identify him. He killed a witness.”
“That’s how brutal of a person this person is. He didn’t have to do it. He just could have left,” Federico added.
Dickey’s public defender, Fielding Pringle, declined to comment Thursday to the SC Daily Gazette. She also declined to comment for an article last year.
Past convictions
Since turning 18, Dickey has been convicted of eight felony charges — mostly for low-level theft and burglary — and pleaded two more down to misdemeanors.
He served three terms in prison: November 2014 to May 2017, April to August 2018, and December 2019 to February 2021, state Department of Corrections spokeswoman Chrysti Shain confirmed.
At age 19, a grand larceny conviction, combined with a conviction for third-degree burglary, landed him a five-year prison sentence, of which he served half.
A drug charge led to his short stay in 2018. He was 23 years old.
A mugshot of Alexander Dickey, who stands accused of murdering Logan Federico on May 3, 2025. (Photo provided by Lexington County jail)
And at age 24, an unarmed robbery conviction resulted in a four-year sentence, of which he served a little more than one year.
Then, in 2023, police arrested him for burglary again.
After the prosecutors and Dickey reached a plea deal, a judge had the option of sentencing Dickey to as much as five years in prison. The judge also could have rejected the deal, keeping to the original second-degree burglary charge that comes with penalties up to 10 years.
Instead, the judge ruled the 411 days Dickey spent in jail waiting for his case to proceed was enough time served. He was let out on two years probation.
The issue, Lexington County’s chief prosecutor told NBC affiliate WIS-TV, was the earlier burglary charges didn’t show up in his criminal history record maintained by the State Law Enforcement Division. So the plea deal treated the burglary as his first for that offense, despite Dickey’s earlier convictions.
Had they known, 11th Circuit Solicitor Rick Hubbard told WIS, his office wouldn’t have struck the deal.
SLED’s explanation was that it never received fingerprints from the 2014 burglary arrest. A receipt of fingerprints is what prompts the agency to add charges to someone’s record.
“A set of fingerprints is the only thing that will identify a subject to their criminal history,” SLED said in a statement Thursday to the Gazette.

title: Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly rallies Iowa educators for Sand’s campaign
description: Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly joined Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand in Des Moines Thursday, saying her tenure shows it is possible to be an effective Democratic governor while working with a GOP-controlled state Legislature. Joining Sand in person at the Iowa State Education Association headquarters, Kelly said when she was first elected in 2018, Kans[...]
text:
Iowa Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand and Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly spoke at an event at the Iowa State Education Association headquarters in Des Moines Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly joined Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand in Des Moines Thursday, saying her tenure shows it is possible to be an effective Democratic governor while working with a GOP-controlled state Legislature.
Joining Sand in person at the Iowa State Education Association headquarters, Kelly said when she was first elected in 2018, Kansas faced a “very similar situation” to Iowa as the state experienced budget problems — including public schools being “chronically underfunded.” Since then, she said, Kansas has “fully funded our schools now for eight years in a row,” alongside making additional investments in public education and special education services.
“None of this has been easy, and none of it happened because one party got its way,” Kelly said. “It happened because we worked across the aisle and stayed focused on our schools. After two terms, I am proud to say we did get things back on track. We balanced our budget, we funded our schools every year, and we built records for business investment and job creation. … What does that prove? That with the laser focus on the issues that matter, you can turn things around. And Rob Sand is that leader.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At the event, educators asked Sand, the current state auditor, what he would do to better support students and staff in Iowa’s public school system. They also asked Sand how he would address changes made in recent years to the state’s Area Education Agencies, which providing services for special education students. While he has said he would support a 5% increase to K-12 funding in his first year as governor, Sand also warned that he would not have the ability to reverse measures passed into law by GOP majorities, under the assumption that Republicans will continue to hold legislative majorities in Iowa.
“I’m not going to be able to unilaterally undo things, and I’m not the kind of person who’s going to stand in front of you and make promises that I know that we have a constitutional system of self-governance that won’t let me keep that promise,” Sand said. “… I know that might sound disappointing, but it’s the truth. Here’s the piece that’s really easy to say that is exciting. More bad bills that hit my desk, I can veto.”
Kelly also said Sand may be in a more advantageous position than herself if elected governor in the Nov. 3, 2026 election. While Kansas has Republican supermajorities in both chambers, Iowa currently has a supermajority in the House and a majority in the Senate. She said working across the aisle in her state became more difficult as “moderate Republicans” were replaced by “MAGA”-affiliated Republicans, but said she has still been able to build relationships across the aisle to accomplish common goals.
“It’s not been easy to get things done, but if somebody knows where they want to go, there are ways and there are people that you will find if you’re willing to talk and be willing to listen … and now you will be able to find those legislators who can modify their approach or their vote to get where you want to go,” Kelly said. “You know, it may have to be transactional. You have to make some deals, and do really what they want over here, so that you can get what you really need over her. But there are ways to do it, and I have no doubt, given Rob’s history as your auditor … the fact that many people have been willing to work with him bodes well.”
She criticized Iowa’s GOP gubernatorial candidate, Zach Lahn, for his approach to state education, while pointing to a regular criticism from the campaign trail that he “still has a home in Kansas” and frequently travels to the state.
Earlier in the week, Kelly had released an advertisement supporting Sand in the 2026 gubernatorial campaign, in which she said though she generally supports Kansans, “in the Iowa governor’s race, I’m supporting the Iowan.”
“Zach, there are no hard feelings, but it is time to come back to Kansas,” Kelly said in the video. “As they say, there’s no place like home.”
Sand and Democrats have regularly criticized Lahn over his Iowa residency status, pointing to reports showing he lived and was a registered voter in Kansas prior to the 2024 election cycle. His residency changed in time to qualify him to run for Iowa governor in 2026. He also regularly travels to Kansas using his private plane – trips Lahn said are because some of his children are located in Wichita.
The two candidates faced off Monday at a debate hosted by KWQC in Davenport, where Lahn addressed some concerns about his residency and travel to Kansas. He said criticisms of his travel and time spent in Kansas were criticisms of his family.
“I’m gonna tell you this right now, this issue is about one thing. It’s about my children. That’s it,” Lahn said. “I have a blended family, and they split time. … I am not going to be intimidated on this.”
The Lahn campaign did not immediately return a message seeking a response for this article.
Kelly also said Lahn’s work in Kansas private schools shows he would not be the best choice for Iowans hoping to improve the state’s K-12 school system. In 2018, Lahn helped launch a private pre-K through 12th-grade school in Wichita, Kansas on the campus of Wichita State University called Wonder. The Kansas governor referenced a report from the Kansas Reflector that found Wonder owned Lahn and his wife Annie Lahn approximately $4.5 million in 2025, and that its expenses exceeded revenues in five of six years of operation.
“His plan for Iowa schools is to model them after the private school he started in Wichita, Kansas. That school is now $4.5 million dollars in debt. Iowa already has a $1.4 billion dollar budget hole. You don’t fix that by importing a failed model.”

text:
President Donald Trump speaks at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on Oct. 2, 2026, as he campaigns in GOP-leaning states ahead of the midterms. (Photo by Dan Anderson/Alabama Reflector)President Donald Trump is planning to fly to Alaska next week for a rally intended to boost the re-election campaigns of U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan and Rep. Nick Begich III.
According to the Trump 47 Committee, an operation of the Republican National Committee and Trump’s Save America PAC, Trump will speak at 3:30 p.m. Tuesday in Wasilla’s Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center. 
The announcement had been expected; Vice President J.D. Vance visited Fairbanks on Monday, and two of Alaska’s three Republican governor candidates had said beforehand that they expected Trump to visit.
It isn’t yet clear whether Trump will endorse any or all three of the Republicans seeking to replace Gov. Mike Dunleavy. 
Polling indicates Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is slightly ahead of Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Vance did not endorse any of the three during his visit to Alaska.
Polls also show Sullivan is in a close race against Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, and Begich is leading independent challenger Bill Hill.
Trump’s visit would be the biggest event in a series of high-profile Republican rallies in Alaska ahead of Election Day. In addition to Vance and Trump, U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, is expected to headline a Republican fundraiser on Oct. 16 in Anchorage.
With Republican polling numbers slipping nationwide, Trump and Vance have been campaigning in traditionally Republican states, including Alabama, Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.
Trump visited Anchorage in July 2022, two years after the end of his first term as President, in order to boost support for Republican candidates: Dunleavy, U.S. Sen. candidate Kelly Tshibaka and U.S. House candidate Sarah Palin. 
Tshibaka and Palin lost their elections; Dunleavy won.
More than 5,000 people attended that Anchorage event, which was held at the Alaska Airlines Center on a Saturday. The upcoming event will take place during working hours, at an arena with a capacity of about 3,500 people.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Todd Johnston, head of WV energy development and competitiveness, exits Morrisey administration
description: Todd Johnston is no longer with the Morrisey administration. He had served under the governor in two roles: deputy chief of staff and director of the state’s energy, infrastructure and competitiveness.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey, with his deputy chief of staff Todd Johnston (right), talked to the press about his "Backyard Brawl" economic development plan on Thursday, Jan. 23, 2025, at the Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (West Virginia Office of the Gov. Patrick Morrisey/Courtesy photo)Todd Johnston is no longer with the Morrisey administration. He had served under the governor in two roles: deputy chief of staff and director of the state’s energy, infrastructure and competitiveness.
Johnston confirmed his exit on Thursday in a phone interview, saying he was proud of the work he accomplished while with the governor since January 2025. 
“We’ve ushered in historic private sector investment of over $96 billion. We’ve implemented policies that put over $5 billion in infrastructure in terms of broadband, water infrastructure and transportation, and we spearheaded the state’s first comprehensive energy policy,” Johnston said. “These are tremendous achievements, and I’ve kind of done what I came to the state to do.”
Johnston, 53, is a Washington, D.C., resident who has split his time between the nation’s capital with his family and West Virginia for the job. 
Tapped by Gov. Patrick Morrisey for the job, Johnston made a two-year commitment to the administration. He is leaving early, he said, due to taking a new job in Washington, D.C. 
“Now seems like the right time. It’s a good transition period,” Johnston said. “It’s been a fantastic ride, and I thank Gov. Morrisey for the opportunity. If given the same opportunity again, I would jump at it in a heartbeat.”
Morrisey’s communications office also confirmed Johnston’s departure in an email on Thursday afternoon. 
“We appreciate Todd’s service and respect the fact that he wants to spend more time with his family. We are grateful for his service and wish him well in his next endeavor,” said Lars Dalseide, communications director for the governor. 
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced at the start of last year that Johnston would step into the role as West Virginia’s energy, infrastructure and competitiveness director. 
Johnston was tasked with marketing West Virginia as an energy powerhouse and working with cabinet secretaries in commerce, environmental protection, transportation and more to attract businesses to West Virginia. Part of those efforts focused on reducing red tape and regulations. 
“I will say it is a Herculean task because it involves managing three different agencies: (Department of Environmental Protection), Department of Transportation and Commerce,” Johnston said. “It was quite an investment of time, and (it) is very tough to do everything at once.”
Johnston noted that he was glad to have led the governor’s “50 by 50” energy generation plan. The strategy relies heavily on the state’s coal and natural gas to increase the state’s energy capacity to 50 gigawatts by 2050. 
He also helped craft and implement the state’s hallmark data center legislation — House Bill 2014 — with the hope of incentivizing data center development.
“We’ve done a number of other things that are just kind of in the vein of good governance that, quite frankly, hadn’t been addressed in over the course of a number of administrations,” Johnston said. 
Johnston’s exit comes about a week after Morrisey administration announced that the state would opt out of consideration by federal officials to be a nuclear development hub. The governor’s heel spin on the federal application came after the Charleston-Gazette Mail and MetroNews reported that states were required to have a plan for handling nuclear energy from beginning to ending, including spent fuel and radioactive waste. 
Morrisey vowed that West Virginia wouldn’t be a dumping ground for nuclear waste and withdrew from federal consideration for the massive project. The programs could generate as much as $10 billion in state and local tax revenue, according to federal officials.
Johnston told West Virginia Watch his departure was completely unrelated from the recent nuclear hub circumstances.
His resume included more than a decade in federal and state government where he served in leadership positions on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works and House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.
Johnston’s departure follows a number of high profile exits in the Morrisey administration, including Dr. Stephen Loyd, who recently resigned as director of the state’s Office of Drug Control Policy. Bureau for Family Assistance Commissioner Janie Cole exited last week, and Tourism Secretary Chelsea Ruby resigned in July after five years in the role.

name: VTDigger
title: Police face barrage of questions but provide few answers about shooting by Williston officer
description:
The injured man suffered a gunshot wound to his hip in the early Thursday morning shooting and was treated at the hospital and released, according to police.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Police face barrage of questions but provide few answers about shooting by Williston officer.
text:
Photo via Adobe Stock

WILLISTON — Questions linger after authorities say a Williston police officer shot and injured a man early Thursday. A press conference by police Thursday afternoon revealed little about what led the officer to shoot the man. 
Police say the matter remains under investigation. 
The man was treated at the University of Vermont Medical Center for a gunshot wound to his hip, Maj. Ashley Barnes, commander of the state police criminal division, told reporters at the press conference. The man has since been released from the hospital, Barnes added.
State police, the agency heading the investigation into the shooting, have not released the man’s name.
The Williston police officer who fired his handgun was evaluated for a minor injury at the hospital and has since been released, Barnes said.
The name of that officer who police investigators say fired on the man has not yet been released either. State police protocol is to withhold the name of an officer involved in a shooting for 24 hours. Williston police said the officer has been put on paid administrative leave. 

READ MORE

When the investigation is complete, the Vermont State Police will turn over the case to the Vermont Attorney General’s Office and the State’s Attorney’s Office for independent reviews of the police officer’s use of force.
Williston officers had responded to a report around 4:50 a.m. Thursday for a road hazard on Route 2A between Butternut Road and Old Creamery Road, Barnes told reporters Thursday. A state police press release issued moments before the press conference stated that that hazard was reported to be downed wires across Route 2A.  
A man driving a car then came upon that scene, police said. 
“A vehicle approached officers, and we’re not exactly sure yet what occurred during that,” Barnes said. “Something led to one of the Williston officers discharging his duty weapon, striking the male.”
Barnes said exactly what took place remains under investigation, declining to elaborate more on what exchanges, if any, may have taken place between the officer and the man who was shot.
Asked if the officer was in danger, Barnes replied, “I don’t know that at this point. We’re going to have to review body cam  and cruiser cam footage.”
He said “some of that footage” has been reviewed by investigators. Asked if police would release that footage, Barnes responded that it would not be released at this time since the matter remains under investigation.
Williston Police Chief Brian Labarge, who also spoke at the press conference Thursday, would not say how many officers from his department had been on the scene at the time of the shooting. 
“Officers were on scene,” he told reporters, refusing to provide a more specific number. The police chief did say that two officers have been placed on paid administrative leave. What role, if any, the other officer played in the incident was not clear.
Larbage wouldn’t say what injuries the officer sustained, or how they may have occurred.
“I’m not confirming at this time who any of the officers or individuals were,” Labarge told reporters. 
A portion of Route 2A near where the shooting occurred was closed to traffic for much of Thursday as detectives investigated and members of the state police processed the scene. It reopened to traffic around 4 p.m. Thursday.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma Jewish charter school expects only 10 students, per email to Tulsa rabbi
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A first-in-the-nation Jewish charter school seeking to open in Oklahoma expects to enroll only 10 students — far short of original projections — in its first year of operation, according to an email the school’s leading founder sent to local faith leaders. The low enrollment goal has raised doubts about the viability […]
text:
Former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch speaks to the Statewide Charter School Board on Jan. 12 in Oklahoma City to present an application to open an online Jewish charter school in Oklahoma. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A first-in-the-nation Jewish charter school seeking to open in Oklahoma expects to enroll only 10 students — far short of original projections — in its first year of operation, according to an email the school’s leading founder sent to local faith leaders.
The low enrollment goal has raised doubts about the viability and local support of Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School as it aims to become the first taxpayer-funded religious charter school in the country.
The Statewide Charter School Board could vote Monday on Ben Gamla’s application to open, according to its next meeting agenda. The board initially rejected the school because it would teach the tenets of the Jewish faith along with secular school subjects, but an Oklahoma City federal judge decided last month a charter school can’t be denied solely because it would provide a faith-based education.
Although it denied the school’s application, the board has advocated for Ben Gamla in court, and it supported a previous attempt to open a Catholic charter school in the state.
“The Statewide Charter School Board will consider the order of the court and may make their decision based on that order on Monday,” the board’s attorney, A.J. Ferate, said. “I do not know and I cannot speak to what decision the board will make, but I do believe that a decision will be made on that.”
The Statewide Charter School Board meets for a hearing on April 29 at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The school’s founders, led by former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, of Florida, first applied in December for state approval. Their application projected Ben Gamla would enroll between 335 and 495 students K-12 in its first year as an online school.
Now, Ben Gamla is preparing to launch in September 2027 as a high school with an “intentionally modest” enrollment goal of 10 students, Deutsch wrote in a Sept. 30 email to a Tulsa rabbi, who publicized the message on Thursday.
Attorneys representing Deutsch, the school and the statewide board declined to comment on the email.
“Although our initial school in Oklahoma will be an online high school, our long-term vision is much broader: to establish Jewish religious charter schools serving students from kindergarten through 12th grade in communities throughout the country,” Deutsch wrote in the email.
Rabbi Daniel Kaiman, who leads Congregation B’nai Emunah in Tulsa, said he was surprised to receive Deutsch’s message and an invitation to apply to be the school’s founding principal. Kaiman is part of a group of Oklahomans who sued to block the school from opening.
In a statement through his legal counsel, Kaiman said the email signals how Deutsch and the proposed school are “completely disconnected from the Oklahoma Jewish community.”
“It also shows how little our community wants this,” Kaiman stated Thursday. “Perhaps most importantly, it shows that this school is nothing but a Trojan horse for creating religious public schools. We don’t need or want this school. We want strong public schools and to keep church and state separate.”
Other Jewish communal leaders received the same or similar email, said Rachel Johnson, executive director of the Jewish Federation of Greater Oklahoma City.
Johnson said she isn’t aware of interest among the local community in enrolling or working for the proposed school.
Although not a recipient of Deutsch’s email, Rabbi Abby Jacobson, of Emanuel Synagogue in Oklahoma City, said she wasn’t surprised to hear the proposed school is expecting so few students.
For years, Oklahoma’s Jewish community has repeatedly said “no thank you” to the idea of a religious charter school in the state, she said.
“I can’t say that no one in the local community would support it, but I would say that I haven’t spoken to anybody who would,” Jacobson said.
The “miniscule” enrollment estimate demonstrates Ben Gamla lacks essential community support and is financially and operationally unviable, wrote multiple national legal organizations — including the American Civil Liberties Union, the Education Law Center and Americans United for Separation of Church and State — in a letter Thursday.
The legal groups are representing Kaiman and other Oklahoma residents fighting the Jewish charter school in court. Their letter urged the Statewide Charter School Board to again deny the school from opening.
The Oklahoma Attorney General’s Office, which also has raised concerns over Ben Gamla’s enrollment estimates, confirmed it received the letter and is reviewing it.
Attorney General Gentner Drummond filed a lawsuit in March in Oklahoma County District Court, contending the Statewide Charter School Board intentionally “manipulated” its vote on the school to benefit Ben Gamla’s chances in court. 
The board solely focused on the school’s religious component and left out other valid reasons for denial, like an abrupt tenfold increase in its enrollment projections, he argued.
In a letter of intent submitted in November, Deutsch initially estimated Ben Gamla would serve 40 high school students. A month later, the school’s formal application projected it would enroll hundreds of students K-12.
The board should have considered that discrepancy a “material deficiency” and grounds for denial, Drummond said.

name: WyoFile
title: The mountain elite: Wyoming’s Amanda MacLeod falls for actors as a Hollywood double
description:
Dancing and ski racing her way through high school gave her the skills to make it in Tinseltown.
The post The mountain elite: Wyoming’s Amanda MacLeod falls for actors as a Hollywood double appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Amanda MacLeod has fallen across silver screens throughout the country while working as a Hollywood stunt double, using skills she learned from skiing and dancing while growing up in Wyoming.
Before she could walk, her father carried her in a backpack while he skied in the Teton backcountry. She was in dance classes by age 4, learning skills that would lay the foundation for a career on stage and in front of the lens.
Through school years, her athleticism grew as she played soccer, cycled, climbed, hiked, danced and paddled, much of it among Wyoming’s hills. Her grandmother was a ballroom dancer, her mother a dancer with the local troupe, her father an avid skier.
“I was dancing and skiing side-by-side my whole life,” MacLeod said. But when she saw a performance by the Diavolo: Architecture in Motion dance company, it swayed her to focus her talents and provoked a fateful conversation.
“Sorry, Dad. I’m going to join the Dancers’ Workshop Junior Company.”
That decision sent MacLeod down a coast-to-coast path — dancing in New York, moving to L.A., working odd jobs and finally, landing on a film set. Among other roles, she was the stunt double for Doug Jones in “Hocus Pocus 2.”
“Which is crazy because he’s a 6’-4” guy, and I’m a 5’-4” woman,” she said. Jones played zombie Billy Butcherson, she his headless double.
“A lot of it is just Doug Jones’s talking head, and then me stumbling around the world,” she said. Her skiing and dancing skills gave her a foundation for soundstage antics.
“If you don’t know how to bail and fall on skis or a bike, if you don’t know how to roll out of that, you’re really going to be in a world of hurt,” she said of learning her art. “Being a dancer has allowed me as a stunt performer to jump into most anything. You know where every part of your body is at all times … something that I haven’t found in any other athletic endeavor. That’s what helps me stumble without hurting myself.”
MacLeod said she knows when she’s hit the mark.
“A stunt person’s favorite thing is when the crew or the director goes, ‘Oh my God, are you okay?’”
Kept up with the boys
“Without my dance background, I would not be where I am in my career,” she said, “and without my extreme sports background, I also would not be where I am in my career.”
Now 37, she forged her ethos in the sometimes cruel crucible of high school and “a patriarchal environment of extreme sports.”
“If you were kind of popular, it was because you could hang and keep up with the boys, or because they wanted to sleep with you,” she said of her formative years. “I was the one who kept up with the boys.”
Dancers provided more inspiration than cliff-jumping dudes. “I saw a couple of big companies from New York and London around my freshman year, and it just put me completely on fire for dance.”
She earned a BFA in dance and choreography from Mason Gross School of the Arts at Rutgers University in New Jersey and became a performance artist in Brooklyn.
“I was doing artsy-fartsy stuff in basements and galleries and what have you, while also working for a nonprofit and a restaurant. I was hitting the ground hard in my 20s. I got kind of burnt out, having to work so hard just to survive.”
“I was the one who kept up with the boys.”Amanda MacLeod
She packed two suitcases and moved to Los Angeles, for a Pilates apprenticeship in Laguna Beach, a discipline that cured a back injury. On a whim, she took a job with a tech startup.
“After six months, I kind of came to,” she said of her corporate stint. “It wasn’t for naught,” she said of the alien culture, because it gave her key communication and networking skills.
In L.A. she made good on a promise she’d made to herself in high school: dancing with Diavolo, the company that had inspired 17-year-old MacLeod to focus on dance back in Jackson.
“The amount of athleticism that that company requires and the strength that it requires — we’re literally running, sprinting, jumping, leaping, and flying 25, 30, feet through the air … caught by a few guys — helped [me] get over this really gnarly disorder,” she said. “And it also inspired me to go, ‘I’m going to join that company someday.’ And 10 years later, I did.”
The experience, and the daily discipline required to keep up, cured her of a troubled eating behavior, she said.
Old white dude with an eye patch
As she became more established, MacLeod began working with art departments on film sets and learning about stunt work.
“It’s like adult playtime,” she said of her work on the movie sets. Then someone said “Oh, you should go to this open call.”
It was a dance tryout that drew 300 dancers, actors and stunt workers, everyone from college cheerleaders to martial artists, gymnasts and parkour athletes.
“And there’s this man, this old, like older white dude, sitting in a chair, bald with an eye patch, and I’m just like, OK, who are you and what’s happening? This is great.
“He’s giving everyone one minute to do a pass. He’ll put two people in front of the whole group and say, ‘Okay, go,’ and you just have one minute to show off some shit, and that’s it.”
MacLeod jumped, dove, and bounced off walls. “And he just went ‘perfect’” she said. “I went ‘OK,’ [and] just walked away because people blow smoke up your ass a lot in this town.”
But she was “perfect” and got a callback, then another. Before long she found herself in front of cameras, working on pre-production for “Avatar: The Way of Water.”
Hollywood has its problems. “There’s still a lot of tropes about women sleeping around for work,” she said. She sometimes wonders, “am I getting hired because this guy’s going to hit on me and try to get me to sleep with him, or is he hiring me because of my skills?”
“I went ‘okay,’ [and] just walked away because people blow smoke up your ass a lot in this town.”Amanda MacLeod
Things are changing and new Screen Actors Guild rules that women should double for women and other guidelines are boosting opportunities. Yet, “it’s still very much a man’s game,” she said. “They have way more jobs.”
Her niche is as a double. “If you can double an actress and become tight with them, you can get carried with them for their career.”
MacLeod sees potential for filming in Wyoming. “Think about outside of Lander, or near the Wind Rivers. There’s so much environment that could be used there. There are plenty of talented cinematographers in Wyoming. There’s a bunch of people that know how to rig that just need the right training.
“We have people who could do it, but they don’t because it’s really expensive to live in Jackson, and there’s no film incentives in Wyoming.”
It would be nice to work in her home state, MacLeod said, in part because “I’m kind of over cities.”
“I’m so grateful for everything I’ve been able to accomplish and do. But none of it matters if I don’t have trees and mountains and rivers to go home to.”

title: Summit pushes for utilities commission action on outstanding pipeline dockets
description: The Iowa Utilities Commission has denied a request from Summit Carbon Solutions, the company seeking to build a carbon sequestration pipeline in Iowa, to consolidate outstanding dockets and schedule a hearing.  The IUC issued hearing schedules for two sections of pipeline in the company’s second phase of the project, but denied Summit’s request to combine […[...]
text:
Kathy Carter, a Floyd County landowner, speaks outside of the Iowa Utilities Commission Oct. 8, 2026 in opposition to a carbon sequestration pipeline. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) The Iowa Utilities Commission has denied a request from Summit Carbon Solutions, the company seeking to build a carbon sequestration pipeline in Iowa, to consolidate outstanding dockets and schedule a hearing. 
The IUC issued hearing schedules for two sections of pipeline in the company’s second phase of the project, but denied Summit’s request to combine the dockets. 
The IUC did not rule on the remaining dockets for phase 2, which could still be consolidated in the future, as Summit has requested. Summit’s phase 2 pipeline routes would add laterals to the pipeline, allowing it to connect to more biorefineries than the original route included. 
In the request, Summit said the IUC has scheduled and held hearings and issued orders for “several other energy infrastructure projects” but has been “ignoring Summit.” Summit’s initial filings for the project were made between October 2024 and September 2025, according to the request, but the company said it has not received the “basic procedural path” forward. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Even if this Commission’s answer is ultimately no—though we see no reason why that would be the case, giving the Commission’s prior rulings—further delay on the bare minimum process (setting a hearing) will irreparably harm Iowa’s reputation,” the company wrote in the request for consolidation.
Summit argued that while other states and the federal government are “speeding up the permitting process, recognizing that energy infrastructure is paramount” the IUC is “making the process longer and more cumbersome.” 
Summit said the drawn-out process is harming the ethanol industry and farmers who want access to the low-carbon biofuel markets the carbon sequestration pipeline would open up. The company said delaying a hearing on the docket is also harming landowners who want their objections heard and rural communities with a stake in the investment. 
Colleen Tucker, a landowner from Mitchell County, addressed commissioners during public comments at a meeting Thursday and said it was “incredibly bold and frankly offensive” for Summit to speak on behalf of landowners in its filing. 
Tucker said the IUC is not responsible for Summit’s investments and that the company’s investment in the project “doesn’t give the company a regulatory shortcut or a cut to the front of the line.” 
IUC, in its order denying the consolidation of dockets, noted the lawsuit against Summit’s permit for phase one of the project as “part of the larger picture” impacting the docket.
Summit’s initial permit for more than 600 miles of pipe through Iowa, phase one of the project, was approved by the Iowa Utilities Commission in 2024, giving the company the right of eminent domain for the project. Landowners, the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter and several counties challenged the permit, arguing Summit should not be considered a common carrier. 
In fall 2025, Summit filed a request to amend its permit with the IUC to no longer travel through South Dakota and to a sequestration site in North Dakota. The lawsuit over the initial permit was partially remanded to the IUC because of the amendment, and according to the IUC response, comments on how to proceed with the permit included a request to keep the Floyd and Ida County dockets in phase two as “stand-alone dockets.” 
IUC held a hearing in September to determine a hearing schedule on dockets for two sections of pipe planned for Ida and Floyd counties, both of which are less than 5 miles. In its responses denying Summit’s consolidation request, IUC finalized hearing dates for the segments. The docket pertaining to Floyd County will be heard March 23, 2027 and the Ida County hearing will occur Feb. 23, 2027. Both will be held in Des Moines and are later than the middle of December hearing dates requested by Summit.
Summit announced in May that it planned to direct the pipeline west toward Wyoming and that it was considering using the CO2 for enhanced oil recovery, a process where the liquified carbon dioxide in the pipeline can be injected into the ground near existing oil fields to help push the oil to the surface. 
Landowner opposition 
Landowners opposed to the project said some of them were denied requests to intervene in the upcoming hearings because, though they live near the proposed route, they don’t own property in the counties. 
Don Johannsen, a Cherokee County landowner, said the route is on adjoining land to his property and would directly impact him.
“They’re assuming that because I’m not on the line in Ida County, that it doesn’t affect me, but it clearly does,” Johannsen said while speaking to reporters Thursday morning. 
Jon Dunwell was recently appointed to serve on the Iowa Utilities Commission. He joined commissioners Oct. 8, 2026 for a public meeting. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The issue of who can intervene has been brought up throughout the Summit proceedings with the Iowa Utilities Commission. Lawmakers opposed to the project, or its use of eminent domain, have proposed legislation to widen the pool of people who could intervene in proceedings. 
Landowners gathered Thursday ahead of the Iowa Utilities Commission’s first monthly public meeting with its newest commissioner, Jon Dunwell, who was appointed Monday by Gov. Kim Reynolds. Those gathered, in their signature red shirts, said they were opposed to the recent appointment and argued Dunwell’s past as a legislator made him partial in the pipeline issue.
Dunwell resigned his seat in the Iowa House of Representatives to accept the commissioner appointment, which will require Senate approval.
Kathy Carter, a Floyd County landowner, said she was “really concerned” with the newest commissioner. 
“Because of his past on the Legislature and his ability to vote, I believe it’s a conflict of interest,” Carter said Thursday ahead of the IUC public meeting. “Anybody who’s been in that position to affect any legislation should not have the ability to vote on the IUC.”
Dunwell voted in favor of legislation in 2025 that would have imposed certain limitations on carbon sequestration pipelines in the state. This bill passed the Senate in 2025 after a group of senators held up votes on budget bills until the body debated the legislation. The bill was ultimately vetoed by Reynolds. 
Dunwell voted against a House bill earlier this year that would have banned the use of eminent domain for carbon pipelines in Iowa, but the bill was not taken up in the Senate. 
During the public meeting, Commissioner Joshua Byrnes, who also previously served as a state legislator, said commissioners are not always able to be “experts” on everything, noting the number of issues the commission handles, in addition to pipeline issues. 
Property rights and the election 
The landowner group said they have sent out surveys to all of the candidates running in state, federal and local races to ask them about property rights. Weston Grow, a Guthrie County landowner, said the group plans to release the responses to the questionnaire next week. 
“Each and every legislator will tell you they are for property rights – they have been for almost six years,” Grow said. “We’re tired of waiting. It’s election time. Just like all the phony political ads we are reading, hearing, and seeing, don’t believe just because a politician says they are for property rights doesn’t mean that they actually are.”

title: Tennessee prepares for heavy rain, strong winds brought by Hurricane Isaias
description: Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring periods of heavy rain and wind gusts to Tennessee this weekend, according to the National Weather Service. The hurricane is expected to intensify as it nears the Gulf Coast and make landfall Friday night, then move through the Tennessee River Valley over the weekend.  While the storm is projected […]
text:
The remnants of Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring periods of heavy rain and wind gusts to Tennessee between Oct. 9 and Oct. 11, 2026. (Courtesy of the National Weather Service)Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring periods of heavy rain and wind gusts to Tennessee this weekend, according to the National Weather Service.
The hurricane is expected to intensify as it nears the Gulf Coast and make landfall Friday night, then move through the Tennessee River Valley over the weekend.  While the storm is projected to weaken before it crosses into Tennessee, the National Weather Service has issued flood watches for most of West Tennessee and Middle Tennessee, in addition to counties along the state’s southern border in East Tennessee from Friday evening through Sunday morning.
A high wind watch is also in place along Tennessee’s eastern border from Saturday morning to Sunday morning.
West Tennessee
Total rainfall is expected to be between one to three inches, though areas near the Tennessee River could see local amounts up to four inches, the National Weather Service reported Thursday.
Rain greater than two inches is most likely along Tennessee’s southern border above Mississippi and Alabama. Memphis has a 49% chance of seeing more than two inches of rain. 
Counties under flood watch include Benton, Carroll, Chester, Crockett, Decatur, Dyer, Fayette, Gibson, Hardeman, Hardin, Haywood, Henderson, Lauderdale, Madison, McNairy, Shelby and Tipton.
Wind gusts could reach 35 miles per hour.
Middle Tennessee
Middle Tennessee is expected to see between one and three inches of rain, mostly on Saturday through Saturday night. 
Counties under flood watch include Bedford, Cheatham, Coffee, Davidson, Dickson, Giles, Grundy, Hickman, Humphreys, Lawrence, Lewis, Marshall, Maury, Perry, Rutherford, Wayne and Williamson.
Wind gusts could reach 40 miles per hour.
East Tennessee
The remnants of Hurricane Isaias are expected to bring “heavy rain and strong gusty winds” to East Tennessee, with gusts topping 70 miles per hour possible in the region’s mountains and foothills, according to NWS.
Gusts between 30 and 40 miles per hour are likely in the Cumberland Plateau.
One to two inches of rain is expected in the Cumberland Plateau, the southern Tennessee Valley and southwest North Carolina.
Counties under high wind watch from Saturday morning to Sunday morning include Bradley, East Polk, Hamilton, Marion and West Polk. 
Counties under flood watch include Bradley, East Polk, Hamilton, Marion, Sequatchie and West Polk.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Ocean County elections board, GOP chair sued over voter challenges
description: The League of Women Voters asked courts to step in after the Ocean County elections board challenged some Democratic and unaffiliated Bay Head voters.
text:
The League of Women Voters asked courts to step in after the Ocean County elections board challenged some Democratic and unaffiliated Bay Head voters. (Photo by Daniella Heminghaus/New Jersey Monitor)The New Jersey League of Women Voters and a trio of Bay Head residents sued the Ocean County Board of Elections and its Republican chairman, George Gilmore, alleging they violated a state voting rights law.
The lawsuit comes after the board warned Democrats and unaffiliated voters on a list compiled by Dennis Shaning, who chairs the all-Republican borough council, that they may be deemed ineligible to vote because their tax bills were sent to an address outside Bay Head. The list excluded Republican voters in the same position, the suit argues.
“The Ocean County Board of Elections has intimidated and discriminated against voters in Bay Head and put unconstitutional barriers in the way of the exercise of their fundamental right to vote,” said Liza Weisberg, supervising attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union of New Jersey, which is representing the plaintiffs.
Voters on the list were told their suffrage may be challenged unless they filled a lengthy questionnaire and attended an Oct. 13 Board of Elections hearing. The deadline to register to vote in the Nov. 3 elections is Oct. 13.
The suit alleges the board violated a recently enacted state voting rights law by attempting to intimidate voters.
It also says the board violated the equal protection clause of New Jersey’s Constitution by leaving in place the registrations of Republicans whose tax bills were sent to an address outside the borough.
“The Gilmore Letters created a separate class of voters — registered non-Republican voters whose tax bills are mailed to addresses outside Ocean County — and treated them differently than everyone else,” the suit says.
Gilmore, who is also chair of Ocean County’s Republican Party, did not immediately return a text message seeking comment.
Last month, Gilmore told the New Jersey Monitor that the elections board is merely following up on a letter it received, a practice the board has done for more than three decades.
“We don’t go out looking for people. We react to challenges that come into the board,” he said.
The suit asks a judge to enjoin the board from weighing the eligibility of voters on Shaning’s list based on their party affiliation, tax bill mailing address, questionnaire responses, and meeting attendance.
Those voters should not be required to cast their vote using a provisional ballot, the suit said. The plaintiffs asked the court to declare the board’s inquest unlawful and award attorneys’ fees and damages under the New Jersey Voter Empowerment Act.
