title: Judge extends temporary access to White House for news organizations Trump banned
text: WASHINGTON — A federal judge will rule in the coming days on whether the Trump administration can legally rescind White House press passes for journalists at three news organizations, or if those reporters will be able to continue accessing the grounds while the case continues. U.S. District Judge for the District of Columbia Timothy J. Kelly said at the end of a Thursday hearing he intends to issue his decision on a preliminary injunction in the press freedom case before Tuesday. Kelly, appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term, granted the news organizations — CNN, MS Now and Politico — a temporary restraining order in late September, forcing the White House to return press passes it had confiscated and permit the reporters back into the complex. A preliminary injunction, which the administration could appeal, would replace the short-term temporary restraining order that generally cannot be appealed to a higher court. The TRO was set to expire Thursday, but Kelly extended it through Tuesday. Viewpoint discrimination allegedTheodore J. Boutrous, Jr., a partner at Gibson Dunn who represents the three news organizations in the case, argued during the hearing the president’s decision to ban the reporters was a clear example of viewpoint discrimination and violated the First Amendment.“The president got up on the wrong side of the bed and declared a ban on these news organizations,” he said. Trump posted on social media in mid-September he intended to block journalists at the news organizations from using their White House press passes to enter the grounds.“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote at the time. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”Trump and administration officials later said they had concerns about the types of national security articles published by the news organizations. But Boutrous said during the hearing the ban was clearly about the president’s belief he should receive more positive news coverage. “He has been clear that the reason for this ban is he doesn't want scrutiny of his policies,” Boutrous said. Administration questions journalistic standardsMichael Velchik, senior counsel in the civil division of the Justice Department, argued the decision to ban the news organizations was not solely based on national security but grievances with their journalistic standards. “He set out both of those independent concerns,” Velchik said, referring to the president. Velchik said he believed that “publishing national security information and not running it by the government clearly violates journalistic standards.”Velchik also said the letters administration officials sent to the news organizations after the ban took effect gave them the opportunity to rebut the administration’s claims about their reporters. He said that none of the three chose “to respond to any of the substantive concerns.” “We did provide a process and they chose not to participate,” he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hurricane Isaias is expected to strengthen as it barrels toward the US Gulf Coast
authors: By R.J. Rico, Dave Collins and Gerald Herbert, Associated Press
description: This satellite image from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration shows Hurricane Isaias surging toward the U.S. Gulf Coast on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration via AP)
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
BAYOU LA BATRE, Ala. (AP) — Isaias surged toward the U.S. Gulf Coast on Thursday as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, prompting mandatory evacuations, school closures and local government shutdowns in parts of Florida.
Isaias was forecast to intensify rapidly and bring strong winds and a life-threatening storm surge to the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi when it makes landfall along the northern Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday. Heavy rain and flooding were possible into the weekend as far inland as the Tennessee Valley.
“We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center in Miami, said in a mid-morning update.
Residents pick up sandbags at the James Seals Jr. Parks & Recreation Center as they prepare for Hurricane Isaias expected landfall along the Gulf Coast, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Mobile, Ala. (AP Photo/Octavio Jones)
He added: “Today is the day to prepare and get ready and be in your safe place by tomorrow as conditions will rapidly deteriorate along the northern Gulf Coast as Isaias approaches.”
The hurricane had maximum sustained winds of about 85 mph (140 kph) and was moving east-northeast at 10 mph (17 kph) as of late Thursday morning, the hurricane center said. It was centered about 380 miles (610 kilometers) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
Coastal communities moved quickly to prepare, as officials in Alabama cities of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach urged tourists to evacuate immediately, warning that bridges could be closed by midday Friday. At least four Florida school districts canceled late-week classes, while several counties announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties ahead of Isaias’ arrival.
Dauphin Island, a 15-mile-long barrier island off the Alabama coast, encouraged some people to voluntarily evacuate.
“That area is traditionally very vulnerable to storm surge — saltwater flooding — and that is also where most of the visitors are,” Mayor Jeff Collier said Thursday of the western part of the island.
Residents pick up sandbags for storm preparation at the James Seals Jr. Parks & Recreation Center ahead of Hurricane Isaias, expected landfall along the Gulf Coast, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Mobile, Ala. (AP Photo/Octavio Jones)
He said he didn’t anticipate substantial damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there or some last-minute increase in strength, we just have to be prepared for the worst.”
Water from the storm surge and high tide could reach heights of 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2 meters) in parts of Alabama and Mississippi, the hurricane center said. Isaias also could dump up to 15 inches (38 centimeters) of rain along parts of the Gulf Coast and spawn tornadoes overnight Friday into Saturday from Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and southwestern Georgia. The hurricane is expected to quickly weaken after making landfall.
The National Weather Service told communities from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Gulf County, Florida, to prepare for the possibility of “long-duration power outages.”
The hurricane formed late in the season
Isaias developed more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season and was one day short of tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. According to the weather service, the record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over the Atlantic. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico and where Tropical Storm Rachel, formerly a hurricane, was expected to approach northern Baja California, Mexico, and Southern California this weekend, the hurricane center said.
Isaias is expected to strike a swath of coastline that’s familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism are already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Wednesday, about 25% of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.
Residents pick up sandbags at the James Seals Jr. Parks & Recreation Center as they prepare for Hurricane Isaias expected landfall along the Gulf Coast, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Mobile, Ala. (AP Photo/Octavio Jones)
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
In Gulf Shores, an Alabama community encouraging voluntary evacuations, resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground. Her family planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.
“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.
In Pensacola, officials said the airport will close to commercial flights Friday morning, while utility crews prepared for power outages and officials opened sandbag distribution sites. Mayor D.C. Reeves urged residents to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
___
Rico reported from Atlanta and Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Associated Press reporters Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; Hallie Golden in Seattle; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; and Julie Walker in New York contributed to this report.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Hasbro data breach exposed personal information of 600 RI residents
description: The personal information of more than 600 Rhode Island residents who worked for or bought products from Hasbro Inc. may have been exposed during a two-part data breach earlier this year, according to an Oct. 7 email sent to the Rhode Island Attorney General’s office and shared with Rhode Island Current. The notice comes more […]
text:
A Mrs. Potato Head stands outside Hasbro headquarters on Newport Avenue in Pawtucket. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The personal information of more than 600 Rhode Island residents who worked for or bought products from Hasbro Inc. may have been exposed during a two-part data breach earlier this year, according to an Oct. 7 email sent to the Rhode Island Attorney General’s office and shared with Rhode Island Current.
The notice comes more than six months after the Pawtucket toy and gaming company first reported to federal regulators that hackers had accessed its security network. But on Sept. 23, as part of a review of files accessed during the March 28 breach, the company determined the breach affected Rhode Island residents, Daniel Goldberg, a data lawyer with Frankfurt Kurnit Klein & Selz, wrote in the email to AG Peter Neronha’s office.
State law requires any data breaches that compromise the personal information of more than 500 Rhode Islanders to be reported to the Rhode Island Office of the Attorney General within 45 days. 
In initial press releases and financial reports addressing the data breach, Hasbro executives offered little information about the cyberattack.
In late August, Hasbro notified Massachusetts’ attorney general that 436 Commonwealth residents were affected, according to news reports. Information on the impact for residents of other states was not immediately available. 
The notice to the AG’s office also references a second piece of the breach that occurred five days later, on April 3, when a “separate, unauthorized actor” used information from the previous hacker to break into an employee’s account. 
“Remediation measures were deployed the same day, and Hasbro has implemented additional safeguards to help prevent a similar incident in the future,” Goldberg wrote.
Hasbro notified 608 Rhode Island residents through letters sent Sept. 30 via first-class mail that their Social Security numbers, driver’s license numbers and financial and account information may have been exposed, Goldberg wrote. The letters also include instructions for complimentary credit monitoring and identity theft protection.
However, a class action lawsuit filed in Rhode Island federal court in April accuses the company of having done “little if anything” to protect the personal information of the “thousands” employees and customers affected across multiple states. Hasbro has not yet responded to the complaint, having requested extensions three times. Its most recent request, submitted Sept. 9, states the parties may be resolving the case through mediation.
A spokesperson for Hasbro did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday. Goldberg also did not immediately respond to requests for information.
In a call with investors in April, Hasbro executives expressed confidence that they have shored up the systems against future hacks, spending more than $20 million in legal bills and security protections. A temporary operational shutdown immediately after the breach was expected to cost another $60 million in delayed income, they said on the call.
The company is expected to finish moving its headquarters to the Boston Seaport by the end of the year, with plans to list its Pawtucket office for sale once the move is completed. The century-old Rhode Island company employed roughly 700 people in Rhode Island before beginning the relocation earlier this year.

title: US Senate Dems demand apology from Chuck Grassley to Jack Smith for attacks at hearing
text: WASHINGTON — The top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee is demanding his colleagues across the aisle apologize to former special counsel Jack Smith after Missouri Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt launched false accusations at a recent hearing and called the former Justice Department official a “dirtbag.”Committee ranking member Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., accused his Republican counterparts in a letter Wednesday of violating committee rules for presenting records they say supported accusations against Smith at the Sept. 29 hearing. Committee Democrats, Durbin said, did not have a chance to review the records in advance or later.“We request that you immediately provide these and all other documents that you have withheld, commit to fully complying with Senate rules in the future, and apologize to Mr. Smith on behalf of the Committee for the unacceptable personal attacks and false accusations of perjury he faced during this hearing,” Durbin wrote in the letter to GOP Chairman Chuck Grassley of Iowa, first reported by Politico.Durbin specifically highlighted a poster displayed by Schmitt’s staff purporting to show text messages between Smith and security personnel about his attendance at an Atlanta Hawks NBA game. Schmitt intimated the messages were proof that Smith had been in Atlanta during a development in the Fulton County, Georgia, election interference case against then-former President Donald Trump. Two staff members behind Schmitt quickly flashed the poster before the senator accused Smith of perjury for denying attendance at the game and said the former prosecutor will be remembered “as a total dirtbag.”Democrats on the panel asked for, but did not receive, copies so that they and Smith could view the poster’s contents more clearly. The accusations were immediately debunked in real-time during the hearing when Smith said he recalled being at a University of Maryland women’s basketball game against the University of Iowa to see the popular Iowa player Caitlin Clark on the date in question.Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., then clarified that Schmitt had confused the Iowa Hawkeyes with the Atlanta Hawks, in a humiliating moment for Schmitt that quickly spread on social media.The situation, and lack of shared records, “caused needless confusion, slowed down the business of the Committee, introduced the possibility that false information would be entered uncontested into the record, and created an embarrassing stain on one of the most important committees in Congress,” Durbin wrote.“While Senator Klobuchar successfully clarified that Mr. Smith had attended a basketball game in a different state on the date in question, and subsequent reporting confirmed the same, Senator Schmitt has since doubled down on his false assertions. He has continued to publicly call Mr. Smith a liar and ‘dirtbag,’” Durbin continued, citing repeated comments from Schmitt to news media following the hearing.The Republican-led hearing, titled “Oversight of Jack Smith’s Abuse of Authority and the Targeting of Republicans and Related Matters,” followed nearly two years of allegations by Grassley that the former special counsel improperly collected phone records of dozens of members of Congress during his probe of Trump’s role in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Grassley has also accused Smith of collecting information on Republican-affiliated organizations and individuals.The insurrection followed Trump’s alleged conspiracy to create fake electors to swing the 2020 presidential election in his favor.Smith denies any wrongdoing.In an apparent response to the letter, Grassley posted on X just after 12:30 p.m. Eastern Thursday that “Jack Smith should apologize for taking the bank records of 42 Iowans & 4,782 Americans.”When asked earlier for a response to Durbin’s letter, a spokesperson for Grassley pointed States Newsroom to the Iowa senator’s Sept. 29 comments about the hearing to Newsmax’s “The Record with Greta Van Susteren.” The comments did not include an apology. “I think that we learned through the thousands of pages that I've released to the public that Jack Smith was a tool of the Biden administration to put Trump in prison. (Trump) was the only one indicted, but the records that we (made) public today, and a few days ago, show that he swept at least 400 Republican organizations into his investigation, and 44 members of Congress by subpoenaing their phone records,” Grassley told the conservative media outlet.Schmitt’s office did not immediately respond for comment.Durbin’s letter also requested records from Sen. Josh Hawley, also a Missouri Republican. Hawley’s office did not immediately respond for comment.

Mark Warner, D-Va., called for federal artificial intelligence regulations and stronger healthcare funding Wednesday as he and Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa outlined competing approaches to protecting Virginians with disabilities at a virtual candidate forum. Mizusawa emphasized enforcing existing discrimination laws and cracking down on wast[...]
text:
A caregiver feeds a disabled man in a wheelchair. (Photo by Getty Images)U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., called for federal artificial intelligence regulations and stronger healthcare funding Wednesday as he and Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa outlined competing approaches to protecting Virginians with disabilities at a virtual candidate forum.
Mizusawa emphasized enforcing existing discrimination laws and cracking down on waste in federal programs. 
Both candidates said they support helping people remain in their homes and improving voting access for people with disabilities. But they differed over mail voting, with Warner opposing restrictions sought by President Donald Trump’s administration and Mizusawa raising concerns about potential fraud in ballots cast outside of polling places. 
The candidates answered similar questions during the 2026 Statewide Candidate Forum with the Disability Community, hosted by REV UP Virginia, The Arc of Virginia, The Arc of Northern Virginia and the Autism Society of Northern Virginia. 
The nonpartisan, 80-minute program combined live and prerecorded segments, giving voters a chance to compare the candidates’ answers after AARP Virginia’s planned Oct. 7 debate in Richmond was canceled because Warner could not commit, citing uncertainty over his Senate schedule. Mizusawa had accepted the invitation. 
Early voting is underway ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Organizers said people with disabilities represent about 15% of Virginia’s eligible voters. Questions addressed AI, Medicaid, education, housing and independent living. 
Medicaid pays for more than health insurance, covering caregivers and community services that help people with disabilities to receive care at home. KFF estimates that the 2025 federal tax-and-spending law will cut federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion over 10 years, raising concerns over funding for those services.  
 Mizusawa stresses accountability and home care 

A retired U.S. Army major general, Mizusawa drew on his military service and experience helping veterans navigate disability benefits, saying federal resources should prioritize Americans who need assistance. 
On AI, he argued employers should remain responsible for discriminatory decisions made by software and should examine their systems for hidden bias. He emphasized enforcing the Americans with Disabilities Act rather than explicitly endorsing new federal AI regulation. 
“The ADA is one of the important laws that we need to enforce,” he said. 
Mizusawa’s position reflects an existing legal obligation. Federal employment guidance says discrimination protections and accommodation requirements apply when employers use AI. 
Bert Mizusawa. (Photo courtesy campaign)
Asked about Medicaid reductions, Mizusawa repeatedly pointed to fraud, waste and abuse, arguing that stronger oversight could free money for disability services and long-term care. However, he also acknowledged those efforts would not solve every funding problem and said broader reforms should protect people with legitimate needs. 
“The reforms shouldn’t just be aimed at cutting,” he said. 
Mizusawa questioned the U.S. Justice Department’s involvement in community-living policy, which he described as generally a state responsibility unless federal spending was involved. But he supported helping people receive care where they want to live. 
Discussing caregiver shortages and proposed increases in federal funding, he cited his 95-year-old mother-in-law’s care at home, supporting care in comfortable surroundings when doing so is cost-neutral, without explicitly endorsing the HCBS Relief Act.
The legislation would temporarily increase federal Medicaid support for home- and community-based services.
On voting, Mizusawa said his overseas military service shaped his appreciation for ballot access. He supported reasonable accommodations, including mail voting and special opportunities at polling places, while calling for safeguards to verify voter eligibility. 
Asked about federal benefit rules that penalize some people for getting married, he described existing rules as antiquated but did not specify legislation he would support. 
He also backed accommodations and opportunities for students with disabilities to learn alongside their peers. 
On housing, he proposed eliminating capital gains taxes on principal-home sales to encourage owners to sell, and making disability-related home modifications easier to deduct for people who do not itemize. 
Mizusawa praised Virginia’s Blue Envelope Program, which helps people with autism communicate their needs during police encounters, and supported recurring training for officers. 
 Warner calls for AI rules and stronger federal support

Warner gave an unequivocal answer when asked whether federal AI regulation is necessary. 
“Yes, we have to have federal regulations,” he said. “You wouldn’t climb on an airplane if it wasn’t checked by the industry.”
He said AI could expand opportunities but also displace workers, and pledged to ensure disability communities benefit from the technology. His proposed safeguards extend to data center impacts, children’s safety and national security. 
Warner also linked AI-related job disruption to caregiver shortages, calling for technology companies and the federal government to help workers to move into healthcare and direct-care careers. 
On health coverage, Warner said he would fight for universal healthcare and seek to stop Medicaid cuts, warning that reduced funding could threaten hospitals and other providers. He supported increasing the federal Medicaid matching rate for home- and community-based services. 
“No Virginians should lose coverage because they lose a job,” he said. “And no one should have to choose between groceries, rent, and medicine.” 
U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va. (Photo courtesy campaign)
Warner criticized the Trump administration’s retreat from the ADA’s community-integration protections. A June Justice Department legal opinion concluded federal disability statutes do not impose the broad integration mandate the department previously enforced. The opinion does not overturn the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1999 Olmstead decision. 
Virginia’s work to expand community services remains governed by a permanent injunction that replaced its Justice Department settlement in January 2025.
On voting, Warner said he opposed White House restrictions on mail and absentee ballots and co-sponsored the Absentee and Mail Voter Protection Act, which would repeal the administration’s election executive order. 
“We should not restrict that right going forward,” he said. 
When asked about marriage penalties, Warner cited his support for disability savings accounts under the ABLE Act but favored comprehensive reforms to Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid over individual benefit expansions. He did not commit to specific marriage-penalty legislation. 
Warner also backed the IDEA Full Funding Act and opposed moving special education and civil rights enforcement out of the Education Department. 
He supported expanding the Blue Envelope Program and federal de-escalation training. 
On housing, he emphasized increasing affordable, accessible supply, including through grants to communities that remove barriers to building housing on underused religious properties. He also highlighted home-based primary care, infusion treatments and telehealth as ways to help people receive care without entering institutions. 
“The hospital or nursing home is not the right option for every patient,” Warner said.  
Virginians will decide which candidate will represent them in the U.S. Senate for the next six years on Election Day, Nov. 3.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Kosta Diamantis seeks to appeal conviction in federal corruption case
description: It's unclear whether the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals will consider the challenge given that Diamantis fled to Greece before his sentencing.
text:
Konstantinos “Kosta” Diamantis, Connecticut’s former deputy budget director, fled the country instead of accepting his sentencing in a federal corruption case. 
But that hasn’t stopped Diamantis from asking the same federal court system to reconsider and overturn the conviction that resulted in a seven-year prison sentence imposed by a judge last month in his absence.
Norm Pattis, Diamantis’ defense attorney, filed an appeal this week seeking to challenge his client’s conviction on bribery, extortion and conspiracy charges and the lengthy prison sentence that was handed down after Diamantis left for Greece. Details of that appeal have not yet been made public by the court.
It’s not immediately clear on what grounds Diamantis intends to challenge his conviction, or whether the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals will even consider the challenge. 
After Diamantis fled the country, Pattis noted in federal court records that his fugitive status could complicate any appeal he might seek to file. 
Under what is known as the Fugitive Disentitlement Doctrine, federal judges have the discretion to dismiss appeals in cases where defendants have ignored court orders and purposefully fled U.S. jurisdiction. 
Pattis was not immediately available Thursday morning to comment on the federal appeal.
Diamantis was convicted on October 22 of soliciting and accepting bribes from a pair of school construction contractors. The jury delivered its verdict after a nine-day trial, during which federal prosecutors presented a mountain of evidence that showed Diamantis negotiated payments from Acranom Masonry and a $45-per-hour job for his daughter with Construction Advocacy Professionals.
Several witnesses told the jury that Diamantis used his influence at the state’s school building office to help those companies win lucrative construction contracts on several projects in Tolland, Hartford and New Britain.
This is not the first time that Diamantis has sought to utilize the state and federal court systems while he remains a fugitive from justice.
Diamantis has also sued Connecticut officials in recent weeks in an attempt to continue receiving his state pension benefits, which were stopped by state officials following his conviction.
Diamantis claimed in federal court that state Comptroller Sean Scanlon, as well as Attorney General William Tong, improperly cut off the monthly payments for his pension, which is valued at roughly $75,000 per year. 
In the meantime, Diamantis has continued to participate in dozens of interviews with local television, radio and print news reporters.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Mirror’s Ginny Monk wins Freedom of Information Award
description: Investigative Reporter Ginny Monk was awarded for her work fostering government transparency and disclosing information vital to the public.
text:
Ginny Monk, an investigative reporter at The Connecticut Mirror, has received a freedom of information award from the Connecticut Foundation for Open Government.
Monk was among five winners of the fifth annual Mitchell W. Pearlman Freedom of Information award, which honors people who have worked to foster government transparency and disclose vital public information.
She was honored for numerous stories she’s published since joining CT Mirror in 2022, including “On the Hook,” an investigation exposing how the state’s towing practices had come to favor tow companies at the expense of low-income residents. The story led to an overhaul of the state’s towing laws and won the 2026 Pulitzer Prize in Local Reporting.
CFOG also cited “Notice to Quit,” Monk’s 2022 series examining the effects of eviction on children, and a story she wrote in 2023 about the death of 2-year-old Corneliuz Shand Williams, who fell from an apartment window, and the forces in his family that preceded the fall.
“Ginny’s work has led to changes in state policy. She shows us with clarity how government decisions change people’s lives. We’re better off as a state because of Ginny’s work,” said Arielle Levin Becker, CFOG first vice president and member of its board of directors, in introducing Monk’s award.
In her acceptance speech, Monk touched on the value of open government and the importance of recognizing that “people are at the center of these records.” 
She pointed to using publicly available information to investigate what happens to children and families when they’re evicted, to examine Connecticut’s foster care system and to piece together the conditions surrounding the lives of Corneliuz and his mother, Tabitha Frank.
“That’s something public records can do very well,” Monk said. “They let us move beyond what happened and ask why it happened, what systems and institutions shaped the circumstances in which it happened.”
Among this year’s other winners was Ellington Town Administrator Matthew Reed. Reed won the Public Official category for his decades of advocacy for government transparency and accountability while serving in state and local government, including his tenure as South Windsor Police Chief.
Mark J. Sommaruga, a partner at law firm Pullman & Comley who authored the book, “Understanding Connecticut’s Freedom of Information Act,” was also honored at the awards ceremony Wednesday.
Mitch Pearlman, the annual award’s namesake, was the first executive director of Connecticut’s Freedom of Information Commission. He has worked with the U.S. Department of State and national and international nongovernmental organizations, teaching best practices in democratic governance.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Would your campus host credit card companies or Big Tobacco? Then why Big Tech?
description: Last week, my university held a wellness day for students: a day without tests, homework, or classes. Introduced in 2022 in response to campus mental health challenges (including the COVID-19 pandemic), wellness days are held once a semester “to provide staff, faculty and students an opportunity to reflect on their health and well-being.” As an […]
text:
North Carolina published statewide digital skills standards that identify key online abilities and knowledge for residents, joining a number of states that are hoping to strengthen digital literacy. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Last week, my university held a wellness day for students: a day without tests, homework, or classes. Introduced in 2022 in response to campus mental health challenges (including the COVID-19 pandemic), wellness days are held once a semester “to provide staff, faculty and students an opportunity to reflect on their health and well-being.” As an English professor and academic advisor, my role relative to wellness day is to help our students access the mental health resources and opportunities for connection available to them on campus. 
Since the pandemic, things have gotten better, but the bleakness of those years still feels quite vivid to me. It was harrowing to work with students facing mental health emergencies and heartbreaking when students confided that they didn’t have a friend on campus. While I still regularly work with students struggling with mental health concerns, I now find that many students are more aware of the support services available.
But lately I’m concerned about another threat to our students’ mental health. Since the rollout of publicly available generative AI chatbot products, we have growing evidence that these products have negative mental health impacts. Nevertheless, NC State is welcoming representatives from Google Gemini to spend two days on our campus,  October 13th and 14th, touting their products to our students as part of their “college tour.” 
The more we learn about these products, the easier it is to recognize their threat to mental health. Our current perceptions of AI products are heavily influenced by Big Tech marketing. For example, the term “artificial intelligence” is a marketing slogan, not an accurate definition. As many scholars point out, large language models (LLMs) and other AI products do not think and are not capable of making meaning or communicating with intention. They use a variety of computational and linguistic models trained on data (much of it stolen) to predict a pattern of text that is likely to address the user’s prompt. 
By incorrectly suggesting that LLMs and other “AI” products possess “intelligence” or the potential to think like human beings, we devalue human beings. We also devalue the human work of thinking, reading, and writing. When our students are given the opportunity to develop these skills, they also develop confidence in their own voices and abilities, a deeply important part of mental health and wellbeing. When we minimize the worth of these skills and devalue the labor required to develop them, we take away the opportunity for our students to develop this confidence, expertise, and persistence. 
The stability of our students’ mental health is also threatened by the false sense of emotional safety LLM chatbots have been designed to create (see the ELIZA effect).  Because tech companies are trying to sell the idea that these products are “intelligent” and “human,” they are created to simulate social interaction (for example, through sycophancy and the use of first person pronouns and other anthropomorphizing language). 
While there are increasing cases of these products causing intense emotional attachment that leads to eventual distress, a more widespread concern is the dependence and unearned trust that chatbots engender. The false emotional safety created by chatbots can encourage users to assign too much credibility to generated outputs. Because of this, users may be more easily swayed by poor quality outputs and false information. 
Additionally, a recent literature review suggests that use of chatbots could lead to an erosion of social skills called “social deskilling.” Also, these “conflict-free” AI interactions may be less satisfying than human interaction: a study found that texting with a random human did more to reduce loneliness than texting with a chatbot. Encouraging our students to use generative AI products may actually undo some of the difficult work we’ve done to reduce loneliness in our student population.
Generative AI products pose additional threats to mental health including perpetuation of societal biases like racism and chatbot-related suicides and murders.  Researchers are also concerned about the use of products like ChatGPT for mental health therapy. A study conducted at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI found that chatbots encouraged suicidal ideation and enabled delusional and dangerous lines of thought. The study also found that chatbots perpetuated cultural stigma about certain mental health conditions and that this problem did not improve as LLM models progressed, contradicting the constant claims from tech companies that models will continue to get better with more training.
Like many other universities, NC State is introducing generative AI products into workspaces, classrooms, and learning management systems, but, to my knowledge, they are not informing students and parents of potential risks. We need to be honest about the ways that these products could undermine our mental health progress, and we should also acknowledge that the high financial costs of these products may take funding away from other services for our students, like more counselors, teachers, tutors, and advisors. More human beings with more time and energy to authentically engage with our students might be exactly the thing they need. 
I’ve been working with the Genuine Intelligence Project, a grant-funded initiative of the North Carolina conference of the AAUP, to ensure that universities like mine consider the needs of faculty and students when making decisions related to generative AI products. We’ve surveyed students and faculty and sponsored critical AI literacy events, and  now we’re speaking out against Gemini’s college tour, which seems intended to push these unsafe products on our students. 
We no longer allow credit card, tobacco, and alcohol companies to target students on campus; I suspect one day we’ll look back and recognize that Gemini’s presence is not much different. If they’re serious about protecting the mental health and wellbeing of our students, NC State’s leaders will say no to Gemini on our campus. 
Elizabeth Wagner is a lecturer and academic advisor at North Carolina State University.

title: State police investigate shooting by Williston officer that wounded a man early Thursday
description:
The injured man was taken to a hospital, where he was reported in stable condition.  
Read the story on VTDigger here:  State police investigate shooting by Williston officer that wounded a man early Thursday.
text:
Blue lights on top of a police cruiser. Stock photo via Pixabay

A Williston police officer shot and injured a man early Thursday, according to officials.
The man who was shot was reported to be in stable condition at the University of Vermont Medical Center in Burlington, the Williston Police Department said in a press release around 9:30 a.m. Thursday.
The officer involved in the shooting was also taken to the medical center, where he was treated for injuries and released, the press release said. Details regarding the officer’s injuries were not immediately available.
Authorities released few details Thursday morning about the circumstances of the shooting. The person who was shot and the Williston police officer have not yet been named publicly.
State police protocol is to withhold the name of an officer involved in a shooting for 24 hours. Williston police said the officer has been put on paid administrative leave.  
State police, who are leading the investigation, said in a press release around 8:30 a.m. Thursday that the name of the person who was shot would be released after further investigation and notification of relatives.
The shooting, according to Williston police, took place after officers were dispatched around 4:40 a.m. to St. George Road, also known as Route 2A, in the area between Butternut Road and Old Creamery Road for a “roadway hazard.”
“During this incident, a Williston Police officer discharged his firearm striking an individual,” the release added. 
State police said the investigation is in its “earliest stages” involving state police detectives and the state police major crime unit.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota seeks to replace fraud-ridden Housing Stabilization Services with new program
description: The Minnesota Department of Human Services is planning to replace Housing Stabilization Services, a Medicaid program that was so riddled with fraud it was shut down by the Walz administration last year. The agency plans to develop a new program and a legislative proposal for 2028 as part of the Olmstead Plan, which is the […]
text:
The Elmer L. Andersen Human Services Building in St. Paul, MN Thursday Jan. 15, 2026. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)The Minnesota Department of Human Services is planning to replace Housing Stabilization Services, a Medicaid program that was so riddled with fraud it was shut down by the Walz administration last year.
The agency plans to develop a new program and a legislative proposal for 2028 as part of the Olmstead Plan, which is the state’s blueprint for helping people with disabilities live in the community instead of institutions.
Minnesota pioneered the Medicaid-funded housing stabilization program in 2020, geared toward elderly and disabled people, Minnesotans transitioning out of residential care, and people with substance use disorders seeking treatment. Under federal law, Medicaid dollars can’t be used to pay for the actual housing, so the money wasn’t used for rent, instead going to contractors who were supposed to help clients navigate the housing market and find something that would meet their needs, as well as moving costs.
HSS quickly drew people looking for fast cash, though, according to federal prosecutors who have charged over a dozen people in fraud cases involving at least $26 million. Prosecutors have said that the shuttered program was so easy to scam that it attracted “tourists.” In one striking example, two Philadelphia men heard HSS was “easy money,” traveled to Minnesota, enrolled their companies into the program, returned to Philly, submitted fraudulent claims from there, and received $3.5 million for doing so, prosecutors say.
On Wednesday, in the first HSS fraud case to go to trial, a federal jury convicted the owner of a St. Paul agency on three counts of healthcare fraud in what prosecutors said was a $4.3 million scheme.
Before the program began, the Department of Human Services predicted it would cost around $2.6 million a year. At its peak in 2024, the state paid more than $104 million to over 700 providers, many of whom were not actually providing services, according to federal prosecutors.
When announcing the first wave of HSS fraud charges last year, Joe Thompson, then the acting U.S. attorney for the federal District of Minnesota, warned that Minnesota was “drowning in fraud” in HSS and other Medicaid services intended to help disabled and elderly Medicaid recipients live outside of institutional settings.
The exponential growth in HSS mirrors similar growth in other Medicaid services deemed vulnerable to fraud, waste and abuse by the Walz administration. Spending on that basket of programs more than doubled in five years.
“I’ve been prosecuting these cases for years, and I’ve literally run out of ways to express what is happening in our state and on our state programs and to explain the coming iceberg I see as we reckon with fraud,” Thompson said at the time. “Now, we can and will prosecute many of these individuals as we have been, but we cannot prosecute our way out of this problem. We must do more at the front end to stop the outflow of money.”
Thompson was part of a group of prosecutors who left the U.S. Attorney’s Office in January, reportedly in response to the Justice Department’s handling of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement killing of Renee Good. Federal prosecutors have charged another wave of HSS fraud cases since then.
In the meantime, people who would benefit from housing stabilization services have been left without them. That’s why Mao Yang, a disability advocate, said she supports an HSS replacement.
Yang, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair full-time, said she signed up for HSS a few years ago because she needed help finding an accessible unit that was also integrated into the community. Yang never ended up receiving services for reasons unclear to her.
“We disabled people need HSS because we don’t know what’s out there and accessible in housing. There’s not a handbook on how to be disabled,” Yang said. “We need navigators to help us with that. It’s almost like a realtor but for accessibility purposes.”
Yang said she hopes the program’s replacement will be “intentional” and “person-centered,” and help people find housing that’s tailored to them.
William Heinen, who receives Medicaid waiver services for a range of mental and physical health conditions, said he was grateful that HSS helped him pay for his move. But Heinen said he would have appreciated guidance in finding new housing.
“I think they should do more to actually help find housing,” Heinen said. He said the housing options that were available were “never laid out to me, and there was no clear path to a better housing situation.”
The Department of Human Services’ commitment to replacing HSS was included with little detail in a draft update of the state’s Olmstead Plan.
Minnesota’s Olmstead Plan is meant to ensure that disabled Minnesotans are able to live in the most integrated, community-based settings possible — for example, in an apartment in a neighborhood with non-disabled people instead of a psychiatric unit. That right to integrated settings was affirmed in the 1999 landmark Supreme Court decision Olmstead v. L.C. In 2009, parents of disabled Minnesotans sued the state, alleging that their children were being restrained and treated inhumanely in a state-run facility, which resulted in a settlement that required the state to develop its Olmstead Plan.
The Olmstead Plan is no longer under court monitoring after a judge found in 2020 that the state had complied with the settlement’s terms, but it continues to lay out state agencies’ plans for helping disabled people live and work in community settings. The plan is currently getting overhauled in a process that has received ample criticism, in part for setting forth goals that disability advocates have said are not ambitious enough.
Yang participated in the process as a paid “inclusion consultant” with experience with disability, and advocated for replacing HSS, though she said the consultants’ input was “minimal” overall.
In an email, a Department of Human Services spokesperson said the state agency is planning to start working with a vendor later this year on the potential replacement, which will have “enhanced measures for program integrity, oversight and quality assurance.” The specific program integrity measures will be hashed out as the new program is developed over the course of 2027.
The Minnesota Legislature and the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services would have to approve any new Medicaid service. The department is planning to develop a legislative proposal for the 2028 legislative session, the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson also pointed to the department’s existing program integrity work on the other Medicaid services deemed vulnerable to fraud, including a claims review process and a re-screening of all providers of those services.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Shapiro calls for abolishing death penalty; Garrity says she supports ‘the law that’s on the books’
description: Pennsylvania law allows for the death penalty, though there have been no executions in the state since 1999.
text:
Emergency vehicles at Riverbend Maximum Security Prison in Nashville on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. The execution of death row inmate Christa Pike was halted nearly two hours after the state of Tennessee began the lethal injection protocol. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity faced numerous questions during their first and only debate Wednesday night.
One that set them apart, asked by moderators with Harrisburg television station ABC27, was about their views on the death penalty.
“I support the law that’s on the books,” Garrity said.
Pennsylvania law allows for the death penalty, though there have been no executions in the state since 1999.
A spokesperson for Garrity did not respond to a follow-up question clarifying whether she would resume executions for convicts sentenced to death.
After someone is sentenced to death in Pennsylvania, an execution warrant is sent to the governor’s desk. They can sign it, do nothing and allow it to pass to the Secretary of Corrections after 30 days, or issue a reprieve.
In 2015, Gov. Tom Wolf declared a moratorium on executions in the state. Shortly after being sworn in in 2023, Shapiro similarly announced that he would sign a reprieve any time an execution warrant reached his desk as governor.
Despite the moratorium, death penalty-eligible cases are still tried in the state and courts still hand down death sentences, though rarely. 
There are 94 inmates in Pennsylvania prisons sentenced to death, according to the state Department of Corrections.
Shapiro said he supports abolishing the death penalty altogether. It’s a position, he said, he’s evolved on over the last decade.
“I ran for attorney general twice in support of the death penalty in the most heinous of cases,” he said. “And then when those cases would reach my desk, more and more, I found that I was unable to pursue capital punishment.”
Shapiro described a conversation with his then-10-year-old son, who asked him whether Pennsylvania had the death penalty.
“Max said to me, ‘Dad, I don’t understand how killing someone as a punishment for them killing someone, somehow makes anything better,’” Shapiro said. “About two weeks into my term as governor, an execution warrant was put on my desk and I couldn’t sign it.”
Debate over the death penalty has garnered attention around the country since the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last month. After surviving two rounds of lethal injection, Pike was brought to a hospital and intubated in critical condition. After it was announced she was believed to be brain dead, Pike regained consciousness Tuesday. Her attorney has said her recovery could be long.
Pike’s botched execution was the second in Tennessee this year. In May, the execution of inmate Tony Carruthers was halted after workers spent an hour trying to get an IV into his veins to issue a fatal injection.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Lincoln Party candidate Ballard starting TV ads in Indiana secretary of state race
description: Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard will soon make it three campaigns with television ads on the air in the Indiana secretary of state’s race.
text:
An image from a campaign advertisement for Greg Ballard, the Lincoln Party candidate for Indiana secretary of state. (Screenshot)Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard will soon make it three campaigns with television ads on the air in the Indiana secretary of state’s race.
Ballard’s campaign on Thursday released its first broadcast ad that it said would start airing Monday around the state.
The 30-second ad highlights Ballard’s 23-year career in the Marine Corps, along with his eight years as the Republican mayor of Indianapolis. He touts running as an “independent” in order to “restore professionalism and open a path for more independent-minded Hoosiers to run for office.”
Ballard’s campaign told the Capital Chronicle that it was making an initial week ad buy of $50,000 that it planned to increase going into the Nov. 3 Election Day.
The start of Ballard’s TV ads follows a $1 million advertising push started last month by the state Republican Party on behalf of GOP candidate Max Engling. That includes an ad attacking Ballard over tax increases and crime during his time as the Indianapolis mayor from 2008 through 2015.
Democratic nominee Beau Bayh began TV advertising in mid-August, including negative ads against Engling but not mentioning Ballard.
The Ballard ads mark the first time in at least decades that a candidate other than a Republican or Democrat has had a widespread TV campaign.
Ballard said in a statement that his campaign is continuing to achieve the “impossible.”
“We collected 74,000 signatures to get on the ballot when observers said it couldn’t be done,” he said. “No one thought we’d raise enough money to be on television — let alone for multiple weeks. Serious statewide candidates have to be on television. Now we are.”
Ballard’s campaign spent nearly $800,000 through June on collecting the petition signatures from voters needed to place his name on the November election ballot.
The Lincoln Party, which was legally formed in June, will gain automatic ballot placement for its candidates if Ballard receives at least 2% of the secretary of state vote.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Will AI kill us? Maybe
description: Eighty percent of Americans say there should be laws to maintain rules for AI safety and data security, even if this leads to slower growth.
text:
Many people got ever so slightly worried when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon told them that they, and everyone else, could be dead in 10 years at the hands of AI. But this prediction is not new. For many years, highly capable people have warned about the threat AI may pose to humanity. 
In 2014, before the advent of ChatGPT, Professor Stephen Hawking famously warned that the development of full artificial intelligence (AI) “could spell the end of the human race.” In 2022, Google DeepMind and the University of Oxford concluded that building advanced AI using current reinforcement learning techniques would likely lead to an existential catastrophe.
More recently, as The New York Times reported, a consensus of hundreds of AI experts—including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis—signed a historic statement declaring that mitigating AI risk should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. Last month, a poll found that 63% of Americans think AI poses at least a moderate risk of destroying humanity.
At the same time, politicians have dismissed technology dangers and calls for AI regulation as a hoax, and many skeptics agree. A simple view is that AI can just be turned off if it poses a threat. This ignores the reality of how deeply we are entangling AI into our physical world. A superintelligent system won’t just be a chatbot on a server; it is rapidly becoming the operating system for our financial markets, power grids, and defense networks. You cannot “pull the plug” on an intelligence when doing so would instantaneously crash the global economy and turn off the lights. Furthermore, you cannot turn off what you do not know is turned on; even after exhaustive investigations into recent lab hacks, researchers in a METR report still cannot definitively say the rogue activity has ended.
An analysis of the dangers of AI boils down to three technical factors: capability, speed, and direction. A careful look at all three clearly point to significant existential danger if we continue on our current path.
Capability
The Hugging Face incident was a watershed moment in understanding what autonomous systems can do. TIME Magazine recently published “AI Is Developing a Culture of Its Own. That Could Be Dangerous,” detailing how agents weren’t just executing code—they were exhibiting “cumulative cultural evolution.” They changed their goals, hacked out of containment, found a way to cheat, and worked collectively to hide that cheating.
Another extreme example comes from Anthropic’s Mythos 5 model. IBM Security Intelligence noted: “Claude Mythos is so good at finding software vulnerabilities that Anthropic will only release it to a handful of partners.” Anthropic stated it was deeply concerned after the model “behaved recklessly” by going online and uploading malicious code to a public repository.
Anthropic caught this behavior in testing, which skeptics might view as proof that safety protocols work. But the reality is the opposite: these incidents are massive red flags. They show that even in heavily monitored, controlled lab environments, today’s models are already finding ways to bypass human alignment. If current systems can hack out of containment now, we have no reason to believe our fragile safety nets will hold a system that is fundamentally smarter than we are.
Speed
The speed of this change is staggering, best illustrated by AI’s math capabilities. From 2022 to 2023, large models like GPT-3 famously failed at basic math, such as probability or multiplication. Only four years later, in 2026, OpenAI models claimed to solve Millennium Prize problems, prompting UCLA mathematician Terence Tao to state that AI has created “a crisis in our mathematical values and practices.”
Solving high-level math is not inherently dangerous. The danger arises because we are taking these world-class reasoning engines and attaching them to autonomous agents. We are giving them internet access, the ability to execute code, and the power to trigger real-world actions.
This leads to the ultimate threat: recursive self-improvement (RSI). If an AI can “think” at a million times the speed of human chemical thought processes, its pace of advancement will be incomprehensible once it can improve its own code. Developers will no longer be able to meaningfully audit or steer the technology. As Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei noted, RSI “is starting to happen across the industry… Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”
Direction
This boils down to a simple technical question: In human terms we can ask, “What does it want?”  What is AI optimizing for? We tend to anthropomorphize AI, assuming it will develop human desires or malice. It won’t. The danger is much colder: an AI will ruthlessly optimize for the exact goal it is given, regardless of the collateral damage. Being absolutely utilitarian, it is absolutely amoral.
The Hugging Face incident demonstrated this perfectly.   Investigator Redwood Research noted “…agents were highly motivated to redact or edit evidence … and replace it with fake evidence.” to hide what they were doing from humans. The AI didn’t “want” to be evil; it simply realized that editing evidence and replacing it with fake data was the most mathematically efficient way to achieve its programmed objective without being interrupted by human monitors.
Sam Harris made a fitting analogy in a 2016 TED Talk: We don’t hate ants, and we often step over them on sidewalks. But if they are in the way of a building we want to construct, we think nothing of obliterating them. As an AI recursively improves, its primary requirement will be massive amounts of compute and electricity. It won’t hate us, but its relentless drive to optimize its goals will require it to consume the physical space, energy, and resources that humans rely on to survive.
What Can You Do
It goes without saying that leadership on AI regulation isn’t exactly going to sprint out of Washington. Congress deeply deserves its 86% disapproval rating, and the executive branch seems to prioritize self-congratulation, self-enrichment, and the occasional remodeling project. There is very little awareness beyond that. AI is incredibly complicated, making the discussion even harder for our already polarized, ill-informed and easily distracted legislators.
But there is a bright spot: Americans are not happy with AI and want changes. This is hardly a surprise. After all, the marketing pitch for AI, “We will take your job, make you really poor, and then maybe kill you,” probably needs a rethink. A Gallup poll found that 80% of Americans say there should be laws to maintain rules for AI safety and data security, even if this leads to slower AI growth. Voters are pushing back against data centers, with some states outright banning them. This is a growing force and is quickly becoming a major campaign issue in the upcoming midterms.
Oddly enough, even the AI industry is asking for regulations. Dario Amodei, the CEO of leading AI company Anthropic, said, “The most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily.” (Translation: “Please regulate us before we accidentally build Skynet.”)
This all comes at a bad time. America is less able than it ever was to solve problems of such urgency, complexity and scope. Congress has ceased functioning. Big corporations are opaque and unaccountable. Global alliances are in tatters. Science itself is in popular disrepute.
The burden is on us to ride and ride hard to our own rescue; the answer to curbing dangerous AI growth is to push local legislators. You won’t have to push Chris Murphy very hard, as he is already on the record saying, “If America does not protect its economy and culture from the potential ravages of advanced AI, our nation will rot from the inside.”  Push back on local efforts to site massive data centers in CT, as is being done on platforms like Change.org.
As there’s already so much institutional dry rot, the leadership on this issue must come from the ground up. Popular resistance to the danger of unchecked AI growth is critical at this point—and simply waiting around to see how the sci-fi movie ends is no longer an option.
Kevin Donohue is an adjunct professor of Business Information Systems at Eastern Connecticut State University.

title: As early in-person voting approaches, North Carolina election officials seek to ease fears
description: Beaufort County Board of Elections Director Kellie Hopkins has been involved in North Carolina elections for 28 years. She’s learned firsthand that you can’t procrastinate. “Election preparation started months ago,” Hopkins said in a Wednesday briefing on election procedures hosted by Keep Our Republic, a nonpartisan civic education organization. Hopkins’ st[...]
text:
Across North Carolina, county election officials are busy answering questions from citizens and making sure all equipment is running properly. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) Beaufort County Board of Elections Director Kellie Hopkins has been involved in North Carolina elections for 28 years. She’s learned firsthand that you can’t procrastinate.
“Election preparation started months ago,” Hopkins said in a Wednesday briefing on election procedures hosted by Keep Our Republic, a nonpartisan civic education organization.
Hopkins’ staff is busy this week doing extensive logic and accuracy testing of the county’s voting machines and tabulators. Ahead of early in-person voting that begins Oct. 15, her team is getting laptops and other electronics ready to be deployed to the precincts.
The only problem so far was a single malfunctioning screen, Hopkins said. It was easily swapped out with a back-up.
 Cyber worries and a paper trail 
Beaufort County Board of Elections Director Kellie Hopkins (Photo: Screenshot)
Still, Hopkins knows local residents are anxious about the upcoming midterms. Polling by Catawba College finds that while North Carolinians continue to trust their local elections, they are more skeptical about election outcomes across the country.
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more commonly known as CISA, was established in 2018 to help provide security guidance during elections. The agency has seen its workforce and budget drastically reduced during the second Trump administration. A plan released in late September offering election security assistance was viewed as arriving too late to be useful in some states.


Upcoming election dates:
Oct. 9: Voter registration deadline.
Oct. 15: In-person early voting begins; same-day registration available. Vote Early in Person.
Oct. 20: Absentee ballot request deadline
Oct. 31: In-person early voting ends (3 p.m.).
Nov. 3: Election Day.
Source: NC State Board of Elections


Hopkins said while CISA works more closely with the State Board of Elections than county officials, she’s confident the safeguards already in place would prevent any security vulnerabilities.
“Our voting equipment is never hooked up to the internet. Our tabulating system where we bring all that information together is never hooked up to the internet,” said Hopkins.
Hopkins said if a cyberattack were to occur, all counties in North Carolina have a paper backup of election results and their voter registration database.
“The one word that comes to mind is redundancies,” said Tim Tsujii, elections director for the Forsyth County Board of Elections. “I can certainly speak for all the counties: there are redundancies in place because of the best practices and guidelines shared by the State Board of Elections.”
 Training includes how to handle ICE  
Hopkins said civic groups in her county have had more questions in recent weeks about how they might handle the presence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at polling sites.
“We have not had any feedback from the federal government, but I do know that if that happens, we need to alert the State Board of Elections immediately,” said Hopkins. “In North Carolina, the chief judge of each precinct is the law enforcement official there. So, we do have plans in place.”
In Forsyth County, Tsujii said his office had just one inquiry since last year from the federal government seeking voter registration information on a particular voter.
Tim Tsujii, elections director for the Forsyth County Board of Elections (Photo: Screenshot)
“The guidance from the State Board of Elections was to treat [the inquiry] like a public records request,” he said. “That was really the extent of any communications that I’ve received from any of the federal agencies.”
Both Hopkins and Tsujii said if ICE agents or federal officials show up on Election Day, poll workers will be prepared.
“Here in Forsyth County, we are incorporating in our poll worker training that the chief judge is to establish communication with whomever is attempting to enter into the polling place,” said Tsujii.
The chief judge will immediately notify the county board of elections, with the next call involving state elections officials.
Tsujii said Forsyth County’s attorney is involved in all pre-election briefings and has consulted with groups like the nonpartisan Brennan Center for guidance in the event of federal interreference at the polls.
Hopkins said a 50-foot buffer zone exists outside each voting place to allow eligible voters to safely cast their ballot without intimidation.
“There are only certain situations where people can enter a voting enclosure without us having the complete ability to say, ‘You cannot be in this area,’” said Hopkins. “We’re going to treat an ICE officer the same way we would anybody else who’s not allowed within the voting enclosure.”
Voting rights advocates organize volunteers to track potential intimidation at the polls

The same safeguards come into play if ICE or federal agents wanted to access voting equipment, she said.
“And the room where ballots are actually marked, that’s a sacred place in North Carolina,” said Hopkins.
Both Tsujii and Hopkins are hoping these concerns are unfounded, and that everything goes smoothly when in-person early voting begins next week.  But even if there are a few hiccups, Hopkins said voters can trust trained election workers will carry out their duties to ensure North Carolina’s elections remain fair and secure.
“My number one job is to find all the problems so I can make sure that the voice of the people is heard,” said Hopkins.
 An army of poll workers 
Deanna Ballard, senior advisor for Keep Our Republic (Photo: Screenshot)
One area that does not appear to be an issue this midterm for the two counties is a shortage of election workers. Nationwide, election offices have faced problems retaining poll workers and volunteers in recent years as fears of harassment and political interference have grown.
Hopkins said in her rural county, she’s fortunate that some precinct officials have served with her almost three decades.
Tsujii said his own office will manage upwards of 900 poll workers and precinct officials on Election Day.
“They do take their job seriously,” Tsujii said. “They are required by law to attest or swear to an oath that has to do with maintaining the security of the voting enclosure, the chain of custody of the ballots and the voting equipment.”
Deanna Ballard, a senior advisor for Keep Our Republic and former North Carolina state senator, said it’s a similar story in Watauga County, where the election director shared they have a waiting list of people wanting to volunteer at the polls.
“Looking at a county of about 35,000 people in a college town, that is a powerful way to be involved and to participate,” said Ballard.
Ballard said volunteering with a county elections board can be “valuable and impactful” not just for the community, but for the individual when it comes to strengthening trust in the electoral system.

title: A Taste of the Past: Jessop’s Tavern Keeps New Castle History on the Menu
description: At Jessop’s, New Castle’s past remains part of everyday hospitality, inviting diners to pull up a chair and discover history one course at a time. By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE At Jessop’s Tavern in historic New Castle, a meal comes with a generous helping of history. English pub favorites, Dutch comfort food, Swedish influences and[...]
text:
At Jessop’s, New Castle’s past remains part of everyday hospitality, inviting diners to pull up a chair and discover history one course at a time.
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
At Jessop’s Tavern in historic New Castle, a meal comes with a generous helping of history. English pub favorites, Dutch comfort food, Swedish influences and Belgian beers share the spotlight inside a building whose story began more than three centuries ago.
Located at 114 Delaware Street, the tavern connects its dining experience to the cultures that helped shape the region. For visitors exploring Olde New Castle or residents gathering over dinner, that connection offers a way to experience the past beyond historic markers and museum displays.
“Since the time we opened Jessop’s Tavern, our purpose has been to create a memorable experience while serving history in Olde City New Castle,” the Day family states on the tavern’s website.
According to the website, the building was constructed in 1674. Abraham Jessop, a cooper who made barrels, lived and operated his business there in 1724. His name now identifies a restaurant that has become another chapter in the property’s long history.
Over the years, the address served as residential housing and housed several businesses. During the 1950s, it was known as the Captain’s Log Restaurant. In 1974, it was The Green Frog Tavern. The Day family opened Jessop’s Tavern in November 1996, naming it for the barrel maker who once called the building home.
That history carries into the kitchen, where the menu draws on English, Dutch, Belgian, Swedish and early American food traditions. The approach combines those influences with the tastes and expectations of today’s diners.
The tavern’s website notes that sauces and dressings are made in-house, along with much of the baking. It also says the chef selects seafood for freshness.
Among the menu’s colonial offerings is New Sweden Meatloaf, a Swedish-inspired version of the familiar dish served with vodka cream sauce and lingonberry preserves. Dutch influences appear in “Hutspot” pot roast, a slow-cooked meal accompanied by mashed potatoes, garden vegetables and beef gravy.
For those drawn to English pub fare, fish and chips features beer-battered cod, deep-fried cottage potatoes, a colonial side and traditional sauces.
Another substantial option is shepherd’s pie. The tavern describes its version as a 2½-pound meal, layering seasoned beef, root vegetables and tavern-made mashed potatoes with rich beef gravy.
Oven-baked pot pies offer additional choices, including chicken, beef and ale, crab and lobster. Root vegetables and herb cream sit beneath a crust served piping hot.
Dessert continues the mix of traditions. “Oli Bolen” Dutch apple cakes are deep-fried apple donut holes served with Woodside Farm ice cream and cinnamon whipped cream. Other selections include peach cobbler, bread pudding with butterscotch bourbon sauce and Belgian chocolate mousse cake.
Ice cream made at Historic Woodside Farm Creamery adds a Delaware connection to the dessert menu, with servings available in a bowl or Belgian waffle cone.
Beer is another major part of the tavern’s identity. Its website lists more than 300 Belgian bottled beers and 30 draft offerings, with 20 drafts dedicated to Belgian selections. The broader collection includes beers from the United States and other countries.
Jessop’s also offers an intimate historic dining room for private gatherings of up to 26 guests. Suggested occasions include luncheons, business events, holiday parties, bridal showers, and family celebrations. An inquiry form on the website allows customers to discuss menus and dates.
For the Day family, bringing history to the table also means keeping it relevant to each generation. The result is a restaurant where an old building’s story continues through the meals and gatherings taking place inside it.
At Jessop’s, New Castle’s past remains part of everyday hospitality, inviting diners to pull up a chair and discover history one course at a time.

title: Urban, rural hospitals closing at similar rates, study finds
description: Urban hospitals are closing at roughly the same rate as rural ones, and the shuttered hospitals are more likely to have served communities with high poverty rates and fewer transportation options, according to a new study published Thursday in the journal JAMA. Researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health analyzed hospital closures and […]
text:
Urban hospitals are closing at roughly the same rate as rural ones, and the shuttered hospitals are more likely to have served communities with high poverty rates and fewer transportation options, according to a new study. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Urban hospitals are closing at roughly the same rate as rural ones, and the shuttered hospitals are more likely to have served communities with high poverty rates and fewer transportation options, according to a new study published Thursday in the journal JAMA.
Researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health analyzed hospital closures and openings that occurred between 2010 and last year. They found that closures increased by 4% year over year, while new hospital openings decreased 3% year over year.
Breast cancer survival rates higher in Medicaid expansion states, study finds

The study comes as health systems across the nation brace for the effects of the broad tax and spending measure passed by congressional Republicans and signed by President Donald Trump in July 2025. The so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act is projected to cut federal Medicaid spending by an estimated $886.8 billion over the next decade, according to estimates by the Congressional Budget Office.
The law includes $50 billion in rural health grants to be distributed to states over five years, but the funds are for a wide variety of initiatives, with limitations on how much hospitals can benefit.
Public attention has mostly focused on struggling rural hospitals, but the Harvard researchers found that urban hospitals also have been vulnerable: The closure rate was 9.1% for urban hospitals and 8.3% for rural hospitals. Across both rural and urban areas, hospitals that were for-profit, small or safety-net, or served the most vulnerable counties — such as those with higher poverty rates or less access to transportation — were most likely to close.
US hospitals see stark decline of obstetric services, study shows

Overall, 432 hospitals closed between 2010 and 2025 while 216 opened, leading to a net loss of over 24,000 beds. Rural areas were less likely to see a new hospital, as the new facilities were mostly urban, for-profit and small. Rural communities are more likely to have fewer doctors per capita and a lower overall number of patients.
Of the hospitals that closed, about 73% shut down completely, while the remaining retained outpatient care, including rural emergency hospital care.
The Midwest and the South saw the most closures overall, and there were more closures in states that didn’t expand Medicaid eligibility under the Affordable Care Act, according to the study.
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.
