Colom’s announcement comes after Gov. Tate Reeves on Tuesday said that Mississippi would not enforce prohibitions against using un-taxed diesel meant for farm equipment in highway transport trucks, after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to try to lower the soaring cost of diesel. 
Colom also aired a new ad on Wednesday as part of a seven-figure ad campaign, highlighting rising fuel and goods costs and advocating a raise to the federal minimum wage.

name: Nevada Current
title: City councilman and state Democratic Party chair compete to lead North Las Vegas
description: North Las Vegas City Councilman Scott Black will face Democratic Assemblymember Daniele Monroe-Moreno in a contentious fight over who will become the city’s next mayor.  Five candidates ran during the primary election, but none were able to secure more than 50% of the vote, leading to a general election run off.  Monroe-Moreno, who came in […]
text:
Scott Black, Daniele Monroe-Moreno. (Candidate photos)North Las Vegas City Councilman Scott Black will face Democratic Assemblymember Daniele Monroe-Moreno in a contentious fight over who will become the city’s next mayor. 
Five candidates ran during the primary election, but none were able to secure more than 50% of the vote, leading to a general election run off. 
Monroe-Moreno, who came in first during the primary, obtained 47% of the vote, or 13,809 votes, while Black garnered nearly 42% of the vote, or 12,198 votes.
Current Mayor Pamela Goynes-Brown served on the council since 2015 and only was elected to her first term as mayor 2022. Goynes-Brown, the state’s first Black mayor, was ineligible to run again because her term as mayor counts against a 12-year term limit of elected service in the city government.
If Black wins, he would only be eligible to serve one term because of term limits, which Monroe-Moreno has argued is a detriment to voters. 
Nevada Current interviewed both Black and Monroe-Moreno ahead of the primary election. 
Monroe-Moreno at the time told the Current the people of North Las Vegas need “a mayor who would be elected that could serve them for the next 12 years if blessed to do so with re-election.”
Though both candidates are Democrats, the race is nonpartisan.  
Monroe-Moreno is the Chair of the Nevada Democratic Party, which Black has argued is the one of the “most partisan jobs in Nevada.”
“Mayor of North Las Vegas is a nonpartisan office, meant to serve every resident,” Black’s website said. “City Hall should answer to neighbors — not hyper-partisan political agendas.”
Previous to serving on the council, Black owned a local marketing firm. He was first elected in 2017 and currently serves as mayor pro tem.
Monroe-Moreno has represented Assembly District 1, which encompasses North Las Vegas, since 2016. Prior to being elected, she was a corrections officer with the North Las Vegas Police Department.
North Las Vegas has come a long way to get back on stable footing since the economic downturn when the city was nearing bankruptcy in 2013.
Black, who is backed by Goynes-Brown, has said he has helped with the economic turnaround and wants to build on the work he has already done on the council.
“When I was first elected, North Las Vegas was really struggling,” his campaign website says, adding that the city is now thriving “with stronger public safety, improved neighborhoods, billions in economic investment, and great hope for the future.”
The city’s unemployment rate, at 5% as of August, still remains the highest among Southern Nevada cities. Monroe-Moreno previously told the Current it was a bad sign the rate remained higher than other cities.
Like in campaigns across the state – and the country – affordability and the high cost of living has weighed heavily on voters. Both candidates have said housing affordability is a priority if elected. 
Monroe-Moreno said she wanted to look at ways the city could crack down on corporate homeowners from purchasing excessive amounts of single family homes.  – state legislative efforts have died at the point of Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo’s veto pen. 
Black said while he has been in office the city has developed “1,400 affordable housing units in our community since 2017,” adding that “we are doing something to create sustainability and access to homes that people can pay for.” 
The Culinary Union attempted to establish a 5% limit on rent increases in the city.
There were conflicting views on whether the union received the necessary amount of votes for the ballot initiative to qualify. In a 4-1 vote, Black was among the majority of city council members that ultimately killed the ballot initiative. 
He previously told the Current that the measure was “a one size fits all” solution that was inappropriate for the community.
Monroe-Moreno said in a previous interview that she wanted to look at ways to address steep rent increases and look at a “stabilization plan of how much rent can go up, so that a family, and especially my seniors, can manage and basically budget.”
In a recent interview with The Nevada Independent, she said she was against the city implementing a form of blanket rent control  but would support stabilization of “rent increases for Nevadans on a fixed income, including seniors, veterans, and those with disabilities.”
Black had a cash advantage with roughly $513,131 cash on hand according to recent campaign finance reports. Monroe-Moreno had about $92,370 cash on hand. 
Former North Las Vegas mayors John Lee and Shari Buck endorsed Black. 
Black is also endorsed by the North Las Vegas Police Association and North Las Vegas Firefighters as well as the Vegas Chamber and the Southern Nevada Home Builders Association.
Monroe-Moreno — the state Democratic Party chair —  is endorsed by top state Democratic leaders, including Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, U.S. Rep. Steven Horsford, whose district includes North Las Vegas, and Nevada U.S. Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen. 
She is also backed by SEIU, Nevada State AFL-CIO, the Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada Action Fund.

name: Michigan Advance
title: I failed calculus twice. Lowering the bar wouldn’t have helped me
description: My first semester in college was a disaster. My second was worse.  I was an engineering major. On my very first Physics exam I earned a 100%, the second 52%, and a whopping 12% on the third. The requirements of my college dictated that averaging less than 60% on “in-semester” exams would automatically produce a […]
text:
Getty ImagesMy first semester in college was a disaster. My second was worse. 
I was an engineering major. On my very first Physics exam I earned a 100%, the second 52%, and a whopping 12% on the third. The requirements of my college dictated that averaging less than 60% on “in-semester” exams would automatically produce a failing grade for the course without being allowed to take its final exam. 
Calculus was not a bed of roses either. I earned 11% on its final exam. I failed calculus again the following semester and got dismissed from the University – that was the rule: fail the same course twice and out you go.
Eventually, the university offered “pardon” exams for dismissed students requiring 70% or better to be re-admitted. I studied calculus all summer and scored 69.5%. It took administrators two full weeks to decide if they will round up. They did. The rest is history.
So, what did I learn over that stressful summer? 
Not that engineering is not for me, not that women cannot do math, not that I’m not smart enough, and not that I don’t “belong.” The University already told me I don’t belong if I am not successful. 



Quotation







Whether for freshmen or upper classmen, poor grades do not cause harm; unfair grades do.


– Dr. Fegin Mekik, Professor of Geology at Grand Valley State University 


What I learned instead was how to master difficult material. My robust college preparation was not enough for the rigors of college. Most importantly, I learned I would not be coddled. 
I now know the point of going to college is to graduate it. Not belong to it. 
Perhaps President Grasso of the University of Michigan and his colleagues were thinking along the same lines when they decided to rescind their new grading policy for some freshmen – removing letter grades and offering pass/fail instead. Or maybe it was the massive pushbacks that caused the reversal in their policy. 
The public made it clear: they expect academic excellence in return for paying tuition.
The officials at the University of Michigan report that they developed the pass/fail policy to help reduce mental health issues among freshmen. Perhaps the real concern behind the now-rescinded grading policy was to keep the freshmen from dropping out – to boost retention – and potentially to recruit more freshmen as the demographic cliff looms. 
Alas, softer grading mars the reputation of the University of Michigan as the flagship of the state and conveys the message to freshmen that the University does not believe they will succeed. This is why their faculty senate pushed back on this new grading policy too.
Similarly, Yale is fighting grade inflation by attempting to place benchmarks on the percentage of students per grade category. But conversely, its faculty senate pushed back with “new grading guidance should minimize student harm.”
The reasoning for protecting students’ mental health through softer grading practices rests on two faulty premises: [1] poor grades cause mental health deficits (“harm”), and [2] post-freshmen students are somehow better at coping with low grades. 
Whether for freshmen or upper classmen, poor grades do not cause harm; unfair grades do. 
Poor grades can either show a student where to better invest their talents or galvanize them into success (as my own example).
High standards for success and the expressed belief that the student can meet them communicate belonging rather than exclusion. Professors and administrators must convey they are taking the students’ intellectual capacity seriously enough to expect excellent work.
From my collegiate teaching experience approaching three decades, poor grades do not result in poor teaching evaluations. What does produce unfavorable evaluations are unfair assessments of student success, wasting precious educational resources, and “dumbing-down” course content. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Moreover, this generation of undergraduates has a life expectancy of 80 – 100 years, and the world population exceeds 8 billion people. So, competition for a job has become fierce compared to my college days 35 years ago. While protecting students from competition in college through softer grading policies may reduce immediate stress, graduates eventually must compete at work and life. Grades must serve as a measure of the skills and knowledge alumni bring to the workforce which is what university reputations live and die on. That is why academic excellence must be the core tenet for all institutions of higher education. 
There is another wrinkle. Artificial intelligence (AI) is not going away, only becoming more capable. This is a nightmare for most educators, especially for subjects like math and writing. While education has surmounted similar threats before, like the calculator and the internet, AI is a tougher challenge because learning requires active intellectual engagement. 
The combination of AI, softer grading, and less competition serve to discourage students from growing their competence. Instead, the key factor that increases a sense of self-reliance and belonging in college is academic success and excellence.
The term academic excellence has become a euphemism for privilege, unfortunately. 
Students from high-income backgrounds are 4 times more likely to succeed in college than those from low-income backgrounds. Furthermore, high-achieving, low-income students often do not pursue education in selective schools. 
But, there is another side to that coin. Precisely because of inequities in college readiness, academic excellence is an equity obligation, rather than an elitist aspiration. 
Educational equity and academic excellence need not be competing goals. Institutions have a responsibility to respond proactively to diverse student needs while ensuring academic standards are maintained. In fact, equity and excellence are mutually reinforcing commitments in undergraduate education.
Colleges must build effective remediation practices and invest resources into not only promoting standards of academic excellence but also creating pathways to success for all students from diverse backgrounds.
So, the bar for excellence need not be lowered (e.g. softer grading); educational opportunities and resources need to be elevated.
Of the 15 public institutions of higher education in Michigan, more than half explicitly tout academic excellence in their promotional materials and strategic plans. So, the softer grading policies the University of Michigan is toying with leave the public wondering why they are straying from the academic excellence they promise.
To bring the point home in real life, who wants to pay for a clumsy ballet performance? Or support an athlete who isn’t willing to sweat? Or a scientist who makes bad predictions?
Success requires hard work, facing challenges, and failure. And success is often unsightly – ballerinas have ugly feet, athletes suffer injuries, scientists often need glasses, and failure bruises everyone’s ego. 
But college is not for learning how to protect one’s ego. College is for learning the skills for lifelong intellectual growth, earning associated credentials to support a well-employed life, and most importantly for having the skills to learn from failure.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico police chief tells lawmakers Flock cameras ‘very valuable’ despite increased criticism
description: The police chief in New Mexico’s second-largest city attempted this week to allay lawmaker fears about one of the most controversial tools in law enforcement: Flock cameras. But by the end of the presentation, some still had big questions and concerns about the technology Democratic-majority Legislature and governor opted to restrict earlier this year.
text:
Las Cruces Police Chief Jeremy Story on Oct. 6, 2026, briefed lawmakers on the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee about how his department uses controversial Flock cameras after the Legislature passed a law restricting them. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)The police chief in New Mexico’s second-largest city attempted this week to allay lawmaker fears about one of the most controversial tools in law enforcement: Flock cameras.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But by the end of the presentation, some still had big questions and concerns about the technology Democratic-majority Legislature and governor opted to restrict earlier this year.
Las Cruces Police Chief Jeremy Story told lawmakers on the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee on Tuesday that his department has access to 43 Flock cameras across the city. They’ve helped detectives close several cases, he said, including several homicides and a bank robbery across the state line in El Paso, Texas.
“If we have a missing person, if we have one picture of that car — even if it has nothing to do with when that person went missing — a lot of times that’s very helpful,” Story said. “When we have a crime where we have either a partial plate or a good vehicle description, that’s where this system becomes very valuable for law enforcement.”
Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham in March signed Senate Bill 40, known as the Driver Privacy and Security Act, into law. It took effect in July and prohibits law enforcement agencies from using data from automatic license plate readers for investigations into “protected healthcare activities,” such as seeking gender-affirming care or an abortion, as well as for public demonstrations or someone’s immigration status.
Critics point to examples the law attempts to address. In Texas, a sheriff’s deputy who did not have a warrant used Flock’s nationwide network to track a woman suspected of attempting to get an abortion, which is banned in the state with few exceptions. At the federal level, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has accessed Flock data through local law enforcement agencies to read license plates. Flock has denied having a contract with ICE. 
Nationally, politicians and civil rights groups have increasingly questioned whether automatic license plate readers — particularly the tens of thousands of Flock’s — risk violating constitutional privacy protections. In Bernalillo County, Sheriff John Allen recently nixed his department’s contract with Flock over the increasing skepticism.
In Tuesday’s presentation, Story sought to push back on some of that. He gave lawmakers a tour through the software by typing in his own license plate number and showing several photos Flock cameras had taken of his pickup truck that week. He then challenged lawmakers to figure out where he was coming from or going to in each of the photos of his truck.
“Try to tell me…where I came from before those hits, where I went after, who was in the vehicle and who was driving,” he said. “The reality is from most of these hits, we can’t determine any of those things.”
Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis), a career prosecutor, said she’s seen firsthand how they’ve been beneficial for criminal investigations. 
Interim committee Chair Rep. Christine Chandler (D-Los Alamos) was not as convinced, though.
She asked Story how he could have accessed the photos of his truck if they weren’t tied to a specific criminal case number. When he responded that he created a case number specifically for this demonstration, she said she was worried that that process could be abused.
“Who has the authority to create these fake case numbers? Because that’s what you’re telling me,” she said. “I was somewhat optimistic about the fact that many of these methodologies are requiring case numbers, but if we also have the ability to do fake case numbers, I’m a little concerned about that. It’s sort of an illusory check on the system.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Aging workforce, immigration crackdown are depleting skilled workers
description: Worker shortages are the top reason for construction project delays, a survey by the Association of General Contractors of America found.
text:
A perfect storm of harsh immigration enforcement, aging journeymen and a building boom for data centers is wreaking havoc on the nation’s supply of skilled trade workers. 
Automakers and construction contractors say they need more access to workers through accelerated training, steady immigration and a cultural shift to encourage young people to do the hard, dirty work of skilled trades. They’re looking for plumbers, electricians, carpenters, machinists and technicians — specializations increasingly in short supply. 
Worker shortages are the top reason for construction project delays, a September survey by the Association of General Contractors of America found. Applicants are there, but half of the contractors who were surveyed said too many job candidates are unqualified and need more training. 
The association cited both the demand for workers building data centers and tougher immigration enforcement as contributing causes for the shortage.  
“Over 50% of craft workers are born outside the United States. We don’t know that they’re illegal but frankly DHS (the Department of Homeland Security) is not being that discriminating in whom they pick up or who feels threatened by them,” said Ken Simonson, the chief economist for the Association of General Contractors of America. One answer is for the government to allow more worker visas for construction and other trades, he said. 
“We’ve been stymied for 20 years or longer trying to get construction treated similarly to agriculture, where if you can demonstrate that there isn’t enough Americans interested in a job you can bring in somebody,” Simonson said. 
Pay is rising for the skilled trades, but it’s hard to say how soon higher wages would attract more people. On social media, trades workers complain of long commutes to work sites, long waits through low-paid apprenticeships and a feeling they’re not valued as much as office workers.
“Getting up at 4am-5am. Driving 50 plus miles to random job sites. Obviously the dirty part which is construction sites and inhaling dust and dirt all day. Seeing people in corporate jobs in nice clothes while I’m dirty going on lunch break,” wrote a 30-year-old on a Reddit social media post in July, concluding that they should have finished a college chemistry degree.
Thousands agreed, including a 31-year-old tradesperson from Michigan who said top pay in their field, plumbing and HVAC, is attractive but that many make less than $70,000. 
“Been in the trades since I was 16 and recently started going back to college,” the person wrote. “Everybody I know who chose a degree over an apprenticeship is starting to outpace me in life buying houses and having kids while we’re check to check and getting less healthy by the day.”
These are the concerns employers have to address if they’re going to find enough workers to build homes, cars and data centers for artificial intelligence. Ford Motor Company and the Ad Council announced a publicity campaign to bring more young people into the trades, with a video declaring “millions of skilled trade jobs are waiting for people ready to do something, with great pay, job security and work you can take pride in.” 
Ford and the alliance didn’t mention immigration enforcement as an issue, but the Association of General Contractors and an unrelated survey of roofers both mentioned it as a prominent factor in reducing the supply of skilled workers. 
John Burns Real Estate and Consulting, an independent housing research company, reported that many of the roofers it surveyed earlier this year saw immigration enforcement as hurting their business. 
“There are no American kids willing to install roofs in Central Texas,” said one roofing contractor in anonymous quotes published by the group. 
“Tough immigration reform and not enough Americans to fill the void,” said another. 
“A lot of these people have been deported. The next generation is complacent and does not want to do physical work,” said a Florida roofer. 
Elizabeth LaJeunesse, vice president for building products research at John Burns, said the vehemence of responses about immigration was surprising. 
“They used terms like ‘They’re hunting our workforce.’ They’re describing disappearing workers,” LaJeunesse said. “Most of these firms are pretty conservative, so this is a real phenomenon we’re picking up on, that level of concern over immigration enforcement.” 
Duane Musser, vice president for government relations for the National Roofing Contractors Association, said the responses are typical of what he hears from members. Immigration as well as better trade education are critical to roofing, he said. 
“Advocating for solutions to workforce shortages, including expanded career and technical education programs and bipartisan immigration reform, is a top priority,” Musser said. 
The DHS told Stateline in an unattributed statement that “those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear” and that “we will continue to enforce our nation’s laws and remove illegal aliens from American communities.” 
In September a Trump-appointed federal judge stayed a federal practice of entering construction sites without a warrant to investigate immigration status. One construction worker of Mexican descent in Alabama complained that he had been detained three times since 2025 despite showing a state driver’s license demonstrating that he was a citizen born in Florida. 
Immigrant workers make up a majority of roofers, painters and stucco masons, according to a Stateline analysis last year.  
The nation will need 1.7 million new skilled trade workers every year through 2035, according to a September report by Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, a trade group including Ford Motor Company, toolmakers and other businesses. Training programs produce just more than half the numbers needed, and only half of those who enroll in skilled training programs finish, the report found.  
Nine states were identified by the alliance report as having high demand but low supply of skilled labor: Arizona, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. 
Florida ranks first for demand for skilled workers, but last for supply, with not enough new workers coming online as building in the state booms and current workers near retirement age. The state’s Association of General Contractors’ chapter hopes the advancements in workforce AI will drive more young adults into construction jobs since those can’t be replaced by chatbots.
Other states have the opposite issue: ranking high for new workers but low in demand for them, based on recent hiring and future projections. 
In the top 10 for worker supply but bottom 10 for demand: Indiana, North Dakota, Oklahoma and Wyoming. 
The alliance report suggested employers themselves need to help train future workers. The companies building data centers, in particular, want those tradespeople.
“America needs hundreds of thousands of electricians, welders and fiber technicians to build AI infrastructure,” said Dina Powell McCormick, president and vice chairman of Meta, in a statement, adding that the alliance is “paying for the training, removing the barriers that keep people from stepping into these careers, and guaranteeing a job at the end of it.”
Shoua Thao, 40,  is straddling the line between trades and AI as a machinist in the computer-assisted manufacturing business known as CNC machining, which uses computer code to control production. The son of Hmong refugees in the Twin Cities area of Minnesota, Thao is now experimenting with AI production techniques. 
“Trades are the one career path that doesn’t lie,” he said. “You can’t hide lower skills in a trade, whereas middle management and white collar jobs are protected by the vagueness of the job.”
Eventually trades could become a more valued career path than college, Thao said, though he has been discouraged at times by low pay and long hours that take time away from family.
“I think it will be a slow process but eventually, sometime in the future, maybe my children’s future, trades will take over,” Thao said.
This story was first published Oct. 8, 2026 by Stateline.

name: Nevada Current
title: District court judge hoping to hold off challenge from attorney in Department 31
description: Clark County Judge Joanna Kishner is among the roughly one-third of Eighth District incumbents who drew challengers in this year’s election. She’ll face attorney Alexandra Beth McLeod in the contest for Department 31.  “Many of us who are experienced and make some of the hardest decisions on the bench seem to have drawn a challenger […]
text:
Joanna Kishner, Alexandra Beth McLeod. (Candidate photos)Clark County Judge Joanna Kishner is among the roughly one-third of Eighth District incumbents who drew challengers in this year’s election. She’ll face attorney Alexandra Beth McLeod in the contest for Department 31. 
“Many of us who are experienced and make some of the hardest decisions on the bench seem to have drawn a challenger this time, and I’m included in that group,” Kishner, who is seeking a third term, told the Current.  
Kishner is a 1989 graduate of UCLA School of Law and was admitted to practice in Nevada in 1993. 
Of the 232 attorneys who evaluated Kishner in the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s Judging the Judges survey, 46.6% said she should be retained. Her highest score was for integrity while her lowest score was for legal ability. 
McLeod says she chose to challenge Kishner because she’s among the lowest-rated judges in the survey. 
Kishner does not put a lot of stock in the survey, noting the attorneys who work for the firms listed as supporters on her website outnumber those who completed the evaluation. Her endorsements, she says, exhibit the “depth and breadth” of her support from the legal community. 
Kishner says she’s never reached out to anyone to complete the survey, “good, bad, or indifferent. So you can appreciate that certain people might choose to fill it out in an election year.”
Still, she says, she’s been able to learn from the comments. 
“Some people don’t like the fact that I explain my rulings, and I think it’s very important so they know it’s a well-reasoned ruling,” Kishner says. 
Kishner notes she handles complex litigation. 
“I am fortunate to have almost all of the social media cases where the State of Nevada has sued a lot of the different entities,” she says. 
That includes Attorney General Aaron Ford’s case against Meta, which, along with other state actions, led to a national settlement of as much as $17.1 billion, along with Meta’s pledge to enact comprehensive child-safety features on its platforms. 
Nevada is guaranteed to receive more than $178 million, according to Ford. 
In the State of Nevada vs. TikTok, a consumer protection case, a “whole bundle of very sophisticated attorneys from around the country raised a lot of challenges to the case being handled here,” says Kishner. 
Kishner says she wrote a “very long decision” addressing those issues on TikTok’s motion to dismiss. Her decision was affirmed by the Nevada Supreme Court, allowing the state to proceed to trial against TikTok. The ruling, Kishner says, has been raised in other cases involving social media. 
Of 155 civil appeals, Kishner has been found in error on 50 cases. 
She is endorsed by dozens of law enforcement organizations, labor unions including the Culinary and Bartenders unions, and a number of community and industry organizations including the left-leaning Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada, the Republican-funded Third Branch PAC, the Israeli American Civic Action Group, Asian American Pacific Islanders, the National Organization of Women (NOW, the Latin Chamber of Commerce, and the Adult Residential Care Providers of Nevada.  
As of July, Kishner had raised $487,000 and had $452,000 in the bank. 
McLeod, a graduate of McGeorge School of Law and a member of the Nevada Bar since 2002, is making her third run for the bench, following losses in 2020 and 2024. She’s represented both plaintiffs and defendants in civil cases. 
She thinks proceedings in Kishner’s court “have gotten a little stale. I commend her for her service but I think it’s time for change.” 
McLeod says her first priority is to present a respectful demeanor. Attorneys who come before Kishner, she says, citing comments from the RJ evaluation,  “are not having a good experience where they are feeling respected as professionals, and they don’t feel that their clients are getting a fair shake. I would bring courtesy back to the courtroom.”
Department 31, which was previously a business court, now hears civil matters. 
McLeod acknowledges the increased use of artificial intelligence in litigation can be confounding – from clients who expect a victory and large judgment after a consultation with ChatGPT, to those who balk at being billed for multiple hours when AI takes minutes to plot their legal course.   
McLeod says her approach to pro se litigants and attorneys who employ AI would be nuanced. 
“The outcome would be the same, but I think that the violation by a trained attorney licensed to practice law would be heavier and would include a referral to the bar,” McLeod says. “Whereas if a pro se litigant were to make the same mistake, there’s no bar to report them to.”
McLeod has raised just under $48,000, including in-kind donations totalling $30,000, and reports $42,000 on hand. Her website does not include any endorsements.

name: Nevada Current
title: Architect challenges incumbent for NV higher ed regents seat
description: A local architect is challenging a first-term incumbent to represent District 4 on the Nevada Board of Regents District 3. The  incumbent, Regent Byron Brooks, is an Army combat veteran who now owns and operates a local bail bonds agency. He faces Erik Swendseid, the vice president at the Las Vegas-based architectural firm EV&A. The […]
text:
Byron Brooks, Erik Swendseid. (Candidate photos)A local architect is challenging a first-term incumbent to represent District 4 on the Nevada Board of Regents District 3.
The  incumbent, Regent Byron Brooks, is an Army combat veteran who now owns and operates a local bail bonds agency. He faces Erik Swendseid, the vice president at the Las Vegas-based architectural firm EV&A.
The Board of Regents oversees the Nevada System of Higher Education, which is composed of two research universities, a state university, four community colleges, and a research institute. NSHE enrolls more than 100,000 students, according to their website, and has a biennium budget of more than $2 billion dollars.
District 3 is contained entirely within Clark County. It includes central parts of the Las Vegas Valley, including around UNLV and part of Spring Valley, and parts of Henderson, including Silverado Ranch and Anthem.
Brooks was elected in 2020 for a six-year term. But, if elected, his second term will only be two years. That’s because the Nevada State Legislature in 2023 passed a bill to reduce the number to regents from 13 to nine. They also shortened the term length of regents from six years to four years beginning with the 2028 election. To align those changes, the winners of this year’s regents races will have truncated terms and have to run for re-election in 2028.
Regents run in nonpartisan races. Because only Brooks and Swendseid filed to run, they did not appear on the ballot in the June primary.
Brooks, according to his NSHE bio, describes his term on the board as being “marked by a focus on accountability, strategic governance, and ensuring Nevada’s higher education system meets the evolving needs of students, faculty, and the state’s workforce.” He has twice served 1-year terms as chair of the board.
In January, Brooks voted against raising tuition between 9 and 12% to cover a budget gap attributed to pay raises. When asked about that vote, Brooks told The Nevada Independent “faculty compensation and student services matter, but tuition should be a last resort. Nevada needs sustainable state investment, greater budget transparency, and funding formula reform to protect affordability, access, and student success.”
Swendseid told the Nevada Faculty Alliance in a candidate survey that he hopes to be a “a pragmatic voice in helping guide our higher education.”
Swendseid is a UNLV graduate who was born and raised in Reno. “I remain deeply connected to the state’s unique character and the people I share it with,” he wrote in a Ballotpedia candidate survey. “That perspective has shaped not only my professional work, but also my belief that systems—whether physical or institutional—should be intentionally designed to serve those who rely on them.”
On his campaign website, Brooks touts endorsements from various law enforcement groups, including the Las Vegas Police Protective Association and Public Safety Alliance of Nevada, and various fellow elected officials, including Mayors Shelley Berkley and Michelle Romero, and legislators like state Sens. Carrie Buck (R-Henderson) and Jeff Stone (R-Henderson).
On his campaign website, Swendseid touts endorsements from the Nevada Faculty Alliance, Vegas Chamber, Veterans in Politics, and AIA Las Vegas.
Notably, several politically active labor unions and organizations, such as the Culinary union and SEIU Local 1107 have not endorsed either candidate in District 3 but have weighed in on other regents races.
Swendseid raised $9,100 in contributions and in-kind donations during the first half of the year. He had $1,510 on hand as of July 1.
Brooks raised $11,300 during the first half of the year but spent almost none and entered the general election cycle with $11,279.
Third quarter campaign finance reports are due to the state on Oct. 15, two days before Nevada’s two-week in-person early voting period begins.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Salt Lake City Council members agree to slow down sale of land near Great Salt Lake to the state
description: Salt Lake City Council members hope to pause before advancing a proposed sale of 900 acres of land between the Salt Lake City International Airport and wetlands.  While the interested buyer is the Utah Department of Natural Resources and its Wildlife Resources division, environmentalists worry that selling the land could be the first of many […]
text:
Birds take flight over the Great Salt Lake, with downtown Salt Lake City visible in the background, on Friday, Sept. 27, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Salt Lake City Council members hope to pause before advancing a proposed sale of 900 acres of land between the Salt Lake City International Airport and wetlands. 
While the interested buyer is the Utah Department of Natural Resources and its Wildlife Resources division, environmentalists worry that selling the land could be the first of many missteps leading to harm to the Great Salt Lake and migrating birds.
Details on the sale are still unconfirmed, according to a report from city staff, including the price of the land. The council still has to approve other processes before the deal is finalized as well, so a vote wasn’t expected at their Tuesday evening meeting. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But, after dozens spoke opposing the sale without more in-depth studies, council members said they would take extra steps before making a decision.
After hearing the comments, Councilmember Dan Dugan said there are conflicts between the management plan proposed by the Department of Natural Resources and federal clean water policy. Also, he said, the city should analyze all options before approving a land transfer.
“Does it require the city to transfer the land to the state, or can we do that ourselves by just transferring it to another one of our departments using (Federal Aviation Agency) money to manage that?” Dugan said. “Can we do it ourselves without giving someone else that responsibility and also that authority to do something that we may not all agree with?”
Chelsea Duke, wildlife lands coordinator at the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, said during the meeting that the agency’s goal in the acquisition is “to protect, conserve, and enhance the wetlands around the Great Salt Lake.” 
Utah’s strategy to fight invasive reeds at the Great Salt Lake? Play the long game and look upstream

The division’s team of full-time biologists would manage the area in conjunction with the state-owned 660 acres adjacent to the land, known as the Blackhawk Waterfowl Management Area, she said, and would work with state, federal, private and nonprofit representatives to restore the wetlands and mitigate invasive species in the system, particularly phragmites, a reed that crowds out native species and draws a tremendous amount of water.
“Our waterfowl management areas are managed in a way to help waterfowl and other migrating bird species,” Duke said, “These properties are closed to public access during specific times of year to protect nesting birds and provide crucial rest areas. Because our (waterfowl management areas) are primarily for wildlife it is also crucial that they remain protected from development.”
If the division were to buy the parcels, Duke said, it is required by state law to write a habitat management plan with input from local government officials, neighboring landowners and others.
But Ren Griffith, policy advocate for the conservation organization Utah Audubon Council, said that protection from development “is only half the question.” 
“The other half is what kind of habitat this land will be. For three decades, the airport has kept this property closed to hunting and trespassing, and it has become a place where migrating birds can rest undisturbed,” she said. 



Let us know what you think...


 


When asked whether hunting would be allowed in the area, the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources said it “hopes to expand waterfowl hunting opportunities and protect the wildlife habitat in the area through this purchase,” according to the city staff report.
If the acquisition goes through, the agency would add the parcel to its Blackhawk Waterfowl Management Area, which has remained closed to the public since it was purchased because it doesn’t have any usable, safe public access points.
“Public access points, parking, motor vehicle restrictions, grazing, and other management decisions will be developed once the property is purchased and (the Division of Wildlife Resources) writes the habitat management plan for the entire (waterfowl management area),” the agency said in its response to Salt Lake City staff.
The Utah Audubon Council supports transferring the land to the Department of Natural Resources with a permanent conservation easement for all 900 acres with some specific terms, Griffith said, like the creation of a hunting-free wildlife rest area within “a meaningful share of the property.”
Neighbors of northwestern Salt Lake City also worry that the sale could essentially undo decades of their land advocacy and negotiations.
Adam Von Maack, representing Gillmor Livestock Corporation, which is owned by a family that has farmed and ranched in the area since 1896, said the family had endured multiple land takeovers from the city as the airport expanded. 
After a decade of planning processes, they understood the city had made renewed commitments to “principles of stewardship, respect for agriculture, and your continued protection of this significant city-owned property,” he said. The sale would “break faith” with the residents in the area.
“You created this mitigation site to replace sensitive lands destroyed by your runway expansion. You took that land from your neighbors to do it, and now you turn your back on it because it’s inconvenient,” Von Maack said.
“The state bought the Blackhawk without usable public access. This transaction seeks to solve their access problem and the airport’s management burden, while neighbors inherit the consequence,” he said. “It also allows the state to bully your area constituents into accepting area policies they spent generations working alongside you reject. Selling to the state removes your ability to protect this land, your constituents, and the city’s documented priorities.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Transgender care takes center stage in Missouri campaign to reinstate abortion ban
description: Jamie Reed stood before a room full of Republicans in St. Louis County in September, clicking through a presentation about pediatric gender medicine. The former social worker at a St. Louis transgender clinic described puberty blockers and hormones in stark terms and warned of what she sees as lasting harm to children. The audience gasped, […]
text:
Supporters of Missouri's Amendment 3, which would reinstate a near-total abortion ban and place a permanent ban on gender-affirming care for minors into the constitution, gather for an informational meeting on Sept. 10 in St. Louis County (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).Jamie Reed stood before a room full of Republicans in St. Louis County in September, clicking through a presentation about pediatric gender medicine.
The former social worker at a St. Louis transgender clinic described puberty blockers and hormones in stark terms and warned of what she sees as lasting harm to children. The audience gasped, groaned and, at one point, a woman called her a hero.
But Reed had come to make a political case, too.
Amendment 3 would reinstate Missouri’s abortion ban with limited exceptions while also constitutionally prohibiting gender-transition treatments for minors. And Reed, who describes herself as a lifelong liberal and supports legal abortion with some restrictions, told the room which part of the measure she thought could help carry it.
“If we talk to people about the trans part of this amendment,” she said, “we can get it to pass.”
That calculation has become increasingly visible in the campaign for Amendment 3, as supporters emphasize restrictions on transgender healthcare in television ads, yard signs and public appearances — even though most gender-affirming medical care for minors is already banned in Missouri.
Chelsea Freels, 20, noticed that strategy as she passed signs on the way to visit her grandmother at the Lake of the Ozarks over the summer.
“Yes on 3,” they read. “Ban transgender surgeries for minors.” 
The signs surprised Freels, who received puberty blockers as a minor in Missouri. Gender-affirming surgeries for minors are already banned, as are puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones.
Two years earlier, Freels, who grew up in St. Louis, helped canvas across Missouri in support of the 2024 reproductive rights amendment. Voters narrowly approved it, overturning the state’s near-total abortion ban and protecting abortion rights until fetal viability.
A year later, the Republican supermajority in the statehouse put Amendment 3 on the ballot. It would ban most abortions, with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies and pregnancies caused by rape or incest during the first 12 weeks.
Polling points to another very close race in Missouri. Abortion access remains popular, as does banning hormone therapy or medications and gender-transition surgeries for minors. 
“It’s really telling that the Republicans have shifted a lot of their messaging about A3 away from abortion,” Freels said. “And towards demonizing children.”
The campaign to ban abortion argues both issues fall under the same goal: protecting children by legislating reproductive healthcare.
“We’re not anti-anyone,” said Amanda Sanders, a spokesperson for Her Health, Her Future, the campaign for Amendment 3. “This is pro-protecting their childhood, their innocence.” 
Many major healthcare coalitions, including the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Medical Association, support gender-affirming care for transgender youth, though surgery is uncommon for minors and some groups recommend deferring it until adulthood. 
Reed has become one of the campaign’s most prominent messengers. She previously worked at a Planned Parenthood clinic in Florida and says she supports legal abortion with restrictions. But abortion is not the focus of her pitch.
PROMO, a Missouri-based LGBTQ+ advocacy group, put up billboards leading up to the November election that read “Trans Missourians are your neighbors” (photo submitted).
Opponents call the transgender provision “ballot candy,” arguing lawmakers added an already-banned practice to make an abortion ban more attractive to voters.
“The politicians pushing Amendment 3 are lying,” said Tom Bastian, a spokesperson with the No on 3 Stop the Ban campaign, which includes Planned Parenthood, Abortion Action Missouri and the ACLU of Missouri. “The facts are that healthcare for transgender youth is already banned in Missouri and it will remain banned no matter how people vote.”
If Amendment 3 passes, Missouri will be the first state to place a ban on gender-affirming care in its constitution. Twenty-six other states have statutory bans in place.
On Tuesday evening, Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe on a webcast fundraiser for Her Health, Her Future, emphasized that Missouri is a battleground for abortion and transgender issues. The message laid out the larger stakes: If Missouri voters champion Amendment 3, other conservative states could follow suit with a similar amendment framework.
“What happens here doesn’t just matter to the people of St. Louis or Kansas City, or Springfield, or the small towns across our state,” Kehoe said. “People around the country are watching to see what Missouri does.”
 ‘Political scapegoat’

“It starts with drag queen story hour and ends with children under the knife,” begins the first of two TV ads for Her Health, Her Future. “Irreversible sex change surgeries on minors, that’s the goal of the trans extremists.” 
Such surgeries were rare in Missouri before the state banned them in 2023. An internal Washington University review found its transgender center stopped referring minors for surgery in late 2018. Six chest surgeries were performed by university physicians on adolescents transitioning to male between 2018 and 2023, but the referrals came from outside providers.
Sara Burke, a Syracuse University psychology professor who studies stereotyping and discrimination, called the campaign rhetoric political scapegoating that could worsen prejudice against transgender people.
“Abortion is quite popular; whereas, there seems to be a wave of knee-jerk, anti transgender sentiment in politics right now,” Burke said. “They’re just trying to score points, and it’s a cynical ploy with real human consequences. Transgender children are highly vulnerable. Treating them as a political scapegoat makes their lives worse.”
Those now championing Amendment 3 point to the August 2027 sunset on the ban restricting cross-sex hormones and puberty blockers as a reason for asking voters to ban something that’s already banned. The ban on gender-affirming surgeries for minors has no expiration.
“We do not want to leave the protections for children to the winds of the political change of whoever is in office in the legislature and courts,” Sanders said. 
Earlier this year, the Missouri Supreme Court upheld the ban on gender-affirming care for minors, known as the SAFE Act, rejecting a challenge brought by families represented by the ACLU of Missouri and Lambda Legal. 
Opponents of Amendment 3 say lawmakers could extend the expiring restrictions before they sunset. 
Asked about the strategy to leave abortion out of TV ads, Sanders said the campaign was leaning into all sides of the amendment. 
“We will continue to put out content on all aspects of this abortion vote,” she said. “But this was so important that I think it could get lost in the conversation if it wasn’t pointed out.”
Opponents argue abortion is what has been lost. 
“The legislature banned transgender care for minors a couple years ago,” Michael Wolff, a retired chief justice of the Missouri Supreme Court and dean emeritus of St. Louis University School of Law, said in a political ad for Stop the Ban. “Misleading? That’s what it is. Don’t let politicians fool us into banning abortion again.” 
A court challenge last year argued unsuccessfully that Amendment 3 violated Missouri’s single-subject rule by combining abortion and gender-affirming care. An appeals court ruled the subjects were sufficiently connected because transition-related treatments may affect fertility and therefore could be considered related to reproductive health care. 
 What is reproductive healthcare?

Reed has become a prominent voice in the Yes on 3 campaign and appears in one of its television ads. Her public profile dates to 2023, when she accused the Washington University Transgender Center of rushing minors into puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones without adequate mental health assessments and failing to fully inform families about potential side effects. 
“I probably was the last expected person to speak in the room tonight,” Reed told the crowd. “And maybe the last expected person to speak up in support of Amendment 3.” 
Those familiar with her story might not be so surprised.
Reed became a national name in the trans healthcare debate in 2023, when she gave an affidavit to the Missouri attorney general with her accusations against the Washington University center. 
Families whose children received care at the clinic for years have disputed Reed’s characterization in testimony and interviews with The Independent, describing evaluations that lasted months and saying providers discussed fertility preservation, including egg and sperm storage.
Reed rejects the idea that she is sacrificing abortion rights to secure a ban on gender-affirming care. She does not believe people can change sex and sees medical transition as harmful to gay and gender-nonconforming people.
“This is a fundamental attack on gender, non-conforming homosexuals,” Reed said. “And for me to have that message in a room of Republicans goes to show how challenging this issue is for the left … it kills me that the Democratic party is willing to die on this hill.” 
TJ Billard, a Northwestern University communications professor who studies media and transgender politics, said pairing abortion and transgender care reflects a broader political argument about gender, sexuality and traditional social roles. 
Billard said describing the transgender provision simply as a political “pill hidden inside the cheese” risks missing why the issues appeal to many of the same voters.
Both can be framed around anxieties over changing ideas about gender and sexuality, Billard said, making transgender issues an increasingly potent political flashpoint.
So far, they said, trans advocates have been woefully unsuccessful in garnering more support in the face of these arguments, which Billard characterized as misinformation and fear-mongering. 
“The vast majority of people had never given thought to a trans person, certainly didn’t necessarily care about trans people, and definitely, even if they opposed it, didn’t think it was a problem at a scale that needed immediate political addressing,” Billard said. 
Anti-abortion divide could complicate Missouri Amendment 3 campaign

A 2025 study by St. Louis University’s Transgender Health Collaborative found that 35% of parents of LGBTQ youth were considering leaving the state; 96% of parents to LGBTQ youth reported feeling the same or more stress and increased concern for their child’s safety.
Katie Heiden-Rootes, a St. Louis University family therapist and researcher who works with transgender young people and their families, said clients have told her the election-year visibility has made it harder to sleep, work and parent.
She accused Missouri Republican leadership of creating “boogeymen” out of the trans community to sway a vote.
“It stokes fear and hatred towards a group of people who really just want to live and be seen as full humans in the state of Missouri,” Heiden-Rootes said. “And that’s not what’s happening right now.”
Kelly Storck, a private practice therapist who focuses on gender care in the St. Louis area, said because of the 2023 law, her minor patients and their parents have to drive to Chicago and beyond to access medical treatment options. Now, she said, they’re also facing a “smear” campaign.
“It keeps people quiet. It keeps people hidden. I promise you legislation like this has killed children and will continue to enact great harms to children,” she said. “They will not see a way or a place for them to exist in the world, because of these conversations, and because these anti-trans sentiments and ideologies exist.”
Chelsea Freels, 20, stands between her parents, Rene and Kyle Freels. The family continues advocating for gender-affirming care for minors in Missouri (photo submitted).
Rene Freels, Chelsea’s mother, still lives in the St. Louis suburbs with her husband. Their home once felt politically insulated, she said. Then Yes on 3 signs appeared in the churchyard down the street.
Chelsea has become more hesitant to visit home, her mother said.
The family has considered moving but decided instead to save money in case they eventually feel they need to leave the country with their daughter.
“Us parents are trying to end this so that when we pass away, our kids don’t have to deal with this type of discrimination, this vile discrimination, so that they just can live their lives free and have free movement,” Rene Freels said. “Nobody’s life is easy, but at least they can just be free to be themselves. But this is just an onslaught against our kids.” 
Chelsea Freels said when she canvassed for abortion rights in 2024, she met conservatives all over the state whose political beliefs were rooted in loving their neighbors and treating one another with kindness. It’s why, she believes, Missourians voted to raise the minimum wage and establish paid sick leave, why they expanded Medicare access and why they voted for abortion rights. 
“When you ask those people if they want to protect the people around them, it’s always a yes,” she said, reflecting on the 2024 election. “And that’s why I’m confident that we’re going to win this one.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska voters should ask better questions
description: Candidates are asking Nebraskans for our votes again. Before we give them one, we should ask for something in return. Give us the facts. Give us the numbers. Show us the data. Then show us the plan. That should be our standard for anyone who wants to be our governor or represent Nebraska in the […]
text:
A sign encouraging Nebraskans to register and get out to vote sits at the Harvest Moon Festival in Lincoln outside a booth for multiple civic advocacy organizations on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Candidates are asking Nebraskans for our votes again.
Before we give them one, we should ask for something in return.
Give us the facts. Give us the numbers. Show us the data. Then show us the plan.
That should be our standard for anyone who wants to be our governor or represent Nebraska in the U.S. Senate.
Nebraska is worth protecting.
There is still something of the frontier in this state. We raise food that feeds people beyond our borders. We have land and water handed down through generations. We still have towns where a farm, business or factory can shape an entire community.
The frontier was never just a place. It was also the idea that people could build something of their own and have a say in what happened to it.
We should not give that away.
Look at Lexington.
Tyson closed its beef plant there in January, eliminating 3,212 plant positions. University of Nebraska researchers estimate the statewide impact could reach more than 7,000 jobs and about $3.3 billion in economic activity each year.
Behind those numbers are paychecks, families, local businesses and a Nebraska community changed by one major employer’s decision.
So what did we learn from it?
How many other Nebraska towns depend heavily on one major employer? Do we know which are most at risk? Who benefits from the choices we make next, and who carries the cost?
Government cannot prevent every plant closure. We should not expect it to. But we should expect our leaders to understand our risks, prepare for them and make Nebraska a place where people want to build, invest and stay.
Our water deserves the same attention.
Water supports our farms, towns, businesses and families. Nebraska’s 2026 Water Quality and Quantity Task Force identified the need to reduce nitrate concentrations in groundwater and protect our water resources for the long term.
What we do with our water is not just a policy question. It is also about what we leave behind.
Someone protected these resources before they belonged to us. We owe the same duty to the Nebraskans who come after us.
That means thinking beyond the next election. It also means thinking beyond Washington.
Too often, our political conversations start somewhere else. Washington has a fight, the parties choose sides, and soon Nebraskans are expected to choose one too.
But Nebraska is not Washington.
We should never become a branch office for a president, political party or national movement.
Our governor’s first responsibility is Nebraska. Our senators should take Nebraska’s interests to Washington, not simply bring Washington’s politics home to us.
So this election, let’s use something simple.
Call it the Nebraska Test.
Whenever a candidate makes a promise, identifies a crisis or assigns blame, ask five questions.
Is it true? Show us the evidence.
Who benefits? Who gains? Who pays? What does the candidate gain by asking us to support it?
How big is it? Give us the numbers and put the problem in perspective.
What’s the plan? Tell us what can actually be done, what it will cost and who is responsible.
How will we know it worked? Give us a result we can measure and check after the election.
“Who benefits?” does not mean someone did something wrong. It means voters should understand who has something to gain, including the candidate asking for our vote.
Use the Nebraska Test at town halls, during debates and when you see campaign ads.
Most importantly, use it on the candidate you already support.
It is easy to demand evidence from the other side. It is harder to look at someone wearing our colors and say, prove it.
And do not give this argument a free pass either. Test it.
A candidate passes the Nebraska Test when ordinary Nebraskans can see the evidence, know who benefits and pays, understand the plan and know what result to expect.
If we cannot do that, keep asking questions.
Nebraska’s independence is worth more than loyalty to any politician.
No party owns this state. No president owns it. No corporation owns it.
We do.
This election, do not just pick a side. Apply the Nebraska Test and make them earn your vote.

name: Missouri Independent
title: As Trump pushes to deregulate AI, Missouri must weigh innovation, risks and cost
description: For most people, the AI debate began with tools such as ChatGPT and questions about jobs, academic integrity, misinformation, and privacy. But AI is increasingly becoming a physical presence as well, through massive data centers, new demands on the electric grid, infrastructure investment and decisions about who bears the cost. That makes the latest developm[...]
text:
Interior of a modern data center (Getty Images).For most people, the AI debate began with tools such as ChatGPT and questions about jobs, academic integrity, misinformation, and privacy. But AI is increasingly becoming a physical presence as well, through massive data centers, new demands on the electric grid, infrastructure investment and decisions about who bears the cost.
That makes the latest developments in Washington especially important. Last month, President Donald Trump announced plans for a new AI adviser and an “AI force,” framing rapid AI development as an urgent national priority in the strategic race with China. The administration’s approach is straightforward: reduce barriers to AI development and let American industry move faster.
That approach reflects one important part of the debate. But researchers, communities, and even leaders within the AI industry are also raising concerns about security, loss of control, and the need for safeguards as the technology becomes more powerful.
Those concerns are growing nationwide. Workers worry about whether AI will replace jobs. Parents are asking how much AI their children should use in school. Consumers are increasingly concerned about privacy, deepfakes, and how their personal information is being collected and used. Communities are also discovering that the AI boom comes with tangible local costs.
This can easily become another broad, polarized debate: accelerate AI or regulate it. But AI is a broad term covering many different technologies and uses, each with its own benefits, risks, and consequences.
Not all AI uses carry the same risks. Using AI to brainstorm ideas is very different from using it to make hiring, lending, or medical decisions. Using AI to help workers do their jobs is different from using it to replace them. Driverless cars raise questions about safety and responsibility. And large data centers bring a different set of concerns altogether, including electricity use, water demand, noise, and the cost of new infrastructure.
Treating all of these technologies and concerns as one big debate over “AI regulation” misses the point. Different risks call for different responses. The real questions are who benefits, who carries the risk, and who ultimately pays the cost.
Missouri is already confronting those questions. One clear example is the electricity demand created by large data centers. A 2025 state law requires the Missouri Public Service Commission to set special rates for large power users, including data centers, so that the costs associated with serving them are not unfairly shifted to households and other customers.
Local communities across Missouri are responding differently, too. St. Louis has chosen to allow data-center development under new zoning, environmental, noise and community requirements. St. Charles has taken a more restrictive approach, effectively barring new primary-use data centers.
These developments point to a broader truth, that the AI debate is really several debates happening at once.
One is about innovation. How can Missouri attract investment, develop AI talent, support entrepreneurs and help existing companies use the technology productively?
Another is about workers. How do we capture AI’s productivity gains without ignoring the disruption it may create for jobs?
Another is about consumers. What happens to privacy when people routinely share personal, financial, or professional information with AI systems?
Another is about children and schools. How can students benefit from AI without allowing it to replace the thinking, writing and problem-solving skills schools are supposed to develop?
And another is about infrastructure. What happens when AI-driven investment creates enormous new demands for electricity, water, land and public infrastructure?
Because these issues differ, they should not automatically lead to the same policy response. But regulation is only part of the challenge. Missouri also has to decide what kind of AI economy it wants to build and where it can create lasting value. States will compete not only to host servers, but also to develop the researchers, entrepreneurs, companies and skilled workers who use AI to create new products and industries.
For Missouri, that means connecting AI development to areas where the state already has strengths: universities and research, health care, agriculture, biotech, advanced manufacturing, financial services and geospatial technology. Missouri should not simply aim to become a place where the AI economy stores and processes its data. It should actively create value from AI.
That does not mean every new regulation is wise. Poorly designed rules can slow innovation, but avoiding regulation altogether carries risks of its own. The better approach is to match safeguards to the technology, its use, and the level of risk involved.
This is not about stopping AI. It is about basic fairness. AI can drive real growth in Missouri, but its success depends on getting the economics and policies right by capturing the benefits, managing the risks and making sure the costs are shared fairly. Missouri can champion AI innovation without asking everyday families to absorb infrastructure costs associated with investments by some of the world’s most resourceful technology companies.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Orphaned cubs abound in Colorado as black bear families struggle to find food
description: Colorado Parks and Wildlife is rescuing more abandoned black bear cubs this year after environmental conditions strained food sources that bears rely on to fatten up before winter. “Extreme drought conditions have limited natural forage in the higher elevations,” said Rachael Gonzales, Colorado Parks and Wildlife Northwest Region spokesperson, in an email to[...]
text:
Frisco Creek Wildlife Rehabilitation Center manager Michael Sirochman scans a cub with a PIT tag reader to make sure the implanted tag is working correctly. The tag allows Colorado Parks and Wildlife staff to know where a bear came from, and if it has been handled before. (Photo courtesy of John Livingston/CPW)Colorado Parks and Wildlife is rescuing more abandoned black bear cubs this year after environmental conditions strained food sources that bears rely on to fatten up before winter.

“Extreme drought conditions have limited natural forage in the higher elevations,” said Rachael Gonzales, Colorado Parks and Wildlife Northwest Region spokesperson, in an email to Colorado Newsline. “Low mountain snowpack and wildfires have added to the reduced availability of natural foods such as berries, fruits, nuts, plants and grasses across Colorado. A starving mother bear’s milk can dry up, forcing her to abandon her cubs, leaving them to search for food on their own.”
Each year orphaned cubs are brought to one of two CPW-licensed wildlife rehabilitation centers where the bears are fed natural foods such as fish and berries, as well as donated peaches from Colorado orchards. Once they’ve reached 60-70 pounds and start to display denning behavior the bears are released back into the wild.
The wildlife rehab facilities also take in injured raptors, beavers, raccoons, bobcats, mountain lions and otters.
By late September, CPW’s Frisco Creek Wildlife Rehabilitation Center in Del Norte had taken in 41 cubs — significantly more than the 29 rescued bears brought to the center last year, said John Livingston, CPW Southwest Region spokesperson. In a typical year, the center cares for roughly 20 bears, he said.
The other CPW-licensed wildlife rehabilitation center is the nonprofit Pauline Schneegas Wildlife Foundation, in Silt. This year it took in more than 30 bear cubs versus the three cubs it cared for last year, said the foundation’s executive director and founder, Nanci Limbach. The center, which is not funded by CPW, averages five to 10 cubs yearly, she noted.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A spring freeze also damaged important food sources.
“It’s been a bad forage year,” said Limbach, adding that in addition to berries, acorns — a highly nutritious fall food — were also lost to the freeze. Plus, “lots of creeks dried off, so lots of bears moved to town. The drought didn’t help but it was the freeze that started all this.”
At the Silt facility, orphaned cubs are fed until they’ve grown large enough to be placed in den boxes attached to large cages, and then in February they are transported to a natural snow cave, from which they emerge in March or April. The Frisco Creek facility has a similar process, and additionally performs “hard releases,” where cubs who weigh at least 60 pounds by November are released to find their own dens for the winter. Cubs that are too small to survive on their own are held in artificial den boxes until they are healthy enough to be released.

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



By late August, CPW officials were finding bear cubs that weighed just 17-18 pounds — the weight they should be in May, said Livingston. The mom was likely already malnourished when she entered the den last year, before emerging in the spring to super dry conditions, he said.
They’re struggling to put on pounds to allow themselves to care for their young, who, by “this time of year should be at least 35-50 pounds,” Livingston said. “That’s the reason for the influx of cubs this year. If a female abandons its cub it’s likely they just can’t provide for them.”
“It’s survival of the fittest in some cases,” Limbach added.
A yearling (a bear between 12 and 24 months) with with burnt paws from the Aspen Acres fire was one of this year’s rescues at the Frisco Creek facility, Livingston said. Bears are dealing with a changing climate, including warmer and shorter winters, he said.
While under CPW captivity, visual barriers allow caretakers to tend to daily feeding and cleaning without the bears seeing them. The goal is for bears not to become comfortable or accustomed to being near humans.
Cubs also become orphaned when a mother is struck by a vehicle, or shot by a landowner defending livestock, or when euthanized by wildlife officials after being caught breaking into houses or attacking humans, Livingston said.
Reported bear incidents in Colorado are at a record high, according to preliminary CPW data for 2026. CPW started its bear reporting system in 2019, to help wildlife managers track bear conflicts in Colorado.
So far, 2026 has seen 3.6 times the five-year average of bear incidents. As of Aug. 31, there were 8,672 reports of bear-related sightings and incidents, compared to 3,680 reports through August 2025.
Ninety-eight bears were relocated in 2026, compared to 33 bears relocated through August 2025. Bears have been euthanized at greater frequency this year — 294 compared to 83 bears euthanized through August 2025.
Bears can spend up to 20 hours a day in late summer and fall searching for food to build up their fat reserves to survive the winter in hibernation. Bears searching for food are more likely to engage in risky behavior such as entering neighborhoods when forage is scarce. Bears caught damaging property or threatening humans can face relocation or euthanasia.
In May, Gov. Jared Polis signed House Bill 26-1342, which strengthens penalties for people who knowingly leave out food or other edible waste that can attract bears. The law does not apply to acts related to agriculture.
