name: Michigan Advance
title: Speaker Mike Johnson talks Iran, public safety with Tom Barrett in Michigan 7th campaign stop
description: MASON — U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson called in air support for Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett on Wednesday as the congressman winds down his reelection campaign to Michigan’s 7th Congressional District seat — a boost he’ll need as he faces a tight race against the progressive Democratic nominee Will Lawrence. The event, held outside […]
text:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana), center, speaks at at campaign stop for U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), right, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026 in Mason, Mich. Also pictured from left to right: Shiawassee County Prosecutor Scott Koerner, Clinton County Prosecutor Tony Spagnuolo, Livingston County Sheriff Mike Murphy, FOP President Michael Sauger, U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township), and U.S. Rep. Dale Strong (R-Alabama). (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)MASON — U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson called in air support for Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett on Wednesday as the congressman winds down his reelection campaign to Michigan’s 7th Congressional District seat — a boost he’ll need as he faces a tight race against the progressive Democratic nominee Will Lawrence.
The event, held outside the Ingham County Sheriff’s Department in Mason, featured Johnson (R-Louisiana), Barrett (R-Charlotte) and U.S. Reps. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township), Carlos Gimenez (R-Florida) and Dale Strong (R-Alabama).
Johnson, Barrett and McClain each addressed the high stakes for Republicans in the 2026 election, including the continuation of President Donald Trump’s agenda in the final two years of his second term.
It also served as an endorsement announcement for Barrett from the Police Officers Association of Michigan and the Fraternal Order of Police. Also giving remarks were POAM President Jim Tignanelli, FOP President Michael Sauger, Livingston County Sheriff Mike Murphy, Clinton County Prosecutor Tony Spagnuolo and Shiawassee County Prosecutor Scott Koerner. Former Eaton County Sheriff Rick Jones was in attendance, as well.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The organizations said they were supporting Barrett because of his support for law enforcement, and his work to secure $2 million in federal funds for public safety initiatives, which have included funding for the Lansing and East Lansing police departments.
It was against that backdrop that Barrett framed the 7th Congressional District race as one of support for public safety officials versus calls to defund them, with Barrett calling Lawrence’s past statements about police funding into question.
“The voters in this district have a choice. Do you want somebody with a record of service like I have in our military, supporting our law enforcement and doing the right thing to keep our communities safe?” Barrett asked. “Or do you want to turn our backs on our police officers, and seek to have them defunded, to take away their dignity, and abolish them altogether?”
To further hammer that point home, Barrett had campaign staff stand — quite literally — in the backdrop of the press conference holding up large posterboards with images of Lawrence’s old social media posts, one of which, posted in May 2020, directly called to defund the police.
Campaign staffers of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) hold up posters of past social media posts by Democratic nominee William Lawrence. Standing next to Barrett is U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana), who joined him on Oct. 7, 2026 in Mason for a campaign event. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Johnson claimed that Lawrence was an avowed socialist and part of a left-wing insurgency taking over the Democratic Party. Johnson further claimed that enacting “communist” policies across the federal government was the ultimate for those who call themselves progressive Democratic socialists.
He urged Michiganders to reject Lawrence and to retain Barrett.
“Tom Barrett stands for common sense. He stands for his community. He stands for public safety, and it’s not just words with him; it’s deeds,” Johnson said. “You have to look at the record and not the rhetoric in a campaign. And in this campaign, in Michigan’s 7th District, you have a clear contrast between two competing visions, two completely different worldviews for who we are.”
Lawrence, in a statement released just prior to Wednesday’s event, criticized Barrett for appearing alongside Johnson and other Republican officials, and sought to tie the event to Barrett’s voting record and positions on Trump’s agenda.
“Tom Barrett’s entire campaign strategy is to stand at the side of extreme Trump administration officials, just like he voted for the Trump agenda 99% of the time,” Lawrence said. “Barrett’s latest guest, Trump’s Speaker Mike Johnson, is against same-sex marriage, stalled the release of the Epstein files, tried to overturn an election, and thinks our communities’ concerns about data centers are a ‘Chinese psyop.’ While voters demand answers for Barrett’s disastrous record in Congress, he is parading around the district with MAGA extremists.”
Johnson and Barrett took questions from reporters following the joint campaign stop and endorsement announcement.
Michigan Advance Fact Check: Tom Barrett’s voting record and Will Lawrence’s goals for healthcare

Michigan Advance asked the U.S. House Speaker if congressional leadership would act to move two important pieces of Barrett-introduced legislation — one that would prohibit local communities from using federal funding to purchase Flock surveillance cameras, and another giving Trump congressional authorization to wage the war in Iran, but with guardrails and an exit plan.
Barrett participated in a debate hosted by WKAR-TV on Tuesday with Lawrence. Both bills came up as key flashpoints in the debate. On the Iran war front, Barrett was one of only a few Republicans to vote against Trump’s ability to continue fighting Iran under the War Powers Act. 
He is also the only House Republican to have introduced a formal Authorization for Use of Military Force. The legislation would have carried the force of law as opposed to the resolutions passed throughout the year. It would have defined, set limits on and detailed a plan to end the war in Iran. His legislation would have ended the war by July 30, if passed. 
The war authorization remains stalled in the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and has not moved since it was introduced in May.
Johnson was asked when either measure would move and whether Barrett could secure action on them before the election, which could have bipartisan support. He praised Barrett’s work in Congress thus far, and said he deserves a lot of credit for that, and gave a rough timeline for Barrett’s legislation.
“Both of those bills will be processed in the lame duck right after the election, when everybody returns to town,” Johnson said. “We have an agenda that stacks so high.” 
The speaker praised his chamber’s ability to pass what he said was nearly 900 pieces of important legislation. He also blamed Senate Democrats from holding up a large majority of the bills his chamber was able to pass.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
When asked again if ending the Iran war was a priority for his majority in the House, or at least taking back its constitutional authority over how Trump wages it, Johnson said the war was going well and that it was winding down, without addressing Trump’s current lack of congressional authorization.
“The effort has worked. Operation Epic Fury was an epic success. We had no choice in the matter,” he said. “I’m on the Gang of Eight. I get the highest level briefing in the federal government. We got the briefing, in a bipartisan briefing, that Iran was dangerously close to having a nuclear weapon. Now, it had been the objective of every administration for 50 years in this country to ensure that the largest state sponsor of terrorism did not have a nuclear weapon. That would be an immediate threat to the security of Americans everywhere and our allies and everybody else. So they had to take care of that. … Now it is winding down.”
Johnson, however, did not speak of that wind-down in terms of an exit strategy, but rather of the United States punishing Iran economically due to its military actions.
“The Iranian currency has a value of almost zero at this point. They have no more assets to sell to anyone around the world. Their economy is in collapse, and they are in a desperate state,” Johnson said. “We have to get the Strait of Hormuz reopened, that is the objective, and it is. We have commerce going through that. We have oil moving through there again, but it is an international waterway that should be open for commerce.”

Johnson added that he believed Iran was “going to be brought to their knees in their economy.”
“They will be forced out of desperation to make an agreement with us and to finish this up,” he said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Doctors know how to treat ectopic pregnancy in Oklahoma. So why are patients still dying?
description: An ectopic pregnancy is not supposed to be a death sentence. As an emergency physician, I know exactly what is at stake when a patient comes into the ER with one. An ectopic pregnancy occurs when a pregnancy implants somewhere it can not grow safely, usually in a fallopian tube. If it continues to grow, […]
text:
An exam room at Stanton Healthcare, an anti-abortion crisis pregnancy center in Meridian, Idaho, is pictured. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for States Newsroom)An ectopic pregnancy is not supposed to be a death sentence.
As an emergency physician, I know exactly what is at stake when a patient comes into the ER with one. An ectopic pregnancy occurs when a pregnancy implants somewhere it can not grow safely, usually in a fallopian tube. If it continues to grow, the tube can rupture and cause catastrophic internal bleeding.
We know what to look for. We know how to treat it. And when we act in time, patients survive.
And yet, a new ProPublica analysis has revealed that deaths from ectopic pregnancy in the United States have nearly doubled, from about 100 between 2014 and 2019 to almost 200 between 2020 and 2025. The increase occurred nationwide, but the climb was much steeper in states with strict abortion bans.
Leitaea Lowrimore, of Oklahoma, sought care at three hospitals across two states as her pain and bleeding worsened, yet did not receive immediate treatment even as doctors acknowledged a possible ectopic pregnancy.
“There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” she later said in a lawsuit, filed in Arkansas, challenging that state’s abortion ban.
As an emergency physician, what is so maddening about a case like hers is that the medicine is not mysterious.
Ectopic pregnancy was once extremely life threatening. In 1880, mortality was estimated at 72% to 90%. By 1990, it had fallen to just 0.14%, thanks to more than a century of advances in diagnosis and treatment.
The problem is not that doctors do not know how to treat ectopic pregnancy. The problem is that too many feel forced to hesitate before they do it.
A few years ago, my colleagues Esther Choo, Monica Saxena, and I surveyed 150 board-certified emergency physicians across the country.
In states with restrictive or semi-restrictive abortion laws, like Oklahoma, 24% reported delays in managing suspected or confirmed ectopic pregnancies. More than half said they had changed their practice to stay within what they understood the law to allow, including ordering additional tests or delaying definitive treatment. Among doctors reporting delays, 58% said they now needed a higher level of diagnostic certainty before acting.
These doctors have not forgotten how to practice medicine. They are practicing differently because the law has changed around them.
Treating an ectopic pregnancy is legal in every state. Abortion bans, in states such as Oklahoma, often include exceptions to preserve the life of a pregnant patient, with some explicitly excluding ectopic pregnancy.
But saying care is technically legal is not the same thing as making doctors feel able to provide it.
Early ectopic pregnancies are not always easy to diagnose. An ultrasound may not immediately show where a pregnancy has implanted. Hormone levels may need to be followed over time.
Emergency physicians are constantly weighing probability, risk, and the consequences of waiting. That is normal medical judgment.
Abortion bans add another calculation that has nothing to do with medicine: What happens to me if I am wrong? Will my hospital support me? Could a prosecutor second-guess the care I provide?
In emergency medicine, waiting for absolute certainty is not always the safer choice. Sometimes waiting is the most dangerous thing we can do.
ProPublica also found that in Texas, a state with one of the country’s most restrictive abortion bans, the number of patients experiencing substantial blood loss from an ectopic pregnancy increased by about 29% between 2018-19 and 2023-24.
The rise in deaths began before the 2022 Supreme Court decision that held the U.S Constitution does not confer a right to abortion. No single analysis can prove the abortion bans that followed that ruling caused every delay or death, but alongside physicians reporting changes in their practice, it is impossible to dismiss the chilling effect as hypothetical. And we should expect findings like this in any state with a total abortion ban.
Lawmakers often point to exceptions in abortion bans as proof that emergency care is protected. But an exception on paper is not the same thing as access to care in practice.
If physicians are ordering extra tests, waiting for greater diagnostic certainty, or delaying treatment for a condition they know how to manage because they are afraid of crossing a legal line, then the exception is not working. It has utterly failed.
I know education matters because I have spent time providing emergency physicians in states with abortion bans with state-specific guidance about what care the law allows.
We are working with doctors, including at the University of Oklahoma School of Community Medicine, to make sure emergency physicians understand what they are empowered to do, even under a total abortion ban.  But education is a workaround, not a cure. No amount of training can erase the fear created by vague laws backed by severe penalties.
That is the fundamental problem with these laws. Emergency medicine does not operate in perfect certainty. Doctors make urgent decisions based on evidence, risk, and the patient in front of us. A legal exception that only feels safe once a patient is unquestionably, catastrophically ill is not a meaningful exception at all.
An ectopic pregnancy should never have to rupture before a doctor feels protected enough to act. We already know how to treat these patients. The question is whether our laws will let us do it before they get sicker.

name: WyoFile
title: Reading with a friend
description:
Treat the American Library Association’s list of the 100 most challenged and banned books as  suggested reading, writes columnist David Romtvedt. 
The post Reading with a friend appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

In the past several years there has been a lot of conflict over the scope and nature of books that can appropriately be provided to adults and young people in Wyoming’s public and school libraries. I thought about this while reading a recent essay by the literary critic and biographer Ruth Franklin on Mark Twain’s novel “Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.” For more than a century, Twain’s story of a young white boy and an enslaved Black man traveling on a raft down the Mississippi River has been considered a central document in our literature and history. But now, the book is often under fire, challenged and sometimes banned from libraries, removed from school curricula.
For her essay, Franklin traveled around the country asking teachers and students about the place of “Huckleberry Finn” in our schools and in society generally. Some say it’s central to understanding our history, a tale of moral awakening that is also a compelling satire of the racist values that were once held by most white Americans. Others believe the book encourages the racial stereotyping we’ve struggled to transcend, that it both reflects and is a form of violence against Black Americans.
Harper Lee’s “To Kill a Mockingbird” is another book that has been both widely lauded and sharply condemned by different readers. And, as with “Huck Finn,” issues around race and racism are at the root of the different views of the book that readers hold. 
With Franklin’s essay in mind, I looked up the American Library Association’s list of the 100 most challenged and banned books in the United States. Here are some of the novels that appear on the list:“Adventures of Huckleberry Finn” by Mark Twain“All the King’s Men“ by Robert Penn Warren“Anne Frank: the Diary of a Young Girl“ by Anne Frank“As I lay Dying“ by William Faulkner“Beloved“ by Toni Morrison“Brave New World“ by Aldous Huxley“The Call of the Wild“ by Jack London“The Color Purple“ by Alice Walker“A Farewell to Arms“ by Ernest Hemingway“Go Tell it On the Mountain“ by James Baldwin“The Grapes of Wrath“ by John Steinbeck“The Great Gatsby“ by F. Scott Fitzgerald“The Handmaid’s Tale“ by Margaret Atwood“I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings“ by Maya Angelou“The Jungle“ by Upton Sinclair“Lord of the Flies” by William Golding“The Lord of the Rings“ by J.R.R. Tolkien“The Naked and the Dead“ by Norman Mailer“Native Son“ by Richard Wright“1984“ by George Orwell“Of Mice and Men“ by John Steinbeck“The Satanic Verses“ by Salman Rushdie“Sophie’s Choice“ by William Styron“Their Eyes Were Watching God“ by Zora Neale Hurston“To Kill a Mockingbird“ by Harper Lee“A Wrinkle in Time“ by Madeleine L’Engle
This group includes Nobel Prize winners Faulkner, Hemingway, Steinbeck, Golding, and Morrison; Pulitzer Prize winners Faulkner, Hemingway, Steinbeck, Sinclair, Penn Warren, Lee, Styron, Mailer, Walker, and Morrison; National Book Award winners Faulkner, Styron, and Walker; Booker Prize winners Atwood and Rushdie; and National Medal of Arts recipient Maya Angelou. These are among the most honored novels of the past century. Why are they so often condemned?
Some of the often-stated reasons for challenging books are that they are pro-socialist or pro-communist, anti-family or anti-religion; that they are obscene, include nudity or are sexually explicit; that they use coarse language, scatological humor or racial stereotypes. Books have been banned for dealing with child sexual abuse, bullying, slavery, firearms, the occult, incest, gambling, infidelity, anarchism and drug and alcohol use. Sometimes it’s the content — suicide, death, abortion, atheism. More recently, books addressing LGBTQ issues have been criticized.
Penn Warren’s “All the King’s Men“ was challenged for “depicting a depressing view of life” while “The Grapes of Wrath“ was challenged for “portraying Kern County, California in a negative light.” Orwell’s “1984“ was charged in one case with being pro-communist and in another with being anti-communist.
I asked several friends to send me a list of their 10 favorite books. They all responded and, over the course of two years, I read every book named and talked about them with the friends who made the lists. Maybe we could do something like that with these controversial books. Pick one I’ve mentioned from the challenged and banned books list and read it with a friend or family member you trust, someone with whom you can speak freely without fear of being judged. After the two of you have read the book, talk about it together. See what happens.

title: Idaho voters can help pick the state’s official gun in 2026 general election
description: This year, Idaho voters have a lot to decide on: Who will be the state’s next governor or U.S. senator? Should two constitutional amendments pass? Should voters pass their own law to repeal the state’s abortion ban? But in the mix is a poll that the Idaho Legislature called for: What should be the state’s […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots during the May 19, 2026, primary election at The Waterfront in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)This year, Idaho voters have a lot to decide on: Who will be the state’s next governor or U.S. senator? Should two constitutional amendments pass? Should voters pass their own law to repeal the state’s abortion ban?
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races.]
But in the mix is a poll that the Idaho Legislature called for: What should be the state’s official gun?
Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. The state Legislature considered a bill this year to allow members of the public to carry concealed guns inside parts of courthouses that aren’t meant for court, like offices for county commissioners and clerks. 
The advisory question on the ballot this year asks voters to weigh in on the Legislature’s possible decision to declare a firearm — out of a mix of well-known Western and American guns — as Idaho’s official state gun. 
If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols, like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. Ten other states have declared state guns, according to the National Rifle Association, a prominent gun lobbying group.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho lawmaker hopes the advisory question will boost voter turnout

One of the lawmakers behind the push for the ballot question, Rep. Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said he thought it might drum up voter turnout during a year when many consequential issues are on the ballot. In election years when the president isn’t on the ballot, like this year, fewer voters tend to participate.
“Voter turnout is always important,” he said in an interview. “… When you have a lot of voter apathy, I think we don’t get as good of results as we could if we had an informed electorate that was actually out and voting.”
The votes won’t be the final say. 
“The results,” the bill says, “will guide the Legislature as to which gun shall be designated the state gun of Idaho.” 
Idaho Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, and Idaho House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, walk Gov. Brad Little out of the House chambers after the governor delivered his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
But Monks said this is the only time he knows of when the state sought public input before designating a state item. 
Monks acknowledges that not everyone loves the idea of declaring a state gun.
“I don’t think you can make everybody always happy. The majority of people in Idaho do have guns,” he said. “We have a pretty high percentage of gun ownership in our state. And so I think it reflects the fact that Idaho is a very gun-friendly state, and that it is an important part of our culture in many aspects.”
He stressed that the push for the ballot question didn’t take much time.
“I had some people ask me, ‘How come this is your priority?’ I’m like, ‘Well, this isn’t my priority. It’s just something we did kind of on the side,’” Monks said. “I put in 12 to 14 hour days there all the time, and I can tell you I spent very little time on this particular issue. I just thought it was a simple way of encouraging voter turnout, and that was it.”
The list of six guns selected by the Legislature for voters to pick between includes a “smattering of well-known American guns,” said Danny Michael, the curator of the Cody Firearms Museum in Wyoming, which collects and displays thousands of guns.
None of the guns on the list, he said, “have a developmental tie to Idaho,” unlike state guns in some other states, including Utah. But several have ties to the West.
 Here’s what you need to know about the guns on Idaho’s ballot:

A digital representation of a Winchester Model 1894. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office)
Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30): The most produced lever action rifle, the gun is one of few firearms used in the West that actually originated in the West, Michael said. 
It was invented by John Browning, a prolific gun inventor who was born in Ogden, Utah, which is near eastern Idaho. The gun is one of the greatest representations of hunting, said Dylan Stocker, who owns Old Arms of Idaho, which sells vintage gun parts across the U.S. 
A digital representation of a Winchester Model 1873. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office)
Winchester Model 1873 (.44-40): Sometimes called the “Gun that Won the West,” the gun became a staple in the early days of Western TV and cinema, topping over 700,000 sales, Michael said. To Stocker, the gun — used for personal security and for supplying food — represents Idaho’s history as a pioneering state. “Idaho was formed by those that were willing to go into the great beyond and get a new life started,” he said. 
But its nickname, Michael said, is a bit of a misnomer; it was a marketing slogan by the gun manufacturer. The gun, he said, often ended up in the hands of Native Americans who were defending the West. He added that the gun became “widely associated with the American West, both through its real-life usage and its popularization in media.” 
A digital representation of a 1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office)
1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver, or “Peacemaker,” (.45 Colt): One of the most collectable firearms, the gun was also a staple in old Westerns, Stocker said. The gun was sold commercially and was adopted by the U.S. military, Michael said. “Troopers at Little Bighorn … would have been carrying Colt Single Action Armies. It would’ve seen military service throughout the Plains Wars and beyond,” he said. Back in the day, most American sheriffs carried the gun, Stocker said. 
A digital representation of an M1 Garand rifle. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office)
M1 Garand rifle (.30-06): A semiautomatic rifle introduced just before World War II, the gun made the U.S. stand out as the only nation routinely using a semiautomatic rifle — which can easily fire repeated shots — when other nations were largely using slower bolt-action rifles, Michael said. Every veteran of that time, Stocker said, “was very familiar with the M1 Garand. And it was one of the technologies … that carried us through.” The rifle is also known for its distinctive ping — when an empty clip ejects.
A digital representation of a Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt pistol. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office)
Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt pistol (.45 ACP): This semiautomatic pistol is still one of the most popular handguns, Stocker said. Adopted in 1911, the gun was used by the military through both of the world wars and up to the 1980s. Today, companies still manufacture the gun. The gun was also invented by Browning, of Utah. It is the state of Utah’s official firearm.
A digital representation of a Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office)
Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle (.30-06): A bolt-action hunting rifle that’s commonly used for hunting. Stocker said the gun has “tremendous accuracy,” and most people who hunt “have shot one or had a friend that carried one.” Even with newer guns available, Michael said he still sees people hunting with the gun because they “trust them a lot when the hunt is on the line.”
 How to decide on the state gun?

When deciding what gun should be the official state gun, it comes down to personal preference. 
Some guns on the list are more popular, like the M1911, which Stocker said is likely personally owned more than any other firearm in Idaho. But, on the other hand, some guns — like the M1 Garand — played a big part in the founding or keeping of the country, and were well-known by veterans, he added. 
While the list doesn’t have guns that were made in Idaho, an Idahoan did play a big role in helping develop technology for one gun that isn’t on the list. Revered gun enthusiast Elmer Keith, based out of Salmon in eastern-central Idaho, developed the cartridge for the .44 Magnum, which was later used by the popular Smith & Wesson .44 Magnum, Stocker said. 
Monks, the lawmaker behind the ballot question, said developing the list was difficult — and lawmakers he talked to opted to leave out assault rifles to instead list more historical firearms.
He said he had no intention to leave out the .44 Magnum. But if that’s what people want as the state gun, he hinted that could be possible — even though voters can’t pick that in November. 
“I don’t want it to sound like ‘We don’t have to do what the people say because … it’s an advisory vote, right?’” Monks said, hinting at its nonbinding nature. “And so, what if we find out here in a little bit that more people were frustrated that that’s not the gun that they wanted. And we could make that our state gun. I think it would probably go a little bit against the grain of what we’re doing in that we’re asking Idahoans to tell us what their favorite gun is, and then we go ahead and do something different.”

title: Voters in midterm elections identify a culprit for rising cost of living: Trump’s tariffs
text:
WASHINGTON — Rebecca Myers lives in one of the nation’s most hotly contested congressional districts, and tariffs were on her mind as she voted early and in-person in Suffolk, Virginia in late September.The 44-year-old trained social worker said she and her husband, who recently retired after 25 years in the U.S. Navy, are raising two children, ages 7 and 9, and forgoing a family vacation to save money.“I'm an educated person, but I'm not going to pretend to be an expert in the economy. All I can say is I know my family's finances very well and I know everything we spend money on has gone up in price.“I understand some of it is due to the tariffs, some of it is due to the war in Iran,” Myers told States Newsroom in an Oct. 1 interview.Myers is among a growing number of voters found to be taking their anger about affordability to the polls this midterm election and blaming President Donald Trump’s tariffs as a culprit for rising expenses. Public opinion surveys bear out Myers is far from alone in making the connection.

 






(Getty images)

“The real top line is that for maybe the first time ever, tariffs are a salient issue at the ballot box,” said Scott Lincicome of the libertarian Cato Institute. “You know, normally trade is a boring issue that nobody really thinks about or cares about.”Myers, who lives in Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District, voted for Elaine Luria, the Democratic candidate and former U.S. representative who is challenging the incumbent Republican, Rep. Jen Kiggans.Kiggans, Myers said, has supported Trump’s “MAGA agenda,” including tariffs.Kiggans’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.Trump opponents seize on issueOrganizers are targeting districts like Myers’, where Democrats could flip seats.“We talk to families every day who are struggling with the things that they need to take care of themselves and their families,” said Sondra Goldschein, executive director of the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy.Her organization, which also has a political action committee that endorses Democrats, recently hosted a “tariff-proof” cooking class in Chesapeake, Virginia, to drive attention to the issue. Attendees received tips like substituting chicken for beef, buying domestic produce, and choosing frozen over canned goods — all which have been affected by Trump’s ever-changing taxes on imports.Goldschein and national organizers are targeting voters not only in Virginia, but in Florida, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Pennsylvania.“This Republican-backed Congress and all of the members that come from states like this have really turned their backs on working families,” Goldschein told States Newsroom during an interview ahead of the cooking class.In a state-by-state breakdown of tariffs, the conservative National Taxpayers Union Foundation and Trade Partnership Worldwide found the top 10 states most affected by Trump’s tariffs — in the tens of billions of dollars — are California, Texas, Michigan, Georgia, Illinois, New York, New Jersey, Florida, Ohio and Tennessee. Virginia, where business owners have paid a collective $6.2 billion in tariffs ordered by Trump since January 2025, ranked 18th.Nearly all are in the midst of fierce battles for U.S. Senate or House seats as tariffs emerge as what critics predict will be a major factor in the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.Ever-changing tariffsNew research shows Trump’s on-again, off-again tariffs on imported goods have cost business owners and consumers billions of dollars. “The typical estimate has it being in the neighborhood of $1,000-plus per year of additional (consumer) costs, and maybe accounting for somewhere between one-half and 1 percentage point of the inflation rate. That doesn't sound like a lot, but if someone came along and gave you a tax increase of $1,100, which is about what this is, you'd feel it,” said Kimberly Clausing, economist and senior fellow at the Peterson Institute of International Economics.Clausing and fellow economist Maurice Obstfeld at the nonpartisan think tank reviewed 13 academic papers from 2025 and 2026 on Trump’s tariffs and the pass-through costs to consumers and businesses.“What makes it a little confusing and hard to measure is that there's been a lot of uncertainty about the trade policy, and so it's come in spurts and reversals and restarts,” Clausing said, adding that some businesses may absorb the new taxes on imports at first but then eventually raise prices later.“It's not like you raise the tariff on day one and (on) day two all the prices have fully adjusted. It's a little slower than that, but you do see absolutely evidence that with time the tariffs are being passed through to consumers, and very little evidence that foreigners are bearing a significant burden,” she said. Trump’s tariff policy has changed more than 50 times since he began his second term in January 2025, according to the Tax Foundation, a think tank that advocates for a slimmed-down tax code and “policies that lead to greater economic growth.”As of Sept. 10, the foundation estimated that Trump’s tariffs will cost each household an average $820 in 2026.While Trump campaigned on the promise that other countries would pay for his tariffs, and vowed the same once he took office again, the statement has always been false, economists have documented. Tariffs are taxes that American businesses and individuals pay upon retrieving their shipments of items they’ve purchased from other countries. The tariffed goods fall into hundreds of categories — anything from machine parts to food.The president’s early round of “emergency” and “reciprocal” tariffs imposed on worldwide goods in April 2025 were struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court in February. Since then, Trump has used three other statutes to justify charging import taxes on goods.Impact spreads across statesThe breakdown produced by the National Taxpayers Union found the biggest effects in states and industries scattered throughout America.Sectors hit hardest by tariffs in the top 10 states include automobiles and auto parts; steel, aluminum and other metals; clothes and shoes; and food and beverages.For example, businesses in Michigan have paid an extra $23 billion on imports, largely cars and trucks. Meanwhile, the food and beverage sector was hit hardest in Florida, where importers have paid an extra $11 billion since Trump began implementing new tariffs in 2025 through Aug. 4, 2026, according to the conservative organization’s analysis that drew from Census Bureau import data.  Bryan Riley, director of the National Taxpayers Union’s free trade initiative, described Trump’s tariffs during his second term as “a very costly policy.” “If you're in a state like Georgia, big tariff costs are mainly because there's a lot of auto manufacturing in Georgia, surprisingly to many people. And then that's not going to be the case in New Mexico, which doesn't have a lot of auto manufacturing, so (there are) less tariff costs and different categories hit in each state,” Riley said. The analysis did not account for any court-mandated refunds the Trump administration must pay back after the Supreme Court deemed the president’s initial emergency tariffs illegal. Those refunds to businesses are not necessarily passed on to consumers.Trump and the cost of livingPolls show voters are growing increasingly frustrated with Trump’s handling of the economy, as his approval ratings plunge, and many of those surveyed are blaming the administration’s trade policy for the rising cost of living.Overall, 69% of American adults, and 52% of Republicans, say Trump is not meeting his promise to fix the cost of living, according to an Associated Press/NORC nationwide poll of just over 2,100 voters from Sept. 24-28.Specifically on trade and tariffs, the survey found that overall 68% of respondents disapprove of Trump’s trade negotiations with other countries, and 64% think the tariffs have gone too far.Lincicome of the Cato Institute said it’s a “shocker” that tariffs are becoming a mainstream concern among voters.When surveying just over 4,100 voters in mid-August, Cato and Morning Consult found 3 in 4 participants said they will consider tariffs when casting their midterm election ballot.Additionally, the survey revealed 74% of respondents — 66% percent of Republicans and 84% of Democrats — blamed Trump’s tariffs for increased prices on items they buy at the store.Lincicome, vice president of general economics for Cato, pointed to his home state of North Carolina, where Roy Cooper, the former Democratic governor now vying for an open U.S. Senate seat, is making opposition to tariffs a centerpiece of his affordability agenda.“It's pretty clear from both the polling and Democrats in not just North Carolina but Georgia and Iowa and other places (candidates) are really chomping at the bit to run on cost of living, and to say they're going to nix all these tariffs. … Even in places like Ohio, where Sherrod Brown is trying to win,” Lincicome said.Brown, a Democrat who served in the U.S. Senate from 2007-2025, was “one of the most consistent protectionists” of domestic manufacturing in the upper chamber, Lincicome said.“Now all of a sudden he's running on nixing the tariffs,” Lincicome said. “Now he's not nearly as vocal as somebody like Cooper or (James) Talarico in Texas or Jon Ossoff in Georgia. He's still saying he's going to get rid of these tariffs, and that's a pretty shocking change.”Trump ‘skillfully used tariffs,’ White House saysThe White House defended Trump’s record on the economy and said he has “skillfully” imposed tariffs.“President Trump signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs, and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs. “The President skillfully used tariffs to renegotiate almost 20 trade deals and level the playing field for American workers and businesses. The Trump administration has consistently maintained that the cost of tariffs will ultimately be borne by foreign exporters who rely on access to the American economy, the world’s biggest and best consumer market,” said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama public universities reach different conclusions on faculty senate, tenure law
description: A state law that weakens faculty senates at public universities formally took effect last week, but Alabama’s public higher institutions have reacted in starkly different ways to it.   HB 580, sponsored by Rep. Troy Stubbs, R-Wetumpka, and signed into law by Gov. Kay Ivey in April, limits the power of faculty senates and also requires […]
text:
Auburn University professor Matt Malczycki protests outside the Auburn University Hotel as the university’s Board of Trustees meets on Sept. 11, 2026 in Auburn, Alabama. Faculty, staff and community members protested the abolition of the faculty senate and changes to the curricula. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

HB 580, which limited the power of faculty senates and required staff to submit to post-tenure reviews, went into effect last week.
The law led Auburn University and Jacksonville State University to abolish and replace their faculty senates and replace them with new entities. Troy and the University of Alabama are maintaining theirs.
HB 580 also provides a compulsory post-tenure review process, which one UA professor said is causing the “most consternation” among her colleagues.




A state law that weakens faculty senates at public universities formally took effect last week, but Alabama’s public higher institutions have reacted in starkly different ways to it.  
HB 580, sponsored by Rep. Troy Stubbs, R-Wetumpka, and signed into law by Gov. Kay Ivey in April, limits the power of faculty senates and also requires staff to submit to post-tenure reviews. The law went into effect on Oct. 1.
The law gives governing boards of colleges and universities more control over tenured professors and faculty representation on campuses, including dismissal of tenured professors, abolition of faculty senates and requiring the creation of a post-tenure review process for schools.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But school administrations have reacted differently to the law. Some moved over the summer to abolish their faculty senates. Others have committed to maintaining them, either as they are or in a weakened form.
Stubbs said in an interview last week he was “pleased to see that they are looking for ways in which they can apply House Bill 580 to the betterment of their universities.”
“Each university has had numerous opportunities to work with us and our team to assist them along the way if they had any needs or requests to gather information or to ensure that they were in compliance,” Stubbs said. “But the bill was written and presented and amended through the process to ensure that we provided the universities with a level of autonomy to allow them to address the things that we wanted them to focus on, but in a way that fit their university.”
Stubbs did not say what the Legislature wanted universities to focus on.
But several universities began moving to implement the bill long before it went into effect. 
In June, Auburn University Board of Trustees voted to dissolve its University Senate and take direct control of curricula, despite an exemption in the law for Auburn and the University of Alabama, which have standing in the state constitution. Shortly after, the Jacksonville State University Board of Trustees voted to dissolve its faculty senate. 
Auburn University faculty protest Board of Trustees’ dissolution of university senate

Auburn’s decision to dissolve the University Senate prompted backlash from faculty members last month, with some saying they didn’t feel like they were being included on campus.
Stubbs said the bill doesn’t stop faculty from expressing themselves on campuses.
“We, as a legislative body, and myself as a legislator, recognize and want the individuals who are responsible for what’s happening on campus— the trustees, the university leadership— we want them to be empowered to address and to be accountable for the things that are occurring on their campuses,” Stubbs said. “Nowhere in the bill does it minimize or eliminate faculty senates. Nor does the bill address that faculty members cannot communicate or share their feelings.”
According to the legislation, faculty senates must “ensure adequate representation of each college and school of the institution; except as otherwise provided by the governing board” and  “require faculty senate leadership positions to be appointed by the university president.” It also requires that faculty senates be limited to no more than 60 members with two members per college or school one appointed by the university president and the other elected.
If a faculty senate body meets the requirements, the university board of trustees does not have to abolish the organization.
‘Far beyond what they were required to do’
Beth Davis-Sramek, president of Auburn’s American Association of University Professors chapter and a business professor at the university, said in an interview Wednesday that the Auburn trustees “went far beyond what they were required to do in that law.”
“There’s nothing in the bill that would suggest that faculty don’t have representation. Our board just decided that we didn’t,” she said.
According to university policy, Auburn’s faculty senate replacement, the Presidential Academic Advisory Council, will have a strictly advisory role despite having some faculty members being elected by their peers. Davis-Sramek said having the elected members serve in an advisory-only capacity could negatively impact the university.
“When faculty are stripped of our collective voice and any kind of meaningful sense of ownership in the direction of the programs in curriculum, because the board has now taken over the curriculum, then that is going to have a really negative impact on the university,” she said. “And more importantly for me, what breaks my heart is that this is going to impact the students.”
Jacksonville State University Board of Trustees dissolves faculty senate, staff council

The JSU Board of Trustees will be presented with an alternative board to represent faculty during a board meeting scheduled for Oct. 19 and 20. The Chanticleer, JSU’s student newspaper, reported last week that the new board will be composed of six elected and seven appointed faculty members.
Lance Ingwersen, a history professor at JSU, said in an interview Tuesday that  “there is no plan B that’s been communicated” if the board does not approve the Presidential Faculty Academic Roundtable.
Some senates remain
Not all colleges disbanded their faculty senates. Troy University announced Monday that its Board of Trustees voted to maintain theirs.
A message seeking comment was left with Lenetra Jefferson, president of the Troy University faculty senate, Tuesday. Jefferson said in the university’s statement the faculty senate “provides the faculty with a voice that can help support both academically and, on the student-supportive side, with the university.”
“We not only share governance here at the university, but we also try to be supportive of the university community as well,” Jefferson said. “We are not the final decision-making body at the university in any way, shape or form, but we’re kind of an advisory council to the administration, and we appreciate that we do have this working role with administration here at the university.”
Ingwersen said the universities deciding to keep a faculty senate showed that other institutions didn’t have to dissolve them.
“It means that the law allowed for faculty senates to continue, and that boards made decisions not to continue them because those are also statutorily created institutions,” he said.
The University of Alabama Board of Trustees also voted to maintain the faculty senate on all of its campuses but will limit the organization to an advisory role. Amber Buck, an associate professor of English at UA, said the board’s decision didn’t change anything the faculty senate was doing on campus.
“Essentially, the board of trustees passed a statement that said the role of the faculty senate is advisory and that it doesn’t make final decisions or speak for the institution itself, which actually has always been the case,” Buck said.
The more pressing changes made at UA, Buck said, come through the post-tenure review portion of the legislation. Under the legislation, governing boards of colleges and universities must have a policy for post-tenure review which includes, but is not limited to, the professional responsibilities of a faculty member; a faculty member’s professional development and revocation of tenure status or other disciplinary action if during the review “incompetency, neglect of duty, or other good cause is determined to be present.”
Buck said that was causing “the most consternation at UA at the moment.”
“I think everyone who has tenure at UA, including myself, works very hard and thinks that we’re continuing to produce research and be excellent teachers,” she said. “And so it feels a little bit like a solution in search of a problem, because we already did have a pretty thorough annual review process for all tenured faculty.”
Auburn has not changed its post-tenure review policy. Davis-Sramek said the board of trustees has signaled a change to the policy is coming in the future.
“They could, for instance, go ahead and adopt our promotion and tenure policy. They could go ahead and adopt our dismissal policy that has academic due process protections in it and just do enough with the post-tenure review policy just to make sure that it is reflective of the law,” she said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: The Democratic Party is gaining ground, even in East Tennessee
description: Democratic candidates in much of the Volunteer State, especially in its rural areas, face a steep hill to climb. Perhaps that is most true in East Tennessee, a region that has voted reliably red for decades. Hamilton County, the urban anchor of Southeast Tennessee with Chattanooga as its seat, hasn’t voted for a Democratic county […]
text:
"I had that same perception that it was more conservative than it actually is,” said Josh Wichman, a Democrat who was elected to the Hamilton County Commission in August. (Photo: Ben Sessoms for Tennessee Lookout)Democratic candidates in much of the Volunteer State, especially in its rural areas, face a steep hill to climb. Perhaps that is most true in East Tennessee, a region that has voted reliably red for decades.
Hamilton County, the urban anchor of Southeast Tennessee with Chattanooga as its seat, hasn’t voted for a Democratic county mayor since the early 1990s, and a majority of its voters haven’t cast a ballot for a Democratic president since Harry Truman in 1948.
The ideological leanings of both major parties have changed drastically throughout American history, but voters in Tennessee’s 2nd Congressional District, centered around Knox County, have elected a Republican to Congress in every election cycle since 1867.
But if the local municipal elections in August are any indication, East Tennessee may be starting to swing left.
Democrats in the Hamilton County elections narrowed the Republican majorities on the county commission and school board, flipping three seats among both governing bodies — with double-digit swings in a district President Donald Trump carried in the 2024 presidential election.
There were similar results in Knox County. Democrats flipped a school board seat, winning majority control of the board. On the county commission, the party gained a district Trump carried by 10 percentage points in 2024.
In both Hamilton and Knox, the Democratic county mayoral candidates — Mark Herndon and Beau Hawk, respectively, who both fell short of victory — dwindled double-digit point losses for the party in both the 2024 presidential election and the 2022 county mayor contests down to four points in both counties.




These gains for the Democratic Party are part of a national and regional trend since Trump returned to office in 2025.
In a December special election for Tennessee’s 7th Congressional District, for instance, state Rep. Aftyn Behn, a Nashville Democrat, lost the race by just nine percentage points in a district Trump carried by 22 in 2024.
In Georgia, Democrats flipped two seats on the state Public Service Commission in November, marking the first time since 2006 that the party has won statewide constitutional offices. A month later in December, Georgia Democrats narrowly flipped a state House seat that Republicans had controlled since 2019.



Quotation







I think what we’re seeing is certainly an emerging, what I would call, a small-d democratic coalition, a coalition of those supporting American democracy.


– Jeremy Strickler, University of Tennessee-Chattanooga


In a special election months later for Georgia’s 14th Congressional District, previously held by former Republican U.S. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene before she resigned after a widely publicized conflict with the president, Republican Rep. Clay Fuller won by just 12 points in a district Trump carried by 37 in 2024.
For Jeremy Strickler, an associate professor of political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, this could be the beginning of an electoral shift, from Washington, D.C. down to the local level in Tennessee, in reaction to the Trump administration polling in the negative on major issues.
“I think what we’re seeing is certainly an emerging, what I would call, a small-d democratic coalition, a coalition of those supporting American democracy,” Strickler said. “That carried over electorally to a lot of these special elections, and particularly in the South, you just see a lot of what feels like the ground is shifting under our feet in a way.”
A matter of turnout
Before Josh Wichman ran for District 8 on the Hamilton County Commission this past election, a Democrat hadn’t contested the seat since 2014. In turn, the district, centered around East Ridge, had been mired by low turnout — just 9.21% of voters in East Ridge showed up to the polls for the local elections in August 2024, compared to over 13% countywide that same cycle.
Fueling Wichman’s win last month — a 10-point swing for Democrats in a district Trump carried by eight in 2024 — turnout in East Ridge shot up to 28.61%, nearly matching the countywide rate of 30.12%.
“I had that same perception that it was more conservative than it actually is,” Wichman said of his district. “I feel like it’s been neglected by Democrats.”
The surge in turnout was seen throughout Hamilton County. The August election saw the most voters go to polls, over 30% of all registered voters, among all local August elections of the past decade, the Chattanooga Times Free Press reported. That was up from the 21.3% turnout in 2022, the previous local election for county mayor and the county commission.



Quotation







The thing I battled the most in the campaign, even talking to very dedicated Democrats, was, ‘This is a red territory. Good luck. I’ll vote for you, but I don’t think you have a chance.


– Knox County Commissioner Brandon Huckaby, a Democrat


Knox County experienced a comparable increase in turnout. Among the county’s nearly 270,000 registered voters, 33.43% cast ballots last month, up from 18.07% in the last local countywide races in 2022.
Knox County Commissioner Brandon Huckaby, the Democrat who flipped a seat previously held by a Republican attributed some of the low turnout of the past to Democratic-leaning voters assuming elections are already lost before they are decided.
“The thing I battled the most in the campaign, even talking to very dedicated Democrats, was, ‘This is a red territory. Good luck. I’ll vote for you, but I don’t think you have a chance,’” Huckaby said.
“They lost the election before Election Day because they have what I call blue-dot syndrome,” he continued. “They think they’re the only Democrat on their street.”
But with a close loss for Democrats in the district in 2022 — just 87 votes — Huckaby said his strategy was to drive Democratic turnout. “We knocked the heck out of some doors,” he said. “We knocked probably 6,000 likely Democratic doors to drive that turnout.”
Beau Hawk, president of the Knox-Oak Ridge Central Labor Council, lost his race for Knox County mayor but narrowed the partisan gap. He is know running for mayor of Knoxville. (Photo: HawkForKnox.com)
Even with this relatively high turnout, most local county seats in Hamilton and Knox are still held by the GOP. As Hawk, the Democratic candidate for mayor of Knox County, pointed out, more Republicans showed up to vote as well.
“We had a dramatic, relatively speaking, surge in Democratic voter participation in this county election,” Hawk said in an interview. “But it was also a higher turnout for Republicans as well, and I don’t necessarily think that’s a bad thing. I think everybody should be engaged in the process.”
Still, for Tennessee Democrats throughout the rest of the state, the key to building upon the momentum from August may not be assuming an inherent conservatism among the electorate and seeking to persuade those Republicans to vote Democratic; it may be convincing people to vote at all.
“Tennessee is not a red state,” Wichman said. “It’s a non-voting state.”
‘An anti-MAGA wave’
In the August election, Democrat Brandy Jenkins, new member of the Knox County Board of Education, did not face an established Republican incumbent, but an upstart candidate more in line with the party’s MAGA arm.
In the GOP’s May primary for the seat, Kristi Kristy, a Republican who had held the seat since 2018, was defeated from her right flank by Bill Sofield, who was endorsed by Moms for Liberty, an organization designated by the Southern Poverty Law Center as a far-right extremist group. With local chapters throughout the country, Moms for Liberty is known to advocate against LGBTQ+ inclusion in public education and for book bans at schools and public libraries.
Before being reinstated in Knox County after a backlash, one of those books was “Roots,” an account of the horrors of chattel slavery published in 1976 and authored by Alex Haley, a Black American who lived in Tennessee during several periods of his life.=
Haley is such a prominent figure in the state that Gov. Bill Lee designated “Roots” as an official state book two years ago. In Knoxville, there is a 13-foot statue of Haley. “It’s a very important book in our city,” Jenkins said.
Knox County votes to challenge Tennessee’s book ban law after “Roots” removal

“Roots” was banned by the Knox County school board in May under a state law enacted in 2022 that requires public libraries to filter content deemed inappropriate for children; in the book, there is a depiction of rape of an enslaved woman that Republicans on the school board had initially found in violation of the state law for detailing “sadomasochistic abuse.”
Following nationwide pushback, Superintendent Jon Rysewyk reversed the board’s decision. In June, previous Republican member Kristy voted with Democrats on the school board to urge the state to reconsider its criteria for book bans. With Sofield running on the GOP ticket in Kristy’s place, Jenkins flipped the seat.
“Why are we discussing this?” Jenkins said how she would respond when questioned by those seeking to ban books. “Let’s talk about what’s really happening in our schools.”
This grounded approach seemed to work, not just for Jenkins, but Huckaby on the county commission as well. His opponent was Sheri Super, vice chair and former chair of the local Moms for Liberty chapter. In the GOP primary, she beat former incumbent Gina Oster, who is closer to the center.
For Huckaby, he doesn’t see the election as a transformational shift away from Republicans, but a backlash against the party’s far-right arm.
“I don’t see an anti-Republican wave in Knox County. What I see is an anti-MAGA wave,” Huckaby said. “It was me, a commonsense candidate against a far-right candidate. It was easy to get those commonsense voters.”
In the election for mayor of Knox County, Hawk saw his relative success as a sign that voters are growing tired of what he described as “pointless national culture war stuff.” The messaging against Hawk on the Republican side, mirroring the party’s national electoral strategy, was largely accusations that the Democratic candidate is a socialist.
One major point of criticism from Republicans was Hawk’s appearance at a 2020 march in Venezuela in support of then-president Nicolás Maduro, a self-identified socialist whom the Trump administration kidnapped and jailed earlier this year.

“I was young and dumb,” Hawk, who is now 35, told the Knoxville News Sentinel in June. Hawk told the Tennessee Lookout that the socialist label and messaging is absurd.
“I’m not even sure how you could enact any kind of socialist agenda when you’re just dealing with potholes and libraries and things like that,” Hawk said. “Do you want to actually have a functioning government or not is the question. If that’s socialist, I guess yeah, I’m a socialist.”
Hawk eventually lost, but only narrowly by four points. Prior Republican County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, the term-limited former WWE wrestler better known by his stage name Kane, won in 2022 by 10 points and in 2018 by 28. 
In Hamilton County, Mayor Weston Wamp faced Herndon, who said he felt compelled to get involved in local politics last year after Republicans on the school board voted to end supplementary mental health services for students.
The local GOP had criticized what it called the provider’s introduction to students of “matters of identity, sexuality and gender” in a statement to the Chattanooga Times Free Press. Herndon’s son Silas, a member of the LGBTQ+ community, died by suicide a few weeks prior to the school board ending the services.
After much local pushback, including from Herndon, the school board eventually reinstated the vendor, along with other options for parents.
Nearly a year later, months after he started his campaign, Herndon found himself in the midst of a local controversy just before the election when it was revealed that he had sent threatening text messages to Republican school board members just after their decision to end the services. (Herndon has since apologized for sending the texts.)
The county GOP and many local Republican officials used the texts to discredit Herndon. Even still, like Knox’s county mayor race, Wamp won by just four points, down from his 16-point victory in 2022.
Reelected: Hamilton County Mayor Weston Wamp was reelected in August by a 4 percentage point margin, down from his 16 percentage point margin in 2022. (Photo: westonwamp.com)
Wamp, his office and the Hamilton County Republican Party did not respond to questions or requests for interviews. Neither did the Knox County GOP or the recently inaugurated County Mayor Betsy Henderson.
Strickler, the UTC political science professor, said that much of what has fueled the GOP’s success over the past decade is Trump convincing these more fringe elements within the party, normally electorally dormant, to turn out and vote.
“The main kind of political effect of Trumpism electorally since he entered the arena in 2016 was bringing out people who had traditionally been disaffected voters,” Strickler said. “Well, they could much easily just go back to not caring about politics.”
In turn, he said, when Trump isn’t on the ballot, like with these local elections, Republicans don’t do as well, leaving an opportunity for Democrats to campaign on anti-MAGA.
“The number of his support has really seemed to be shrinking and independents are very much turned against Trump,” Strickler said. “I think that’s what we’re seeing, but whether or not it’s durable is the open question.”
The future of Tennessee Democrats
Even with the party’s gains last month, Tennessee Democrats face a high hurdle in forming a meaningful coalition. Not only do Republicans control most local seats in Hamilton and Knox counties, the statehouse has been governed by a GOP supermajority since 2013.
For Democrats like Wichman in Hamilton County, turning the tide for the party starts with delivering results locally. As seen elsewhere across the country, that means, he said, focusing on making life more affordable.
“We have a really good opportunity right now to show residents of Hamilton County what Democrats are interested in and what we can do, but we have to be able to show action,” Wichman said. “We have to be able to show them that we can get things done.”
In Knox County, Huckaby said Democrats must start tying the struggling economy to the Republican Party more broadly, not just its MAGA wing.
“The Republicans have been in control. Affordability isn’t getting better. Infrastructure is getting worse,” he said. “Then you can tie it to a party instead of a faction.”
Hawk, who recently announced his run for Knoxville mayor in the election next year, said there needs to be more politicians willing to enact meaningful change — in both parties.
“So many of the issues that we are dealing with from the local level to the national level, they are solvable. It’s just a matter of political will. Do we want to actually put government to work for everyday people or not?” Hawk said. “I think there’s a lot of people in both parties that would prefer to just keep it as is.”
For Herndon, creating true change falls on the public.
“We’ve got to raise the bar. The bar has been lowered so much that people have forgotten that we have to hold our elected officials accountable to something, to someone,” Herndon said. “That someone, when everything else fails, is us.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Parents in Wallback work to open Clay County’s only childcare center
description: Clay County now has its only childcare center after parents worked together to get a facility certified and opened.
text:
Trailblazer Learning Academy in Wallback, West Virginia, opened this month and is Clay County’s only childcare center. (Courtesy photo)Clay County now has its only childcare center after parents worked together to get a facility certified and opened. 
The rural county lost its only childcare center four months ago, leaving families with no local options. Some parents were forced to leave their jobs.
Allie Vaughan, who serves on the board for Trailblazer Learning Academy, had expected to send her infant son to the county’s previous center before its closure.
“It was really devastating to find out that our county wasn’t going to have a licensed daycare anymore, and we were kind of just scrambling. So, a bunch of parents came together to start Trailblazer Learning Academy,” Vaughan said. 
“Not having a childcare facility has really stunted where Clay County could go. It really sent us back,” she added.
Trailblazer Learning Academy in Wallback opened earlier this month and can serve 27 children. Those spots filled up quickly, and there is already a waitlist for care. 
“It’s definitely an urgent need,” said Carrie Osborne, director of Trailblazer Learning Academy. Her daughter attended the county’s previous childcare center before it closed.
“A lot of our parents work for the school board or in town here or in our county. It doesn’t make sense for them to have to drive an hour away to take their kids somewhere to drive an hour back to go to work,” Osborne said. 
More than 28,000 children currently lack access to care because West Virginia providers don’t have enough available slots. Rural counties across the state sometimes have just two providers.

The West Virginia Chamber of Commerce has linked the state’s lack of availability to the state’s abysmal workforce participation rate. 

Families on average spend over $10,000 a year on childcare in West Virginia. The median household income in Clay County is around $42,300.
The majority of parents needing care in Clay County rely on the state’s childcare assistance program, Vaughn said. The state-run program provides financial assistance to eligible families who are working or enrolled in school; the funds are distributed to child care centers serving the eligible families. 
Vaughn said their team faced hurdles getting the center open since June, especially when it came to making sure the center could accept childcare subsidy payments from the state. She expects that they’ll be fully able to serve children enrolled in the childcare assistance program by the end of the week. 
Trailblazer Learning Academy staff are already hoping to expand, looking for a building or land in Clay County to serve additional children, especially older children and those in need of after- school care. 
Around 70% of families at the center use the state’s childcare assistance program, Vaughn said, but the state’s current subsidy rate doesn’t match the true cost of care. 
This could be a barrier to growth if not addressed, she said.
The child center is reliant on grants and the limited private-pay parents to make up the subsidy program’s reimbursement rate, according to Vaughn.
Trailblazer Learning Academy in Wallback, West Virginia, opened this month and is Clay County’s only childcare center. (Courtesy photo)
“It just makes it really difficult when you come from a small, low-income county, how we’re able to serve the county when we’re not raising rates to meet inflation,” Vaughn said. “I totally understand the struggles that our state has with income, but just looking at it from that lens, it impacts our center and how we’re able to expand.”
Along with typical childcare hours, Trailblazer Learning Academy offers drop-in care for people who do not need full-time care. This is helpful for grandparents who are raising their grandchildren, Osborne said.
“We have a lot of grandfamilies too in our county. So you know, if they need to go to a doctor’s appointment, that’s great for drop-in care,” she said.

title: First-time candidate running as independent for US House in North Dakota
description: A newcomer to North Dakota politics is running for the state’s sole U.S. House seat. Helene Neville sought the endorsement of the Democratic-NPL Party, but finished third, leading her to file for office as an independent. “I’m just running to serve,” Neville said in an interview with the North Dakota Monitor. “This is one of […]
text:
Helene Neville speaks to delegates at the Democratic-NPL state convention on March 27, 2026, in Bismarck. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)A newcomer to North Dakota politics is running for the state’s sole U.S. House seat.
Helene Neville sought the endorsement of the Democratic-NPL Party, but finished third, leading her to file for office as an independent.
“I’m just running to serve,” Neville said in an interview with the North Dakota Monitor. “This is one of the most consequential Congress’ in history, and we better get it right this time.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Neville, a Philadelphia native who has never sought elected office before, said she watched her mother run for local office in Pennsylvania when she was younger. Even though her mother did not win, Neville said it showed her the importance of public service. 
Now living in Jamestown, Neville is a former travel nurse and worked as a public health consultant in eight states. She garnered national media attention after spending years running solo across every state in the country and parts of Mexico, Canada and Puerto Rico, traveling nearly 17,000 miles on foot to promote healthy living.
“I’ve always wanted to run for office my entire adult life,” she said. “Most of the running around the country was because I wanted to get a good landscape of who our people are, what our people are going through and what they want.”
In 2020, she moved to Bismarck and worked at a local hospital before collapsing during a shift. She was diagnosed with Stage IV non-Hodgkin lymphoma and celebrated her five years of remission in May. She is the author of multiple books. 
Affordability
Neville said the affordability crisis makes it difficult to manage a family budget with costs continuing to rise.
Price increases could have been addressed by Congress, Neville said, but its members have become complacent. She said she supports term limits for members of Congress and wants to prohibit stock trading by members of the federal government to reign in what she sees as corruption.
3rd Democrat announces campaign for North Dakota US House seat

Neville said President Donald Trump has lied about who is paying for his import tariffs, and added that Canada may never resume normal trade with the U.S. based on how the country is being treated.
“The cost was pushed back to us,” Neville said. “We are paying for Trump’s mistake and corporations’ greed.”
She said healthcare affordability concerns could be addressed by breaking up the health insurance and pharmaceutical monopolies, which would lead to lower costs.
She said she is opposed to cuts to earned benefit programs like Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid.
“We’re not spending enough on these people,” Neville said.
Artificial intelligence
Neville said artificial intelligence companies should be held responsible for the products they create. Criminal charges and civil cases should not be off the table, if their products break the law or cause damages, Neville said.
She also took issue with secrecy around the AI companies and the data centers providing them with data.
“You can’t run something that sophisticated, that advanced, without saying what your plan is and telling everybody what it is,” she said. An international agreement is needed for AI products since those products are being used worldwide, she added.
Election security
Neville said federal elected officials should “stay the hell out” of elections in every state.
“I think they are using fear tactics because we already have those things in place,” Neville said. 
Neville is running against Republican incumbent Julie Fedorchak, Democratic-NPL candidate Trygve Hammer and frequent candidate Charles Tuttle, who also is running as an independent.

 Catching Our Eye

• In closing. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Jo Ingles reports, “Candidates for Ohio governor roll into final weeks of campaign with closing messages.”
Acton said as governor, she’ll push for a tax cut for working families and would help with health care costs by making drugs more affordable, alleviating medical debt. And she said ensuring data centers pay their fair share would making costs lower for everyone, including small businesses…
Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy has also been traveling the state, promising to lower costs. One thing he’s touting is how he worked with his running mate, Senate President Rob McColley (R-Napoleon), to bring the legislature back in session last week to pass a 90-day suspension of the state’s fuel tax.
• Refugees. WYSO’s Shay Frank reports, “‘There is no place to go.’ Ukrainian family battles red tape trying to remain in the U.S.”
The family came legally through a two-year renewable admission program called parole, which is granted to immigrants on a case-by-case basis for urgent humanitarian reasons.
They’re among the estimated 240,000 Ukrainians who received parole as of 2025, when the “Uniting for Ukraine” program was paused. Many, like Tetiana’s family, are stuck in legal limbo, waiting to find out if they’ll be able to renew their parole and remain in the U.S.
“Going back to Ukraine isn’t an option for many and for most and going to Europe, a lot of programs have closed and so these people are in limbo. There is no place to go,” Tetiana said.
• Husted embracing Trump. Cleveland.com’s Anna Staver reports, “In tight Ohio Senate race, Husted embraces Trump support, but that comes with risks.”
President Donald Trump keeps coming to Ohio to lend Sen. Jon Husted the one thing he can’t get on his own: Trump’s turnout. “I’m going to ask you to just pretend that I’m running,” Trump told the crowd Saturday at Butler High School near Dayton.
But that support comes with risks. The closer Husted stays to the president, the more he risks absorbing blame for voter frustration over the cost of living, the war in Iran and data centers.
• Mail-in ballot requests. Signal Ohio’s Andrew Tobias reports, “Ohio mail-in ballot requests plummet compared to recent midterm elections.”
The drop comes as President Donald Trump has made unfounded claims that voting by mail is rife with fraud while also trying to exert federal control of the process. In-person early voting meanwhile was up in all 56 counties where data is available.

The Colorado Capitol is pictured on the opening day of the Colorado Legislature, Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Attorney General Phil Weiser entered the home stretch of the 2026 governor’s race with a significant financial advantage over his Republican rival, Victor Marx, disclosures show.
Weiser’s campaign raised nearly $1.7 million in the third quarter of 2026, and reported $724,879 in cash on hand as of Oct. 1. That was Weiser’s best quarterly fundraising total since the first quarter of 2025, just after he launched his campaign for governor.
Weiser, who has served two terms as Colorado attorney general, is considered the race’s heavy favorite. He defeated U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet in the Democratic primary for governor in June, overcoming lopsided spending by a billionaire-funded super PAC supporting Bennet’s campaign.
