name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Turek, Hinson talk legislative track records at US Senate debate
description: U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and Iowa Rep. Josh Turek spoke about their track records as lawmakers as they met for their first U.S. Senate debate Wednesday, discussing their previous votes — and planned actions if elected — to address rising costs for Iowans. Hinson, a Republican representing Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, and Turek, a Democrat […]
text:
U.S. Senate candidates Ashley Hinson and Josh Turek take questions during a debate on Oct. 7, 2026, at Iowa PBS in Johnston. (Pool photo by Cody Scanlan/The Des Moines Register)U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and Iowa Rep. Josh Turek spoke about their track records as lawmakers as they met for their first U.S. Senate debate Wednesday, discussing their previous votes — and planned actions if elected — to address rising costs for Iowans.
Hinson, a Republican representing Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, and Turek, a Democrat representing Council Bluffs, are running in the Nov. 3 midterm election to replace U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst and serve alongside Sen. Chuck Grassley.
Though Iowa currently has an all-GOP federal delegation, the Senate race — alongside several House races in Iowa — are considered by political forecasters to be among the most competitive in the country in the upcoming midterms, and could play a pivotal role determining control of Congress.
Turek and Hinson will be at the top of Iowa’s ticket on the November ballot. As the two faced off at a debate on “Iowa Press” Wednesday evening, the candidates brought up some of the top criticisms leveled against them in campaign ads in a race that generated more than $90 million in ad spending through the end of September.
Many of the ads targeting Hinson in the campaign have focused on her increase in personal wealth since first taking office in Washington, D.C., in 2021. A progressive news organization, Heartland Signal, published an analysis of federal financial disclosures of Hinson’s finances between 2021 and 2026 that found Hinson increased her wealth by up to 10 times since entering Congress.
Turek and Democrats have also criticized her for retaining private stock in Elliott Hartman Agency, an insurance company founded and sold by her husband, while saying she supports a ban on stock trading by members of Congress.
When Turek brought up her and her family’s personal wealth during the debate, Hinson said her opponent was lying, and said she and her family sold all public stocks shortly after she took office in 2021.
“Look, my husband built a successful business that he sold in 2021,” Hinson said. “I made the decision as well when I got to Congress — because I do think we need to clean up Washington D.C. … We decided to sell our individual stocks right away in 2021. So we made it very clear that I want Iowans to know the decisions that I’m making in Washington, D.C., have nothing to do with the inside information I might be getting as a public servant.”
Turek also criticized Hinson for taking “$50,000 of taxpayer dollars, even though she’s a multimillionaire, to give herself a luxury D.C. apartment.” Hinson responded that this was per diem pay, meant to provide housing for members of Congress, that is only paid when lawmakers are in session.
“That’s the only day you can actually take it, and I use that, you can use it for a hotel or your apartment,” Hinson said. “So I think it’s important to note that my opponent, who did not show up to work, still took the full per diem here in Iowa — the same program that exists for lawmakers here. So you took the per diem, you stole from taxpayers. You should refund that money.”
Hinson and Republicans have repeatedly brought up Turek missing votes as a member of the Iowa House in 2026. According to an analysis of voting records, Turek missed 58% of Iowa House votes this year — but his campaign says he has participated in 81% of votes since first taking office in 2023.
Turek said during his time in the Iowa Legislature, he has been recognized as one of the “most effective” and bipartisan state lawmakers, referencing a Center for Effective Lawmaking report, and said he was willing to work “behind the scenes” to move many measures forward as a member of the minority party in the Iowa Legislature.
“When I joined the Iowa Legislature, I was told, ‘Josh, you’ll never get a subcommittee. You’ll never get a committee. You’ll certainly never get anything signed by the by the governor,'” Turek said. “And I said, ‘No, I refuse.’ We can come up here and have the monkey push the red button over and over. And so, I did the hard work behind the scenes and I built strange bedfellows. I built relationships across the aisle where I would say, ‘Look, maybe we disagree on 90, 95 percent of policy, but we agree on this, and we can do some good things here. Because honestly, I believe more than even Republican versus Democrat, what Iowans want is they want someone that is going to go up and work hard to provide solutions to people’s problems through bipartisan policy.”
The Democratic candidate criticized Hinson for backing policies of President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans that he said are making life more unaffordable for Iowans, such as the “One Big, Beautiful Bill,” and cited her votes against measures to restrict Trump’s powers over tariffs and to continue the war in Iran.
“When she’s been up in D.C., she has voted in favor of cuts to healthcare in a state with a healthcare crisis and a cancer crisis … just to give tax breaks to billionaires,” Turek said. “And additionally, five times in favor of the tariffs that have decimated rural communities and farmers, and seven times voted in favor of this war in Iran, which has led to increase in gas prices, diesel prices at an all-time high, and fertilizer prices. Iowans would have been better off had she not been up there in D.C. voting.”
Turek has said he would support repealing the OBBB, which makes substantial cuts to Medicaid, while adding that he would support keeping some portions of the law such as the cuts to taxes on tips and overtime.
Hinson has argued her support for the 2021 law has led to lower costs for Iowans through tax cuts, and has said the law protects Medicaid funding for those most in need, and also ensures “people who are gaming the system aren’t getting these benefits, and people who are illegal are not getting these benefits.”
She also discussed her September vote against a war powers resolution that would have required congressional approval for Trump to continue his war in Iran — a measure two other Iowa Republicans, U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn voted for — and said, “I don’t think we need another resolution, and I certainly don’t want to see the president not be able to do an orderly end to this war.”
“We do need to bring it to an immediate and successful end, and to me, that means not allowing them to have a nuclear weapon and making sure that we’re working with and protecting our allies in the region,” Hinson said. “My bottom line is protecting the taxpayers’ dollars. Also, as a mom, I think about the men and women who are fighting, right? I have a 15-year-old and 13-year-old boy. I don’t want this to be a forever war. So, I want to make sure we do everything we can. I trust in our U.S. military, the greatest fighting force in the world, to bring this to a close as quickly as possible, because I know people are getting squeezed.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Sharp divides in Indiana secretary of state debate over noncitizen vote, spending audit
description: Republican Max Engling leaned into blocking noncitizen voting as a top priority as he and the other three Indiana secretary of state candidates debated Wednesday night.
text:
The Indiana Debate Commission hosted a debate on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, featuring, left to right, Libertarian Lauri Shillings, Republican Max Engling, Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard and Democrat Beau Bayh. It was moderated by University of Indianapolis political science professor Laura Merrifield Wilson. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)

Republican Max Engling leaned into blocking noncitizen voting as a top priority as he and the other three Indiana secretary of state candidates debated Wednesday night.
Engling maintained that he was the only candidate firm on that issue — arguments that Democrat Beau Bayh called “ridiculous” and Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard labeled “ludicrous.” Libertarian Lauri Shillings described Engling’s push for tighter voter rules as unnecessary.
Bayh kept up his persistent push for an independent audit of what he calls corrupt spending by current Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales, whom Engling defeated for the GOP nomination.
Ballard used the televised matchup, sponsored by the nonprofit Indiana Debate Commission, to assert that an overhaul of the state’s Election Commission and Recount Commission was needed to remove political bias.
Here are key topics that emerged in the hour-long debate:
Quarrel over noncitizen voting
The sharpest exchanges of the night came over Engling’s arguments that other candidates weren’t as dedicated to blocking noncitizens from voting.
“They all said it was unduly burdensome to verify if you’re a U.S. citizen to be voting in our elections. That is a very big problem and they all said it,” Engling said. “The question was: Do we need to ensure that it’s only U.S. citizens voting in our elections? The answer is an absolute ‘yes,’ and I’m the only candidate that has said that and put that straightforward.”
Republicans have won every election for the office since 1994.
Ballard, who was a two-term Republican mayor of Indianapolis, quickly retorted Engling’s statement.
Libertarian candidate Lauri Shillings listens to a question. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)
“That’s a ludicrous assertion. We all think that,” Ballard said. “That’s ludicrous.”
Other candidates pointed out that voting by noncitizens is already illegal.
Bayh said during the debate that he supported Indiana’s current voter ID law and told reporters afterward that “our elections are safe and secure in our state.”
“Max is making this up because he wants to stoke fear and divide people and dissuade you from participating,” Bayh said. “People should have faith in our elections. We have 92 county clerks from both major political parties who do a fantastic job on a bipartisan basis, making sure these things run smoothly.”
Engling, who most recently was a top staffer to Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, said he would advocate for Indiana to adopt driver licenses with different backgrounds for noncitizens as a further safeguard against them casting election ballots.
Shillings said after the debate that Engling was “looking for a problem that doesn’t exist.”
“What he’s trying to do is bring the Republican SAVE Act and shove it down into our realm, and I think it’s unnecessary entirely,” she said. “We already have checks and balances in place to prove citizenship when you register to vote and our clerks do a great job of catching that.”
Bayh aims to keep Morales an issue
Bayh never mentioned Morales’ name during the debate, but repeatedly brought up the spending controversies from his time in office.
Democratic candidate Beau Bayh responds to a question. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)
“The current secretary of state has spent $92,000 of your taxpayer money on a luxury SUV for himself,” Bayh said. “He’s hired members of his family, six-figure positions. He’s taking trips all over the world and won’t tell us who’s paying or the purpose of the travel. He’s given out millions of dollars in no-bid state contracts to his largest campaign donors. That’s unacceptable.”
Bayh said he would immediately start a forensic audit of Morales’ spending and pledge to not give any contracts to campaign contributors.
Engling countered that he would support a review of the secretary of state’s office by the state inspector general.
“I am the only candidate that has actually done something about the issues that we’ve seen in the office,” Engling said. “I ran at the (Republican) convention and replaced the current secretary of state. I am the Republican candidate in this race, and I’m pressing forth to win, to bring new processes, to bring new procedures into this office.”
Republican candidate Max Engling responds to a question. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)
After the debate, Bayh said an inspector general review was insufficient and that Engling “wants to kick this can down the road, pretend like this corruption never happened.”
“The inspector general was appointed two years ago by the Republican governor, who’s Max Engling’s biggest supporter,” Bayh said. “For two years, the inspector general has looked at the purchase of luxury SUVs in this office, has looked at no-bid contracts to large donors and has looked at unexplained world travel and hiring relatives, and not taken action.”
Voting change priorities
Bayh highlighted his support for ending straight-ticket voting and allowing citizen-led ballot initiatives — both issues that Democrats have unsuccessfully pushed for several years in the Republican-dominated Legislature.
“We’re one of only six states in the country which has a straight-ticket voting system,” Bayh said. “What this means is that the first page on your ballot won’t have a list of names or offices on it. It’ll have political parties — red team, blue team. That reinforces some of the worst instincts of tribal politics.”
Engling said after the debate that he believed voters should have the option of casting a straight-ticket ballot. 
He derided citizen ballot initiatives as “a way for folks that cannot work an issue through the Statehouse to try and evade the Statehouse.”
Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard responds to a question. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)
“Very often what we’ve seen is that ballot initiatives are sponsored by folks with millions and millions of dollars to try and do something that the state didn’t want to do through their elected legislators,” Engling said.
Ballard pressed his desire to revamp the state’s Recount Commission and Election Commission, both of which are now controlled by appointed Republicans and Democrats.
Ballard faulted the setup for the lack of investigation into complaints about possible improper campaign donations.
“Because there’s two Republicans and two Democrats on that Election Commission, they’re not meeting either because they don’t want to meet,” he said. “Those duties should be handed off to administrative law judges.”



About the office
The secretary of state is an administrative official who broadly oversees statewide policies for elections, which are run by county officials. The secretary, by law, is chair of the Indiana Recount Commission.
Other office responsibilities include the registration of businesses and nonprofit organizations, regulation of the securities industry, commissioning of notaries public and the licensing of motor vehicle dealerships.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: As state considers vaccine changes, new online tool examines sickness, death, cost impacts
description: What would result if Florida reduces the number of vaccines Florida children are required to receive to attend school and daycare? The answers to those questions may be found on an interactive dashboard dubbed VaxImpactMap, published by the Emory Rollins School of Public Health at Emory University. Lead developer Ben Lopman, a professor of epidemiology […]
text:
Chickenpox appears as a rash that turns into itchy, fluid-filled blisters that eventually scab over, according to the CDC.(Photo via the CDC) What would result if Florida reduces the number of vaccines Florida children are required to receive to attend school and daycare?
The answers to those questions may be found on an interactive dashboard dubbed VaxImpactMap, published by the Emory Rollins School of Public Health at Emory University.
Lead developer Ben Lopman, a professor of epidemiology and global health at Emory Rollins, says he and other researchers at the university have been studying vaccine efficacy for more than a decade. 
They’ve been working on the VaxImpactMap for about nine months.
The latest version comes as the DeSantis administration moves ahead with plans to eliminate four vaccines from the list of shots children are required to take to enter public school or daycare.
The Florida Department of Health will hold a rule-making workshop on the proposed new regulation Thursday in Lake Mary. Public testimony on vaccine mandates leans toward the passionate, with two general camps — people who support vaccines and those who are hesitant.
“The intention of the model was kind of not as an advocacy tool, but really just to to lay out, you know, what would be the real consequences in terms of health and economic impacts of of these potential declining vaccine coverages,” Lopman said, underscoring that the data behind the dashboard are “robust and well established.”
He added: “Our intention was … to provide tangible estimates to policymakers as well as the public of what vaccines do and what the consequences would be of declining coverage. And I hope that policymakers, when they’re weighing a decision like the Florida rule change, weigh the costs and benefits of their decisions.”
To date, he said, response has been positive.
“We’ve heard from state health departments that are using the tool. We’ve heard from professional organizations like the American Academy of Pediatrics using the tool, as well as parents and the general public,” he said.
Expanded tracker
VaxImpactMap initially was released in February but tracked only three vaccines. The expanded version released in September added three, allowing users to track six vaccines in all — rotovirus, pneumococcal conjugate, pertussis, varicella, Hib, and RSV.
The map shows and how percentage declines in vaccine uptake over time could affect the number of hospitalizations and deaths from disease; increase health care costs; and lower productivity across the nation.
“The reason we chose these initially is because these are vaccine-preventable diseases that cause acute disease in young children. And what that means is that if vaccine coverage declines, we’ll see pretty immediate impacts of that,” Lopman told the Florida Phoenix. 
“But they are six different vaccine-preventable diseases, and they have their own epidemiology, they have their own vaccine coverage and their own kind of policy debates going on around them.”
The proposed rules under consideration in Florida would eliminate four vaccines the DOH now requires through rules and regulations that children receive to go to school and daycare: varicella, pneumococcal conjugate, haemophilus influenza type b (Hib), and hepatitis B.
VaxImpactMap includes information on all those vaccines except hepatitis B.
For Florida the map shows:

Five years of a 10% decline in varicella uptake could result in 24,900 new chickenpox cases; 222 additional hospitalizations for chickenpox, two additional deaths, and a $54 million increase in healthcare costs and lost productivity.
A similar dip in vaccination coverage for pneumococcal conjugate in Florida could result in 143 additional cases of that disease; 118 increased hospitalizations and four additional deaths; and an $8.3 million hit in healthcare costs and productivity losses.
Five years of a 10% decline in Hib vaccination in Florida could result in one additional case of Haemophilus influenzae disease, one hospitalization, and an estimated $34,200 in additional costs.

Findings can be modified by the percentage decline as well as time horizons, allowing users to choose as little as a 1% decline over one year to as much as 20% decline over 20 years.




Quotation







And I hope that policymakers, when they're weighing a decision like the Florida rule change, weigh the costs and benefits of their decisions.


– Benjamin Lopman, professor of epidemiology and global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health.


What stood out to Lopman about the research, he said, were the costs associated with declining vaccination rates.
“Varicella is the cause of chickenpox, and while many people don’t perceive this as a severe disease, there are, like, many kids that have severe outcomes from this, require hospitalization, [and] that has impacts in terms of healthcare costs, but also parents and kids missing work and missing school. So, there’s this whole range of economic impacts that occur that go beyond or in addition to the disease itself,” he said.
He noted that the lower the baseline vaccination rate, the bigger the implications of declining rates.
For example, Texas’ vaccination rate for varicella during the 2025-26 school year was 92.9% and California’s was 95.4%. The national rate was 92.2%.
A 10% decline in varicella vaccination rates in Texas over five years could spike chickenpox cases by an additional 30,700, lead to 277 additional hospitalizations and three additional deaths, and cause a negative-$66.7 million financial impact.
By contrast, a similar decline in California’s varicella vaccination rates could mean 11,600 new chicken pox cases, 111 additional hospitalizations, one additional death, and a $25.5 million negative economic impact.
“Florida already has lower coverage than many other states, and because of the way vaccines work and herd immunity, the lower your coverage is, actually the more you have to lose. Because if coverage declines further, there will be more disease,” he said. “So, any decline in Florida actually might matter more than in other states because the coverage already is relatively low.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blumenthal talks Trump, war — but not age — during ‘In the Room’
description: Asked about the prospect of running again in 2028 at age 82, Blumenthal pivoted, quoted Mark Twain and added: “This is my why moment.”
text:
On a stage in Fairfield — with four stops behind him and two more ahead at opposite ends of Connecticut — it was as good a time as any for U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., to field questions about aging and the prospect of running for a fourth six-year term in 2028 at age 82.
Blumenthal, who lives in Greenwich, began his day Wednesday with an event in Hartford, then ones in Norwich, Mashantucket and New Haven. After a one-hour conversation with Executive Editor Elizabeth Hamilton for The Connecticut Mirror’s “In the Room” series, it was to be back to Hartford to accept an award and then down to Stamford.
“So, it’s been a light day,” Blumenthal said, smiling.
At the CT Mirror event, held at the Sacred Heart University Community Theater in downtown Fairfield, Hamilton tried with limited success to engage the senator in a conversation about age and the road ahead. Another term would keep him in the Senate until age 88.
“How are you thinking about this issue?” Hamilton asked. “Because 88 —”
Blumenthal interrupted.
“Here’s the thing, Beth. As I go around the state of Connecticut, and I do travel a lot, I show up. I’m proud of showing up, and I listen,” Blumenthal said. “What I hear from people is, ‘Thank you for fighting. Thank you for standing up. Thank you for standing strong against this [Iran] war — senseless, reckless war.’”
The audience began to applaud. 
Blumenthal barely paused.
“‘Thank you for fighting the increasing cost of living.’ The price of diesel is 80 plus percent higher than it was just a year ago,” he continued. “The price of heating oil is 86%. We’re facing a perfect storm for consumers. ‘Thank you for fighting for lowering costs. Thank you for fighting ICE. Thank you for fighting the Department of Homeland Security that is brutally and inhumanely enforcing these laws.’ ”
There was more applause. 
And more to his answer to the question he interrupted.
“People want a fighter. People want someone who is willing to stand up and take stands, and they want candidates with courage and character,” Blumenthal said. “I hope I fit that profile. I’m more energized than ever right now because of this challenge that our democracy confronts. You know, this is why I became a public official. Mark Twain used to say that the two most important days in your life are the day you were born and the day you figure out why. 
“This is my why moment.”
Blumenthal, a former U.S. attorney and Connecticut attorney general, said Democrats regaining the majority in November would mean congressional investigations of President Donald Trump’s business dealings from the White House. The president has disclosed his income was $2.2 billion last year, nearly quadruple from 2024.
“In this administration, there is a through line of corruption,” Blumenthal said. “The president made $2 billion last year, $1.4 billion of it from crypto. I guarantee it’s not by dint of any intelligent investing. It’s because foreign governments have stacked cash in his crypto enterprises — World Liberty Financial, his meme coin.”
World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company started by Trump and his sons, sells a digital currency, a stablecoin. The senator has hopes of becoming chairman of the Homeland Security’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, a role he held when Democrats last held the majority.
“There is a kind of intertwining or interlocking of corruption that over that next two years, if I am chairman, I would try to uncover and untangle,” he said. “And I wouldn’t have prosecutorial authority. I’m not the U.S. attorney anymore or the attorney general, but we could at least uncover it.”
As Blumenthal was speaking, CBS reported that Trump was floating the idea of the federal government developing his Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Fla., as a presidential retreat for future presidents. There was no discussion of cost.
Blumenthal, whose relationship with Trump has been fraught since the president’s first tenure in the White House, said he was hopeful Trump would enforce the Russia and Iran sanctions bill he negotiated with the late Lindsey Graham. The measure was named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
“The president has to enforce the law, and I don’t think I’m revealing any secret here that the president doesn’t seem to have a lot of respect for the law. He has broken the law in the way that he’s used his existing tariff authority,” Blumenthal said. 
Blumenthal, as was Graham, is an admirer of Ukraine’s resistance to Russia and a strong proponent of the U.S. taking stronger steps in defense of Ukraine. He said the Russia sanctions bill includes “incredibly scorching, wide-ranging sanctions against financial institutions, oligarchs, energy companies tied to Russia.
“What Ukraine has done is going to go down in the history of warfare as one of the most extraordinary achievements of all time,” Blumenthal said. “When you think back to four years ago, almost five years ago now, and our own military said that Ukraine was going to fall in a matter of weeks.”
Blumenthal smiled recalling his travels with Graham.
“I don’t think we voted the same way more than a handful of times, but we traveled to Ukraine probably eight, nine times together. I’ve been there 11 times, most recently,  a little more than four weeks ago,” he said.
Blumenthal said he hoped Republicans would urge the president to use the tariff tools handed him by the two senators.
Hamilton tried to end the event on a light note, asking Blumenthal about his reading habits. 
“I am reading an absolutely chilling book on biological warfare,” Blumenthal said.
“Oh, that’s happy!” Hamilton said.
Blumenthal said he is reading the nonfiction book “Biological War: A Scenario.” The New York Times called it “a sobering new book” in which “Annie Jacobsen considers the potentially civilization-ending impacts of biological war.”
The senator recommended it.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Federal judge releases 50 people to date in wrongful arrest class-action lawsuit
description: A federal judge has ordered the release of 50 people from jail since the end of July because the U.S. government wrongfully arrested them in Montana, according to Upper Seven Law, representing the plaintiffs. Andres Haladay, senior legal counsel with Upper Seven, said Wednesday the federal government has continued to ignore an earlier court order […]
text:
A sign marking entry into Cascade County along Highway 89 taken on March 30, 2024. (Photo by Nicole Girten/Daily Montanan)A federal judge has ordered the release of 50 people from jail since the end of July because the U.S. government wrongfully arrested them in Montana, according to Upper Seven Law, representing the plaintiffs.
Andres Haladay, senior legal counsel with Upper Seven, said Wednesday the federal government has continued to ignore an earlier court order that said those arrests were illegal.
The people have been detained on immigration holds, at least some in Cascade County Detention Center.
Sunday, the law firm said it had secured the release of 40 people since the end of July in the class-action lawsuit.
Tuesday, Upper Seven said the U.S. District Court of Montana ordered the release of another 10 people, all found to be wrongfully arrested.
“The rule of law does not differ on the basis of race, language, sex, or immigration status,”  Upper Seven said in the post. “We will not stand down.”
The case started when U.S. Customs and Border Patrol arrested Jesus Verde Hernandez near Lewistown and detained him in the Cascade County Detention Center.
Upper Seven successfully argued his arrest and that of others held in Cascade County, including a father and child, was illegal.
Haladay said, and Judge Brian Morris agreed, the federal government needs to have a warrant before arresting a person or must believe the person is in the country without proper documentation and is also a flight risk.
The lawsuit is filed against Cascade County Sheriff Jesse Slaughter and authorities with other federal agencies, including the Havre Sector of Customs and Border Patrol, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office has argued the federal government produced a warrant after arrests took place.
Citing active litigation, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment Wednesday on the high number of improper arrests the judge said the federal government made or if it planned to change its immigration operations in Montana
Haladay told the Daily Montanan the government is inserting “boilerplate language” – or language that has been copied verbatim multiple times – that describes a near identical reason officials believe the detained people are flight risks.
But Haladay said the justification for holding them takes place after a person has already been handcuffed and detained.
“Some of these later orders point out that they (government officials) can’t do that,” Haladay said.
In one release order, for example, Morris said officers need to determine a person is a flight risk before an arrest.
The judge said that means seeking specific evidence ahead of time, such as whether a person has family, property or other ties to a community.
“Nothing in the record indicates that the officer collected this information before (the resident’s) arrest,” the order said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Dyed diesel still currently illegal on Montana roads, despite executive order
description: The Montana Department of Transportation said in a social media post on Wednesday that red dyed diesel is still illegal on Montana roads, despite a recent executive order from President Donald Trump. “Montana statute banning the use of dyed diesel on the state’s public roads remains in effect,” a Facebook post from MDT says, adding […]
text:
Trucks line up at a shipping terminal. (Justin Sullivan | Getty Images)The Montana Department of Transportation said in a social media post on Wednesday that red dyed diesel is still illegal on Montana roads, despite a recent executive order from President Donald Trump.
“Montana statute banning the use of dyed diesel on the state’s public roads remains in effect,” a Facebook post from MDT says, adding the department will share more information when it receives it.
Announced on Monday, the federal executive order allows for wider use of dyed diesel, which is exempt from federal fuel taxes. It does not change individual state taxes. Trump said he issued the order to help ease soaring fuel prices.
Red dyed diesel is not allowed for on-road use and is specifically directed toward farm equipment or recreational equipment. Some states, including South Dakota, have used the announcement to widen dyed diesel usage.
The diesel, which is identical to standard diesel fuel, is dyed red as a way to alert law enforcement.
The fuel is not sold at all gas stations and retails for around $1 per gallon cheaper than other diesel because it does not include state and federal taxes. Those taxes often go toward road and transportation projects, but since red dyed diesel is used in agricultural and recreational equipment that do not travel on roads, it’s exempt from those taxes.
Burning red dyed diesel in a vehicle or truck leaves a red residue that tells authorities that it’s being used in that particular vehicle, which can be ticketed for not paying the fuel tax.
In Montana, a first offense is a fine up to $1,000, a second offense is a fine up to $5,000, and third and subsequent offenses carry a $535 minimum fine and potentially jail time.
The move comes in the midst of a severe spike in cost of materials using oil in the United States as war in the Middle East has severely hampered maritime global trade and throttled oil transportation.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: 2 Utah sheriffs are charged with obstruction in case tied to Kouri Richins prosecution
description: A current and former Utah sheriff are charged with obstruction of justice in a case tied to the high-profile prosecution of Kouri Richins.
text:
Kouri Richins listens to statements written by her children during her sentencing in 3rd District Court in Park City on Wednesday, May 13, 2026. At right is defense attorney Kathy Nester. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)A current and former Utah sheriff are both charged with obstruction of justice in a case tied to the high-profile prosecution of Kouri Richins, the realtor convicted of poisoning her husband with a fentanyl-laced cocktail and then writing a children’s book about grief. 
Court records unsealed Wednesday in Utah’s 3rd District Court show Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby and former Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds were charged by grand jury on Sept. 24. They have pleaded not guilty. 
The criminal case against Rigby was the second filed within a week against a sitting public official in Utah. A Republican state lawmaker from Layton, Rep. Trevor Lee, resigned last week after he was charged with fraud. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Grand juries are common in the federal court system, but rare in Utah’s state courts, where prosecutors tend to file charges and a judge decides later at a preliminary hearing if there’s enough evidence for a trial. 
The indictments take the place of that preliminary hearing, prosecutors on the case against the sheriffs said in court filings. Under state law, grand juries must include at least nine and up to 15 members, and can only return an indictment if ¾ vote in favor. 
As sheriffs, Rigby and Edmunds have been in charge of law enforcement in Utah’s two most affluent counties. The specifics of the allegations against them were fully redacted from charging documents unsealed Wednesday, an unusual occurrence in the state court system. Prosecutors in Summit County argue in court filings that the indictments should be made public under the First Amendment. 
Attorneys for Rigby and Edmunds said in court filings they don’t want the indictments released without redactions, raising concerns about pretrial publicity given intense public interest in the Richins case. A hearing on those arguments is scheduled for Nov. 4. 
The bulk of available information about the indictment comes from those motions, with Edmunds’ attorneys saying the charge against him arose from a statement he’s accused of making in an interview in March. The indictment also ties the charge to “alleged misconduct involving a sheriff’s deputy, an anonymous letter, and State of Utah v. Kouri Darden Richins,” they wrote in a court filing dated Oct. 2. 
Rigby’s attorneys wrote that the case against him is “predicated on allegations that he interfered in State v. Kouri Darden Richins — a prosecution that received extensive local and national media coverage.”
Wasatch County sheriff under criminal investigation for actions tied to Kouri Richins trial

Both men are charged with obstruction of justice: Rigby with a more severe second-degree felony count of obstructing in a criminal proceeding; Edmunds a third-degree felony of obstructing in a criminal investigation. Rigby also faces an additional charge of making a written false statement, a misdemeanor.
The charges follow coverage of the investigation by the Utah Investigative Journalism Project for Utah News Dispatch, which reported that in January of this year, Rigby “allegedly presented an anonymous letter to Summit County Sheriff Kacey Bates” containing severe allegations about a Summit County sheriff’s deputy.
That deputy, Eric Mainord, was challenging Rigby in the race for Wasatch County sheriff and was also a detective on the Richins case, the Utah Investigative Journalism Project reported. 
Rigby lost the June Republican primary election to Jeremy Hales, the county’s emergency manager. Mainord withdrew from the race before the primary. 
Edmunds was Summit County sheriff from 2003 to 2014, KPCW reported, while Rigby started the job in Wasatch County in 2019. Their attorneys did not immediately respond Wednesday to emails requesting comment. 
Richins, sentenced in May to life without parole for the murder of her husband Eric Richins, was ordered this week to pay more than $55 million to his estate as a result of a wrongful death lawsuit filed by his sister. Her trial was among the highest profile in the nation this year, followed extensively by news media and court watchers across the country.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Huckabee, Arkansas officials mark 3rd anniversary of Oct. 7 attack on Israel
description: Arkansas elected officials, faith leaders and U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee decried what they described as a rewriting of the history surrounding the deadly 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel as they marked the third anniversary Wednesday.  “If Israel wanted to commit genocide, they could have done it in two and a half hours. They […]
text:
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee shakes hands at the Arkansas Capitol prior to a commemoration of the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas elected officials, faith leaders and U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee decried what they described as a rewriting of the history surrounding the deadly 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel as they marked the third anniversary Wednesday. 
“If Israel wanted to commit genocide, they could have done it in two and a half hours. They have the military capacity. Gaza is the size of Las Vegas. They intentionally did not,” Huckabee, the former Arkansas governor and father of Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, told attendees at the Capitol for the commemoration held by the National Association of Christian Lawmakers.
About 1,200 people were killed and more than 240 taken hostage by Hamas fighters in the early morning attacks on Oct. 7, 2023. More than 74,000 people have been killed during Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, according to the territory’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its figures but says around half were women and children. The military campaign has displaced around 90% of Gaza’s population and destroyed vast areas.
Biden denounces deadly Hamas attack on Israel: ‘There’s no justification for terrorism’

The widespread destruction has garnered international criticism and accusations that Israel is committing genocide, while U.S. military support for the nation has grown more polarizing in the years since the attacks.
Wednesday’s event at the state Capitol featured remarks from Sanders, Attorney General Tim Griffin and others. Many thanked Sanders and the Legislature for their support of Israel in the years since the attacks.
“In 2024, my predecessor came to this building carrying footage recorded by the terrorists themselves on Oct. 7,” said Israel’s Consul General to the Southwest Adi Farjon Israel. She said more than 100 members of the Arkansas Legislature attended a screening of that footage.
“That matters, because three years later, some are trying to rewrite what happened on Oct. 7,” Farjon Israel said. 
Farjon Israel commended the move by the Legislature last year to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s definition of antisemitism, which came as part of a law requiring public schools and universities to treat harassment or discrimination with “antisemitic intent” the same as they would treat any other form of discrimination prohibited by state or federal law.
Speakers sometimes used graphic terms when describing the violence of the attacks, which targeted a music festival as well as civilian homes. 
“We can’t even understand the pain the Jewish people are going through these days, and the world is celebrating, and shouting, ‘From the river to the sea,’” said Albert Veksler, co-founder of the Jerusalem Prayer Dinner, referring to a controversial phrase that has been adopted by pro-Palestinian protestors and vilified by Israel’s supporters. 
A ceasefire that took effect in October halted the heaviest of the fighting, though Israel strikes have continued. A United Nations commission established to investigate allegations of humanitarian and human rights law violations in Israel issued a report last year saying Israel had committed genocide in the territory — findings the nation has denied.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Warmer soil and a warmer, wet winter expected in Iowa with super El Niño
description: Weather patterns across Iowa, influenced by an abnormally strong El Nino pattern, will likely impact fall nutrient applications for farmers, according to weather and crop scientists in the state.  Climatologist for the state of Iowa Justin Glisan said Wednesday on a webinar hosted by the Iowa Farm Bureau Federation that the “cake is already baked” […]
text:
A farmer tills a harvested corn field in late October, 2024 near Boone. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Weather patterns across Iowa, influenced by an abnormally strong El Nino pattern, will likely impact fall nutrient applications for farmers, according to weather and crop scientists in the state. 
Climatologist for the state of Iowa Justin Glisan said Wednesday on a webinar hosted by the Iowa Farm Bureau Federation that the “cake is already baked” for a “very strong” El Niño event, beyond what has been “seen in the observational record.” 
El Niño is a pattern observed when ocean temperatures in the equatorial Pacific are unusually warm, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The warmer water, or cooler water in the event of a La Niña year, influences weather in the U.S. and around the globe. Glisan said there is a “huge plume of very warm surface-based waters” in the eastern equatorial Pacific that is leading to what has been described as a “super” El Niño. 
Analogs from past strong El Niño years and climate outlooks from NOAA indicate that Iowa will have warmer, wetter conditions through fall and winter. 
“Warmth is the theme here through fall and into winter with strong El Niño events,” Glisan said. “Generally, when we see warmer temperatures with these El Niño events, typically less snowfall, but more episodic snowfall events – we get more snow within a shorter period of time.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While the forecasts show potential for more precipitation than normal in October and November, Glisan said these months are typically fairly dry, so Iowans should not expect “September behavior” to return. Glisan said last month was one of the wettest Septembers on record, with parts of the state reporting some rainfall 25 days out of the month. 
Shawn Richmond, with Iowa Farm Bureau Federation, moderated the webinar and noted the wet conditions from September have delayed harvest activities for farmers. 
“We’re also forecasting some challenges that’s going to create, beyond harvest, with nutrient applications,” Richmond said. “Especially as it relates to the guidance we have on the conditions we want to have when we’re putting nutrient applications in the ground.” 
Wetter, warmer soils
Glisan said that following a September with precipitation patterns that mimicked wet spring months, soils are generally wetter. According to the latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, around 40% of sub and topsoil in the state had surplus moisture conditions at the end of September. 
Soggy soil creates a thermodynamic lag, Glisan explained, meaning soil temperatures will “hang on longer” than they have in recent years.
Warmer soil temperature through the fall is significant because agronomists recommend waiting to apply fall fertilizers until soil temperatures are around 50 degrees Fahrenheit “and falling.” 
Daniel Andersen, a professor at Iowa State University and a manure extension specialist, said that with anticipated warmer soil temperatures, manure application windows might be slightly later than normal. 
Andersen said he also anticipates that farmers will have longer to apply manure before the ground freezes thanks to the forecast warmer temperatures brought on by the strong El Niño. Farmers prohbited by Iowa law from applying manure to frozen or snow covered ground, because there is high risk of the nutrients running off the soil .
“It’s hard to predict next year’s weather in the fall, but given where we’re at, if you can wait until 50 degrees and cooling, we should be in good shape,” Andersen said. 
Andersen said Iowa does a “pretty darn good job of trying to manage our manure as a crop resource” but said there is “still room for improvement” when it comes to the balance of nutrients that will help feed crops and the amount that is lost to the environment.
Environmental groups and some researchers have pointed to fertilizer run off and manure application as cause for high nitrate concentrations in Iowa’s rivers. More strategic fertilizer application is a key component of the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy, which aims to reduce the nitrogen and phosphorus entering Iowa’s watershed.
Cooler soil temperatures lead to a significant decline in soil microbial activity. Mike Castellano, an ISU professor and lead of the Iowa Nitrogen Initiative, explained that microbes in the soil take organic material in fertilizers and transform it into things like nitrate which is “easily lost to the environment.”
Delaying fertilizer applications until microbial activity declines in cooler soil temperatures can reduce soil nitrification and in turn, the amount of nitrate that could potentially run off the soil. 
“We expect the relative rate of the transformation of ammonium to nitrate to be about a third of its maximum,” Castellano explained, pointing to research of soil temperatures. “So it’s still not zero at 50 degrees.” 
How do manure management plans work in Iowa?

Castellano said more and more he is seeing farmers apply fall fertilizers with nitrification inhibitors, which he said is valuable since there is still some nitrification happening even at lower soil temperatures. 
Andersen said especially if farmers can’t wait for soil temperatures to drop, they should consider adding an inhibitor – additives that work to reduce the number of soil microbes that convert ammonium to nitrate. 
“If there’s a year I was going to pick an inhibitor or really pay attention to waiting, this is the weather condition that I’m really focused on,” Andersen said. “A time period when we know the fall will be warmer than normal, and a time period where we’re starting that fall with a wetter profile and making the risk of more tile drainage next spring probable.”
Castellano said that wet soil, in addition to warm soil, encourage soil microbe activity. 
“Unfortunately, in this year, we know that we have pretty good soil moisture this fall, maybe too much, and we also have those high temperatures, and so we really need to think about managing our fall nitrogen,” Castellano said. 
Castellano said there is “little difference” in nitrate loss for fields applied under best management practices in the fall versus those applied in the spring. Castellano said fall application, however, “opens up” the spring season for farmers to spend time doing other things, including conservation work. 
He said the Nitrogen Fertilizer Application Consultation Tool, or N-FACT, from the Iowa Nitrogen Initiative is one tool farmers can use to optimize their fall applications. The online tool helps farmers determine optimal nitrogen application rates for their farm based location, precipitation and residual nitrogen in the area. 
Farmers in certain counties can also apply for free nitrogen soil testing with the Iowa Nutrient Research & Education Council and Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Help crops and reduce flooding and pollution with new approach to drainage, speaker tells farmers
description: BROOKINGS — Farmers could reduce their reliance on groundwater, help mitigate downstream flooding and improve crop yields during droughts by storing their drainage water in a pond or wetland, according to a speaker at the Eastern South Dakota Water Conference. Chuck Brandel is a drainage expert with ISG, an engineering and architecture firm with offices […]
text:
Chuck Brandel, a drainage expert with ISG, an engineering and architecture firm, delivers a presentation about “drainage water recycling” to the Eastern South Dakota Water Conference on Oct. 7, 2026, in Brookings, South Dakota. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)BROOKINGS — Farmers could reduce their reliance on groundwater, help mitigate downstream flooding and improve crop yields during droughts by storing their drainage water in a pond or wetland, according to a speaker at the Eastern South Dakota Water Conference.
Chuck Brandel is a drainage expert with ISG, an engineering and architecture firm with offices in South Dakota and other states. He delivered a presentation about “drainage water recycling” to conference attendees at South Dakota State University’s McCrory Gardens Education and Visitor Center.
Brandel said the practice capitalizes on water moving through existing networks of perforated pipes buried beneath a crop field, called drain tile, which farmers install to remove excess water from the soil. Instead of allowing that water to drain away, drainage water recycling stores the water in ponds or wetlands and uses it for irrigation when the farmer wants it. 
‘Wild places are worth fighting for’: Concern grows for receding South Dakota wetlands

“In some cases, you can gravity-feed your tile system into a low spot,” Brandel told South Dakota Searchlight after the presentation, “and then you’re pumping that back out and putting that back on the field.”
Brandel said the practice could do a lot for South Dakota, such as reducing downstream flooding and farm-chemical runoff, improving crop yields by making more water available for irrigation during droughts, and reducing the amount of groundwater used for irrigation. A prior speaker presented a chart showing irrigation accounts for 86% of South Dakota’s water use. 
Multiple speakers at the conference said South Dakota needs more water to keep up with development and population growth projections. Some South Dakota water systems depend on pockets of groundwater known as aquifers.
Brandel said the reduction in groundwater use for irrigation could be substantial if drainage water recycling is widely adopted. 
“If you build enough storage, you could potentially switch it all over,” he said, referring to individual farmers’ irrigation.
An Environmental Defense Fund estimate says building a pond, wetland or other storage area for a drainage water recycling system could cost $10,000 to $20,000 per acre-foot of storage. An acre-foot is the volume of water needed to cover 1 acre of land to a depth of 1 foot. The estimate lists additional costs to install drain tile, irrigation and other parts of the system.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas state tax revenue tops estimate by 6.1% in first quarter of budget year
description: Kansas tax collections in the first quarter of fiscal year 2027 wildly exceeds the official projection by $147 million on $2.57 billion in actual receipts.
text:
Kansas House Speaker Dan Hawkins, left, says he welcomes the Kansas Department of Revenue report showing the state government collected $147 million in taxes than anticipated during the initial three-month period of the 2027 fiscal year. The photograph of Hawkins, a candidate for state insurance commissioner, a Jan. 8, 2026, meeting at the Capitol. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The state of Kansas collected $147 million more in taxes than anticipated during the first quarter of the fiscal year as income, sales and excise revenue exceeded expectations by a combined 6.1%, state officials reported.
Fiscal analysts predicted revenue from corporate and business income taxes, retail sales and compensating use taxes, tobacco and liquor taxes, oil and gas severance taxes, as well as insurance premium and motor carrier taxes, would bring in $2.42 billion in July, August and September. Actual receipts during the three-month period were $2.57 billion, or $147 million more than expected in the first quarter of the 2027 fiscal year.
The report from the Kansas Department of Revenue showed taxes collected by the state during the first quarter of the 2026 fiscal year amounted to $2.36 billion. That was $208.5 million, or 8.8%, less than in the same point in the current fiscal year.
“Three months into the new fiscal year, the results are encouraging,” said House Speaker Dan Hawkins, a Wichita Republican. “There will always be ups and downs from month to month, but after a full quarter, these are numbers worth paying attention to.”
The Republican-controlled Kansas Legislature and Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly produced state budgets the past two years that spent approximately $700 million more than the state generated in tax revenue. If the state’s revenue trend held through June 2027, it could moderate implications of overspending.
In the first quarter of this fiscal year, Kansas took in $53.8 million more than anticipated in corporate income tax and $50.7 million more that projected in individual income tax. In addition, revenue from sales exceeded the projection by $30.6 million.
“We’ve spent years proving that every additional dollar that comes into Topeka doesn’t automatically have to become another dollar of government spending,” said Hawkins, a candidate for state insurance commissioner.
In September, corporate income tax receipts submitted to the state government were $58.2 million above the official estimate, while individual income tax collections were $13.3 million below the prediction. Retail sales taxes owed the state hit $308.6 million in September, which was $2.8 million above the estimate.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump auto-enrolls 10s of millions in child investment accounts
description: Every child in the U.S. with a valid Social Security number is now enrolled in a tax-advantaged investment account, titled a 'Trump Account.'
text:
WASHINGTON — Every child in the United States with a valid Social Security number is now enrolled in a tax-advantaged investment account, titled a “Trump Account,” President Donald Trump announced Wednesday.
Parents must claim the accounts by downloading a Trump Account mobile app. Children born from 2025 through 2028 will automatically receive a one-time deposit of $1,000 from the U.S. government, once parents or guardians officially claim it. 
Children born before the eligibility window, up to age 10, can receive a $250 deposit donated by the Michael and Susan Dell Foundation, of Dell Technologies fortune.
Surrounded in the Oval Office by U.S. Treasury Department officials, business moguls and a half dozen children holding a banner reading, “Thank You for Trump Accounts,” the president said parents and guardians have voluntarily created accounts for 8 million children since the July 4 launch.
“With today’s announcement, we’re building on that success by 70 million accounts of children across America,” Trump said. “Put very simply, this money is your child’s future.”

A letter sent to parents about Trump Accounts for their children. Credit: States Newsroom Photo

The White House estimates over 60 million accounts have been added via auto-enrollment, but did not provide a specific figure.
The president signaled to the children standing by the Resolute Desk and said, “These beautiful young children are extremely rich — they are now, and they will be in the future, extremely rich. So they have something to look forward to.”
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the accounts mark the “beginning of the ownership society.” 
“I was talking to these great young people earlier,” he said. “They already know about compounding. They understand how the stock market works. … I think this is going to be a real-time financial literacy project.”
Investments from government, philanthropy
More than $4.5 billion has been deposited into the accounts since July 4, according to the White House.
Trump said Wednesday “much of that” has come from large donors, including the Dells, and Altimeter tech investment firm founder Brad Gerstner, who attended the announcement.
Parents and guardians have claimed roughly $2.6 billion in philanthropic contributions to date, with more available, according to the White House. The U.S. Treasury has so far seeded the accounts with $1.3 billion.
Another $638 million has been deposited into the accounts from friends and family of the individual accountholders, according to the administration.
Family and friends can contribute up to $5,000 annually to the accounts. Parents and guardians can elect to divert pre-tax contributions from their paychecks directly into their child’s account. Employers can match up to $2,500.
Over 70 companies have signed on to contribute to accounts of employees’ children, according to the White House.
Certain contributions, like the government’s one-time $1,000 deposit and contributions from state and local governments and nonprofits, do not count toward the $5,000 cap.
Susan Dell said she has received letters from parents and grandparents who have claimed the contribution from her foundation.
“It’s not just the money that matters — that does matter — but knowing that someone believes in you and your future that matters just as much,” she said. “These accounts are ready. They’re waiting for you, and they have money in them. So claim your child’s accounts and start adding money to their accounts and preserving a wonderful future for them.”
The Dell Foundation targeted the contributions to 25 million children from ZIP codes with median family incomes of up to $118,000.
The Trump administration is directing families to the website trumpaccounts.gov to find how to download the app and manage the account.
The White House estimates the government’s $1,000 seed money could grow to approximately $6,000 by age 18, if the family never contributed another dollar, assuming historical return data.
A child’s account that receives the maximum family and employer contributions of $5,000 at the start of each year could grow to nearly $200,000 by age 18, assuming a 7% annual rate of return, according to a Fidelity Investment hypothetical example, not adjusted for inflation. 
Used for retirement, education or down payment
The Trump Accounts, as named in the 2025 law dubbed “the big beautiful bill,” are structured like a traditional individual retirement account, but with different investment features and restrictions.
Money in the account can be invested in mutual funds or exchange traded funds that track the returns of large American companies, for example the S&P 500 index.
Investments will legally belong to a minor, but can only be managed by a parent or guardian until a child’s 18th birthday. 
The accounts are bound by certain restrictions, including a prohibition on withdrawals until age 18, when the account essentially becomes an individual retirement account subject to tax penalties for early withdrawal before age 59.5.
Some penalty-free exceptions include accessing the cash for a first-home purchase of up to $10,000, birth or child adoption fees up to $5,000 and qualifying medical expenses.
This story was first published Oct. 7, 2026 by States Newsroom.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska gubernatorial candidate settles campaign finance complaint with state regulators
description: Alaska gubernatorial candidate Treg Taylor has agreed to pay a fine and update his campaign disclosure reports as part of a settlement with state regulators to resolve a campaign finance disclosure complaint.  The complaint challenged Taylor’s failure to disclose details of more than $187,000 in expenditures to a handful of campaign consulting businesses.  C[...]
text:
Former Attorney General Treg Taylor speaks at a Sept. 8, 2026, gubernatorial candidate forum held by the Last Frontier Republican Club at the Petroleum Club of Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Alaska gubernatorial candidate Treg Taylor has agreed to pay a fine and update his campaign disclosure reports as part of a settlement with state regulators to resolve a campaign finance disclosure complaint. 
The complaint challenged Taylor’s failure to disclose details of more than $187,000 in expenditures to a handful of campaign consulting businesses. 
Commissioners with the Alaska Public Offices Commission, which regulates lobbying activity and  financial disclosures for campaigns and elected officials, unanimously approved the settlement agreement at a hearing on Tuesday. 
Taylor, a former state attorney general, is one of three Republicans plus one Democrat running for governor on the November ballot. 
Taylor was previously investigated by APOC this summer after failing to properly file campaign disclosure reports on time. The commission recommended he be decertified as a candidate for governor.  Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, who oversees the Alaska Division of Elections, initially agreed but then reversed her decision and reinstated him on the ballot. Taylor has also contributed hundreds of thousands of his own money to his campaign, far exceeding the limit, and violating campaign finance laws. 
The approval was one of four complaints commissioners heard on Tuesday, including complaints challenging inadequate campaign disclosures from Republican gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson, and independent candidate for lieutenant governor Zac Johnson,  who is running with Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.   
The complaint settled Tuesday came prior to Taylor’s decertification and reinstatement on the ballot. Christopher Constant, a former Anchorage Assembly member, made the complaint and identified 24 alleged violations, including inadequate details of how Taylor’s campaign spent more than $187,000 at several businesses.  
Under Alaska law, candidates must report campaign spending. Candidates must report details about the vendors they pay for goods and services and on the purpose of the expenditures, including additional details for advertising or campaign consultants. Details are not required of law firms. 
After an investigation, APOC staff found that in Taylor’s financial reports ahead of the primary election, he failed to disclose the purpose of expenditures totalling more than $187,000 to three firms and one individual. Those included 1892 Inc, a political consulting firm, where the campaign’s spending totaled more than $103,000; Fulcrum Intel, an intelligence firm, where the campaign spent more than $17,000; Sugarhouse Strategies, a political communications firm, where the campaign spent more than $26,000; and a series of monthly payments to Evan Lee totaling $40,000. 
Instead, Taylor’s campaign had described the expenditures as “retainers” or “research.” APOC found that it was in violation of campaign disclosure rules.
Under the terms of the settlement, Taylor agreed to amend his campaign finance reports to include those details and full descriptions of the expenditures within five days, and pay a penalty. 
Failing to provide timely and accurate reports incurs a maximum civil penalty of $50 per day under Alaska law, which resulted in an initial penalty of $8,350 for Taylor.
But APOC staff deemed there were mitigating factors, based on criteria set in statute, that warranted lowering the fine to $1,087.50. APOC staff noted it was Taylor’s first election cycle and said he had a “good filing history” and status as an “inexperienced filer,” which warranted a reduced penalty.
Kim Stone, a campaign disclosure coordinator with APOC, said Wednesday by email that he is considered to have a good filing history despite his previous failures to comply with campaign finance law because the latest violations pertain to Public Official Financial Disclosures. “For this reason, APOC treated them as separate provisions, and the violations of 26-10-CD were Mr. Taylor’s first under AS 15.13,” she said. 
At the hearing on Tuesday, Chris Moses, an attorney representing Taylor, made brief comments to the commission. He said Taylor agreed with the settlement and the campaign had already prepared the updated financial reports. “Taylor has not objected to the complaint,” he told commissioners. “So we would just ask that you accept the consent agreement as proposed and close this matter out,” Moses said.
The Taylor campaign did not answer questions about the services rendered by the businesses in the complaint on Tuesday or Wednesday. 
APOC is further considering complaints filed against Wilson, with decisions expected in the next few weeks. On Tuesday, commissioners decided not to take action on a complaint against Johnson after APOC staff found that the allegations of improperly disclosed income from properties in Indiana was unsubstantiated.

title: Idaho US Attorney Bart Davis announces retirement from Justice Department
description: Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho.  Davis, who is 71 and in his second term as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, will retire Oct. 17, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho said. […]
text:
U.S. Attorney for the District of Idaho Bart Davis in his Boise office. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho. 
‘The best job I ever had’: Bart Davis returns as Idaho’s chief federal litigator 

Davis, who is 71 and in his second term as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, will retire Oct. 17, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho said.
“I am unable to overstate the privilege it has been to work with the dedicated and remarkable women and men of the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Davis said in a written statement. “These great lawyers and support staff faithfully enforce the law, work to keep Idaho and our country safe, support our law enforcement partners and protect the civil rights of others. I am proud of the work they do every day.”
President Donald Trump nominated Davis for U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho last year, and the U.S. Senate confirmed Davis on Oct. 7, 2025 – exactly one year before Davis announced his retirement. 
Davis previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho from 2017 to 2021 during Trump’s first term. 
Prior to serving as U.S. attorney, Davis practiced law in Idaho Falls and served in the Idaho Senate for 19 years. 
Davis, a Republican, served as Senate majority leader for 15 years, where he was regarded as a powerful and intelligent legislative leader.
“Bart Davis has served the State of Idaho and our country with distinction throughout a remarkable career,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a written statement. “His sound legal judgment, deep knowledge of Idaho and unwavering commitment to doing what is right have been invaluable to our state.”
Davis also served as co-chairman of the 2021 Idaho Commission for Reapportionment, which was charged with redrawing Idaho’s congressional and legislative boundaries following the 2020 census to ensure political representation is proportional. 
During a 2025 interview with the Idaho Capital Sun, Davis called serving as U.S. attorney, “the best job I ever had.”
“… to work with these people who are genuinely trying to even handily apply the laws of the United States of America,” Davis said. “It impressed me then, and it impresses me now.”

 Governor says Davis strengthened relationship between Justice Department and Idaho

Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho is responsible for prosecuting federal crimes in Idaho, defends the United States in civil cases and collects debts owed to the United States, the office said.
In the past year under Davis’ leadership, the office said it has filed 298 criminal charges, including 103 drug trafficking cases, 89 violent crimes cases, 69 immigration cases and 22 fraud cases.
“During his time as U.S. Attorney for Idaho, Bart strengthened the relationship between Idaho and the U.S. Department of Justice and represented our state with integrity and professionalism,” Little said. “ We will miss his counsel, his wisdom and his steady leadership. I am grateful for Bart’s many years of service and friendship, and I wish him all the best as he enters retirement and has more time to enjoy with his wife, children and grandchildren.”
Davis and his wife, Marion, have six children and 14 grandchildren. Davis and Marion recently celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary.

title: State senator accuses Lincoln of improperly taxing non-city residents, demands refunds
description: LINCOLN — A Lincoln state senator accused city officials Wednesday of improperly taxing residents outside city limits and pledged to seek legislation to force refunds to taxpayers. State Sen. Beau Ballard, one of 10 state senators whose districts include part of Lincoln, announced his office had received evidence from constituents that the City of Lincoln […[...]
text:
State Sen. Beau Ballard of Lincoln, standing, talks with State Sen. Jared Storm of David City. March 20, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A Lincoln state senator accused city officials Wednesday of improperly taxing residents outside city limits and pledged to seek legislation to force refunds to taxpayers.
State Sen. Beau Ballard, one of 10 state senators whose districts include part of Lincoln, announced his office had received evidence from constituents that the City of Lincoln has been assessing its 1.75% sales tax on residents outside city limits within the surrounding 3-mile extraterritorial jurisdiction. Lincoln has a population of about 291,000, according to the Department of Revenue.
Lincoln city officials argue that the allegation has no merit and that it’s the Nebraska Department of Revenue that is in charge of overseeing, collecting and returning sales tax revenue to cities.
The seven-member Lincoln City Council. Top row, from left, Sändra Washington, Justin P. Carlson, Tom Beckius and James Michael Bowers. Bottom row, from left, Tom Duden (vice chair), Brodey Weber (chair) and Bennie Shobe. (Photo courtesy of City of Lincoln)
Ballard is calling on the city to audit its books and refund every dollar he says was improperly collected. He said he’ll push 2027 legislation to force the refunds, plus interest, either way. His idea would also force the city to conduct a 20-year lookback and return any such tax dollars.
“Families in the ETJ don’t get to vote in city elections, but we now have evidence from constituents that the city has been collecting city sales and occupation taxes from residents of the ETJ,” Ballard said in a statement.
Ballard’s northwest Lancaster County Legislative District 21 includes part of Lincoln and its ETJ.
City of Lincoln spokesperson Garret Swanson said city officials don’t receive or retain the business tax returns necessary for the audit Ballard proposes, unlike the Revenue Department.
“If a business believes sales tax was collected in error, the Nebraska Department of Revenue has an established process to review the matter and issue a refund when appropriate,” Swanson said in a statement.
Between January 2006 and July 2026, the Department of Revenue returned $1.72 billion in local sales tax revenue to Lincoln, according to data from the department. In the past year, the city has received $132 million in sales tax revenue, an average of $11 million each month.
Under state law and department regulations, cities can leverage a local sales tax up to 2 cents on top of the statewide 5.5-cent sales tax rate. Anyone who makes a taxable purchase in such a city pays the tax. The state also takes a portion of the local tax for administrative purposes.



Retailers must collect sales taxes at the rate at the point of delivery of goods or services, according to a department information guide on state and local sales taxes.
Ballard told the Nebraska Examiner that the evidence he’s seen from constituents is taxes on packages they ordered online or on business services at their home. For example, he cited a constituent ordering a shirt from Old Navy, which might be only a $1.20 tax but is still too much.
He said city officials should have looked more at the issue and listened to voters sooner.
“If the city says that they want to point the fingers at the Department of Revenue, that’s fine, I’ll work with the Department of Revenue,” Ballard said. “The real problem is the City of Lincoln has  been collecting this tax without any red flags raised.”
Nine of the 10 Lincoln and Lancaster County state lawmakers who served during the 2023-24 legislative session joined a town hall at Union College on Dec. 18, 2023, in Lincoln. Back row, from left, are State Sens. Beau Ballard, Carolyn Bosn, Eliot Bostar, Myron Dorn, George Dungan and Lincoln Chamber of Commerce president and CEO Jason Ball. Front row, from left, are State Sens. Jane Raybould, Anna Wishart, Danielle Conrad and Tom Brandt. Not pictured: Sen. Rob Clements. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Ballard said his proposed legislation is still at the “beginning stages” and couldn’t say what interest rate he might consider on refunds. He is also proposing that the city quarterly reconcile its sales tax revenues to promptly return any improperly collected taxes to ETJ residents.
“Just trying to figure out what the best way is to remedy this situation for Nebraskans that should not have been taxed,” Ballard said.
The 2027 proposal would focus on Lincoln, but Ballard said he could be open to other senators expanding the law to more cities. Lincoln is the only city of its size — a city of the “primary class” — so legislation can target the city and not be unconstitutional “special legislation.”
The Nebraska attorney general — current Attorney General Mike Hilgers lives in Lincoln’s ETJ — would have the authority to enforce compliance with the proposed law. Ballard succeeded Hilgers in the Legislature in 2023 and previously worked for Hilgers.
The Lincoln city budget is made up primarily of local property taxes and sales tax revenue. If the money is returned, Ballard said, he doesn’t want to hurt the city financially but the focus is on righting a wrong he expects has been going on for multiple years. He said legislation is needed to iron out the possible refund mechanism, which could allow payments over time.
This November, Lincolnites will consider five proposed amendments to their city charter. The last — Ballot Question 6 in Lincoln — would allow residents in the 3-mile ETJ to vote in municipal elections, excluding bonds.
Ballard, who supports the proposed amendment from the Good Government Lincoln campaign, said if the measure passes, the tax concerns become less of an issue because those voters can vote for city representation. But Ballard said he’s focused on returning taxes to residents.
If Lincoln delays compliance, Ballard said he’s considering forcing the city to pay a penalty to the state.
“This city has a pattern of dragging its feet on basic duties, including recently refusing to avoid its constitutional responsibility to put charter amendments before voters,” Ballard said. “Given the city’s disregard of its duties, it may take a penalty to get the city to stop taxing people it has no right to tax.”
