name: Mississippi Today
title: Feds announce takedown of ‘major’ drug and gun trafficking ring after string of arrests in Delta, Tupelo
description: The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives announced on Facebook on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, that its agents made arrests throughout Greenville and Tupelo over a two-day operation, recovering multiple guns and "significant quantities" of illegal narcotics.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
OXFORD — Authorities dismantled a “major” Mississippi drug and gun trafficking ring after arresting 14 suspects in Greenville, Leland and Tupelo late last month, federal officials announced Wednesday.
Officials said the arrests targeted street dealers in a trafficking ring that stretched across the northern part of the state. Federal authorities said they went public with the arrests after months of covert operations, as part of an ongoing crackdown on trafficking in Mississippi.
“We have a problem with violent crime, and when I say ‘problem,’ it doesn’t do justice to this,” said Scott Leary, U.S. attorney for Mississippi’s Northern District.
Joshua Jackson, special agent in charge of the Bureau of the ATF division overseeing Mississippi, announces his agents’ takedown of a trafficking ring in the Delta and Tupelo at the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Oxford on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Local police, state officers and federal agents banded together to execute the operations. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
Federal law enforcement banded with local police and state officers to conduct the string of investigations that resulted in the arrests — called Operation King’s Conversion, Operation Delta Fury and Operation Real Deal. Two of the operations targeted drug trafficking in the northern stretch of the state while the other investigated the flow of Glock switches into Mississippi — illegal devices that turn a regular, semi-automatic handgun into a machine gun.
Authorities identified the suspects through dozens of undercover buys of firearms, fentanyl and methamphetamine — sometimes purchasing up to $1,500 worth of illicit goods at a time, said Joshua Jackson, special agent in charge of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives division overseeing Mississippi. 
The suspects face federal charges, including drug distribution, carjacking and illegal possession of a firearm and machine gun. Leary, whose office is prosecuting the cases, said authorities saw a drop in local crime following the arrests.
Shootings and narcotic deals in Tupelo and Greenville sparked the operations, which Jackson said were a spinoff of an earlier investigation that ended in February. Officials said the crackdown is in its next phase in other parts of north Mississippi, as part of a local, state and federal effort to stem violent crime and the flow of drugs.



Few places in America see gun killings as often as some parts of the Delta. Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows that Washington County, home to Greenville, saw the nation’s third-highest rate of gun killings from 2022-2024 — over five times the rate of Chicago’s Cook County.
“Next, we’re going to other communities around the state, around the Northern District of Mississippi, using the same sort of concepts and techniques that we know that work, that we are efficient and focused as we move forward,” Jackson said. “We’re going to have other announcements and other arrests because this is not stopping.”
The partnership behind the operations — the Homeland Security Task Force — was specifically developed to go after crime connected to foreign cartels and gangs, which Leary said are often the source of drug and gun trafficking in communities.
Scott Leary, U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Mississippi, announces his office’s prosecution of 14 suspects who were arrested on federal drug and firearm charges at a press conference in Oxford on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
The arrests come after a recent string of trafficking sweeps across the northern part of the state ensnared officers and civilians alike. Last October, the FBI announced that it arrested 14 law enforcement officers as a part of a wider drug and corruption operation that stretched from the Mississippi Delta into Memphis.
Some of the officers were accused of providing protection to undercover FBI agents posing as members of a Mexican drug cartel in exchange for bribes. The main defendant in the case, former Hollandale Police Chief Brandon Addison, pleaded guilty in March to his involvement in transporting and distributing illegal drugs.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Federal audit says Arkansas mishandled reports of child abuse and neglect
description: A federal audit found Arkansas mishandled thousands of reports of child abuse and neglect, including allegations of rape and video surveillance in children’s bedrooms. The Sept. 29 report from the Office of Inspector General in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services surveyed 27,690 reports the Arkansas’ Division of Children and Family Services reje[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)A federal audit found Arkansas mishandled thousands of reports of child abuse and neglect, including allegations of rape and video surveillance in children’s bedrooms.
The Sept. 29 report from the Office of Inspector General in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services surveyed 27,690 reports the Arkansas’ Division of Children and Family Services rejected and 21,268 reports it accepted between Oct. 1, 2023, and Sept. 30, 2024.
Auditors estimated from their studies of samples of the reports that 99%, or nearly 21,000, did not comply with Arkansas’ child abuse screening, assessment or investigation requirements.
The division incorrectly rejected reports of children being watched by video while undressing and failed to contact law enforcement about findings of sexual abuse and life-threatening harm to children, according to the audit.
Auditors found “systemic weaknesses” in Arkansas’ processes for assessing and investigating reports of child maltreatment, the report states. Some processes “did not fully reflect current practices,” and some investigators did not follow the rules.
Arkansas child welfare agency denies prosecutor access to internal files in teen’s severe abuse

The report was prompted in part by a Mountain Home child abuse case that became public last year. The state determined 29 allegations of abuse against the teenager were unsubstantiated, and the child was abused for years before the mother and stepfather were sentenced to more than 40 years in prison earlier this year. 
In the time since the audit was conducted, Children and Family Services “has undertaken significant work to strengthen investigative practice, policy, training, supervision and technology,” and many of the changes are a direct response to the audit, division director Tiffany Wright and Maj. Jeff Drew, commander of the Crimes Against Children Division of the Arkansas State Police, wrote in their response to the findings.
State officials faced questions from lawmakers last year about the Mountain Home abuse case. Republican Rep. Ryan Rose of Van Buren said Wednesday that state officials could not “explain away” the problems in the system. 
“This audit confirms what we feared: children who cried out for help had their pleas muffled,” Rose said.
 What the audit found

Arkansas officials agreed with auditors that nine rejected maltreatment reports in a random sample of 70 should have been accepted, including an 11-year-old child’s disclosure of rape by a family member at the age of 6.
“Hotline operators screened it out because they believed that a young child might not have a clear understanding of the word ‘rape,’” the report states.
Child abuse hotline operators rejected four other reports after inappropriately determining there was not enough evidence to launch an investigation.
“For example, a mandated reporter stated that a child disclosed being molested by a half-sibling when she was younger,” the audit states. “However, the report was screened out because of a lack of specific details, and the hotline did not conduct a follow-up to obtain clarifying information.”

OAS-25-06-038 
Arkansas child abuse investigations must be complete in 45 days, but auditors found 32 investigations in a random sample of 140 were completed between one and 200 days too late.
The state also failed to begin child abuse probes in a timely manner and interview all required parties in some of its investigations, the report found.
“Failure to initiate investigations within required timeframes places children at risk of continued child abuse or neglect,” the report states.
Wright and Drew took issue with this statement in their response to the report.
“The stated objective and methodology of the audit…do not appear to include an assessment of whether any child in the sample experienced harm or an increased risk of harm as a result of an identified deficiency,” they wrote.
 Recommendations and disagreements

Federal auditors gave the state six recommendations for how to fix the problems found, and the division fully accepted three.
The state agreed to revise its Child Abuse Hotline manual to clarify definitions of child maltreatment and guidance for how to identify and locate children mentioned in reports, among other things. The state also agreed to strengthen its documentation requirements and to review its policies to ensure they follow state law.
State officials had misgivings about the auditors’ other three recommendations but agreed to take them into account to an extent.
Auditors and state officials disagreed over whether investigating previous rejected reports of child maltreatment were necessary due to how much time had passed since the reports were filed. State officials also disputed auditors’ claim that insufficient staff training was the only reason for the problems found in the audit.
“The state agency pointed out that the audit findings also demonstrated the need for consistent supervisory oversight, clear expectations, accountability, and system supports that help staff apply those requirements and practice,” the report states.
Effort to upgrade Arkansas child welfare computer system fails after two years

Auditors determined that the state’s Children’s Reporting and Information System, also known as CHRIS, did not “clearly distinguish between custodial and noncustodial parents.” State officials agreed to improve the system’s documentation capacity but “did not concur with any implication that the current CHRIS configuration demonstrates that required parent interviews were not conducted,” the report states.
In 2022, Children and Family Services entered into a multimillion-dollar contract with a Chicago-based software company to update the reporting and information system. 
The project ended in 2024 after Wright and other Department of Human Services officials were frustrated by its lack of progress, but the agency said last year that CHRIS still met the child welfare system’s needs.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Dysfunction continues at Canton charter school while its fate remains unclear
description: Buses arrive to pick up children attending SR1 College Preparatory and Stem Academy at the end of the school day, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Canton.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
The Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board will have a new leader come January. 
What remains uncertain is whether the board has information it needs to resolve an issue that has loomed for months: whether to revoke the charter of SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy.
The board has set a meeting for Oct. 14 to form a search committee to replace Executive Director Lisa Karmacharya, who plans to retire Jan. 1. 
“I had this incredible opportunity to begin the work and build the plane while we were flying it,” Karmacharya said of her tenure. “So it was an amazing opportunity and exhausting at the same time, but one that I will absolutely cherish for the rest of my life.”
Meanwhile, the board still needs to make a decision about the Canton school’s charter. In May, Kim Turner presided over a hearing where the board built its case for revoking the charter. Last month, the board asked Turner to provide an update about her recommendation by Sept. 30. The board also requested that Turner provide a recommendation by Friday.
Hearing officer Kim Turner asks questions during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
With those deadlines in mind, authorizer board members set a goal to decide on the charter at their Oct. 26 meeting but can’t act without Turner’s recommendation.
Karmacharya confirmed Tuesday the board had received no communication from Turner. But when Mississippi Today reached out again for confirmation on Wednesday, board attorney Dillon Pitts responded, “We can confirm receipt of both in a timely manner. No further comments.”
Lisa Karmacharya, executive director of the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board, listens during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
As the delay drags on, so does the dysfunction within the charter school. Three charter school employees, including the provost, resigned last month, according to a report Karmacharya provided to the board on Sept. 21. An administrator, and not a chef or designated child nutrition department employee, was preparing food in the cafeteria for students, according to Karmacharya.
An inspector who worked for the charter board found the child nutrition department was not complying with federal guidelines that ensured student meals had the proper nutritional value and were stored at a safe temperature, among other standards.
The charter school has been plagued by dysfunctional leadership, money woes and compliance issues in its cafeteria and special education department. All were highlighted in the case the authorizer board presented to Turner in May. Mississippi Today spoke to 13 former SR1 charter school employees about disorganization in the school’s business office and attempts by leadership to deceive regulators.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Matos, Loughlin spar over Trump, groceries and gasoline in second LG debate
description: Rhode Island Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos and her Republican challenger, former state Rep. John Loughlin, met Wednesday afternoon for their second televised debate in less than two weeks, sparring over grocery stores, gas prices, and how much blame to assign to President Donald Trump for Rhode Islanders’ problems. Unlike the candidates’ pretaped Sept. 25 matchup […[...]
text:
NBC 10 moderator Gene Valicenti speaks with Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, center, and Republican challenger John Loughlin after Wednesday’s lieutenant governor debate at the Providence Performing Arts Center on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos and her Republican challenger, former state Rep. John Loughlin, met Wednesday afternoon for their second televised debate in less than two weeks, sparring over grocery stores, gas prices, and how much blame to assign to President Donald Trump for Rhode Islanders’ problems.
Unlike the candidates’ pretaped Sept. 25 matchup at WPRI 12, Matos and Loughlin went at it live from the Providence Performing Arts Center lobby, with Gene Valicenti moderating the 30-minute WJAR NBC 10broadcast. A gubernatorial debate was scheduled to follow at 7 p.m.
Matos found fault with the current administration in Washington for rising costs and what she described as insufficient federal investment in the Ocean State. To Loughlin, these problems were largely self-inflicted.
“The administration in Washington didn’t give us the worst roads and bridges in America,” Loughlin said, then listed a number of other local failures. “Those are homegrown problems.”
Most intriguing RI race to watch? New UNH poll shows LG Matos in tight race with Loughlin

In response, Matos acknowledged the state received money for the Washington Bridge rebuild from Trump’s administration — but the state has received federal funding from “many other administrations in Washington, not just this one.”
“But this one made it worse because he decided to give a big tax break to the rich people, to his friends,” Matos said of Trump.
Though ideologically distant, Matos and Loughlin were more closely aligned in a University of New Hampshire poll released Sept. 24, which found the two candidates vying for the state’s second-in-command role were basically tied in tentative voter support. The online poll of 598 likely voters was conducted Sept. 17 to 21 and found the incumbent Democratic lieutenant governor with support from 48% of likely voters. Loughlin had support of about 44% of likely voters — a narrow difference reduced to basically zero by the survey’s 4-point margin of error. An additional 7% of voters were undecided. 
Matos, 52, has been lieutenant governor since 2021, when she was appointed to fill the vacancy created after Dan McKee became governor. Reelected to a full term in 2022, Matos last month bested four other Democrats in a crowded primary. Loughlin entered the race last year and ran unopposed for the Republican candidacy.
Loughlin, 67, served as a state representative for District 71, which covers Tiverton, Little Compton and Portsmouth, from 2005 to 2010 and was House minority whip in his final year at the State House. An Iraq War veteran and retired Army Reserve lieutenant colonel, Loughlin is no stranger to live media, having hosted a Saturday radio program on WPRO-AM from 2012 until the launch of his campaign last year.
When Valicenti asked why Matos should be replaced, Loughlin replied, “I think that she’s done a decent job as lieutenant governor,” then added, “I think I could do a better job.”
The general election is set for Tuesday, Nov. 3. The deadline to apply for a mail ballot is Tuesday, Oct. 13. Early in-person voting will begin the following day on Wednesday, Oct. 14.
A behind-the-scenes view of NBC 10’s live lieutenant governor debate in the Providence Performing Arts Center lobby on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, between Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos and Republican challenger John Loughlin. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Different visions for a limited office
The list of contenders who sought the lieutenant governorship this election year is lengthier than the list of duties afforded to the office, which are constitutionally few compared to other states. 
Still, one obligation hovers over the office, as outlined in the state constitution, which defines the lieutenant governor’s time to shine as “[w]hen the governor-elect shall die, remove from the state, refuse to serve; become insane, or be otherwise incapacitated.”
That leaves the officeholder to use their limited powers in creative ways. In her tenure, Matos has focused heavily on grocery access and affordability as one of her key issues, and she reiterated this theme Wednesday. She pointed to successful legislation she promoted that prohibits new restrictive covenants from being applied to former grocery store properties. The covenants are a means of barring competing supermarkets from filling the spaces once inhabited by markets that close their doors.
“John, does she get credit for that?” Valicenti asked.
“Well, I mean, it’s an achievement,” Loughlin replied. “I thank you for doing that.”
But he said it was a modest achievement overall, and one which he thought would not have much immediate effect since existing restrictive covenants can remain in play for years, if not decades.
“I tried to explain to you before,” Matos shot back. “I think you don’t understand the law.”
She said that, if still in office next year, she plans to pursue legislation that would strip away “restricted covenants on the buildings that already have it.”
Loughlin expressed his desire that the office become more independent and proactive, and take on a larger role in oversight. His chief example was his May 11 call for a state inspector general, which he believes helped motivate legislative leaders to issue their own proposal for the new oversight role. 
The House of Representatives introduced their own proposal on May 14, three days after Loughlin’s promise to create the position via the lieutenant governorship if he’s elected. 
“Conversation could happen for a long time,” Loughlin said. “Nothing has happened until I made them push it across the finish line.”
Following House leadership’s successful proposal, five finalists are now under review for the inspector general role.
Matos countered that the proposal has been floated for years in the General Assembly, including by Democratic Rep. Charlene Lima.
“I don’t believe that having a press conference pushed the [House] Speaker to make the decision,” Matos replied.
As they did at the Sept. 25 debate, Matos and Loughlin again disagreed on how to get Rhode Islanders’ energy costs lower. This time around, the influence of Trump on gas prices emerged as a major point of contention. 
Matos credited Trump’s “illegal war” as the cause of gas prices being “so high.”
Loughlin stated the war in Iran has “no impact” on domestic natural gas prices, and that Rhode Island should broaden access to pipeline capacity so it can obtain cheaper domestic gas. 
“You said that the war is not increasing the price of gas,” Matos said shortly after. “Have you been at the gas station?” 
“Natural gas, Sabina, there’s a difference,” Loughlin said.
The half-hour debate also touched on the Washington Bridge, the return of Providence schools to municipal control, how the office can work across the political aisle, and Rhode Island’s business climate.
Matos, who filed a post-primary report with the Rhode Island Board of Elections for the 33 day-period ending Oct. 5, had about $43,000 cash on hand after raising about $40,000 in private contributions and receiving $174,350 in public matching funds. She spent more than $196,000 during the reporting period.
Loughlin had $22,813 cash on hand as of Oct. 5, after raising about $39,000 and spending $40,000 since July 1, according to his third-quarter campaign finance report. 
You can watch the debate on WJAR’s website.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Democrat Rebecca Bennett campaigns with Gabby Giffords in push to flip House seat
description: Democrat Rebecca Bennett enlisted former Congresswoman Gabby Giffords in her bid to flip the House seat now held by GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr.
text:
Former Congresswoman Gabby Giffords, left, and Rebecca Bennett, the Democratic candidate for the 7th District House seat, hold hands during a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]NEW PROVIDENCE — Former Rep. Gabby Giffords, whose gun safety group has spent big to unseat Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in North Jersey’s 7th District, visited New Jersey Wednesday to stump for Kean’s Democratic challenger, Rebecca Bennett, in the state’s most competitive congressional race.
Giffords’ stop at the New Providence Memorial Library, where she joined Bennett and local advocates for a roundtable discussion on reducing gun violence, came as polls show affordability remains voters’ top priority with the election just a month away.
But the gun lobby’s systematic effort to dismantle New Jersey’s famously tough gun laws through the courts underscores the need for voters to elect representatives who support background checks, secure storage requirements, assault weapon bans, and “red-flag laws” that allow authorities to seize firearms from people deemed dangerous, the panelists said.
“We have federal agencies, the federal courts, and Congress itself that are taking actions to weaken gun regulations and undercut the laws that states like New Jersey have passed. So that is why this is so important. This moment and this seat,” said Assemblyman Vincent Kearney (D-Union).
Bennett, a former Navy pilot, said she’s ready to “turn the seat blue in November, so we can have a gun safety majority in Congress next year.”
“This is absolutely going to be a priority for me,” she said. “We are traumatizing a generation of kids because our elected officials in Washington are failing to solve this crisis that we are dealing with in this country.”
Bennett had a very receptive audience, with red-shirted members of Moms Demand Action for Gun Sense in America filling every row and applauding throughout. Andrea Podgarsky, who co-leads the group’s elections advocacy, said flipping Kean’s seat is one of their main goals this year.
The panelists included a range of people impacted by gun violence.
Rebecca Bennett, the Democratic candidate for the 7th District House seat, holds a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Andrea Podgarsky with Moms Demand Action speaks during a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Andrea Podgarsky with Moms Demand Action speaks during a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Campaign materials for Democratic House hopeful Rebecca Bennett on display at a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)A.J. Ford of Bergen County takes a selfie with Rebecca Bennett, the Democratic candidate for the 7th District House seat, during a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Former Congresswoman Gabby Giffords, left, listens as Rebecca Bennett, the Democratic candidate for the 7th District House seat, speaks during a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026.(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Former Congresswoman Gabby Giffords, left, and Leslie Wald of New Providence speak during a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Assemblyman Vincent Kearney speaks during a gun safety roundtable at New Providence Memorial Library on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Giffords survived being shot in the head in 2011 during a “Congress in Your Corner” event in her Tucson, Arizona, district, where a gunman opened fire, murdering six people and injuring 12 others.
“Words once came easily. Today I struggle to speak. But I’ve not lost my voice. America needs all of us to speak out, even when you have to fight to find the words,” Giffords said.
Kimberly Banks lost her 19-year-old son, Samaad Z. Frazier, to gun violence in 2019 and afterward started a group, One Family One Fight, to advocate for more and better prevention. She told listeners her son was slain in Somerville by five people, including two 16-year-olds, two 18-year-olds, and a 21-year-old. New Jersey law prohibits people under 18 from buying any firearms and those under 21 from purchasing handguns.
“How did they get these guns? How was this even possible? We need to keep guns out of the hands of people legally prohibited from having them,” Banks said.
She implored Bennett, if she makes it to Congress, to prioritize cracking down on illegal gun trafficking and investing in mental health and career-readiness programs focused on helping at-risk youth.
“When gun violence has taken so many lives, prevention cannot wait,” Banks said.
Union County Sheriff Pete Corvelli and Kearney, a former 911 dispatcher who’s now a deputy in Corvelli’s department, talked about how loosening restrictions on things like large-capacity magazines, silencers, and assault weapons endangers officers and echoed Banks’ call for more federal action on illegal guns.
“Four out of five crime guns in New Jersey are traced and were originally purchased in other states. That’s a gap in federal law, and that’s why who we send to Washington really matters,” Kearney said.
Bennett bashed President Donald Trump’s record on gun safety, noting that he eliminated the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention, made it harder to regulate firearm sales, and cut federal funding for community violence intervention and mental health programs.
Kean has Trump’s endorsement, and the National Rifle Association gave him a B grade (Bennett got an F) in their recent ratings of political candidates who’ll be on November’s ballot.
“It’s very clear we need to make a change in Washington,” Bennett said. “I’m going to work every day to make sure that we are keeping our kids and our communities safe, unlike my opponent, Tom Kean Jr., who is just going to do whatever the National Republican Party tells him to do. I want your kids and mine to be free from gun violence, and you can count on me to do just that.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: EPA head announces oil and gas emission rules rollbacks during visit to Santa Fe
description: The head of the Environmental Protection Agency announced plans Wednesday for further cancellations of Biden-era oil and gas regulations aimed at reducing emissions of climate-warming gasses while on a visit to New Mexico. Environmental groups protested the proposals and urged New Mexico to codify the regulations in state law.
text:
Environmental groups protested outside the Santa Fe Convention Center on Oct. 7, 2026 while EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced to oil and gas executives and officials revisions to a Biden-era methane emission reduction rule. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)The head of the Environmental Protection Agency announced plans Wednesday for further cancellations of Biden-era oil and gas regulations aimed at reducing emissions of climate-warming gasses while on a visit to New Mexico, as environmental groups protested the proposals. 
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced a second rollback of rules during the annual meeting of the New Mexico Oil and Gas Association. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work. They can’t do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens,” Zeldin said in a statement. “The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the U.S. can reach its full energy potential.” 
The 2024 EPA methane rule created performance standards to reduce methane and smog-forming organic compounds from new, modified and reconstructed oil and gas infrastructure. The rule also created a super emitter program to identify and investigate large leaks or releases of methane located at or near an oil and natural gas facility.
During his speech in Santa Fe, Zeldin announced that the EPA is “days, not weeks” from proposing to eliminate the super emitter program. He added the EPA will propose to revisit the overall approach to regulating associated gas from oil wells. 
Environmental groups apart of a the New Mexico Methane Table coalition march towards the Santa Fe Convention Center in New Mexico on Oct. 7, 2026 while EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the revisions to the methane rule. (Photo by Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)
Groups protesting Wednesday included the Sierra Club Rio Grande chapter; the Environmental Defense Fund; New Mexico Interfaith Power and Light; and Healthy Climate New Mexico. They said the planned revisions will further harm the environment and set back states that have enacted stricter regulations on methane pollution.
Nini Gu, with the Environmental Defense Fund, told Source NM that satellite images from the Delaware subbasin, which covers areas of New Mexico and Texas, showed that New Mexico had 60% less methane pollution than Texas, where operators face weaker emission standards. With the geography and industry being similar in both states, the disparate results are “mainly due to regulations,” Gu said.
Gu highlighted New Mexico’s attempt to codify elements of the 2024 methane rule into state law. In August, the New Mexico Environment Department proposed the creation of a state super emitter program which would identify large methane leaks through satellite and aircraft imagery.
The New Mexico Environmental Improvement Board will host a hearing on the proposal starting on Dec. 1, which Gu said is “an opportunity for New Mexico to codify its own regulations to reduce methane emissions. 
“That can happen in spite of what the EPA does,” Gu said.
The Environmental Defense Fund noted in a statement Wednesday praised Colorado and New Mexico’s work to implement tougher methane standards. 
 “At a time when Americans are facing high energy costs, EPA should not give oil and gas companies more room to waste a domestic resource, adding to the nearly $7 billion in lost energy value since the Administration stopped enforcing key methane protections,” said Jon Goldstein, with the Defense Fund. “Rolling back these safeguards would mean more wasted energy, more methane pollution and greater health risks for communities living near oil and gas operations.” 
Missi Currier, New Mexico Oil and Gas Association president and CEO, told Source NM the organization will carefully review Zeldin’s announcement. 
“NMOGA and our membership support clean, reliable, affordable energy, and practical policies that reduce emissions, protect public health, and provide certainty for energy producers and consumers,” she said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Marsh-building river diversions have local support at the Bird’s Foot Delta, but money still needed
description: Fishermen and property owners in lower Plaquemines Parish are optimistic about a plan for how to rebuild lost wetlands at the Mississippi Delta, though state officials still need to line up more than $150 million to pay for the project.
text:
A boat travels near the Cypress Cove Marina in Venice, Louisiana. A coastal restoration project in lower Plaquemines Parish looks to revitalize wetlands that were damaged by the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)VENICE — Fishermen and property owners in lower Plaquemines Parish are optimistic about a plan for how to rebuild lost wetlands at the Mississippi Delta, though state officials still need to line up more than $150 million to pay for the project.
Members of the Louisiana Coastal Restoration and Protection Authority sought input from locals and fisherman who live and work around the southernmost tip of Southeast Louisiana. They were given the floor Tuesday night at a community meeting held at the New Orleans Big Game Fishing Club in Venice on the Bird’s Foot Delta Hydrologic Restoration Project.
The project would open and close some of the both natural and human-made channels of water in the delta to use river water and sediment to revitalize the adjacent marsh.
Fishermen and longtime residents of Plaquemines Parish voiced general support for the project at the meeting.
Earl Armstrong Jr., a cattle rancher and lifetime resident of Pilottown, spoke about the power of restoring the river’s flow to under-nourished wetlands.
“I know all these areas like the back of my hand, “ Armstrong said. “If we can get all this water that’s being lost … you’ll have a lot better chance trying to build up places downriver.”
Brent Roy, a charter captain and fisherman who operates out of Venice, agreed that the marsh west of South Pass, where the river and sediment flow are higher, looks healthier than the east side. He called the Bird’s Foot Delta plan “a great project” and suggested the CPRA also consider building a barrier island to contain the fresh sediment.
Baker said the CPRA “would love to” pursue a barrier island project, but that the cost is prohibitive.
“If I had all the money in the world, I would do it, but then that still doesn’t fix why I’m losing all this [sediment],” he said.
Everett Marks, a landowner in Plaquemines Parish, shared concerns with the CPRA’s tentative plan to place dredged sand from the channel clearing near his private duck hunting property, bringing up the issue of whether the state would try to claim ownership. Despite this, he indicated he would be willing to work with CPRA to find a place to put sediment that would not disrupt duck hunting on his private land.
“Great project, I’m for the project,” Marks said. “I’m just not for the sand being dumped on private property. There’s got to be some other place to dump the dirt.”
Over the past 40 years, more than 26,000 acres of wetlands have been lost on the southeastern end of the delta’s tip from sea level rise, sediment deprivation and impacts from the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010.
“This is the closest land mass to the oil spill, the Bird’s Foot Delta,” said Todd Baker, the CPRA’s project manager. “Because it’s not Grand Isle or a Florida beach, there weren’t a lot of people out there with cameras filming everything that was going on. So it was able to sit in this (oil-damaged) environment for a very long time.”
To revitalize the area, the plan proposes the removal of sand shoals from the Pass a Loutre navigation channel that have “plugged up” water flow downriver, Baker said. The plan also calls for closing several small channels along the western side of the larger South Pass and opening others on the eastern side to deliver more river water and the valuable sediment it carries to deteriorated marsh areas.
“It really is an opportunity to do whole ecosystem restoration,” Baker said, adding that project models expect to build at least another 1,000 acres of wetlands.
By opening up avenues for flow to the east, Baker said the project aims to use the Mississippi River’s natural power to build land more efficiently than humans could alone.
For example, sediment flow to wetlands east of South Pass will increase by a substantial 40%, according to projections.
“We have a problem out here, and we’re not gonna attack the symptom,” Baker said.” We’re gonna attack the problem.”
Engineers have been designing the Bird’s Foot Delta project since 2020, spending $2.7 million of the $6 million from the BP Deepwater Horizon settlement dollars allocated for [insert description]But it will take a lot more money to see the plan through to completion. Officials said at the meeting they expect total costs to run anywhere from $144 million to $176 million.
Baker said the price tag has such a large range because the rising cost of diesel fuel makes dredging costs hard to predict.
“But also, this is the Mississippi. We don’t know how much sand we’re gonna have over the next few years, where it’s gonna deposit,” he added.
Baker said the CPRA plans to ask for more BP settlement dollars to fund the project by the end of 2027 to hopefully begin construction on the project by early 2028. The CPRA is part of a panel of federal trustees that has to approve how settlement dollars from the Deepwater Horizon oil spill are spent to restore damaged areas of the coast.

name: WyoFile
title: Task force ditches Wyoming-run health insurance plan idea, mulls unorthodox service models
description:
Legislature-assigned panel studying healthcare affordability in Wyoming examines several alternative pricing structures. The task force hopes to continue work next year. 
The post Task force ditches Wyoming-run health insurance plan idea, mulls unorthodox service models appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A legislative task force studying health insurance affordability in Wyoming has declined to advance a proposal to create a state-run catastrophic health insurance plan, citing the unlikelihood that it would move the needle on premium costs. 
Following further study, it “doesn’t really appear to be a good cost driver, or to bring costs down, as premiums would probably actually have to be fairly high to cover everybody in the pool,” Legislative Service Office Attorney Anna Johnson said Tuesday. “So at the end of the day, I don’t think it would be as much of a cost saver as originally hoped.”
The task force came to a similar conclusion for a concept to create a state-administered division to negotiate, purchase and distribute medical devices to participating healthcare facilities in an effort to reduce acquisition costs through coordinated purchasing.
With those off the table, the Health Insurance Affordability Task Force continued Tuesday to explore alternative models and strategies used by other states to help allay costs. Those included a public service commission that could regulate some hospital costs and a utility model for paying for core hospital services. 
At the end of the meeting, task force members agreed they would like to continue the conversation, voting to ask the Legislature’s Management Council, which serves as the Legislature’s leadership, to continue the group’s work into a second year. 
Even when the ideas don’t gain traction, said Co-chair Sen. Tara Nethercott, R-Cheyenne, the discussion is worthwhile. 
The process has forced lawmakers and industry leaders “to think outside the box, which is what we need you to do, and to think more collectively as a state to provide and deliver these services to the people of Wyoming in a way that’s never been done before,” Nethercott said. “Because trying to overcome the increasing costs of healthcare is going to require something different. This is the start of being challenged, and it will continue.” 
Costs of care
When the Management Council convened the task force, it brought together lawmakers with representatives from hospitals, medical associations, insurance companies and the health department to understand the high costs of medical insurance in Wyoming and explore ways to allay them. 
The issue is top of mind for many residents; a statewide survey of registered voters earlier this year found that 81% say the cost of healthcare is an extremely or very serious problem. 

A customer looks over an insurance benefit statement. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 

Wyoming residents experienced the highest price jumps in Affordable Care Act premiums in the country after the expiration of Enhanced Premium Tax Credits at the end of 2025. The demographic most impacted includes working families that earn more than 400% of the federal poverty level.
According to a Wyoming health department presentation, ACA enrollment in Wyoming fell from 46,643 in 2025 to 37,643 in 2026, a drop of 9,000.
But the Affordable Care Act is only one factor driving healthcare costs in Wyoming. During its meetings this summer, the task force spent hours exploring factors ranging from how medical devices are priced, how costly hospital billing mistakes can be and the impacts of malpractice insurance.
Also discussed was the state-operated public health insurance plan. The Wyoming Health Department first brought the plan into public consideration when it applied for federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds last year. The idea was to protect residents from financial ruin by covering healthcare emergencies like a car accident or a bear attack.
Further study this summer prompted the task force to abandon that idea, however. Instead, the task force Tuesday explored several novel models related to the way patients pay doctors and how costs are regulated. 
Out of the box
Department of Health Director Stefan Johansson stressed that the ideas presented to the task force were exploratory.
“The whole point here with looking at the different types of models or concepts … is a difficult one because there’s no easy answers,” he said. “This is pretty outside-of-the-box thinking.”
One concept would entail paying for certain, core hospital services under a
public utility framework. The concept would categorize those core services as essential, akin to infrastructure like water, electricity and roads that people pay utility bills for. That would uncouple essential services from ones that are more elective, and thus shoppable on the free market. 
“We’re kind of at this precipice where the consumer or the patient is being priced out of healthcare. That’s what we’re trying to correct.”Rep. Lloyd Larsen, R-Lander
The task force also learned about healthcare sharing ministries, which are not technically insurance. Instead, the way these nonprofit, faith-based organizations function is through members contributing monthly funds to help pay for each other’s medical expenses. 
“For our members, it’s more than a way to just address healthcare costs, it’s an expression of their faith in action,” Lindsey Swindle, director of government and policy affairs at Christian Care Ministry, told the task force. 
Another novel model discussed was direct primary care, in which patients pay a membership fee directly to a doctor or clinic, bypassing traditional insurance. The model has shown positive results as doctors are able to spend more time with a smaller pool of patients, but it can also have drawbacks, task force members said. 
Ultimately, the members agreed that there’s more work to be done around the issues of healthcare costs, leading to a vote to ask the Management Council to continue the effort. It’s too important not to, said Co-chair Rep. Lloyd Larsen, R-Lander.
“We’re kind of at this precipice where the consumer or the patient is being priced out of healthcare,” Larsen said. “That’s what we’re trying to correct.”
Without “something significant happening,” Larsen added, medical costs and insurance claims will continue to rise at a rate consumers can’t keep pace with.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont governor’s race will test voters’ appetite for raising new taxes — or cutting them
description:
There’s broad consensus that affordability is a problem, one political observer said. But Amanda Janoo and Phil Scott hardly see eye-to-eye on how to solve it.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont governor’s race will test voters’ appetite for raising new taxes — or cutting them.
text:
Republican Gov. Phil Scott, left, and Democratic nominee for governor Amanda Janoo. Photos by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The leading candidates for governor of Vermont this year agree that the state is unaffordable for too many people. But Amanda Janoo and Phil Scott have different ideas for how to solve that problem — and say each other’s plans won’t cut it. 
Janoo, the Democratic nominee and an economist from Burlington, says a key part of her agenda is raising new revenue for state services by increasing income taxes on Vermont’s wealthiest residents, as well as boosting taxes on some second homes and large technology companies.
Scott, a Republican who is running for a sixth term, says he’d do nearly the opposite if he gets reelected: propose a package of tax cuts or credits. He has already directed the heads of state agencies to prepare spending plans for the upcoming fiscal year that account for less state revenue, anticipating the possible impacts of levying lower taxes.
Two years ago, frustration over rising property tax rates to pay for schools was the animating issue in Vermont’s elections for statewide offices and seats in the Legislature. This year’s election raises a different — but related — question, said Alex Garlick, an associate professor of political science at the University of Vermont: Will voters elect a governor who’s pitching more taxes to pay for a broader array of public services?
Janoo has proposed, for example, using new tax revenue to make sure everyone in the state can see a primary care doctor, free of charge. She hopes this sets Vermont up to implement a system where all healthcare services are free, as it tried to do more than a decade ago, only to abandon the effort after determining it wasn’t financially feasible.
“I think there is consensus that affordability is a problem. And healthcare is a major part of that. But the approach of how to get out of that is unclear,” Garlick said. 
In Janoo’s primary win over the childcare advocate Aly Richards, he added, one of the key differences was Janoo didn’t shy away from saying that she supports new taxes.
“And I see this election as kind of a litmus test on that,” Garlick said. 
The governor argues that his so-far unspecified tax reduction plan will put more money in Vermonters’ pockets and encourage more people to move to the state. Only with a larger tax base can Vermont solve its biggest challenges, he said, which include the high cost of healthcare as well as a lack of workers and housing they can afford.
In contrast, “why is their answer to every problem always another tax, fee and more spending?” his campaign said in a social media post last month, referring to Janoo and Democratic leaders in the Legislature. “That’s what got us into the affordability crisis and no amount of new spending or higher taxes is going to get us out.”
But Janoo — who says some details of her tax proposals will need to be worked out in the future — thinks Scott’s decade-long refrain as governor against new taxes and fees hasn’t helped the state make progress. She says the state already has access to the resources it needs to solve its biggest challenges, if only it would better use them.
“Phil Scott’s definition of affordability is tax cuts. My definition of affordability is: How affordable is your life? And, you know, basic needs?” she said in an interview. “Taxes are one of the levers, or tools, that we can utilize as a way to achieve that.”
Taxing the rich
Janoo has sustained support for an idea that’s made inroads with left-leaning members of the Legislature in recent years: raising taxes on high income-earners. This year, a version of the proposal got significant airtime in a key House committee but ultimately did not have enough support from Democratic leaders to advance beyond that.
Her campaign has proposed a 2% tax surcharge on personal income over $250,000 and an 8% surcharge on personal income over $500,000. Together, these measures would raise $344 million in state revenue each year, according to estimates from Fair Share for Vermont, a group that has lobbied in Montpelier for those proposals.
Janoo was part of that advocacy effort before running for governor and says her proposals are based on the group’s modeling. Revenue garnered from the surcharge plan would effectively replace, in Vermont, the tax cuts included in last year’s Republican-led federal tax and spending law, according to Fair Share for Vermont.
Broadly, Janoo said her goal is to use the surtax revenue to fund primary and preventive healthcare for all Vermonters, regardless of their insurance coverage. She’s previously estimated that such a system would cost more than $300 million. Janoo said in an interview, though, that the details of which services the surcharge would pay for would need to be worked out with legislators after she was elected. 
Vermont would not be the first state to raise income taxes on wealthy people. Several other states, including two in New England, have similar policies in place. Since 2023, Massachusetts has had a 4% surcharge on income over $1 million; and starting this year, Maine has levied a 2% surcharge on income over the same amount. 
If Vermont’s goal is to bring in as much new revenue as possible from a new tax, it makes sense the threshold starts at a relatively lower level of $250,000, so that as many people pay it as possible, said Robert McClelland, a senior fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, a nonpartisan think tank in Washington, D.C.
He said some questions to consider about the proposal are whether it would be indexed for inflation — so that it continues to impact only the wealthiest people — and whether married people’s income would be counted together or separately when calculating who meets the surtax threshold. If married people’s income is counted together, it could create a “marriage penalty,” he said, which might not be a good policy decision.
Scott, for his part, has been a sharp critic of the tax surcharge idea and contends that it would drive businesses and wealthy individuals out of the state at a time when Vermont needs to be growing its population, not losing more residents.
“You’re raising a tax on a group that I don’t think will pay it, because I think they’ll make a decision at that point as to where they live,” he said earlier this year. 
Vermont has a neighboring state, New Hampshire, with no income tax — which could draw some people across the border, McClelland suggested. But he said there is little evidence from elsewhere in the country that significant “tax flight” would occur. 
In Massachusetts, the so-called “millionaire’s tax” has exceeded projections for how much revenue it would bring into the state each year it’s been in effect since 2023. Supporters there argue this would not be the case if wealthy residents were leaving in large numbers to avoid paying the new charge. 
“The best evidence is, that’s not much of a concern. People tend not to do that,” McClelland said. 
For some people, “if you threw an extra 8% on their income above $500,000, they’d say, that’s it. I’m done,” he added. “But one also can imagine there’s a lot of people who love Vermont — and they’re not going to move, no matter what.”
Taxing second homes 
At a campaign town hall in Newfane last week, Janoo got a rousing ovation and even some loud cheers for another tax proposal: raising taxes on some second homes. 
Her campaign platform draws a distinction between types of housing that she thinks are good for a community — primary homes, affordable housing, homes owned by small landlords and “modest family camps” — and those that she has described repeatedly as “extractive” of the types of housing people who live in the state need. The latter includes “luxury second homes, commercial vacation rentals, vacant investment properties” and those owned by large corporations and private equity, her website states.
She’s proposed imposing a higher tax rate on the latter types of housing, which would discourage wealthy investors from buying up properties and allow the revenue to be “reinvested to reduce property taxes for Vermont residents,” according to her site.
Her platform doesn’t list a specific dollar amount that could be raised from those taxes. In a social media post in May, she cited a figure as high as $1 billion a year, though later told VTDigger and Vermont Public that “was a rough estimate of the potential long-term revenue” and not an amount that the state could immediately count on taking in.
Janoo said in an interview that it was hard to give a solid estimate because so much work would need to be done first to determine which types of properties would be taxed in what way. VTDigger and Vermont Public reported that even counting the number of second homes in the state is complicated, much less deciding how to tax them.
The idea is, at least, popular: in a recent Vermont Public poll, 57% of respondents said they thought that the state should impose a new yearly tax on second homes.
Scott, at a press conference last week, wouldn’t directly say whether he’d support new taxes on certain types of second homes. He said he’s waiting for more analysis of the idea by the state Department of Taxes before making up his mind. 
Still, the governor said, “I would prefer not to raise any taxes” at all.
Taxing big tech
Another one of Janoo’s proposals is to tax the revenue that large technology companies earn from digital advertisements. She says tech companies collect troves of data on Vermonters to target them with ads, but in her view the state gets little benefit in return. She called it another “extractive” process, as is corporate ownership of housing. 
Revenue from the tax would be invested in community broadband projects, local journalism and other initiatives, Janoo said. She also hopes that taxes on big tech companies dissuade them from running targeted ads, in the first place.  
“We don’t have billboards in our state. Why don’t we discourage digital advertisements? Nobody likes them, anyway,” Janoo said.
Numerous other states have considered or enacted some form of tax on digital advertising, some of which are similar to Janoo’s proposal. In August, a Maryland court struck down a digital advertising tax in that state after finding it violated federal internet tax freedom law, though state officials have since appealed that decision.  
One of the challenges for Janoo’s proposals might not be whether or not they will discourage business from operating in the state, but rather, the cost the state would have to take on to administer them, Amanda Gregg, an associate professor of economics at Middlebury College, said in an interview.
“This happens in Vermont. What I see is that sometimes, our reach exceeds our grasp administratively,” she said. “We have a small state government.” 
Broadly, Gregg said she thinks Scott is right to be concerned about the impacts of new taxes on the state’s demographics and businesses. But she also said that voters are eager for new ideas, like the ones Janoo is proposing. 
Recent polling and campaign fundraising data suggests Janoo has built significant momentum around the state in recent months, especially compared to most other Democrats who have run against Scott in years past.  
Even Scott acknowledged last week, at his press conference, that Janoo’s ideas were generating excitement. Janoo is “a different voice and I think that people just are looking for change,” he said. “And she’s very articulate.”
He contended that the change voters should support is sending more of his Republican allies to the Statehouse, rather than replacing him with a Democratic governor. 
But Janoo’s ideas are “popular for a reason,” Gregg said. “It feels like doing something — and it addresses a sense of unfairness.” 
Olivia Gieger contributed reporting.

Jim Risch, who’s in his 18th year as a senator. Achilles was […]
text:
Independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles, left, and Independent Leadership Council co-founder Adam Brandon speak about Achilles' commitment to not caucus with either major party, to only serve two terms, hold public town halls and participate in debates if elected. Achilles held the press conference on Oct. 7, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles on Wednesday pledged to not caucus with either party if he’s elected. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Achilles, who served in the Idaho Legislature as a Democrat before announcing his independent run for U.S. Senate, is running against incumbent Republican Sen. Jim Risch, who’s in his 18th year as a senator.
Achilles was joined at the Idaho state Capitol in Boise by Adam Brandon, the co-founder of a national advocacy organization promoting independent candidates called the Independent Leadership Council. Achilles also committed to serve a maximum of two terms, hold town halls in each of Idaho’s 44 counties every two years, and to engage in public debates. 
Brandon previously was president of FreedomWorks, which helped tea party candidates get elected to office. That organization dissolved in 2024, Politico reported.  
“Every vote that he casts, both parties are going to have to come to him for his vote to represent the state of Idaho, and I think that is incredibly incredibly powerful,” Brandon said.
Idaho US Senate candidates weigh in on tariffs, Iran War, federal spending and more 

In the letter Achilles signed to make these commitments, he said the U.S. Senate rules would still guarantee him a committee seat despite not caucusing with the major parties. 
The two independent U.S. senators — Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont — both caucus with Senate Democrats. When King won his election in 2012, he announced he would caucus with the Democrats because it would allow him to participate more in the committee process, PBS News reported at the time. 
Committee assignments are largely decided by party leaders and then formally voted on by the entire Senate. 
During the event, Achilles also signed a sworn, notarized statement that would resign him from office in 2039 — meaning if elected, he would only be able to serve two, six-year terms. A spokesman for the Achilles campaign said the letter will be sent to either the governor’s office or secretary of state to keep. 
“We’re serious about this,” Achilles said Wednesday. “That’s it. I don’t want to spend more than 12 years in D.C. I love Idaho’s mountains. I want to get back here and get my skis on and do what I love doing. So two terms. That’s it.”

text:
People walk into the Traill County Courthouse in Hillsboro, North Dakota, on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)A judge has upheld a North Dakota environmental agency’s permit issued for what is planned to be the state’s largest dairy farm.
The Dakota Resource Council challenged the Department of Environmental Quality’s permit for the Herberg Dairy in Traill County. The animal feeding operation permit covered areas such as manure management and water water discharge for the planned 25,000-cow Herberg Dairy southeast of Hillsboro, near the Red River.
Landowner group sues over Wahpeton water sale for large dairy

It is one of two large dairies being built in North Dakota’s Red River Valley by Riverview, based in Morris, Minnesota. 
East Central District Court Judge Susan Bailey issued the ruling affirming the permit Oct. 1. Bailey heard arguments on the permit challenge in July in Hillsboro. 
Dani Replogle is the attorney for the environmental group Food and Water Watch that represented the Dakota Resource Council.
“My main takeaway from the opinion is that this is just another instance of courts deferring to agencies despite evidence showing that they (the agencies) are not doing their job,” Replogle said Wednesday. “North Dakotans deserve better.”
The lawsuit named Riverview as well as the Department of Environmental Quality.
“We appreciate the court’s review and decision,” the agency said in a statement. “We remain committed to a thorough, transparent permitting process grounded in sound science and consistent application of the law to protect human health and the environment.” 
Riverview officials did not return voicemail or email messages sent Wednesday. 
Jim Murphy, economic development director for Traill County, said Riverview has started construction in earnest on the Herberg Dairy, after initial work on housing for dairy workers. 
The Dakota Resource Council and a group of Wahpeton-area landowners also have filed suit against the North Dakota Department of Water Resources. They are challenging a water sale for Riverview’s other Red River Valley milking operation, the Abercrombie Dairy in Richland County.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Coordinated lawsuits against in-state tuition for immigrants a ‘threat to rule of law,’ groups say
description: TOPEKA — A nationwide campaign to dismantle access to in-state college tuition for children of immigrants is “as much a threat to rule of law as what we see in the streets,” said an attorney for a Latino civil rights organization. A coalition of advocacy groups released a report Wednesday detailing the coordinated nature of the […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on Oct. 2, 2026, as he campaigns in GOP-leaning states ahead of the midterms. (Photo by Dan Anderson/Alabama Reflector)TOPEKA — A nationwide campaign to dismantle access to in-state college tuition for children of immigrants is “as much a threat to rule of law as what we see in the streets,” said an attorney for a Latino civil rights organization.
A coalition of advocacy groups released a report Wednesday detailing the coordinated nature of the Trump administration’s efforts to eliminate in-state tuition for students who are brought into the U.S. as children and attend public universities and colleges.
Kansas is one of 24 states and Washington, D.C., in active litigation with the United States government over its tuition policies. In September, a federal judge appointed by President Donald Trump struck down Kansas’ law, leaving immigrant students without the access to the in-state higher education they qualified for since 2004.
“The students in these lawsuits are not outsiders,” said Gabby Pacheco, president and CEO of The Dream.US, one of the report’s authors. “They’re students who grew up right here in our backyards, in our country, in our communities, and they are embedded in our states.”
The median age of arrival for students in the U.S. is 4 years old, Pacheco said during a virtual press conference Wednesday. There are 8,800 students, about 4,500 of whom have graduated college, represented in the 26 total lawsuits across 24 states and D.C. Immigrant students and graduates are asking to be treated the same as the classmates they’ve grown up with, Pacheco said. 
Their families have been contributing to states across the country not just with their labor but their taxes, she said. She called the lawsuits “self defeating.”
“Not only are they threatening and harming the dreamers and their opportunities for their future, but the future for the broader states and the communities that they live in,” Pacheco said.
Kansas is uniquely positioned among the coordinated series of lawsuits, said Thomas Saenz, president and general counsel for the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, or MALDEF, during a virtual press conference. The federal case against Kansas has been appealed to the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals, where a panel of judges will review whether the decision to overturn the law will stand and whether a group, Kansas Students for Affordable Tuition, can intervene in the case.
The appeal, however, is preceded by one in a case against Oklahoma. That case is “well ahead” of Kansas’, and Kansas’ case doesn’t yet have a briefing scheduled, while Oklahoma’s has been fully briefed, Saenz said. It’s unlikely Kansas’ will make it to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Judges across the country are split on whether these state tuition laws are in conflict with federal law, as the Trump administration argues. In Minnesota, a decision went in favor of students. In Illinois, a judge ruled in favor of the U.S.
Saenz said the Trump administration has used “very sharp tactics” to prevent outside parties from becoming involved in the cases. Saenz said the cases are just as much a part of the Trump administration’s immigration policies as immigration enforcement raids and “as much a threat to rule of law as what we see in the streets.” 
In Kansas, that has included Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, who tried to intervene in the case and defend the state law. 
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, a Republican, sided with federal prosecutors, culminating his years-long push to rid the state of its tuition equity law.
Kobach said in a non-binding legal opinion published in February that the law ran afoul of federal statutes, classifying in-state tuition for immigrant children as “tuition at greatly reduced rates” and “therefore a public benefit forbidden to illegal aliens.”
The Republican-controlled state Legislature attempted to overturn the law earlier this year, but Kelly vetoed the legislation, allowing immigrant students to receive in-state tuition until the court blocked the law in September.
Saenz pointed out Kelly is term-limited and could be replaced by a Republican governor in January, eliminating a barrier to passing legislation.
But, at this point, Saenz said, “there’s no reason currently for the state Legislature to do anything.”
The cases are “fundamentally about the nation’s talent pipeline,” said Miriam Feldblum, president, CEO of President’s Alliance, an organization involved in releasing Wednesday’s report.
It is “about the immigrant domestic talent pipeline that goes through our nation’s colleges and universities, and that spurs innovation, that fuels our workforce, that enables states and communities to prosper,” Feldblum said. “This is about both individual lives, and this is about the communities that they support, and the institutions and states that they enable to prosper.”
If there isn’t an attempt to defend in-state tuition for immigrant students, Feldblum predicted the ripple effects will be visible for decades.
