name: Connecticut Mirror
title: With eye on gavels, CT Dems envision oversight if they win majority
description: Members of CT's delegation are starting to sketch out what a Democratic return to power could look like from the highest echelons in Congress.
text:
They first need to win their own reelection races — and their party needs to gain control nationwide — but members of Connecticut’s delegation are starting to sketch out what Democrats’ possible return to power could look like from some of the highest echelons in Congress.
If both of those scenarios happen, nearly all of the Democrats in the delegation will vie for the top spot on their committees, giving Connecticut’s delegation the potential for outsized influence in the new session of Congress next year.
Democrats are looking to take back the House and the Senate, though the odds look better in the former. While uncertainty remains, that hasn’t stopped Connecticut Democrats from giving early previews of how they envision their potential roles as leaders of committees. 
And there’s a common theme in all those plans: oversight of the Trump administration.
“Connecticut, for a really small delegation, we’re going to punch well above our weight, and most of that is due to Rosa DeLauro’s likely appropriations chairmanship,” U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, D-4th District, said. “Rosa’s role there, Joe Courtney’s role on Armed Services, my role on Intelligence — from the standpoint of the power of the purse, I think is going to be really powerful check and balance.”
Some of these high-ranking positions wouldn’t be new for Connecticut’s House members. DeLauro, D-3rd District, was previously chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee and has served as the ranking member since 2023 when Republicans took back the majority.
Courtney, D-2nd District, has also served in both the majority and minority on the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee. And Himes ascended the leadership ladder on the House Intelligence Committee, becoming ranking member in 2023. All three have maintained productive working relationships with the GOP chairs of their respective committees and subcommittees.
This time, U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, will make a foray into running for leadership, on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. She’s mounting a challenge in what’s becoming a crowded race for either the gavel or ranking member.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., holds up a document during Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s testimony before the House Appropriations Committee, Tuesday, June 2, 2026 in Washington. Credit: Allison Robbert / AP

Pursuit of the gavel
As a fixture on the Appropriations Committee, DeLauro sits on an influential panel that crafts spending bills, allocates money and funds the government.
Her current role as the Democratic ranking member comes at a time when there has been a major strain between the executive and legislative branch regarding federal funding. The power of the purse resides with Congress, but the White House, led by Russell Vought at the Office of Management and Budget, has sought to claw some of that back, whether through rescissions or the impoundment of appropriated money.
DeLauro, 83, said she doesn’t take either race for granted and currently doesn’t face any challengers for the chair. But in her potential quest for the gavel, she hopes to restore education and job opportunities that could help address the higher cost of living and restore her committee’s authority on grants and other funding.
“I want to, as I have done in the past, continue to use the appropriations committee as the way to look at how in fact we address this affordability issue, how we put money back into people’s pockets, how we provide the services in all of the areas that have a real effect on their economic security and their lives,” DeLauro said.
She also works on the defense budget that could top $1.5 trillion, based on the request by the Trump administration at a time when the war in Iran has stretched into its eighth month. DeLauro acknowledged the dependence of the defense industry and contractors on Connecticut’s budget but said she’d want to work on improving funding for domestic programs and social services.
“Understanding that Connecticut is a defense-dependent state, I vote for the defense budget,” DeLauro said. “I deal with helicopters, engines, submarines, but I want to address the balance between what we are spending for education and health and transportation and housing, etc., with what we are spending with regard to defense.”
DeLauro also envisions handling some oversight “in my lane” by taking a look at where federal dollars are flowing and whether some money “has been transferred illegally.” 
“It won’t be frivolous, and I don’t want to take on anybody else’s jurisdiction,” she said, “but as it has to do with taxpayer dollars and the use of taxpayer dollars.”

House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., left, confers with Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking member, as the panel holds a hearing on worldwide threats, at the Capitol, in Washington, Wednesday, March 26, 2025. Credit: J. Scott Applewhite / AP

Unlike most of Congress’ committees, Himes, 60, serves on one of the more secretive panels because of the confidential nature of intelligence matters.
His job as ranking member places him in the “Gang of Eight,” a group of the Republican and Democratic leaders in the House and Senate plus the chairs and ranking members of both intelligence committees. Because of that, he typically gets a heads-up on major military actions, though that wasn’t the case with Venezuela and Iran.
The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence has oversight over U.S. intelligence agencies as well as some issues concerning the Pentagon and other government agencies. As a potential chairman, Himes previewed oversight as a main objective.
“What I can talk about is an effort we’re going to make to try to shine a light on some of the entities who have bent a knee to Donald Trump’s demands,” Himes said, referring to law firms, universities and corporations that do business with the intelligence community. “We’re going to shine a light on instances where contractors and others did the administration’s bidding, either illegally or, if not illegally, at least in ways that raise pretty ugly conflicts of interest.”
Himes has already issued warnings to defense companies about cooperating with congressional oversight, specifically on a potential investigation into corporate donations for the construction of the White House ballroom. But if he gets the chance to become chair, he said, he’s cognizant he’ll need some amount of buy-in from Republicans during such a polarized time.
“I think it’s really important that our oversight efforts appeal beyond just the Democratic Party,” Himes said. “That people really understand why what we’re doing is important for the country and the health of the country rather than for Democrats who may be very angry at Donald Trump.”

Rep. Joe Courtney speaks during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall, on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Courtney’s work on the Seapower Subcommittee has a lot of crossover with the defense industries that power much of Connecticut’s workforce and economy.
Some of his focuses will be on the Department of the Navy, submarine programs, and the AUKUS agreement between the U.S., U.K. and Australia that will have to meet deadlines on the delivery of Virginia-class submarines.
“I think oversight of this administration is obviously going to be very strong in general with some of the executive orders and different actions that the president has taken,” Courtney said. “But I think we have our work to do too in Seapower, as far as making sure that the right investments are being made to deal with what’s happening out there in the world.”
Courtney, 73, also see opportunities for oversight, whether that’s on the Air Force One plane gifted by Qatar as well as the White House’s battleship proposal. He also believes oversight over the war in Iran and U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s tenure will be “front and center” for the full House Armed Services Committee.
“That’s another one we would be looking at in terms of making sure it’s the property of the government and not an individual,” Courtney said, regarding Air Force One.
Hayes, meanwhile, would be a newcomer to leadership on the House Education and the Workforce Committee.
She recently threw her hat into the race to lead the panel for Democrats. So far, Hayes and Oregon Rep. Suzanne Bonamici are challenging the current top Democrat on the panel, U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia.

U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes joins other officials in Danbury, Conn. on Aug. 26, 2026 to condemn the actions of ICE, which detained dozens of people Monday and Tuesday.  Credit: Ryan Caron King / Connecticut Public

Education is one of her top priorities, especially as a former teacher in Waterbury. She currently serves as ranking member of the House Agriculture’s Subcommittee on Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture.
Hayes, 53, didn’t offer details about what that could look like because of her reelection race in the 5th Congressional District against Republican Chris Shea. The sprawling district in the western part of the state is viewed as Connecticut’s most competitive seat at the federal level, compared to the races of her colleagues. This year, though, election analysts see it trending even more toward Democrats.
“I’m not commenting on a chair race because I am in a district where I have to win first,” Hayes said in a statement. “I have declared my intention to run for the top Democrat on the Committee of Education and Workforce and will shift my focus to that race after the Election Day.”
One loss in seniority for Connecticut’s delegation comes after U.S. Rep. John Larson’s defeat in the August Democratic primary for the 1st Congressional District. He lost a four-way primary amid calls for generational change.

U.S. Rep. John B. Larson address supporters as he concedes to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin during a primary election watch party at Connecticut River Academy at Goodwin University in East Hartford on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Larson, 78, sought to leverage his seniority in his campaign, touting that if Democrats take back the House, he’d go back to holding the gavel of the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security and get a vote on his bill to raise Social Security benefits, which has stalled for years. That will be a live issue in the next Congress after a recent report estimated that the retiree trust fund will dry up in the early 2030s.
Larson lost to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, who’s favored to win the deep-blue district. Bronin faces Republican physician Amy Chai in the Nov. 3 general election.
The rest of the House delegation will also need to compete in the midterms to secure another term. Their Republican challengers — Chris Lancia running against DeLauro, Michael Goldstein challenging Himes, and George Austin looking to unseat Courtney — argue the Democrats’ work on committees hasn’t provided enough for Connecticut or has been a distraction as they focus on boosting their national profiles.
“I’d rather focus on things that are going to help the state of Connecticut,” Lancia said.
The view from the upper chamber
Taking the Senate will be a tougher feat for Democrats.
Democrats have been feeling more emboldened about retaking the Senate, though the map is more complicated than the House’s. Democrats will need a net gain of four seats to win the majority. That includes flipping GOP-held seats, some in deeper-red territory, while defending a few of their own vulnerable senators in tougher states.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., shakes hands with Donna Ganger, the mother of Renee Good, who was killed by federal agents in Minneapolis in January, before a Congressional spotlight hearing on Capitol Hill, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

Both of Connecticut’s U.S. senators currently hold minority leadership positions on some of their committees. Neither is up for reelection this year.
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal said he’d hope to serve as chairman of the Homeland Security’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations — a role he previously held when Democrats were in the majority — and the Veterans’ Affairs Committee. He didn’t give a preview of what that work could look like if his party is in the majority.
“I’m not jinxing it,” Blumenthal said, adding that he’s “focused on electing Democrats, as many as possible, so we will be in the majority.”
But as the current ranking member on both of these committees, Blumenthal, 80, has already sought to wield some investigatory power, even from the minority, and without subpoena power. That includes a recent investigation into a cryptocurrency firm and a series of public forums on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s practices.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., left, and Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., confer at the start of a Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing, at the Capitol in Washington, Thursday, June 18, 2026. Credit: J. Scott Applewhite / AP

U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, meanwhile, currently serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee that deals with funding for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
Funding for DHS got contentious over the last year, with Democrats pushing for any new money to be contingent on implementing ICE guardrails. The agency was in a record-long shutdown that ended in the spring. 
But it’s unclear if Murphy, 53, would stay in that role or look to become chair if Democrats took back the Senate.
“I don’t know that I’d stay as DHS chair,” Murphy said. “I think there will be a lot of movement.”
Back to the majority?
A return to the majority in either chamber of Congress is not a guarantee, even with historical trends, polling and Trump’s sagging approval numbers.
And if Democrats have a good night on Nov. 3, it remains to be seen if it would be a “blue wave” election as it was for the party in the 2006 and 2018 midterms. There’s at least one unpredictable factor — redistricting — that could scramble the race for the House.
Plus, Republicans have a major money advantage over Democrats that’s expected to deluge the airwaves and other forms of media for the next four weeks.
And coming off of Democrats’ disastrous 2024 election that ushered in Republicans’ political trifecta the past two years — control of the White House, House and Senate — the party is still working to build back trust with voters.
While frustrations persist for some of Trump’s policies and decisions, Connecticut Democrats acknowledged voters still aren’t completely sold on their party’s brand. And they will need to use their time in the majority, if they get it, to reinforce that they’re paying attention to voters and try to quickly deliver on lower costs of health care, housing and other necessities — and not just being an anti-Trump vote.
DeLauro and Himes echoed an urgency that Democrats need to follow through on their rhetoric around affordability and balance that with their opposition to Trump and his actions.
“We’re not going to win because all of a sudden they have Kennedy-like inspiration about the Democrats,” Himes said. “The American people don’t much like the Democrats today. They despise what this president has done to their well-being.”
“If we ever win the presidency, we better implement those effing policies immediately,” he said about cost-of-living measures. “No more bullshit about rolling out stuff six years down the road, because that’s a recipe to get tossed right back in the minority.”
Constituents who are ideologically aligned with members of Connecticut’s delegation are pushing them to fight back against certain policies. Some want them to go even further, and that frustration at lawmakers and officials was palpable at a press conference following ICE’s operation in Danbury in August.
Even if Democrats are victorious in November, there’s a level of expectation-setting that Democrats say they’ll need to do, given limitations of being in the majority in either one or two chambers while Trump has another two years of veto power.
Beyond committee work, some of the priorities of the delegation include more work on the child tax credit, the renewal of the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired last year, reauthorization of an apprenticeship law, lower costs of prescription drugs and more work on infrastructure. 
DeLauro continues to point to the courts being a backstop, but she argues, “public outcry gets things changed.” She noted the quick reversal of the administration around $2 billion in federal grants focusing on mental health and substance abuse that were reinstated within 24 hours after their termination.
“What we have to do is to manage those expectations, because even if God’s in his heaven and all’s right with the world with this, it’s going to take some time to get things done,” she said. “It doesn’t happen automatically, and I’m saying that to people.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: In wake of high profile death, new report on domestic violence in NH proposes changes
description: A group working to improve the state’s response to domestic violence incidents is proposing nearly a dozen recommendations for how the state can better protect victims — including harsher penalties for repeat offenders and training 911 dispatchers on the dynamics of domestic violence. The New Hampshire Domestic Violence Fatality Review Committee was establis[...]
text:
The New Hampshire Domestic Violence Fatality Review Committee — which includes representatives from the New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence — is calling on the state to implement 11 reforms meant to strengthen the response to domestic violence incidents. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)A group working to improve the state’s response to domestic violence incidents is proposing nearly a dozen recommendations for how the state can better protect victims — including harsher penalties for repeat offenders and training 911 dispatchers on the dynamics of domestic violence.
The New Hampshire Domestic Violence Fatality Review Committee was established by state law after the death of Marisol Fuentes-Huaracha, who was shot by her estranged husband in July 2025 in a case that a state review committee later found was mishandled. At the time of her death, lawmakers had already approved legislation — Senate Bill 140 — to establish the committee modeled after similar groups convened in the past. Gov. Kelly Ayotte signed it into law later that month. The committee was tasked with reviewing specific deaths with the goal of determining what lessons the state can learn. Fuentes-Huaracha’s was the first death the committee reviewed, and members released their first report this week.

 Domestic violence helpline

	If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, you can call New Hampshire’s statewide helpline at 866-644-3574 for free and confidential support 24 hours a day.

From 2022 through 2025, 44 out of the 68 homicides in New Hampshire were related to domestic violence, according to the committee. In 30 of those 44, a firearm was used. Twenty of the perpetrators were romantic partners and 22 were family members; in two, the victim and perpetrator were neither intimate partners nor family, but the death was connected to domestic violence. (For example, an estranged husband killing his wife’s current partner, or a bystander being killed during a domestic violence incident.)
“This report creates hope that systems will change to intervene in domestic violence situations sooner, both to protect victims and to hold offenders accountable,” Lyn Schollett, executive director of the New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence, said. “This report demonstrates a true commitment by a wide range of professionals to do things differently, and that’s groundbreaking.”
Three of the committee members represented the coalition or organizations involved in the coalition. The committee also includes members of the judicial branch, law enforcement and prosecutors.
To better respond to these tragedies, the committee proposed 11 policy and practice changes in its report.
“Create an enhanced level of offense for subsequent domestic violence convictions.”
The committee wants repeat domestic violence offenders to be charged with felonies. In New Hampshire, a domestic violence conviction alone is a class A misdemeanor unless the person uses or threatens to use a deadly weapon (in which case it is a class B felony). Under the committee’s proposal, the first offense would remain a misdemeanor, but subsequent offenses would become felonies. In the report, the committee said the Department of Justice, which is represented on the committee, would coordinate with state lawmakers to work on this goal.
“Explore domestic violence compliance efforts within the court system.”
The committee wants the judicial branch to assess its practices and consider creating a specialized process to monitor whether someone is complying with court orders, such as protective orders. A protective order is issued by a judge to keep a potential perpetrator from traveling within a certain distance of or contacting a potential victim, for example.
“Explore evidence-based risk assessment tools or guides to be used by judges in both civil and criminal cases.”
The committee also proposed creating tools or guides that can be used by judges to evaluate the level of danger for a potential victim. This might look like a rubric designed to assess the risk that an offender commits more violence against their partner or family, or to assess the likelihood they kill their victims. The committee said that the judicial branch may look to tools already created by domestic violence prevention organizations.
“Assess the disparities between counties for accountability for offenders, including but not limited to pre-trial and post-trial services.”
Different counties have different resources and infrastructure in place for law enforcement, prosecutors and judges to respond to domestic violence. The committee wants the New Hampshire Department of Justice to assess those disparities with a focus on what stakeholders believe is working, what they believe is failing and what they think might help. The report also outlined domestic violence-related homicides by county:

Hillsborough and Merrimack counties each saw 10 such deaths from 2022 through 2025.
Rockingham and Strafford counties saw six during the same time period.
Coös County saw five.
Cheshire and Carroll counties saw four each.
Grafton County saw three.
Sullivan and Belknap counties saw none.

“Increase knowledge on domestic violence protective order violations and appropriate charges.”
The committee wants the Department of Justice and the Police Standards and Training Council to develop or identify training that can help law enforcement officers better understand what constitutes a violation of a protective order and what criminal charges to bring. These trainings are particularly important when state law or case law change, the committee noted. It wants the New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence and law enforcement agencies to be involved in this.
“Train dispatchers and call takers on the dynamics of domestic violence.”
The committee reviewed the recordings of dispatch and 911 calls as part of its work. It believes the New Hampshire Emergency Dispatchers Association should create statewide standards for training dispatchers and call takers — an effort the association is already working on — that incorporates the dynamics of domestic violence. It encouraged the association to collaborate with the New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence on the content of the training and standards.
“Strengthen organizational responses to compassion fatigue and secondary traumatic stress among law enforcement and prosecution personnel.”
The committee defined compassion fatigue as “the cumulative physical, emotional, and psychological toll experienced by professionals who regularly work with people in pain, trauma, or distress,” and noted that law enforcement and prosecutors are vulnerable to the phenomenon. The committee wants state lawmakers to broaden required training for emergency response and public safety workers to cover compassion fatigue for law enforcement and prosecutors. It also wants prosecutors to be defined under state law as emergency response and public safety workers. Additionally, the Police Standards and Training Council should include protocols for addressing compassion fatigue in its model law enforcement protocols, the committee said.
“Explore the creation of Domestic Violence High Risk Response Teams.”
The Domestic Violence High Risk Team Model, created by the Massachusetts-based Geiger Institute, is a nationally recognized approach to domestic violence intervention. It involves creating teams across law enforcement, prosecution, probation/pretrial services, parole and corrections. The teams try to identify the most dangerous cases early, increase access to support services for victims, and better monitor offenders and hold them accountable. The committee plans to research what it would take for the state to create such teams.
“Promote system-based victim advocacy for criminal cases handled in Circuit Court.”
Every county attorney’s office has victim advocates who help the victims of a crime navigate the criminal justice system as their alleged perpetrator is prosecuted. The committee wants the state to explore grant opportunities that might provide funding for police departments to start their own similar programs as well.
“Revive domestic violence coordinating councils.”
In the 1990s, New Hampshire established domestic violence coordinating councils designed to identify and address domestic violence-related issues specific to their local community. The committee suggested re-establishing these committees.
“Expand ACERT teams to additional communities where appropriate.”
Adverse Childhood Experience Response Teams seek to respond to traumatic events occurring to children before age 18, such as abuse, neglect or household dysfunction. The state currently has nine such teams serving 17 communities. The committee thinks the state should create them in more communities.
On the committee are Attorney General John Formella; Cristina Brooks with the Merrimack County Attorney’s Office; Deanna Campbell, a New Hampshire public defender; Janet Carroll with the SANE Program and New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence; Ellen Christo with the New Hampshire judicial branch; Mike Donati with the Division for Children, Youth and Families; Jennie Duval, the New Hampshire chief medical examiner; Jessica Erazo, with New Hampshire Legal Assistance; Katja Fox, director of the New Hampshire Division of Behavioral Health; Amanda Grady Sexton with New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence; Ryan Grogan with the Portsmouth Police Department; Scott Hampton with Ending the Violence; Michael Mosher with the Jackson Police Department; Kevin O’Meara with the Manchester Police Department; Peggy O’Neil with WISE; Shanna O’Rorke with the Cheshire County Attorney’s Office; and Sean Smarz with the New Hampshire State Police. 
The committee will continue meeting and is required to release a similar report in October 2028.
“It is critical that we improve protections for victims of domestic violence so that our state never sees another tragedy like the murder of Marisol Fuentes in Berlin,” Ayotte said in a statement. “… I look forward to working together to implement these recommendations and strengthen our laws so we can prevent future tragedies and ensure victims have the protection they deserve.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Sparrows Point shipyard could bring thousands of jobs, promises billions in investments
description: President Donald Trump joined state and local leaders Tuesday to welcome a huge new shipyard that will bring billions of dollars of investment and thousands of jobs to Sparrows Point in Baltimore County.
text:
President Donald Trump at Tradepoint Atlantic in Sparrow's Point. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)President Donald Trump joined state and local leaders Tuesday to welcome a huge new shipyard that will bring billions of dollars of investment and thousands of jobs to Sparrows Point in Baltimore County.
Anduril Industries is set to invest $3.7 billion to construct a new shipbuilding facility at the Tradepoint Atlantic terminal on the site of the former Bethlehem Steel plant. The Arsenal-2 facility will manufacture components for Virginia-class nuclear submarines, reinvigorating the area’s historical manufacturing industry.
“Anduril chose Sparrows Point, in part, because of what this waterfront has done for this country,” Anduril Industries co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf said Tuesday. “Bethlehem Steel Mill here became the largest steel producer in the world. During the Second World War, hull after hull of Liberty ships were built at the shipyard on this site.
“That legacy doesn’t need to stay in the past. In the years ahead, Arsenal-2 will bring thousands of skilled manufacturing jobs back to the site and returns Sparrows Point to shipbuilding,” Schimpf said.
Moore says White House prevented him from speaking at Anduril announcement

Arsenal-2 will be a 2-million-square-foot “software-defined shipyard” on Sparrows Point. State officials say it is expected to bring a total of 14,000 jobs to Maryland, including 3,100 permanent jobs.
Additionally, the shipyard is expected to generate $2 billion in annual economic output, and deliver more than $300 million in wages each year, according to state estimates.
The company said site preparation and permitting will begin immediately, with construction to start as soon thereafter as possible. Initial production at the site could begin as early as 2030.
With the construction of the new shipyard Trump said the United States is “is going to remain the undisputed naval superpower of the world.”
“The workers of Baltimore and the shipyard here at Sparrows Point have been a vital part of the American industrial strength for literally over 100 years along these very shores,” Trump said. “Right here in Sparrows Point, you’ll build the next generation of American submarines, including autonomous subs … We’re going to have the finest ships anywhere in the world with the help of everyone here today.”
Notably missing from Tuesday’s ceremonies was Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, though several state lawmakers were in attendance. While the Moore administration said it has been involved in two years of discussions to bring Anduril to Maryland, officials with the governor’s office say he was disinvited from the event after the White House got involved.
But Schimpf gave him and other local leaders a shout-out during his remarks.
“An event of this magnitude and building a shipyard of this size comes with an equally long list of people who we need to acknowledge and thank,” Schimpf said. “Gov. Moore, County Executive [Kathy] Klausmeier, the federal congressional delegation, as well as state and local leaders throughout Maryland have all moved with urgency to bring industrial investment of this scale to Baltimore County.”
Attracting new companies to the state has been a priority of the Moore administration as it tries to revitalize the state’s stagnant economy, and counter ongoing budget woes. The administration says federal decisions under the Trump administration have exacerbated those challenges.
Co-founder and CEO of Anduril Industries Brian Schimpf. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
Lawmakers face another year in the coming legislative session with a steep budget shortfall, as spending is expected to outpace revenues by $3 billion in fiscal 2028.
Senate Budget and Taxation Chair Guy Guzzone (D-Howard), who attended the Tuesday event, said that the new shipyard construction is an “extraordinary” opportunity for Maryland to work with a major corporation that will bring in “lots of jobs.”
“It may be the very beginning and could lead to other companies coming to Tradeport Atlantic,” he said.
The shipyard construction will be “the largest job creator in Maryland in over a decade” according to a prepared statement from the governor’s office released Tuesday morning. Additionally, state and local officials plan to create a workforce training center near Tradepoint Atlantic to support the new shipyard.
“With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs,” Moore said in a written statement. “We thank Anduril for choosing Maryland, and we’re ready to build the future of the aerospace and defense economy together.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Billionaire Diane Hendricks helps Wisconsin Republicans defend legislative majorities
description: Billionaire Diane Hendricks recently contributed millions to help Republicans in their efforts to defend their legislative majorities, which are in jeopardy for the first time in more than 16 years. Hendricks and the billionaire couple Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein have flooded Wisconsin’s midterm elections with money this year. According to a recent WisPoli[...]
text:
Wisconsin State Capitol (Wisconsin Examiner photo)Billionaire Diane Hendricks recently contributed millions to help Republicans in their efforts to defend their legislative majorities, which are in jeopardy for the first time in more than 16 years.
Hendricks and the billionaire couple Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein have flooded Wisconsin’s midterm elections with money this year. According to a recent WisPolitics analysis, the three billionaires have given more than $73 million to Republican committees and candidates in 2026. 
Individuals in the state of Wisconsin can only give $1,000 each to state Assembly candidates and $2,000 to individual candidates for state Senate. However, there is no limit on the amount donors can give to party committees, meaning an unlimited amount of money can be sent to and spent on behalf of candidates through the parties. 
Hendricks’ contributions are part of an effort to help Republicans maintain control of both houses of the state Legislature, which they have held since 2011. They currently hold a 54-seat majority in the 99-seat state Assembly and a 17-seat majority in the 33-seat state Senate. Democratic lawmakers are looking to hold all of their current seats and pick up five additional seats in the Assembly and at least two seats in the Senate. 
Sen. Patrick Testin (R-Stevens Point) told the Examiner in August that the billionaires have been strong supporters of Senate Republicans and “despite the criticism leveled against those individuals, what never gets a light shined onto it is the money that comes in from states like Illinois, New York, California, billionaires and multi-and mega-millionaires from the liberal elite who have flooded Democrat coffers for years.”
But the WisPolitics analysis found there was no comparable donor to the Democratic committees or campaigns in 2026 and no one donor has contributed as much over the past 17 years as each of the three GOP billionaires have donated in 2026 alone.
The Republican Assembly Campaign Committee reported raising $6.17 million from July 1 through Sept. 23. The majority of the funds — $5.5 million — were contributed by Hendricks.
The committee reported spending $9.5 million and having $11.16 million in the bank at the end of the fundraising period. It also provided $4.87 million in in-kind contributions to candidates across the state. 
The Assembly Democratic Campaign committee reported raising $6.01 million during the same time period and spending about $3 million. The committee reported having $5 million on hand at the end of the fundraising period. Top Democratic contributors were Wendy Munger, who contributed $1 million and Lynde Uihlein, a family member of the Republican donors, who provided $250,000.
In many races, Republican candidates are not receiving large cash donations to their campaigns, but are receiving in-kind contributions of mailing, TV and online advertising. 
In Assembly District 85, Rep. Pat Snyder (R-Weston) reported raising $31,870. His Democratic opponent, John Kroll, reported raising $84,294. However, Snyder outpaced Kroll in in-kind contributions receiving $642,899 from the Republican Assembly Campaign Committee and the Republican Party of Wisconsin. Kroll received $271,317 in in-kind contributions, which were contributed by the candidate, the Assembly Democratic Campaign Committee and the Democratic Party of Wisconsin.
In Assembly District 88, Rep. Benjamin Franklin reported raising $20,030. His Democratic opponent, Brandy Tollefson, reported raising $53,650. However, Franklin received $675,043 in in-kind contributions, while Tollefson received less than half of that amount — $307,172 — in in-kind contributions. Franklin spent $39,411 and Tollefson spent $93,277.
The Committee to Elect a Republican Senate reported raising $2.28 million. Hendricks contributed $1.75 million of that. The committee reported spending $2.6 million and having $4.96 million on-hand at the end of the period.
The State Senate Democratic Committee reported raising $1.24 million and spending $2.03 million. It had $1.3 million in the bank at the end of the report. The top donations were $500,000 from Sarah O’Neill of New York and $225,000 from the Democratic Party of Wisconsin. 
In the four most closely watched state Senate races, the contributions of the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate are playing a large role in the GOP campaigns, including through cash donations and in-kind contributions. 
In Senate District 21, Republican candidate Jim Croft reported raising $1.1 million, but only raised $15,000 from individual donors; the majority of the $1.1 million was contributed by the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate. He spent a little more than $1 million.
Democratic candidate Trevor Jung reported raising $816,707 and spending $1.05 million. About $725,000 of his total came from the State Senate Democratic Committee.
In Senate District 5, Rep. Robyn Vining (D-Wauwatosa) raised $79,321, more than Republican candidate Mike Roberts, who raised $34,092. Roberts received more in-kind contributions than Vining, however, totaling more than $145,000 from the Republican Party of Wisconsin and the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate. 
Will Karcz, spokesperson for the State Senate Democratic Committee, said in a statement that “Wisconsin voters have shown us that their votes cannot be bought by the billionaire donors Republicans rely on to prop up their failing candidates.”
According to a July analysis of past races by Marquette Law School fellow John Johnson, money does matter in these races, but “it’s clear that money doesn’t ‘buy elections’ in any crude way. Candidates routinely win after being outspent by their opponent — a fact not limited to the Wisconsin legislature.” 
Johnson wrote, “the hypothesis is that in districts where the Democrat accounts for more of the spending, that Democrat will do better relative to the performance of the Democratic candidate for governor or president in that district.”
More important than the relative amount of money each candidate has, according to Johnson, is the name at the top of the ticket in any given election.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Urban League asks: ‘Is the American Dream dead?’ In Kansas and US, obstacles look overwhelming.
description: The National Urban League, in its latest and 50th edition of the State of Black America, asks a haunting question: “Is the American Dream dead?” This question has a particular resonance with Black Americans as the nation marks its 250th birthday, but also a particular answer. American enslavement lasted some 246 years. Segregation, another 89, […]
text:
The American flag flies at the Lower Fox Creek Schoolhouse, built in 1882, at the Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve near Strong City. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)The National Urban League, in its latest and 50th edition of the State of Black America, asks a haunting question: “Is the American Dream dead?” This question has a particular resonance with Black Americans as the nation marks its 250th birthday, but also a particular answer.
American enslavement lasted some 246 years. Segregation, another 89, and that just takes us to 1954. Racists killed teenager Emmett Till in 1955. Also that year, Rosa Parks and other Black citizens in Birmingham, Alabama, began boycotting city buses.
The Urban League’s State of Black America highlights a nation still finding its footing in its climb toward a just society. Violence seemed the predominant weapons of the past, whereas today, the cudgel is economic. Consider the report’s findings.
From November of 2025 to February of 2026, 567,000 Black men and 250,000 to 300,000 Black women lost their jobs. Since then, the number of Black women who lost their jobs has jumped to that roughly 600,000 number.
Those losses amount to a loss in Black households of a staggering $87 billion. Black America finds itself in recession-like conditions, namely, surging unemployment, sector-specific contractions, and policy-driven shocks.
The report noted that Black households had 15 cents for every dollar owned of a white household.
The report described stalled progress: “Policy changes under the present administration have pushed the American Dream further out of reach for Black Americans than at any point since the Civil Rights Movement.”
Those policy shifts didn’t just impede progress; they rolled back gains won over decades.
“While the 2021-2024 period saw historic lows in Black unemployment and poverty rates, subsequent shifts in diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and federal civil rights oversight have reversed or erased much of that momentum,” the report reads.
The current administration has launched explicit attacks on Black workers, Black history, and Black institutions.
I’m pointing now to the firing of Black military leadership; the temporary scrubbing Jackie Robinson from a government website; firing Carla Hayden, then the Librarian of Congress, via email and doing so by addressing her by her first name.
Two great Black intellectuals saw this coming decades ago.
One of those men, noted political science professor Ron Walters, wrote about this subject in his 2003 book, “White Nationalism, Black Interests.”
Walters, a Wichita native and an architect of the Congressional Black Caucus, said extremists began pursuing “a more explicitly white nationalist agenda,” after the 2000 election.
“We appear to be living in an era when a dominant sector of the white majority seems to have lost confidence in the promise of a liberal democratic state (and) is proceeding to concentrate economic and social power within its own group, using control over political institutions of the state to punish presumptive enemies,” the late-Walters wrote.
This wasn’t a pendulum swing, he wrote, but rather a “several-decades-long white nationalist movement committed to reinstating and strengthening racialized hierarchies of power and privilege.”
Noted historian John Hope Franklin referenced this subgroup in 1969. Franklin described the tendency to ignore or omit Black history as “uninformed, arrogant, un-charitable, un-democratic and racist history.”
Continuing, he said, “It has thus spawned and perpetuated an ignorant, self-seeking, super-patriotic, ethnocentric group of white Americans.”
 The report speaks to its deja vu findings.
“For the 50th anniversary edition of the State of Black America … we examine how this pattern has repeated across 250 years of American History. We document how each attempt to guarantee every American the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness has been met with racism, social violence, and political retrenchment.”
Still, hopefulness shapes the report.
“We also chart a way forward,” it reads. “America is changing racially, culturally, and economically, and a new technological revolution is reshaping what is possible. We believe the future holds real promise, if we demand it.”
It poses another question as haunting as its title: “What becomes of an America where millions support policies that threaten individual freedom and physical safety rather than securing every person’s right to a full life?”
That question shadows a history long in sacrifice but short in appreciation. It spans the Revolutionary War, the Civil War, two world wars and today. In each theater, the nation’s Black inhabitants bet their lives that America might finally reward their allegiance and patriotism.
The past decade has revealed, however, that fully a third of the nation pines for a pre-civil rights America.
The Urban League asks if the American Dream is dead.
Black America might respond with a question of its own: “How can the American Dream be dead for those of us who embody it, who forced it to live up to its ideals, and who loved it when it hated us? How can it be dead, when it has always been alive in us?”
Mark McCormick is a journalist and a nonprofit executive. He’s also the author of four books including “Barry Sanders: Now You See Him” (a New York Times bestseller), “Some Were Paupers. Some Were Kings: Dispatches from Kansas,” and his latest, “Kansas Matters: America’s Social Faultlines.” Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana DNR plans public wildlife land at former Newport Chemical Depot
description: Fifteen years after agreeing to acquire a large swath of the former Newport Chemical Depot for conservation, Indiana is still working to complete the $10 transfer — and planning to manage the additional land without more money or staff. The Indiana Department of Natural Resources has not yet acquired the roughly 1,705 acres in Vermillion […]
text:
The former Newport Chemical Depot property includes forest and agricultural land intended for conservation, prairie restoration and protection of Indiana bat habitat. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Fifteen years after agreeing to acquire a large swath of the former Newport Chemical Depot for conservation, Indiana is still working to complete the $10 transfer — and planning to manage the additional land without more money or staff.
The Indiana Department of Natural Resources has not yet acquired the roughly 1,705 acres in Vermillion County, according to agency spokesperson Emma Balzer. But she said a 2011 agreement outlining the unusual deal remains in place and its terms have not changed.
“The department is working through the process, including completing the necessary survey work,” Balzer said in a written response to the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
Under the agreement, the Newport Chemical Depot Local Redevelopment Authority intended to convey a 1,093-acre forested parcel and a 612-acre agricultural parcel to DNR during 2026, although it did not establish a more specific deadline. The land would be limited to conservation purposes, including prairie restoration, wetlands banking and preservation of Indiana bat habitat.
The agreement called for DNR to pay $10 for the land if the transfer occurred in 2026, with the property’s future use restricted to conservation. Had DNR accepted the property earlier, it would have owed $3,000 per acre — more than $5.1 million for the full 1,705 acres.




Quotation







This is a beautiful area, and it’s an important area, and it’s really an opportunity for the state to do something in a very cost effective way.


– John Ketzenberger, director of government relations for The Nature Conservancy in Indiana 


Balzer said the original agreement remains in effect and that its terms have not changed.
The agency did not provide a projected acquisition date or say what must be completed beyond the survey work.
John Ketzenberger, director of government relations for The Nature Conservancy in Indiana, said the organization is hopeful DNR will complete the acquisition.
“We’ve all been worried about the deadline because it’s right upon us,” Ketzenberger said. “But we’ve gotten an assurance from DNR that they intend to do that. It’s just a matter of getting everything worked out.”
The DNR acquisition is roughly one-quarter of the overall site. The redevelopment authority owns and operates the broader 7,000-acre Vermillion Rise Mega Park, which includes land dedicated to industrial and economic development.
Former military land
The property is part of the former Newport Chemical Depot, located about 25 miles north of Terre Haute and several miles south of the town of Newport, between the Illinois border and the Wabash River.
The installation was used for military manufacturing and later for the storage and destruction of the deadly nerve agent VX. A federal base-closing commission recommended shutting it down in 2005 after completion of its chemical demilitarization mission.
The Army subsequently conveyed more than 7,200 acres associated with the chemical depot, according to federal Base Realignment and Closure records. The local reuse authority was established to guide the former depot’s conversion to civilian use and economic development.
Federal records also show that buildings involved in VX neutralization were demolished because of possible contamination. Historical military environmental reports identified explosives, heavy metals and other contaminants at sites across the former installation.
Story continues below.
SIGNED - 2011 Recitation of Intent
 
DNR did not identify a specific environmental obstacle when asked whether cleanup obligations, liability or other environmental issues could affect its acquisition. Its response instead emphasized the challenge of managing the property with existing resources.
“It’s not your typical transfer,” Ketzenberger said, noting the need to identify conservation easements, other potential encumbrances before getting a clear title. “But what we’ve been led to believe is that it’s just a matter of time, of working through that paperwork, which gives us a little hope because for a long time we thought that they were just going to let it go.”
Balzer said additionally that DNR “is working to find solutions to properly manage the additional acres while maintaining the same budget and staffing level.”
The proposed acquisition comes amid an agencywide spending reduction at DNR.
The agency’s 2026 fiscal plan called for a $10.7 million appropriation cut, a $6.6 million reserve and savings from eliminating or holding open 100 full-time positions. The plan also proposed reducing intermittent staffing.
DNR officials did not say how many employees would be assigned to manage the Newport property.
Ketzenberger said managing the land as a fish and wildlife area makes sense because that designation generally requires less manpower than some other state properties. But he said the state must still invest in restoration and continued upkeep.
“We’re just hopeful that … they will … make the investment to ensure that … the restoration is done at a high quality level and that it’s managed then afterwards,” Ketzenberger said. “And by that, it may be doing prescribed fire or other conservation management practices to ensure that it stays viable for the long term and doesn’t just become an overgrown mess.”
Public access planned
DNR intends to make the land publicly accessible and place it under the Division of Fish, Wildlife and Nature Preserves, Balzer said.
The agency’s current plan calls for managing the Newport land as a satellite property of Deer Creek Fish and Wildlife Area.
The state wildlife area began in 2010 with the transfer of 1,962 acres from the Putnamville Correctional Facility to DNR. Later additions brought the property to 2,175 acres, according to the agency.
The main wildlife area is near Greencastle in Putnam County, while the former Newport depot is farther west in Vermillion County. DNR did not provide an estimate of the annual cost of managing the satellite property, nor did the agency identify how many employees would be responsible for it or say when public access could begin.
John Ketzenberger, director of government relations for The Nature Conservancy in Indiana (Photo courtesy TNC Indiana)
The 2011 agreement requires the parcels to be used exclusively for conservation after their transfer to DNR. Before the transfer, it allowed the agricultural parcel to remain in agricultural or conservation use and required the forested acreage to be managed for conservation.
Ketzenberger called the prospective acquisition “the bargain of the century.” He said the forest offers intact habitat, while more than 600 agricultural acres could eventually be restored as prairie, wetlands, woods or another habitat type selected by DNR.
The protected Indiana bat habitat is only one part of the property’s value, he said. Wetlands and floodplains can help reduce flooding, while the land’s location along the Wabash River places it within a migratory route used by sandhill cranes and other birds.
“It’s all part of an interconnected landscape, and when we tear it up as we have, then it makes it … harder to realize the benefits from that landscape,” Ketzenberger said. “And that’s why this, you know, it’s 1,700 acres, which is in Indiana a large parcel.”
He also pointed to the potential for hunting, fishing, trails and other outdoor uses if DNR opens and develops the property for recreation.
“Those kinds of recreational opportunities are critical, and in that part of the state, they’re just not abundant,” Ketzenberger said. “This is a beautiful area, and it’s an important area, and it’s really an opportunity for the state to do something in a very cost effective way.”
The agreement was executed in August 2011 by representatives of DNR and the Newport redevelopment authority. It did not detail why the parties selected 2026 for the significantly reduced transfer price.
Ketzenberger said he believes agricultural agreements covering part of the property needed to expire before the transfer could occur, contributing to the long wait.
DNR officials said the acreage, boundaries, ownership terms and conservation restrictions contemplated in the agreement have not changed.
Ketzenberger said The Nature Conservancy remains optimistic that “the state is able to complete the deal and … make it what it potentially can be.”
“You can imagine a prairie, or … whatever else is restored out there — wetlands, whatever they deem important,” he said. “It becomes an area that, from a picture, it may look unremarkable, but when you get on site, you can see numbers of birds and critters and chances to take in the beautiful nature of that area.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Controversial Pierce Co. factory farm appeals groundwater decision
description: A factory farm in Pierce County filed a lawsuit late last month appealing an administrative law judge’s decision that the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources didn’t include enough groundwater protections when approving a permit allowing the farm to expand from 1,700 to 6,500 cows.  The Ridge Breeze Dairy in Maiden Rock has long been the […]
text:
Opponents of the Ridge Breeze Dairy expansion watch the contested case hearing Tuesday against the farm's permit in the standing room only overflow room at the Eau Claire State Office Building. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)A factory farm in Pierce County filed a lawsuit late last month appealing an administrative law judge’s decision that the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources didn’t include enough groundwater protections when approving a permit allowing the farm to expand from 1,700 to 6,500 cows. 
The Ridge Breeze Dairy in Maiden Rock has long been the subject of local activism against the expansion, which is expected to generate 78 million gallons of manure every year. The initial DNR permit process drew significant public participation. 
The dairy is owned by the Appleton-based Breeze Dairy Group, which operates a number of farms in the state — some with a history of manure spills. 
Communities across Wisconsin are facing the effects of massive factory farms on their local water, particularly rural areas where residents get their drinking water from private wells. The groundwater around the Ridge Breeze site already has elevated nitrate levels, which have been linked to blue-baby syndrome, thyroid disease and colon cancer.
The DNR approved the expansion permit in February 2025. During the application process, the agency had to send the permit back to the farm operators once because it named nearby properties as sites for planned manure spreading although those property owners were never contacted.
After the approval, a group of local residents and the advocacy group Grassroots Organizing Western Wisconsin filed a lawsuit alleging that the permit did not do enough to ensure that the area groundwater was protected. 
Two days of hearings were held in Eau Claire in March and in August Administrative Law Judge Angela Chaput Foy ruled in favor of the residents, sending the permit back to the DNR to include a process through which the agency can verify that the farm isn’t harming the groundwater. 
“By omitting a mechanism to verify actual compliance, the Department has issued a mandate while simultaneously denying itself the tools or data necessary to know whether that mandate is broken,” Chaput Foy wrote.
In the lawsuit, filed Sept. 23 in Outagamie County Circuit Court, the farm argues that it’s “aggrieved” by being forced to verify it is following the law, mostly because it would have to pay the cost of digging groundwater monitoring wells. 
In recent years, Wisconsin factory farms and their allied advocacy groups have also filed lawsuits that argue the DNR lacks the authority to regulate their pollutants at all. 
Ridge Breeze argues that state law doesn’t include a mechanism through which the DNR can verify compliance with groundwater standards in a factory farm’s permit. 
“The ALJ concludes that the lack of mechanisms in the Permit to verify that Ridge Breeze’s practices comply with the standards is inherently contradictory to the mandate to assure compliance with those standards,” the lawsuit states. “The Decision thus improperly conflates the statutory requirement to assure compliance with a (non-existent) obligation to prescribe conditions that verify compliance. Nothing in [state statute] requires the DNR to require groundwater monitoring or some other mechanism to ‘verify’ compliance or detect non-compliance.”
The dairy points to parts of Chaput Foy’s decision in which she finds that the provisions included in the initial permit should be strong enough to protect the groundwater. 
“By disregarding substantial record evidence that showed the terms prescribed in the Permit were reasonable and sufficient to assure compliance with groundwater standards — including the ALJ’s own conclusion that the permit ‘sets Ridge Breeze up for anticipated compliance’ — the Decision is outside the range of discretion conferred upon DNR and is unreasonable, arbitrary and capricious, and should be reversed and/or remanded to the agency,” the lawsuit states. 
Danny Akenson, an organizer with GROWW, said in a statement that Ridge Breeze appealing the decision shows the farm cares more about its bottom line than being a good neighbor. 
“We fought for three years to make sure the state has a way to determine whether Ridge Breeze is contaminating our groundwater, and the judge agreed with us,” Akenson said. “Factory farm special interests care more about protecting corporate profits than protecting the groundwater Wisconsin families rely on. Ridge Breeze may have deep pockets for legal fees, but we’re organized, and we’re not going to let them off the hook.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore says White House prevented him from speaking at Anduril announcement
description: Gov. Wes Moore planned to be on hand for Tuesday's announcement of a massive economic development project at Sparrows Point, but said he was uninvited by the White House after President Donald Trump said he was coming, the latest spat between the two.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore, right, said President Donald Trump said he would not be allowed to speak at Tuesday's announcement of a new Anduril Industries shipyard in Sparrows Point; the White House denied the claim. (Trump from a White House screen shot; Moore by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)It was called the biggest private investment in the state in a decade, with state and federal dignitaries on hand Tuesday to celebrate Anduril Industries’ plan to spend billions, and create thousands of jobs, at a new Sparrows Point shipyard.
Noticeably absent from the officials on stage, however, was Gov. Wes Moore (D). He said he was uninvited by the White House after President Donald Trump announced plans to show up.
“I will not be there later on today,” Moore said earlier Tuesday, after a debate with GOP gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox. When asked if his absence from the Tradepoint Atlantic event was at the direction of the White House, Moore said, “That is correct.”
Moore said he’s proud of the facility and the deal state officials helped bring to fruition after more than a year of negotiations. 
“We’re excited about what it’s going to mean to the area,” Moore said. “But if the president of the United States wants to bring the circus into town and tell me that I’m not allowed to speak despite the fact that we were the ones that helped bring the deal, then I will let the circus be conducted while I go back to work for the people of Maryland.”
The White House said Tuesday that Moore was invited to attend — as a guest — and that President Trump is willing to collaborate with anyone if it means bolstering the country’s manufacturing sector.
“It’s unfortunate that the Governor is now making a multi-billion dollar announcement about himself by throwing a tantrum over a federal initiative that will bring sorely needed jobs back to his state thanks to President Trump,” the White House statement reads.
But Moore administration officials said the governor was part of the program, only to be told by the White House that he couldn’t speak.
“Gov. Moore has always said he will work with anyone when it comes to delivering for Marylanders, but bow to no one when it comes to standing up for them,” a spokesman for Moore said. “The governor is proud to welcome Anduril to Baltimore County and the thousands of permanent jobs this investment is bringing to our state.”
The Moore administration got ahead of the event by announcing details of the deal in a news release posted at 9 a.m. Tuesday.
The 2-million-square-foot submarine manufacturing facility is expected to provide more than 14,000 jobs, with 3,100 of them being permanent, according to a news release from the governor’s office. The facility will produce parts for Virginia-class nuclear submarines and is expected to open in 2030.
Tuesday is not the first time Trump and Moore have sparred.
Trump has repeatedly attacked Baltimore and Maryland, as he does many blue cities and states, threatening in 2025 to send National Guard troops to Baltimore because the city was “so far gone” with crime. Moore, pointing to falling crime rates in the city, said Trump should come walk the streets of Baltimore and see for himself, but to otherwise “keep our name out of your mouth.”
In an August 2025 Cabinet meeting, Trump called Baltimore a “hellhole” he wouldn’t want to walk through. Moore, at the time, added that President Trump was simply spouting “nonsense” from the Oval Office and making false claims without ever visiting the city.
The sparring has continued, with Moore blasting Trump’s cuts to the federal workforce and Trump, earlier this year, disinviting Moore and Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, both Democrats, from a National Governors Association dinner at the White House, among other slights.
Trump made no mention of the governor Tuesday, but others did.
“An event of this magnitude and building a shipyard of this size comes with an equally long list of people who we need to acknowledge and thank,” said Anduril Industries co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf. “Gov. Moore, County Executive [Kathy] Klausmeier, the federal congressional delegation, as well as state and local leaders throughout Maryland have all moved with urgency to bring industrial investment of this scale to Baltimore County.”
Sen. Guy Guzzone (D-Howard), who was at Tuesday’s event, said, “The State of Maryland was involved [in landing Anduril]. The governor had every right to be there and every right to speak.”
— Maryland Matters reporter Danielle J. Brown contributed to this report.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC governor candidates agree on abortion, differ on gambling and Medicaid
description: COLUMBIA — In the only scheduled gubernatorial debate before the election, Democrat Jermaine Johnson and Republican Alan Wilson sparred Tuesday night over questions about data centers, Medicaid expansion, and a state hate crime. Perhaps more surprising is where they agreed. In a state where legislators debate abortion every session — sometimes several times[...]
text:
Democrat Jermaine Johnson and Republican Alan Wilson debate Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, in the studio of WIS-TV, a Gray Media station, in Columbia, South Carolina. The studio was closed to the public and other media. (Screenshot of the livestream from Gray Media)COLUMBIA — In the only scheduled gubernatorial debate before the election, Democrat Jermaine Johnson and Republican Alan Wilson sparred Tuesday night over questions about data centers, Medicaid expansion, and a state hate crime.
Perhaps more surprising is where they agreed.
In a state where legislators debate abortion every session — sometimes several times a year — both agreed the state’s abortion restrictions should go no further. Both pledged they “would not seek to make them even more restrictive.”
The contest pits Johnson, a state representative since 2020 who opposed all GOP anti-abortion laws, with Wilson, the state attorney general since 2010 who’s defended them in court.
When the nominees were asked if the 2023 state law, which bans abortions six weeks into a pregnancy, is “strong enough,” Wilson sought clarification.
So, “leave the exceptions in place?” he asked to the show-of-hands-only question.
“Correct,” replied WIS-TV moderator Judi Gatson, causing both to raise their hands.
The Legislature’s most strident abortion foes want to go a lot further. In April, senators advanced legislation that not only banned abortions from the onset of a pregnancy but also deleted exceptions and threatened to send women to prison for two years for seeking an abortion. The bill, which divided the GOP, never got a floor vote.
But there’s a strong chance the legislation will return next year.
Wilson’s team confirmed after the debate that he believes the six-week law should stand. It allows exceptions for a fatal fetal anomaly and allows victims or rape or incest to get an abortion until the 12th week of pregnancy.
Gambling
Two other show-of-hands-only questions showed opposing views on gambling.
The odds of SC legalizing more gambling could change with next governor

Asked if they would support allowing casinos in South Carolina if voters approved a “statewide referendum,” only Johnson raised his hand.
On the flip side, only Wilson raised his hand when Gatson asked who would oppose casino gambling “even if voters support it.”
That assumes the Legislature passes a law putting the question on a general election ballot, with the earliest being November 2028. In South Carolina, there’s no such thing as a voter-led ballot referendum. Only supermajority approval by both chambers can put a question on November ballots. And that’s highly unlikely for a question involving casinos.
Historically, legislators have been reluctant to alter South Carolina’s anti-gambling laws. That’s changed in the last few years, with increasingly more Republicans willing to legalize sports betting, authorize a casino, or even bring back forms of video gaming.
One thing that’s stopped gambling bills from gaining traction is Gov. Henry McMaster’s opposition. Overriding his guaranteed veto would take supermajority approval, which supporters haven’t had.
Wilson’s answers Tuesday are further indication he would continue to be a veto threat, at least when it comes to casinos. At a GOP primary debate in April, Wilson said he “could never be against the faith community and the law enforcement community when it comes to this.”
Data centers
On data centers, Johnson and Wilson argued, even though their positions were very similar.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both said communities should decide whether a data center becomes their neighbor.
“That’s why,” Johnson said, he introduced a resolution in April calling for a moratorium on all data centers in South Carolina. The bill never received a vote. Wilson blasted the proposal as taking away choice from a community that may want a data center for the property taxes it pays.
“If you don’t want a data center, you don’t have a data center,” he said. “But if you are a community who sees the value or benefit of a data center, then we should provide you with a statutory and regulatory framework, guardrails” that require them to generate their own energy and mitigate noise, light, and other pollution.
In a rebuttal, Johnson said that was the purpose of his moratorium — to pause data centers until the General Assembly can create that framework.
Healthcare
On improving access to healthcare, Johnson said expanding Medicaid is a must.
South Carolina is among 10 states that never expanded Medicaid eligibility to cover all adults with incomes up to 138% of the federal poverty level, as intended by the 2010 federal health care law commonly known as Obamacare.
Johnson noted that his mother, who’s diabetic, recently had to have a leg amputated, and that a ZIP code in north Columbia has one of the nation’s highest rates of amputations due to diabetes, as reported by The State newspaper in 2022.
“We have to do this, not just for us, but for the people of South Carolina, for all mothers and sons, and to make sure that everybody gets the healthcare they need,” said Johnson, of Hopkins.
Wilson recalled his family’s own “terrifying” ordeal as his wife Jennifer battled breast cancer, saying he wants “every single family” to have the same access to healthcare. But expanding Medicaid isn’t the answer, he said, repeating South Carolina Republicans’ long-held argument that the state can’t afford it.
He pointed to North Carolina’s experience as evidence: The neighboring state’s expansion took effect Dec. 1, 2023. Advocates hoped that would change minds in South Carolina. But it was not the example they hoped. In April, North Carolina legislators passed a $319 million bailout to keep the program afloat through the end of June after failing to pass a state budget last year.
The massive federal tax policy law signed by President Donald Trump in July 2025 made Medicaid expansion more expensive for states. South Carolina hospitals are set to take a multimillion-dollar annual cut starting in 2028 due to one of the law’s tax changes. But the law’s biggest cost-cutting measures don’t apply to South Carolina.
Hate crime
South Carolina remains one of only two states without a specific hate crime law.
Asked how they would work with the Legislature to get one passed, Wilson said he supports legislation that would allow prosecutors to add prison time to the sentences of people convicted of committing a crime due to their victim’s race, gender or sexual orientation.
“So, if you were killed because you’re gay, or killed because you’re a conservative person on a public college campus, we can prosecute you and we can enhance that penalty by even more. So, I’m open to that,” Wilson said, adding that he’d have to “talk to the Legislature when I become governor.”
That so-called enhancement legislation is what the GOP-dominated House has passed twice since 2021. The most recent version that cleared the House would have added up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine to the sentence of a hate-motivated violent crime.
But the Senate has never taken a floor vote on the legislation.
Johnson, who believes “we absolutely need a hate crime,” accused Wilson of being dishonest.
“Now, I don’t know why my opponent just said all those words up here, but we all know that he has stood against a hate crime law here in South Carolina,” he said. “We see these counties all over South Carolina enacting their own ordinances in the counties, and he has issued opinions against them.”
AG’s opinion says only SC legislators can create a hate crime. But 2 dozen local laws still stand.

That’s a “categorically false” misrepresentation, Wilson shot back.
Johnson was referring to an opinion from the attorney general’s office last October that hate crime ordinances in municipalities across South Carolina would likely be struck down if someone challenged them. The ordinances may violate the state constitution’s ban on local governments creating criminal law, the analysis concluded. The opinion was sought by the city attorney for Greenwood.
That was a legal opinion on the constitutionality of local ordinances, Wilson said, not his opinion on statewide legislation.
Who’s ‘new’?
Both candidates talked about changing the status quo and working to make life more affordable.
Johnson said he’d usher in a “new South Carolina,” while Wilson said he represented a “new generation of leadership.”
McMaster, who was attorney general prior to Wilson, leaves the governor’s office as the longest-serving and oldest governor in state history.
Both candidates questioned the other’s ability to actually create change.
Johnson repeatedly referenced “24 years,” which is how long there’s been a GOP trifecta at the Statehouse. Wilson’s part of that ruling party, he said.
The last Democratic governor, Jim Hodges, lost his 2002 bid for re-election. Republicans gained the majority in the Senate following the 2000 election, when one Democrat switched parties. That was six years after Republicans gained control of an evenly divided House because a Democrat voted for a Republican speaker. Republicans have been growing their majorities since. The 2024 election gave the GOP supermajorities in both chambers.
Wilson pointed to Johnson’s track record: Of the 70 bills he sponsored, none passed. “How can you bring transformative change as an outsider, but you can’t even get bills passed” as a legislator, Wilson said.
“When you’re a Democrat, it is not about getting bills passed. It is about working with everybody and being the co-sponsor” on legislation that becomes law, Johnson said.
Not on the debate stage were two third-party candidates for governor: United Citizens candidate Michael Addison and Green Party candidate Walid Hakim.
