title: Cox’s ‘pro-human AI’ order directs state government to use ‘responsible’ artificial intelligence
description: Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on Tuesday signed an executive order meant to “promote responsible AI use within government” by using “pro-human” principles when evaluating artificial intelligence tools.  The executive order sets a “structured, pro-human framework for artificial intelligence integration across state government,” the governor’s office said in a news re[...]
text:
Gov. Spencer Cox speaks with members of the media during the PBS Utah Governor’s Monthly News Conference at the Eccles Broadcast Center in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026. (Pool photo by Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune) Utah Gov. Spencer Cox on Tuesday signed an executive order meant to “promote responsible AI use within government” by using “pro-human” principles when evaluating artificial intelligence tools. 
The executive order sets a “structured, pro-human framework for artificial intelligence integration across state government,” the governor’s office said in a news release. 
It’s meant to advance Utah’s Pro-Human AI Initiative, an effort launched in December 2025, by directing state agencies to “maintain rigorous safeguards for human agency, data privacy and trust” while also using AI to “enhance public services and improve efficiency,” the governor’s office said. 
AI may soon be in more healthcare processes in Utah under new state agreements

Under the executive order, state government agencies are directed to require AI literacy training for employees while also requiring them to use AI tools to “streamline internal processes and radically improve citizen-facing applications.”
“The choice between innovation and safety in government is a false one,” Cox said in a prepared statement. “AI represents a generational opportunity to better serve Utahns, but technology must always remain accountable to the people.”
Cox added that by “ensuring our approach is strictly human-guided and human-enhancing, Utah is demonstrating how state government can lead the nation in deploying cutting-edge technology while preserving individual liberty, privacy, and human dignity.”
The governor’s order tasks the Department of Government Operations “to lead the state in the use of AI-driven process improvements, choosing tools that adhere to Pro-Human AI principles.” 
It also requires the Division of Technology Services to coordinate with the Division of Human Resources Management to design and implement a “comprehensive AI literacy training strategy for all state agency employees” as well as “specialized training for agency AI leads.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Under the order, all state agencies are also required to “evaluate opportunities for optimizing and transforming state government business functions through the use of AI technology in a cost-effective manner.” They’re directed to “actively investigate and propose areas where citizen-facing government processes and automated workflows can responsibly be optimized or transformed using AI technology.” 
Marvin Dodge, commissioner of the Utah Department of Government Operations and a member of the Pro-Human AI Task Force, said in a statement that “state government must exemplify both operational excellence and ethical responsibility as we adopt these powerful technologies.”
“Through comprehensive employee literacy, robust technical safeguards, and privacy-preserving digital identity frameworks, we are empowering our workforce to innovate safely and deliver faster, more transparent outcomes for all Utahns,” Dodge said.

The co-chairs of Utah’s Pro-Human AI Initiative — Margaret Woolley Busse, commissioner of the Utah Department of Commerce, and Jefferson Moss, commissioner of the Governor’s Office of Economic Development — also issued a joint statement applauding the executive order, calling it a “vital action” for the effort.
“By establishing these standards, state agencies are empowered to harness AI tools dynamically and efficiently while preserving public trust, transparency, and accountability,” Busse and Moss said.

title: Utah health officials issue ‘urgent’ warning about kratom, ‘cat’s claw’ products after overdoses
description: The Utah health officials are warning against substances marketed as herbal products that produce psychoactive “highs,” saying they may contain dangerous semi-synthetic kratom chemicals. The warning comes after four Utahns died of overdoses linked to “high-potency, illegal chemical compounds” found in the products, according to a news release from Utah’s Dep[...]
text:
Buzzers Cat's Claw tablet packets. (Photo courtesy of Utah Department of Agriculture and Food)The Utah health officials are warning against substances marketed as herbal products that produce psychoactive “highs,” saying they may contain dangerous semi-synthetic kratom chemicals.
The warning comes after four Utahns died of overdoses linked to “high-potency, illegal chemical compounds” found in the products, according to a news release from Utah’s Department of Health, Poison Control Center and Department of Agriculture and Food. No additional details about the deaths were released.
The state had issued a similar warning in July following one death and multiple severe health incidents involving cat’s claw tablets that were found to contain kratom alkaloids.
Pure leaf kratom remains legal in Utah, but lawmakers this year banned adulterated kratom products containing extracts or semi-synthetic chemicals that increase potency.
Utah’s kratom ban takes effect: Adulterated products should be off shelves starting today

The agencies said the products often sold online, in smoke shops and convenience stores under brand names like “Buzzers,” purport to contain “cat’s claw” or Uncaria tomentosa, which is not harmful in its natural form. But testing by the Department of Agriculture identified semi-synthetic kratom alkaloids in the tablets, including mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI) and dihydro-7-hydroxymitragynine (MGM-15), which the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration classified as Schedule I controlled substances in August.
The agencies warned the substances “carry severe risks of addiction, dangerous withdrawal symptoms, overdose, and death.” 
Because the substances act on the body’s opioid receptors, naloxone, an overdose reversal medication, can be used in response to an overdose, the agencies advised. For people experiencing addiction, medical treatments for opioid dependence and withdrawal are effective. Anyone experiencing withdrawal should seek immediate medical attention.
While synthetic kratom alkaloids are illegal in Utah, the agencies said they can still be found for sale. Anyone who sees kratom extracts or semi-synthetic kratom products being sold in the state are asked to report them to the Department of Agriculture and Food by emailing udaf-kratom@utah.gov.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvanians call on Shapiro, lawmakers to pass data center moratorium
description: Speakers at the rally were critical of Shapiro for his initial embrace of Amazon and other tech companies as they scoped out sites. The development guidelines that now encompass much of the commonwealth’s data center policy are too little, too late, they said.
text:
Maya K. van Rossum, founder of Green Amendments for the Generations, speaks at a rally where advocates demanded a statewide moratorium on data center development Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026 at the Pennsylvania Capitol. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The state Capitol rotunda echoed with dissent Tuesday afternoon as dozens called on Gov. Josh Shapiro and lawmakers to enact a statewide moratorium on data center development.
At least 100 data center projects are proposed around the commonwealth, according to Shapiro’s office. 
In August, he signed an executive order removing all proposals for the facilities  from the state’s Fast Track permitting process and requiring developers to comply with responsible development standards.
But speakers at the rally were critical of Shapiro for his initial embrace of Amazon and other tech companies as they scoped out sites. The development guidelines that now encompass much of the commonwealth’s data center policy are too little, too late, they said.
“While he was cheerleading for this industry, communities, real communities like mine, were burdened with figuring out the consequences in real time, without a serious statewide framework of how to accommodate these kinds of developments at scale,” said Stuart Day, a Lawrence County farmer and co-founder of Ohio Valley Allies.
Day compared data center speculation to the commonwealth’s natural gas fracking boom in the 2010s, which former Gov. Ed Rendell compared to a gold rush. He later admitted he had regrets about prioritizing the economic benefits of shale gas development over the environment.
Data center development, Day said, is another example of rural economic colonialization, where land, labor, and resources are exploited and the value goes elsewhere.
“Data centers are simply the most recent incarnation of this very old pattern,” he said.
Shapiro spokesperson Rosie Lapowsky described the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development Standards, enacted by Shapiro’s order, as the strictest in the nation. They’re designed to place legally binding requirements on developers to protect communities and the environment, ensure data centers pay for their own power and infrastructure and create well-paying jobs.
“Developers who want to do business in Pennsylvania need to meet these requirements, earn community support, and be good neighbors — if they can’t do that, they should look somewhere else,” Lapowsky said.
The rally, organized by the Better Path Coalition, brought together advocates for  rural communities, faith groups and immigrant rights.
Maya K. van Rossum, founder of Green Amendments for the Generations, speaks at a rally where advocates demanded a statewide moratorium on data center development Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026 at the Pennsylvania Capitol. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
State lawmakers have introduced at least 80 bills this session dealing with data centers but few have become law. In July, Shapiro signed the state budget, which included legislation requiring larger data centers to report their energy and water usage to state regulators.
But data center opponents called on the General Assembly to pass Sen. Katie Muth’s (D-Chester) bill to impose a three-year moratorium on new development to give local officials time to assess risks and enact protective measures to ensure public safety.
They also delivered letters to Shapiro’s office, including one signed by 80 doctors, nurses and other health care providers opposing the construction and operation of hyperscale AI data centers in Pennsylvania due to the health harm, environmental impacts, and the burdens they would place on communities. 
“Once a center is operational, pollution from diesel and gas generators are known to have severe health impacts,” said Josephine Gingerich of Physicians for Social Responsibility PA. She noted recent studies have suggested data centers could contribute to roughly 600,000 additional asthma cases a year nationwide and 1,300 premature deaths from the condition. 
Teofilo Reyes of Make the Road Pennsylvania noted artificial intelligence and data centers drive the mass data integration and surveillance technologies U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement uses.
“Pennsylvania should not be a testing ground for mass surveillance,” Reyes said. “It should lead the country in protecting our privacy, our communities, and our freedom.”
Elected leaders  in Pennsylvania have a duty under the state constitution to protect the environment from the degradation threatened by data center development, said Maya K. van Rossum,
The founder of the Green Amendments for the Generations called on elected officials to act to protect Pennsylvanians’ rights under the state constitution. Enacted in 1971, the constitution’s Environmental Rights Amendment creates a powerful right of the people to healthy environments and protected natural resources, van Rossum said, but it also gives leaders a duty to preserve them.
“Good government officials, like all of us here today, recognize that protecting our environment is good for everyone, regardless of our politics, where we live, our personal beliefs or our priorities,” she said, adding that good food, outdoor recreation and property values all depend on environmental quality.
“Knowing all of this,” she continued, “Pennsylvanians are offended that data center developers keep walking into our communities, declaring that they have rights, declaring that they have rights to build their data centers and devastate our environment, overwhelm our communities with massive development and unending noise, light, and pollution.”

name: VTDigger
title: Federal boost advances West Brattleboro Terrace redevelopment
description:
A $1.75 million federal award moves forward a $19 million plan for 30 energy-efficient homes for older residents.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Federal boost advances West Brattleboro Terrace redevelopment.
text:
U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., visits the former Melrose Terrace site in West Brattleboro to discuss $1.75 million in federal Community Project Funding for its redevelopment on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Photo by Kristopher Radder/Brattleboro Reformer

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Oct. 6, 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — Brattleboro Housing Partnerships celebrated $1.75 million in congressionally directed funding for the redevelopment of Melrose Terrace as West Brattleboro Terrace.
The approximately $19 million project will replace remaining buildings outside the floodway with 30 energy-efficient units for residents age 62 and older. Other funding includes $3.8 million from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board, $1 million in National Housing Trust funds, $815,000 in equity and nearly $3 million in tax credits. 
Redevelopment follows damage wrought by Tropical Storm Irene in 2011, which prompted the relocation of residents to new Brattleboro Housing Partnerships developments at Red Clover Commons. Completed flood mitigation work is now anticipated to protect housing along the brook while restoring flood plain capacity.
At the celebration Tuesday, U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., called the redevelopment “a smart community development project.” Christine Hazzard, executive director of Brattleboro Housing Partnerships, said she expects a groundbreaking in the next few months and a ribbon-cutting ceremony in early 2028.
Melrose Terrace was developed in 1966 with 80 households and was significantly affected by Irene. Completed flood mitigation changes the flood map and protects housing along the brook.
“This was the first property developed by the town-formed Brattleboro Housing Authority,” Hazzard said. “The property was developed to provide housing for many of Brattleboro’s lowest-income elderly residents and in the late 1990s began including adults with disabilities. Vermont’s only example of mid-20th century garden apartment design with winding walkways and ample green space, this property has been loved by most people who have lived here and for all of us who have gotten the fortunate opportunity to work in this space over the 60-year history.”
Hazzard said communities throughout Vermont “will need to find ways to preserve their historic downtown and village centers and housing that are along the floodway by creating space for the water to go.”
“This will hopefully create parcels of land across Vermont outside of the floodway for future use,” she said.
Hazzard thanked Chris Hart, former executive director of Brattleboro Housing Partnerships, M&S Development and the BHP Board of Commissioners. 
“Fifteen-year projects need a champion,” Hazzard said, “and Brattleboro Housing has been that champion when making every major decision on this project.”
Hazzard said Balint “has been with us throughout this whole way and was a firsthand participant in the development of Red Clover Commons One and Two, and the story of Melrose Terrace, and she has undoubtedly supported the progress each step.”
“It takes a lot of people to bring a project like this across the finish line,” Balint said. “And although we’re not at the finish line yet, I’m grateful that we are working together every step of the way.”
Balint called Brattleboro “home to me.”
“This is my hometown, and this is where I live,” she said. “This is where I’m raising my kids. This is a special community, and I made a commitment to myself when I was in the state Legislature, and again, when I was fortunate enough to be able to represent Brattleboro in Congress, that I was going to always have a special eye for the southern part of the state because I know oftentimes we feel like we get forgotten down here, so this is exactly where I want to be today.”
Balint said she’s “so proud that even in the midst of all of this dysfunction in Washington, D.C., that we can be here today celebrating some good that came out of it.” Brattleboro needs about 500 new units of housing right now, she estimates. 
Balint said the Melrose Terrace redevelopment is about “making sure that people can retire with dignity in a beautiful place, a place that feels like home.”
Rural communities struggle with similar issues, Balint told reporters, including housing and healthcare. Lawmakers from different parties finding common ground makes programs such as congressionally directed funds “continue to work even when you have forces that would like it so that we don’t get anything done,” she said. 
“For me, it’s making sure that the more rural areas don’t get forgotten when it comes to rehabbing housing and building new housing because we have the same struggle that is happening in Chittenden County,” she said. “We have a very low occupation rate, and so it’s very obviously very special for me to be able to do this here in Brattleboro, but I feel that way whenever we are able to invest in housing because I know it’s one of our biggest challenges right now.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont summer food aid for families expires this weekend
description:
Time is running out for most families to use grocery benefits that help feed children during the months when schools aren’t in session.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont summer food aid for families expires this weekend.
text:
An aisle in a grocery store with canned food items. Photo via Adobe Stock

Most families that receive Summer EBT food aid have until Oct. 10 to hit the grocery stores and farmers markets and use the benefits before they expire.
The federally funded program provides support for qualifying Vermont families, including those who receive free and reduced-price school lunches, to buy groceries for their children during the summer. The electronic benefits are valid for about four months after families receive them, according to a memo from the Vermont Agency of Education. For most families, that means they expire Oct. 10, the agency said. 
Food costs in the Northeast have risen 2.9% over the past year, according to an August study by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. 
Vermont is in the top three nationwide for the biggest grocery price hikes from 2024 to 2025, rising 7% during that year, according to a study by the Consumer Affairs Journal of Consumer Research.
For families, the costs hit hardest in the summer, when children don’t receive school-provided meals as they do during the year, according to Tim Morgan, deputy director of programs at the advocacy organization Hunger Free Vermont.
“And for families that qualify, Summer EBT provides a grocery benefit that can make a huge difference to filling that gap,” Morgan said. 
Summer EBT benefits were issued for more than 38,000 school-age Vermont children this year, according to the Education Agency memo. Eligible households receive $120 for each school-age child.
The benefit cards can be used at grocery stores, online retailers and farmers markets to buy foods such as fruits and vegetables, whole grains, meat and dairy products, according to the state’s Vermont Summer EBT web page.
In early September, Summer EBT benefit cards for over 12,000 children still had a balance of more than $20, according to the Education Agency memo. More than $1.4 million in benefits could be returned to the federal government if left unused, it said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: On his way out of Congress, Rep. Burgess Owens still sees his future in education
description: As Utah Republican Rep. Burgess Owens prepares to turn off the lights and close the door to his career in public office, he finds himself ending on the same note that sparked his interest in government. And he says he’ll now pursue similar ventures in the private sector. After retiring from the NFL in 1983, […]
text:
Utah Republican Rep. Burgess Owens speaks during an interview hosted by the Sutherland Institute on Oct. 6, 2026. (Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)As Utah Republican Rep. Burgess Owens prepares to turn off the lights and close the door to his career in public office, he finds himself ending on the same note that sparked his interest in government. And he says he’ll now pursue similar ventures in the private sector.
After retiring from the NFL in 1983, he aimed to focus on solutions for at-risk children and kids getting out of the juvenile justice system, he said during an interview hosted by the conservative think tank Sutherland Institute on Tuesday. And that’s what led him to pursue a seat in the U.S. House.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Well, I realized that if things didn’t change in D.C. then that was not going to happen. So I decided to start this journey in D.C.,” Owens said. “What has happened now, after six years, the last years, is the dream I began 40 years ago is now coming to fruition.”
He referred to the initiatives he pushed as chair of the U.S. House Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Development, including efforts to expand school choice offerings at the federal level, as well bills he sponsored, including the MATCH Act, which creates “Learning and Employment Records,” allowing employers to hire based on verified skills and credentials.
Facing new congressional boundaries, Utah Rep. Burgess Owens won’t seek reelection

His school choice proposal to expand K-12 educational options nationwide passed through the 2025 spending package known as the “Big, Beautiful Bill,” and the MATCH Act passed in committee to be considered by the full House. 
“I left the NFL with a focus on helping out at-risk kids. There’s nothing more important than doing it through the workforce process and good education,” Owens told Utah News Dispatch after the panel. “So, I hope that’s going to be the legacy that, in generations to come, might not know my name, but I’ll be part of a good group of people that decide to put together some good policies.”
Owens announced he wouldn’t seek reelection in March after a lawsuit he filed alongside Republican Rep. Celeste Maloy contesting Utah’s new congressional maps failed. However, he didn’t address the anti-gerrymandering legal fight in his lengthy social media post announcing his retirement from Congress.
“I will finish this term fully committed and fully accountable. My final political sprint will be here in Utah and across the country, helping my colleagues expand our Republican majority,” Owens said then. “Though this chapter closes, my commitment to advancing opportunity, advocating for our children, and strengthening families will continue in new ways.”



Let us know what you think...


 


The Utah Republican was elected to Utah’s previous 4th Congressional District in 2020, when he prevailed over the Democratic incumbent at the time, Ben McAdams, by tight margins. He served three consecutive terms. 
Now, he said, he’s ready to focus his attention where he feels most comfortable: the private sector.
“You know, being a politician is work, and I don’t mind it. But I love being in the private sector,” he said. “So I’m excited about being in Utah and take some of the things we’ve done over the last couple of years, and now implementing it, helping Utah to really take advantage of it. So it’s a great chapter for me. I’m looking forward to it.”
His private sector pursuits are still to be determined, but he said he’s passionate about the Learning and Employment Records effort he pushed in Congress, and he may work on expanding that system. He also sees himself finding solutions for states to “understand” and “work through” school choice.
But, for now, he knows that he’s staying in Utah.
“Utah’s home. Six kids and 19 grands here in Utah,” he said. “This is home for good.”

name: VTDigger
title: Lt. gov. candidates largely agree on politics, clash personally
description:
Lt. Gov. John Rodgers and challenger Molly Gray met Tuesday for a tense debate hosted by Vermont Public.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Lt. gov. candidates largely agree on politics, clash personally.
text:
Republican Lieutenant Governor John Rodgers, left, and Molly Gray, a Democratic nominee to be the lieutenant governor. Photos by Glenn Russell
Incumbent Lt. Gov. John Rodgers and Democratic challenger Molly Gray mostly challenged each other on past experiences rather than policy in a debate Tuesday afternoon. 
“My opponent and I agree with one thing,” Rodgers said. “And that is that we can’t afford the status quo.”
Rodgers and Gray, the executive director at Vermont Afghan Alliance, talked bipartisanship, education, healthcare, property taxes and rural-urban divides in a debate hosted by Vermont Public. The candidates agreed that Vermont needs to lower the cost of living and support the state’s rural population. Deflections and personal attacks, however, left little room for policy outlines.
Throughout the debate, Rodgers accused Gray of political opportunism and questioned her rural credentials and schooling, while Gray defended her education and later accused Rodgers of bullying.
In an opening question, moderator Mikaela Lefrak asked the candidates to discuss how they will fulfill the duties of the role, which has little authority in passing legislation. They agreed that the role should not be seen as a ceremonial one. Gray, who previously served as lieutenant governor from 2021-2023, said the job should be used to advance state priorities and address federal overreach. Gray did not run for reelection in 2023, instead making an unsuccessful bid for the U.S. House of Representatives. Rodgers criticized that decision noting that his time in office has been spent focusing on “constituent work.” 
“When you look at the two of us who’ve each had two years there, I used the office to help Vermonters, and my opponent used the office to run for Congress,” he said.
Throughout their campaigns, both candidates have touted their rural upbringings. While the candidates agreed that legislators in Montpelier are disconnected from the state’s farmers, Rodgers, 61, of Glover, brought up Gray’s high school education at Stratton Mountain School, a private boarding ski academy. 
“I don’t think it’s appropriate to make light of that,” Gray, 42, of Burlington, responded, noting that she had received a scholarship having learned to cross-country ski while growing up in Newbury. 
They also agreed on education spending, healthcare, land-use policy and property tax. Gray said she would advocate for universal primary care and affordable housing, noting a five-point housing plan she’s proposing. On high property taxes, Rodgers, who served in the Legislature for 16 years, recalled an amendment he proposed on Act 46 in 2015 that would have mitigated education costs but ultimately wasn’t passed into law. 
“It is clearly the same folks that are supporting my opponent that have caused us to get here,” he said, speaking to Vermont having one of the highest property taxes in the country. 
Rodgers also said that Gray has yet to explain how to pay for universal primary care. 
“What I believe is that we have a responsibility to consider recouping the Trump tax cuts and possibly increasing the tax on luxury second homes in Vermont, not hunting camps, not workforce housing, and investing that directly into a program that we know brings down costs, helps stabilize our education system and provides Vermonters meaningful property tax relief,” Gray responded.
Gray won the Democratic primary in August. After her unsuccessful bid for Congress in 2022, she served as the first executive director of the Vermont Afghan Alliance, a nonprofit which supports Afghans resettling across the state. This, she said, allowed her to see “the cruelty and inhumanity of the Trump administration up close.”
Rodgers has also previously spoken against the Trump administration’s cuts to Medicare and Medicaid, tariffs and the detentions of migrant workers.
Before his 2024 Republican bid for lieutenant governor, Rodgers served in the Legislature as a Democrat. During the debate, he said that he felt disappointed in the impacts of Democratic policies on the working class. 
“Their policies are literally crushing them,” he said. “I have a long history of being independent, no matter what party I was part of, because I work for Vermonters”
During a segment where the candidates could offer questions to one another, Rodgers asked Gray why she had not spoken out against labor violations on her family’s farm in 2024, which found unfit living conditions for migrant workers. The case was resolved and closed in January 2025. 
Gray responded that she was on the ballot, not her family. 
“I’m a little bit caught off guard here, and I’m a little bit shocked,” she said. “Vermonters have a chance in this election to really think about the type of leadership they want in the state. When I think about what we see nationally right now, I think about what I want for my kids. I don’t want a self-serving, self-interested bully.”
She then asked Rodgers if he could change anything he had done in office he had regretted. 
“I mean, quite frankly, I can’t think of any mistakes,” he said, noting speaking against the Trump administration and constituent work.
Rodgers questioned whether Gray had encouraged Democratic leaders to bully state Rep. Leanne Harple, D-Glover, who told Gray in a phone call that she was supporting Rodgers. Gray said she couldn’t speak on “anything that happened after” she received a call from Harple. She then criticized Rodgers for his “small, petty, personal” attacks throughout the debate, saying that leadership means focusing on “big issues” in the state.
“It’s showing up every single day, making sure that Vermonters feel protected … We’re not bullying other candidates. We’re not bullying other people into providing support for us. And I think that’s what Vermonters deserve right now.”
Vermont Public is hosting debates between candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives and governor later this week. The general election takes place Nov. 3.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore and Cox bring heat to debate, but will it alter the race?
description: Gov. Wes Moore (D) and his Republican challenger Dan Cox each presented their vision of a state under their leadership in an hour-long debate Tuesday that quickly showcased the expected lines of attack and the animosity between the two candidates.
text:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox, right, and Gov. Wes Moore (D) meet for a debate Tuesday at the Maryland Public Television studios in Owings Mills. (Photo by Larry Canner Photography/Courtesy of MPT)The lone televised debate between the two leading contenders for governor looked very similar to their debate four years ago.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) and his Republican challenger Dan Cox each presented their vision of a state under their leadership. But the hour-long debate in Owings Mills quickly showcased the expected lines of attack and the animosity between the two candidates.
Cox, who lost to Moore four years ago, painted the governor as a tax-and-spend liberal and at times accused his opponent of lying. Moore at every turn tied Cox to President Donald Trump and portrayed his opponent as a MAGA acolyte, quoting a former governor who once called Cox a “Q-Anon whack job.”
And, to the surprise of none, both Cox and Moore left the Maryland Public Television studios saying they felt good about their performance.
“I appreciated the chance to come and speak directly to the people of Maryland, and saying that despite the assaults that we have seen from the president, and frankly, a Trump agenda that Dan Cox has said himself that he backs 100% of the time, that there’s been no state that’s been greater affected, but there’s been no state that’s been more effective when it comes to dealing with it,” Moore told reporters after the debate.
Cox said in an interview after that he spoke on behalf of Marylanders, and urged Moore to agree to additional debates at one of the state’s historically black colleges and universities.
Third-party candidates decry exclusion from only debate of the governor’s race

“I wanted to speak for the people of Maryland, and I felt we got some of that done,” Cox said. “I appreciate this opportunity. I thank the governor for the opportunity to come here.”
In the end, however, it is not clear the policy differences, wrapped in heated exchanges and one-liners, will change the trajectory of the election with four weeks left.
Cox trails Moore by 27-points in a poll released Tuesday morning before the debate.
Two third-party candidates on the ballot were not included in the debate: Green Party nominee Andy Ellis and Working Class Party nominee Cathy White each polled at 3% in the survey. below MPT’s threshold of 10% to qualify for the debate.
Mileah Kromer, director of the Institute of Politics at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, which did the poll, said before the debate that Cox’s inability to bring in voters from outside his party and a lack of money are hurdles.
“If he does really, really well on the debate, he’ll get the benefit of some post-debate coverage,” Kromer said Monday before the poll release. “Without money to wage a campaign, or frankly having the individual characteristics that appeal to unaffiliated voters and moderate conservative Democrats — the things that are necessary to like to take a really strong debate showing and then turn it into momentum — he just doesn’t seem to have any of those things.”
The debate Tuesday afternoon in Owings Mills is likely the only one between the two major party candidates. Cox on at least two occasions called on Moore to participate at a forum at Morgan State University or Coppin State.
Moore was noncommittal.
“I’m ready for the next question,” Moore said following Cox’s attempt to goad the governor into another event.
Cox opened the debate focused on affordability issues, high electricity prices, business closures and tax increases he said are on the horizon.
Moore, speaking to voters, acknowledged the economic tribulations and blamed them on Trump.
“I do want to level with you: I do know the past year and a half has been hard,” Moore said. “I do know that while we have had many successes together as a state, that we are still fighting against Donald Trump’s illegal tariffs, still fighting against these endless foreign wars, and still fighting against these cuts to health care…. this is the agenda that Dan Cox says he supports 100%.”
Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox speaks to reporters after his debate with Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Oct. 6, 2026, at Maryland Public Television. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
But when Moore was asked if he would raise taxes to close projected multibillion-dollar structural budget gaps in coming years, the governor focused on increasing private investment in the state.
“So, you saw the governor not answer the question about will he raise taxes,” Cox said in response. “I can look in the camera, governor, and say I will not raise taxes and fees on my watch, and you have not been willing to do that.”
The animosity between the two candidates appeared 15 minutes into the one-hour debate.
At one point, Cox invoked the name of Gov. Larry Hogan, crediting the Republican leader — whom he once tried to impeach — for his budget management and criticizing Moore for projected budget gaps.
Moore fired back that Hogan “called you a Q-Anon whack job and said he’d never support you because you’re not fit to lead.”
At various points in the debate, the two accused each other of lying about the other’s records.
When Cox called on Moore to release his military records, Moore said Cox defined patriotism “by putting on a red cap” — a reference to the red Make America Great Again baseball caps worn by some Trump supporters. Then he criticized Cox for his involvement in busing protestors to the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6.
“Oh please,” Cox interrupted.
“It is not, ‘Oh please,'” Moore said. “It’s that when I had a chance to express my patriotism, I used it to protect us. When you had a chance to express your patriotism, you used it to try to destroy us.”
“That’s a lie and that is an absolute lie,” Cox said. “It’s a falsity, just like every other thing that seems to come out of this governor’s mouth.”
Both candidates were asked to explain their change in positions on data centers.
Cox was a member of the House of Delegates in 2020 when he supported tax breaks for data centers. Now Cox is calling for a statewide moratorium.
“Well, the data centers of seven years ago are not the data centers today,” Cox said adding that the today’s centers are larger, consume more energy and use up too many resources.
“I will make sure the people of Maryland are protected in their water, in their land, and in the future,” Cox said. “And I pledge that to the Maryland people.”
Gov. Wes Moore (D) speaks to reporters after his debate with Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox on Oct. 6, 2026, at Maryland Public Television. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Moore has publicly supported data centers but recently signed an executive order calling for more state scrutiny of data centers. He also said he would push to repeal tax credits for the facilities, part of what he called a “progression on data centers.” The reason for the change was twofold, he said.
“One is because I listen to the people, and … we are watching data centers that are now having a greater pull and a greater draw,” Moore said. “But what’s also happening simultaneously … we have Donald Trump, who has removed all guardrails because he has called this growth of data centers essential to beating China, and has called AI a hoax, and so it is important that we step in.”
Cox called Moore’s executive order little more than a stunt.
“Political theater, ladies and gentlemen,” Cox said. “That’s what you’re seeing here. The executive order, so-called, does not put a moratorium, even though a majority of counties have done so.”
A question to Moore on the ability to deliver big projects quickly focused on replacing the Francis Scott Key Bridge. Several large projects such as the bridge and the Purple Line remain unfinished. Moore’s promise to build the east-west Red Line in Baltimore has yet to break ground, nearly four years after he announced it. And the Key Bridge completion was pushed back from 2028 to 2030, the last year of the coming term.
Moore vowed the Key Bridge “will be opened in record time.” He said a recent decision to change contractors was “an important cost saving measure”
Cox was quick to criticize the governor’s management of the rebuild, saying a state website on the project has incomplete or inaccurate information.
“There’s demolition not finished yet, and yet your your little website says that it’s done,” Cox said. “Well, guess what? People can’t drive on a website. They need a bridge, and I’ll build it.”
Cox mocked what he called a “turtle noise permit” referring to an underwater noise monitoring effort to determine harmful effects on aquatic wildlife in the areas around the bridge project. The Republican claimed the monitoring causes too many delays in construction and that the project should continue “24/7.”
“That’s the way it needs to happen,” Cox said. “I love turtles too, but I love Dundalk more.”
Both candidates at times avoided inconvenient questions from the panel.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Cox sidestepped a question about protections for LGBTQ students in schools. He called the issue “nuanced” and turned his answer to economic issues.
“But at the end of the day, I want everybody to understand: Every person in Maryland has to open their electric bill. That’s what this governor is hurting you with,” Cox said, reeling off a list of what he said are possible looming tax increases. “This is hurting every community.”
Cox was asked if he regretted working with lawyers who attempted to overturn the 2020 election, organizing buses to the Jan. 6 rally that turned violent at the U.S. Capitol, and calling Vice President Mike Pence a traitor on social media.
Cox said he regretted the social media post but called the question “political TMZ” and said it was not what voters wanted to hear.
“I think we need to focus on the issues of the people of Maryland,” Cox said. “And I absolutely have always had the people of Maryland in my heart and mind.”
The governor had similar moments, avoiding questions about whether he had regrets about embellishing his military record, claiming a Bronze Star that he did not receive until years later.
And when asked about serving the full four-year term, Moore, often talked about as a 2028 presidential hopeful, would only say, “I’m committed to the people of Maryland.”
“I just want to be clear, Dan Cox seems to be more concerned about my future than the future of the people of Maryland,” he said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘Election Day gimmick’? As NC lawmakers eye gas tax cut, Stein questions timing
description: State lawmakers return to Raleigh Wednesday for a special session to address high gas and diesel prices. It’s unusual for legislators to summon themselves back to Raleigh so close to an upcoming election. So it was surprising to many when House Speaker Destin Hall and Senate Leader Phil Berger announced the session on social media […]
text:
While the cost of regular unleaded has dipped slightly in October, North Carolina motorists are still struggling with the high price of fuel. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) State lawmakers return to Raleigh Wednesday for a special session to address high gas and diesel prices.
It’s unusual for legislators to summon themselves back to Raleigh so close to an upcoming election. So it was surprising to many when House Speaker Destin Hall and Senate Leader Phil Berger announced the session on social media Saturday. They offered few specifics, only calling for “real relief” for families.
Gov. Josh Stein said Tuesday that, while he’s pleased there is an acknowledgement by Republicans that North Carolina families are struggling, the timing is suspect.
“Clearly, their poll numbers are really bad because they’re coming back right before the election to take this action to help themselves,” Stein said. “It’s as if they’re taking this emergency action to deal with what must be a polling emergency.”
Gov. Josh Stein discussed the gas tax at a Oct. 6 press conference on affordable housing. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Stein said there’s no doubt that the war against Iran has led to a dramatic uptick in the price of gas and diesel since February. But, he added, perhaps lawmakers should be open to addressing other pocketbook concerns.
“I’ve asked them to join me in dealing with affordability — add a Working Families Tax Cut and add a child tax credit. They did not include those things [in the budget],” said Stein. “Instead, they continue to have tax giveaways to big corporations, to shareholders, many of whom don’t even live in North Carolina.”
Several states have suspended gas taxes in recent weeks ahead of the midterms.
“What I hope is that this isn’t just an Election Day gimmick,” said Stein.
The governor’s comments came at a celebration of new affordable housing in downtown Raleigh.
Last week, Stein directed the North Carolina Department of Revenue to allow highway use of red-dyed diesel fuel penalty-free through the end of the year. Farmers have stores of non-taxed dyed diesel on hand for off-road use. The governor’s office said allowing on-road use during this year’s harvest will save the state’s agricultural producers money.
By lowering costs for farmers, Stein is hopeful that it lowers the pressure on grocery costs for everyone.
With election pressure mounting, states move to suspend fuel taxes

Whatever the legislature approves this week, Stein said there must be balance. He said the state cannot allow its roadways and infrastructure to crumble.
“It’s critical that whatever the legislature does, they not only provide relief to people at the pump, but that they protect the Department of Transportation’s highway work, because we’ve got to repair our roads,” said Stein. “We have to build new roads. We are a growing state.”
As for whether Stein would sign a bill to suspend North Carolina’s gas tax that’s currently 41 cents per gallon, the governor wasn’t tipping his hand on Tuesday.
“We’ll have to see how they’ve drafted it,” he said.

title: New Mexico AG challenges federal commission’s review of proposed Project Jupiter gas pipeline
description: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez is pushing back against the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s review of a proposed gas pipeline intended to power the Project Jupiter data center, calling it “inadequate.” Texas-based Energy Transfer early this year asked federal regulatory officials to approve construction of a gas pipeline, known as the “Gr[...]
text:
A map of the proposed pipeline Energy Transfer submitted in its early 2026 application to the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. (Photo courtesy of FERC)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez is pushing back against the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s review of a proposed gas pipeline intended to power the Project Jupiter data center, calling it “inadequate.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Texas-based Energy Transfer early this year asked federal regulatory officials to approve construction of a gas pipeline, known as the “Green Chile Project,” to serve the Oracle and OpenAI Project Jupiter data center under construction in Doña Ana County.
In a Monday filing with the commission, Torrez argued that federal regulatory officials have not adequately assessed the proposed pipeline’s environmental impact because their assessment did not include the environmental impacts of Project Jupiter itself. Source NM previously reported that the data center’s power system could emit more greenhouse gases annually than New Mexico’s largest cities combined.
“The commission is asking us essentially to consider the fuel line from a car’s gas tank to its engine wholly separate from the rest of the vehicle and to completely ignore the emissions coming out of the tailpipe,” Torrez wrote. “Project Jupiter in its current form cannot function without the pipeline, and this pipeline has no reason to exist other than to provide fuel for Project Jupiter.” 
Torrez also wrote that regulatory officials aren’t meeting their responsibilities as described in the National Environmental Policy Act, which says that officials can only conduct an environmental assessment of a proposal like this — rather than a more exhaustive environmental impact statement — if the proposal does not have “a reasonably foreseeable significant effect” on the environment.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Plans for the pipeline initially described it as a $60 million project that would carry gas from El Paso to Project Jupiter. It fits into Energy Transfer’s broader Desert Southwest Pipeline Expansion Project, though, which aims to build a data center-serving pipeline that stretches from Texas to Phoenix.
The plan has hit several roadblocks in the months since then. New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands Stephanie Garcia Richard, who is running as the Democratic nominee to be lieutenant governor, twice rejected Energy Transfer’s requests to build a portion of the pipeline on state trust land. In August, Energy Transfer’s federal regulatory filings showed that company officials expected the pipeline to be delayed to 2027.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Hospital worker fired for Facebook video that revealed patient information
description: An Iowa hospital worker who posted a Facebook video showing off her Harry Potter-themed office was fired after it was discovered the photo revealed protected patient information. State records indicate Alicia Keffer worked for the Lucas County Health Center as a full-time clinic referral clerk from March 2025 until her firing in August 2026. As […]
text:
An Iowa hospital worker was granted unemployment benefits after she was fired for posting a social media video showing off her Harry Potter-themed office that also inadvertently revealed protected patient information.An Iowa hospital worker who posted a Facebook video showing off her Harry Potter-themed office was fired after it was discovered the photo revealed protected patient information.
State records indicate Alicia Keffer worked for the Lucas County Health Center as a full-time clinic referral clerk from March 2025 until her firing in August 2026.
As a referral clerk, Keffer was responsible for processing and scheduling patient referrals. According to the findings of the administrative law judge who presided over Keffer’s recent hearing on unemployment benefits, Keffer decorated her office with Harry Potter collectibles and memorabilia in July 2026.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On July 30, 2026, she allegedly recorded a short video of her decorated office space, and then posted the video to a local bakery’s Facebook page, intending only to show off her Harry Potter merchandise. Unbeknownst to Keffer, her computer screen was visible in the video and displayed protected health information for “several patients,” the judge found.
The same day the video was posted, another hospital employee saw the video on the bakery’s Facebook page and alerted their superiors. The hospital allegedly contacted Keffer and the bakery and both agreed to take down the video.
On Aug. 7, 2026, the hospital fired Keffer for violating its privacy policies. Prior to her dismissal, she had never received any warnings or discipline for her conduct in the workplace.
Administrative Law Judge Patrick Thomas recently ruled Keffer was entitled to unemployment benefits, noting that in order for her to be disqualified based on carelessness, there must be wrongful intent.
While Keffer’s conduct violated the hospital’s policy, Thomas ruled, the “weight of the evidence indicates that (her) decision to post the video was an isolated instance of poor judgement, arising from inadvertence and ordinary negligence.”
As the disclosure of protected information was the result of a mistake, and Keffer had never previously been disciplined for similar conduct, the hospital had not met its burden of proving disqualifying, job-related misconduct, Thomas ruled.
Other Iowa healthcare professionals recently fired or sanctioned for alleged patient-privacy violations include:
— Kimberly Hettinger, a registered nurse who has practiced in Manchester and been an Iowa-licensed nurse since August 1987. The Iowa Board of Nursing recently charged Hettinger with violating the confidentiality or privacy rights of a patient or client. The board alleges that at some undisclosed time in the past, Hettinger “accessed family member medical records outside the scope of her employment duties.” The board has not disclosed where Hettinger worked at the time.
In a recent settlement agreement with the board, Hettinger agreed to accept a warning and complete 30 hours of educational training on patient confidentiality.
— Kelcey Bohlke, who worked as a full-time registered nurse for Family Health Care of Siouxland from July 2024 until her firing in July 2026. According to the findings of the judge who presided over her recent hearing for unemployment benefits, Bohlke received a message from her daughter’s new school on July 7, 2026, informing her the school needed her daughter’s immunization records to complete her enrollment. Bohlke then pulled up her daughter’s medical records on the computer and printed a copy, prompting a colleague to remind her she should have obtained prior approval to access patient files.
Bohlke was unable to locate her supervisor to report the incident but acknowledged her actions later that day when asked about the situation. She was fired and later was awarded unemployment benefits by Administrative Law Judge Patrick Thomas, who characterized her actions as a momentary lapse of judgment rather than a willful or wanton disregard of the employer’s interests.
— Amber Peterson, who worked as a dental assistant and surgical technician for Mississippi Valley Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery from August 1999 until June 2026 when she resigned. According to the findings of the judge who presided over her recent hearing for unemployment benefits, Peterson was questioned by her superiors on June 2, 2026, about using her phone to take a photo of a patient’s X-rays. She allegedly admitted doing so, stating the patient was her boyfriend and she had sent him the photo via text message.
The clinic proposed a three-day suspension and additional training on patient-privacy provisions of the federal Health Information Portability and Accountability Act, but Peterson opted to resign, according to state records. She was then denied unemployment benefits, with Administrative Law Judge Stephanie Adkisson ruling her resignation was “not based on good cause but rather was because she was upset after being notified she was being disciplined for violating patient privacy.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Keffer, Peterson and Hettinger for comment. Bohlke declined to comment on her case.

title: Trump sixth U.S. president to be named an admiral in Nebraska’s ‘Great Navy’
description: GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — President Donald Trump is the sixth U.S. president to be named an admiral for the largely honorific Great Navy of the State of Nebraska. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen bestowed the largely honorific title Monday during a midterms rally headlining Trump. It’s not unusual for governors to bestow the honor on friends or […]
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen announces he has inducted President Donald Trump as the newest "admiral" of the largely honorific Nebraska Navy  in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds for a midterms rally featuring the president. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — President Donald Trump is the sixth U.S. president to be named an admiral for the largely honorific Great Navy of the State of Nebraska.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen bestowed the largely honorific title Monday during a midterms rally headlining Trump. It’s not unusual for governors to bestow the honor on friends or celebrities and dignitaries who visit Nebraska.
After a more than 20-minute speech Monday, Pillen laughed and asked the crowd to “let me have one little fun thing here yet this afternoon before, I hope, I haven’t indulged too long.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and President Donald Trump lead a “USA” chant during a midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, that Trump headlined on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The governor remarked that, as Nebraska’s chief executive officer, he’s also the commander of Nebraska’s Air and Army National Guard. But, tongue-in-cheek since the 1930s, the governor also oversees a “Great Navy.”
“Triple land-locked state — our navy — and oh, by the way, home of the largest, most sustainable underground aquifer in the Western Hemisphere,” Pillen said.
The honor began in 1930 when then-Gov. Charles W. Bryan went on vacation and his lieutenant governor, T. W. Metcalfe, wanted a way to honor his friends, according to the Nebraska State Historical Society. So the acting governor created the Great Navy and named the first admirals.
Trump is at least the sixth U.S. president to be named an admiral and the first since President George W. Bush (2001-09), who was recognized for his service following the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, according to the Nebraska Admirals Association.
The other honored presidential admirals: Ronald Reagan (1981-1989), Gerald Ford (1974-77), Harry S. Truman (1945-53) and Franklin D. Roosevelt (1933-45).
Trump asks Nebraska to ‘pretend’ he’s on the midterm ballot

Other famous admirals listed by the association:

Gene Autry, the “Singing Cowboy.”
Comedian and radio/TV star Jack Benny.
Comedian Johnny Carson.
Talk show host Dick Cavett.
Actor Bing Crosby.
Actress Sandy Dennis.
Screenwriter and director Costa Dillon.
Queen Elizabeth II, who served from 1952 until she died in 2022.
Basketball player Julius Erving.
Astronaut and former U.S. Sen. John Glenn, who represented Ohio.
Former Secretary of Defense and former Sen. Chuck Hagel, who represented Nebraska.
Mountaineer Sir Edmund Hillary, the first person to summit Mount Everest.
Comedian and actor Bob Hope.
Animator and filmmaker Chuck Jones.
Civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr.
Advice columnist Ann Landers.
Gen. Douglas MacArthur, a U.S. military leader during World War II and the Korean War.
Comedian and actor Bill Murray.
Former U.S. Sen. and former Nebraska Gov. Ben Nelson.
Golfer Jack Nicklaus.
Husker legend Tom Osborne.
Golfer Arnold Palmer, nicknamed “The King.”
Olympian Mark Spitz, a nine-time gold medalist in swimming.

The honor is among Nebraska’s highest civic honors as a largely honorary designation. The award carries no military rank, duties, pay or other special privileges.
Pillen’s office also allows a process to request admiralships. At least the nominator or nominee must be a Nebraska resident. No self-nominations are accepted. The governor has “full discretion” for any requests.
An admiralship appointment reads as follows —
“Know Ye, that reposing special trust and confidence in the patriotism valor, fidelity and abilities of _________ and knowing him to be a good fellow and a loyal friend and counselor I have nominated and do appoint him an Admiral in the Great Navy of the State of Nebraska. He is therefore called to diligently discharge the duties of Admiral by doing and performing all manner of things thereto belonging. And I do strictly charge and require all officers, seamen, tadpoles and goldfish under his command to be obedient to his orders as Admiral — and he is to observe and follow, from time to time, such directions as he shall receive, according to the rules and discipline of the Great Navy of the State of Nebraska. This commission to continue in force during the period of his good behavior, and the pleasure of the Chief Admiral of the Great Navy of the State of Nebraska. Given under my hand in the City of Lincoln, State of Nebraska, this _________ day of _________ in the year of our Lord.”

text:
President Donald Trump dances after headlining a midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)GRAND ISLAND, Neb. — Thousands of Nebraskans flocked to Grand Island to see a presidential rally in the city for the first time in 20 years.
Plenty more Americans tuned in virtually, and an “unwelcoming committee” protested just about half a mile away. President Donald Trump’s visit — a string of midterm visits to help shore up Republican support — marks the first time a president visited Grand Island since 2006. 
In those midterms, President George W. Bush rallied support for Nebraska candidates and others. Voters in Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District, which includes Grand Island, also first elected U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith of Gering in 2006 after his eight years in the state Legislature.

Smith is now asking for an 11th term against the Democratic Party’s Becky Stille of South Sioux City, Legal Marijuana NOW Party’s David Else of Overton, Working People Party’s Macey Budke of North Platte and registered nonpartisan Mark Cohen of Lemoyne.
Also in 2006, then-U.S. Sen. Ben Nelson, a former governor, became the last Democrat to win Nebraska statewide. Nelson handily beat Pete Ricketts, 64%-36%, yet Ricketts would go on to safely win Nebraska’s governorship in 2014 and 2018. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen appointed Ricketts to the U.S. Senate in 2023, and he won a two-year term in 2024.
Ricketts and Pillen face closer-than-expected reelection bids this year. Trump disparaged their leading opponents, registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn and former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz, respectively. Osborn told KETV Newswatch 7 that the visit “speaks volumes” if Ricketts needs backup, while Walz similarly told the station the rally shows Pillen is “really nervous.”
Osborn defied expectations in 2024 and gave U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer a close race in her reelection bid. Also on the 2026 Senate ballot are Legal Marijuana NOW’s Mike Marvin (who dropped out), Working People’s Robin Richards and the America First Party’s Chuck Conboy.
Walz is the most well-funded Democrat seeking the governorship since 1990, when Nelson unseated Republican Gov. Kay Orr. Also running for governor in 2026 are Legal Marijuana Now’s Rick Beard and America First’s Brett Lindstrom, a former state senator. However, Pillen maintains a nearly 9:1 lead in cash on hand — $7.5 million as of Sept. 29 to Walz’s $860,000. Neither Beard nor Lindstrom has reported raising or spending more than $5,000 in total.
Trump also appeared on stage Monday with U.S. Rep. Mike Flood, who faces Democrat Chris Backemeyer and Libertarian Nik Sandman, both of Lincoln, and Attorney General Mike Hilgers, who faces Democrat Jocelyn Brasher of Omaha.
A Grand Island-area state lawmaker told the Nebraska Examiner that Monday’s event helps drum up voters as much as it “restores” and “recharges” Trump’s strength. Pillen also named Trump as the newest admiral in the honorary  “Great Navy of the State of Nebraska.”

title: New Mexico solar grants reduce energy costs for public buildings in rural areas, state officials say
description: Solar projects at public buildings funded by the Local Solar Access Fund generated a 53% reduction in energy costs on average for predominately rural communities in the state since the program began accepting applications in January, New Mexico Finance Authority program chief John Brooks told lawmakers on Tuesday. Brooks spoke at a meeting of the interim Fin[...]
text:
Rural areas reduced energy costs due to state solar energy project grants, state officials told lawmakers in the interim New Mexico Finance Authority Oversight Committee on Oct. 6, 2026. A lion’s share of grants went to rural areas, far exceeding the legal requirement, officials added. (Photo by Anna Padilla/Source NM)Rural governments in New Mexico are reducing energy costs due to a state grant to build community solar projects, state officials told lawmakers on Tuesday. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Solar projects at public buildings funded by the Local Solar Access Fund generated a 53% reduction in energy costs on average for predominately rural communities in the state since the program began accepting applications in January, New Mexico Finance Authority program chief John Brooks told lawmakers. Brooks spoke at a meeting of the interim Finance Authority Oversight Committee in Santa Teresa.
The Local Solar Access Fund sets aside $20 million for grants meant for solar energy and battery storage projects in rural and underserved communities. Counties, municipalities, school districts and tribal governments are eligible to apply for the grant, Brooks said. 
The goal of the fund is to reduce the burden of energy costs in low-income communities; support the local renewable energy workforce in New Mexico; and enhance community resilience during environmental emergencies, according to Brooks’ presentation to the committee. 
The law requires 60% of the total funding to go to rural communities. Of the current 34 approved grants, Brooks noted, 31 serve rural areas across New Mexico.
Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) was a sponsor of the 2025 legislative bill that created the fund. She called the results so far “heartwarming” and that it lives up to the original concept of the bill.
“We didn’t envision the funds going to big land developers or private equity firms,” Caballero said. The purpose was to allow rural and low-income communities to “enter into the renewable energy world in a manner that would not cost them outrageous amounts.” 
The money pays for both project and technical assistance grants. Project grants, up to a maximum of $1 million, help applicants plan, construct and install solar energy systems. In September, 21 project grants — totaling $18 million — were awarded after meeting all eligibility criteria and undergoing New Mexico Finance Authority staff review, Brooks said. An estimated 91% of the allocated project grant funds went to rural communities.
Technical grants, up to a maximum of $50,000, help applicants with professional grant writing services for future federal or Local Solar Access Fund project grant applications. In June, 13 technical assistance grants were awarded, totaling $650,000. Of that total, 92% went to rural community applicants, Brooks said. 
Roybal Caballero underscored that the grants also help dispel fear or misunderstandings about renewable energy in New Mexico. Whatever socioeconomic background a New Mexican comes from, Roybal Caballero said, “we want those residents to understand that renewable energy is accessible to them and it’s affordable.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Gov. Healey steps in again as Brigham nurses near an indefinite strike
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: Nurses authorized an indefinite strike last week, and the Massachusetts Nurses Association said it submitted the required 10-day notice for an "unfair labor practice" strike to Mass General Brigham.
text:
Gov. Maura Healey on Monday urged one of the state’s biggest health care employers to “reopen negotiations now” with nurses ahead of an anticipated strike set to begin October 14 at Mass General Brigham.
“Yes. I’ve been clear with both parties. Get back to the table. MGB needs to open discussions, open negotiations, and get back to the table,” Healey told reporters in Everett when asked if she’s involved in any talks. “Our health care workers need to be treated fairly.”
Nearly 4,000 Brigham and Women’s Hospital nurses plan to start the strike unless they reach a contract deal with Mass General Brigham leadership. They want cost of living increases, affordable health insurance, limits on the use of temporary travel nurses and protections around patient care. MGB says nurses receive annual raises and that the system proposed a new increase for nurses at the top step of their wage scale. 
“I don’t want to see people out on strike,” Healey continued. “MGB needs to reopen negotiations now.”
Nurses authorized an indefinite strike last week, and the Massachusetts Nurses Association said it submitted the required 10-day notice for an “unfair labor practice” strike to MGB. 
A five-day work stoppage in July did not break the contract negotiation stalemate. Healey at the time met privately with MGB and MNA leaders in an unsuccessful attempt to prevent nurses from walking off the job.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Corrections head says settlement likely in suit over sending people on probation to ICE
description: New Mexico Corrections Department Secretary Alisha Tafoya Lucero said Tuesday that her department is moving toward settling a lawsuit over state officers’ practice of referring people on probation to federal immigration agents for arrest and deportation.
text:
New Mexico Corrections Department Secretary Alisha Tafoya Lucero told lawmakers Oct. 6, 2026, that the department is working toward a settlement in a lawsuit alleging probation officers referred New Mexico residents to ICE for deportation. (Courtesy U.S Department of Homeland Security)New Mexico Corrections Department Secretary Alisha Tafoya Lucero said Tuesday that her department is moving toward settling a lawsuit over state officers’ practice of referring people on probation to federal immigration agents for arrest and deportation. 
Movement toward a settlement  – with terms that were not immediately clear – with the New Mexico State Ethics Commission marks the potential end of an unusual legal battle waged in state and federal court for more than a year involving a state agency using taxpayer funds to avoid complying with a law the Legislature passed in 2025. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Nondisclosure of Sensitive Personal Information Act prohibits state employees from disclosing New Mexico residents’ personal information – including immigration status – to federal agencies, except in limited circumstances. 
The State Ethics Commission last September sued Tafoya Lucero, saying the agency had repeatedly violated the privacy law, which went into effect in July 2025. 
The lawsuit said New Mexico probation officers lured at least three people with probation appointments to state offices, where U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were waiting to arrest them.
Subsequently released materials, including emails and other correspondence that Source NM reviewed, showed that the probation department referred at least 20 additional people on probation to ICE between October 2024 and May 2026, and regularly tipped off ICE agents when a probationer was scheduled for a probation appointment. At least five of those referrals came after the state privacy law went into effect. 
The Corrections Department, which hired an outside lawyer for this lawsuit, has previously argued that federal law trumps the state privacy act and that the case is more appropriate for federal court than state court.
Tafoya Lucero appeared before the interim legislative Courts and Criminal Justice Committee on Tuesday. She said the concerns her department’s lawyers initially had about the state privacy law were “remedied,” and the department is now “definitely working to come to settlement.” 
The secretary did not weigh in on the specific allegations in the lawsuit regarding probation officers she oversees, though she said all staff are now trained on how to comply with the law. She also defended the Corrections Department’s choice to fight back against the law in court as a result of confusion over how to implement it. 
New emails allege New Mexico probation officer ICE referrals more widespread than previously known

“We were never in disagreement with what the policy of the law was,” she said. “It was just a matter of, we needed clarification to make sure that how we implemented it was accurate.” 
Sen. Antoinette Sedillo Lopez (D-Albuquerque), who sponsored the 2025 privacy law, told Tafoya Lucero she found it “shocking” that the Corrections Department did not immediately comply with the law. 
“I’m glad you’re going to settle it,” Sedillo Lopez said. “I lament the thousands and thousands of dollars that have been wasted in fighting this.”
Tafoya Lucero did not specify what the terms might be of a settlement, or how soon it might arrive. The State Ethics Commission’s lawsuit seeks court orders requiring the Corrections Department to implement department-wide training regarding the law, as well as technological changes to prevent probation officers from being able to access a database to learn a probationer’s citizenship status.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia Republicans urge Spanberger to call special session for fuel-tax holiday
description: Virginia Republican leaders on Tuesday called for Gov. Abigail Spanberger to summon lawmakers to Richmond and suspend the state’s gasoline and diesel taxes for 90 days, arguing that the temporary break would help families, farmers and trucking companies cope with high fuel prices.  Diesel prices have climbed sharply amid disruptions to global fuel supplies f[...]
text:
Republican lawmakers are urging Gov. Abigail Spanberger to call a special session to suspend Virginia’s gasoline and diesel taxes for 90 days to ease fuel costs for families and businesses. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)Virginia Republican leaders on Tuesday called for Gov. Abigail Spanberger to summon lawmakers to Richmond and suspend the state’s gasoline and diesel taxes for 90 days, arguing that the temporary break would help families, farmers and trucking companies cope with high fuel prices. 
Diesel prices have climbed sharply amid disruptions to global fuel supplies from the war with Iran and other pressures on the international market. 
Gathered at Owens Market Deli and Truck Plaza in Bedford County, Republicans said stronger-than-expected state revenues could replace the money normally collected from the taxes to give residents relief. They want lawmakers to act before the General Assembly returns for its 2027 session in January. 
“Basically, this should be a bipartisan issue,” said House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, R-Scott. “This is about giving our voters, our constituents, Virginians, a temporary pause in the gas tax, so that life becomes more affordable.”
A Spanberger spokesman said the governor is considering options to provide relief while blaming the increase in fuel prices on President Donald Trump’s war with Iran. 
He said Spanberger is also “assessing all available options to address the extra costs” while “working to create long-term solutions to make the commonwealth more affordable so families can keep more of what they earn.”
Virginia currently taxes gasoline at 32.6 cents per gallon and diesel at 33.6 cents. If the entire cut reached consumers, someone buying 15 gallons of gasoline would save $4.89.
Del. Scott Wyatt, R-Mechanicsville, estimated a 90-day suspension would cost the state about $410 million. He said revenue collections running ahead of projections would give the state room to absorb the loss. 
Del. Wendell Walker, R-Lynchburg, said lawmakers could replace the transportation money when they return to Richmond next year. Fuel taxes help pay for road construction and maintenance, so replacing that revenue would be a central part of any legislation.
For Christian Snead, who owns a Bedford County trucking company with 28 vehicles, the immediate concern is what happens every time one of them needs fuel. 
“Fuel is a necessity for us, it’s an operating expense, not something we can live without,” Snead said at the event.
Diesel was posted at $5.99 a gallon at the truck plaza Tuesday. Removing Virginia’s excise tax would reduce that to about $5.65 if the entire savings were passed along to customers. 
Snead said higher fuel costs eat into his company’s margins and eventually show up in the prices customers pay for goods moved by truck. 
“Let’s give businesses the ability to recover,” he said. 
U.S. Rep. John McGuire, R-Goochland, also took a prominent role in Tuesday’s event, defending Trump’s energy policies four weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. 
Asked whether Trump should pursue an end to the war with Iran to help bring down fuel prices, McGuire argued that keeping more American refineries would have left the country less vulnerable to disruptions overseas. 
“Obviously, we all want to find a solution the right way. But in the meantime, let’s give Virginia some relief at the pumps,” he said. 
Kilgore added Virginia lawmakers should focus on what they can do at the state level. “We can’t control what’s going on in Washington or what’s going on in Iran,” he said. 
Tuesday’s event came a day after Trump signed an executive order temporarily allowing broader highway use of red-dyed diesel, which usually is reserved for off-road uses such as agricultural equipment. 
Trump’s order directs federal officials to determine whether applicable federal excise tax payments can be deferred through Dec. 31 without interest or penalties. It also directs officials to explore ways, including legislation, to forgive those deferred taxes. Deferring a tax does not by itself eliminate the obligation to pay it. 
Part of Bedford County falls within the 5th Congressional District, where former U.S. Rep. Tom Perriello, the Democratic nominee, is trying to unseat McGuire. Republicans have held the seat since Perriello lost reelection in 2010, although its boundaries have changed since. 
A Washington Post-Schar School poll released last week found McGuire leading Perriello 51% to 45% among likely voters in a district that Trump carried by 12 points in 2024. 
McGuire used the appearance to criticize Perriello’s past support of cap-and-trade legislation and Spanberger’s climate policies, arguing that Democratic energy legislation has contributed to higher costs at the pump.
Perriello has also put affordability at the center of his campaign. He told The Mercury last week that ending the Iran war would be among his priorities if elected to Congress. 
Republicans have tried the gas-tax approach before. 
They proposed a similar 90-day holiday in March as fuel prices climbed. Spanberger responded at the time by blaming Trump’s decision to launch the war with Iran, saying Virginians were “feeling the brunt of the president’s actions at the pump and grocery store.” 
Republicans returned Tuesday to Spanberger’s own emphasis on affordability, arguing that suspending the gas tax would give consumers some immediate relief. 
Kilgore said the differences in fuel taxes among neighboring states are particularly noticeable in Southwest Virginia, where drivers can easily cross state lines to refill their tanks. 
Other states are considering or have already taken similar steps. Georgia suspended its motor fuel excise taxes from Sept. 29 through Oct. 29. Lawmakers in North Carolina plan to return for a special session Wednesday to consider fuel-tax relief.
