name: National
title: New York governor declares measles emergency
description: NEW YORK — Facing a surge of measles cases in New York state’s rural counties, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul issued an executive order on Monday allowing paramedics, pharmacists, midwives and other non-physicians to administer vaccines. Hochul’s decision to declare a “state disaster emergency” comes amid the nation’s worst measles outbreak in more than 30 yea[...]
text:
A worker applies an adhesive bandage to a child at a vaccination clinic in Minneapolis’ Corcoran Park in August 2023. Minnesota and other Democratic-led states have sued the federal government over relaxed childhood vaccination standards, and New York has declared a state of emergency as measles cases surge in neighboring Pennsylvania (Photo courtesy of the City of Minneapolis)NEW YORK — Facing a surge of measles cases in New York state’s rural counties, Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul issued an executive order on Monday allowing paramedics, pharmacists, midwives and other non-physicians to administer vaccines.
Hochul’s decision to declare a “state disaster emergency” comes amid the nation’s worst measles outbreak in more than 30 years and an eruption in neighboring Pennsylvania that is the largest that any single state has experienced since the early 1990s.
As of Oct. 3, New York had reported 108 total cases, its highest number since 2019. Pennsylvania has recorded more than 1,000 cases this year, and state officials there have attributed five deaths to the disease (so far the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has only confirmed two of them.) There have been no deaths in New York.
As of October 1, the CDC had recorded more than 3,887 confirmed cases this year in the United States.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test,” Hochul said in a news  release.
Also on Monday, New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, announced that the state would join 15 other Democratic-led states in suing the Trump administration over its decision to scale back the childhood vaccination schedule. Joining in the lawsuit are the state attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin, and the governor of Pennsylvania.
Measles is a respiratory virus that leads to symptoms of fever and rash, and can cause serious health complications, such as pneumonia and even death. It’s highly contagious and can be contracted through exposure to contaminated air or surfaces. It is entirely preventable, however, with the two-dose MMR, or measles, mumps, and rubella, vaccine.
Children under a year old, who are typically too young to receive the first dose of the vaccine, are highly susceptible.
Through a robust vaccination campaign, measles was declared to be effectively eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, according to the CDC. But during the COVID-19 pandemic, anti-vaccination sentiment began to rise, and measles cases have surged over the past  two years.
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is an outspoken vaccine skeptic and has opposed vaccine mandates. Under Kennedy, the agency has called into question the safety and efficacy of vaccines and  recommended fewer vaccines for children. The move has prompted most states to unlink their vaccine guidance from federal recommendations and form their own health alliances and standards.
Combined with efforts by Republican-leaning states to weaken vaccine mandates, the federal shift has contributed to a decline in the vaccination rate among kindergarteners and a resulting increase in measles cases.
According to health policy research group KFF, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccination for the 2025-2026 school year, compared with 95% in the 2019-2020 school year. During the last school year, 39 states had MMR vaccination rates below 95% — the minimum considered necessary to prevent community spread, according to KFF.
Katrine Wallace, an epidemiologist at the School of Public Health at the University of Illinois Chicago praised governors for taking action to stop the spread of measles. But Wallace said it’s critical that the federal government encourage people to get vaccinated to slow the spread of the disease.
“There really isn’t a national promotion of ‘Hey, we’re having an outbreak right now. Please vaccinate your kids. The MMR is safe and effective, and it prevents measles.’ That’s not being pumped out on social media. That’s not being put on TV,” Wallace said. “So this administration is not promoting the best tool that we have to prevent severe disease from viruses.”
Nationally, the CDC reports that 352 people have been hospitalized this year due to measles. Of the 3,887 confirmed cases, 61% are people younger than 19 and 95% were not vaccinated or had an unknown vaccine status.
According to CDC data, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, Wisconsin, Texas, and Virginia are experiencing the highest number of cases.
The rise in cases under Kennedy’s leadership has prompted Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro to call for the secretary’s ouster.
“He’s making it harder for governors to be able to keep people safe in our communities. I’m actually shocked that the president is letting him get away with this,” Shapiro said in a recent NBC News interview. “I don’t know why he’s still allowing him to even serve in the role”.

title: Tina Peters met with Trump to discuss election plans, former Trump administration attorney says
description: A former U.S. Department of Justice attorney said Monday that former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters met with President Donald Trump at the White House to discuss “election integrity” and plans for upcoming elections.  Ed Martin, who left his position with the Justice Department to take on legal work related to upcoming elections, told Real […]
text:
Then-Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters attends the Western Conservative Summit in Aurora on June 4, 2022. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)A former U.S. Department of Justice attorney said Monday that former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters met with President Donald Trump at the White House to discuss “election integrity” and plans for upcoming elections. 
Ed Martin, who left his position with the Justice Department to take on legal work related to upcoming elections, told Real America’s Voice that Peters, a Republican who was convicted of multiple felonies for her role in a security breach of her office’s election equipment, met with Trump to talk about federal involvement in the November midterm elections.
“It is a local election … there is local control. However, the laws that govern the system, like safety and national security, are federal laws,” Martin said. “And so, when Tina Peters, you know, famous Colorado clerk, was in the Oval Office today just two hours ago talking about this question, the president’s taking it seriously.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The nature of the plans Peters and Trump discussed are unclear.
The White House does “not comment on private meetings that may or may not have happened,” spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement. Adrienne Mazzone, publicist for Peters’ attorney Peter Ticktin, said Ticktin cannot discuss or confirm matters that fall under attorney-client privilege. An unnamed source confirmed to ABC News that Peters and Trump met Monday.
Martin said if Congress does not pass the SAVE America Act, which would implement a nationwide requirement that voters show documents proving their citizenship, “the president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said that foreign adversaries have access to voting machines in the U.S., but his department provided no additional details to PolitiFact to clarify what Mullin meant by that. He said adversaries “can change voter registration and your vote,” but voter registration does not involve voting machines, and there’s no proof that foreign actors have tried to manipulate voting machine security controls, an election technology expert told PolitiFact.
The department said it has $1 billion in taxpayer dollars prepared to protect elections, with specific requirements for any government entity to receive grant funding. More recently, department officials said it does not plan to send Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to patrol polling places, but voter advocates remain skeptical of that claim, The Associated Press reported.
While courts have blocked many of his efforts, Trump has taken action to target mail ballots, including an executive order that would have implemented requirements for states to notify the Postal Service if they intend to allow ballots to be sent through the mail.
Trump has repeatedly claimed that mail-in voting is susceptible to widespread fraud. There is no evidence for that, and fraud with mail-in ballots is extremely rare. Colorado’s post-election audits regularly confirm that ballots are counted accurately. Trump voted by mail in Florida’s GOP primary this year and in recent days encouraged supporters to vote any way they can, including by mail.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis cut Peters’ prison sentence earlier this year, and the Colorado Department of Corrections released her in June.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: What did people who went to Trump’s Nebraska rally have to say?
description: While the perception of Republicans seems gloomy ahead of the midterms, thousands came to see and support President Donald Trump at his rally.
text:
Thousands of Nebraskans gather in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds for a midterms rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)GRAND ISLAND — While the national perception of Republicans seems gloomy ahead of the midterms, thousands in Grand Island came to see and support President Donald Trump at his rally in the ruddy red state. 
As expected, the people waiting in line and attending the rally were strong Trump supporters. Some were traveling from other states for the Cornhusker State visit, as the president is in a midterm campaign blitz. Nebraska has a few races that are viewed as competitive, including the Senate and 2nd Congressional District races. 
Doris, who didn’t want to give her last name, said she traveled from Omaha to the Trump rally because she loves America and wants to keep it free. 
“Freedom in America is very important to me, and Trump is all about America,”  Doris told the Examiner. “It’s so invigorating to be with these same kind of people that have the same beliefs … and trust in Trump.”
Chea Polonia, an Omaha resident, said she helped make calls to elect Trump in 2016 because she didn’t want to vote for former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. A former Democrat, she said she voted for Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Chea Polonia of Omaha at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, before a midterms campaign rally featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“It wasn’t about him, and then the day of the (2016) election, I was there, and he won, and we didn’t think he’d win,” Polonia said. “Everybody hated him — the media, the people — and it was so — honest, it was so spiritual, it changed my life.”
Polonia wore a hat referring to Trump as “bullet proof” and  a necklace with Trump’s signature line, “Make America Great Again.” On her hip, as well as hanging off her neck, were keychains she created resembling the president, which she calls “Pocket POTUS.”
The audience was very friendly to Trump and the other Republican elected officials on stage. Nebraska 3rd Congressional District Rep. Adrian Smith led a “Go Big Red” chant. Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen got loud applause when he said, “Boys are boys and girls are girls … over my dead body that any boys are going to play sports against my granddaughter in Nebraska.” 
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ walk-on song was “Thunderstruck” by AC/DC, and he started his speech by saying, “D.C. Democrats have lost their minds.” 
Trump said the audience at Pinnacle Bank Expo Center was part of the “greatest political movement in the history” of the U.S.
The crowd chanted “four more years” during the rally.
Outside the venue, there was Trump merchandise ranging from hats, figures, stuffed animals and jackets. Vendors would walk up and down the line with carts filled with hats, yelling that if people didn’t buy a hat, they could be mistaken for a Democrat. 
Susie Wilkinson, a Kearney resident, said she was excited to be in the same room as the president. Wilkinson, who has been a Trump supporter since 2016, said Trump is doing a good job during this second term.
Attendees wait to enter a midterm rally at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, ahead of an appearance featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Marlene Nabel, who lives in Garfield, Kansas, said Trump is the best president and is fighting to make the country great again. 
“We need everybody to get out and vote, so socialism doesn’t take over our country,” Nabel said. “I’ve never been so involved in politics as I am now that I’ve got grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and I’m fighting for them. … I will fight with Donald Trump to make this country great.” 
Nabel said she used to be a Democrat around a decade ago when Trump was first running for office, but after watching how the news media treated him and how the Democrats – she called them “hateful” — were handling the country, she switched parties. 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already started.
Examiner Reporter Zach Wendling contributed to this report.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Commission denies CMP request for temporary rate increase
description: The Maine Public Utilities Commission Tuesday denied a request from Central Maine Power to enact a temporary rate increase.  At the Tuesday meeting all three commissioners voted to deny the request, primarily because the parties to the rate case could not reach an “undisputed” amount for the increase, as required under state law.  “When we […]
text:
On June 23, the Public Utilities Commission joined staff at Lewiston Public Library, where people filled the room for a public hearing on Central Maine Power's rate case. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)The Maine Public Utilities Commission Tuesday denied a request from Central Maine Power to enact a temporary rate increase. 
At the Tuesday meeting all three commissioners voted to deny the request, primarily because the parties to the rate case could not reach an “undisputed” amount for the increase, as required under state law. 
“When we deliberated the dismissal of CMP’s last rate case, I indicated an openness to temporary rates given the anticipated delay resulting from terminating that proceeding,” said Commission Chair Philip Bartlett. “But to grant a request for temporary rates, there needs to be a clear amount that is not in dispute. In my view, that is not the case here.”
CMP is seeking to increase its revenue by $189 million, and while that case is pending before the commission, the utility requested a temporary rate increase to provide $69.3 million. 
CMP estimated the proposed temporary rate would mean an increase of $7 a month for the typical residential customer using around 550 kilowatt hours each month. 
Commissioner Patrick Scully also noted that state law gives the commission the option to grant a temporary increase, but it does not have to allow it, even if there is an undisputed amount. 
“I view temporary rates to be the exception and not the rule, and not typically available in most cases, barring a showing of extreme need or the potential of serious harm to the utility or its ratepayers,” he said. “In this case, I do not see that a few months of more time to reach a fully considered outcome in this complicated case will result in significant harm to either.”
Commissioner Carolyn Gilbert also noted that the commission is scheduled to make a final ruling in the case in the spring.
“It seems like we’re actually getting fairly close to the end of the case, and so I think we would benefit from letting the full case run before deciding on a rate increase,” she said.
CMP did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday, but in a statement last week after commission staff recommended against the rate increase, the utility said the decision would have consequences beyond the rate case, extending financial uncertainty for the company. 
“​​CMP has already been forced to defer planned capital work, including projects intended to make power available, strengthen reliability, improve resilience and modernize the system, and will continue to do so,” the utility said. “CMP will now also be forced to evaluate workforce levels and hiring plans that support current operations and future needs.”
CMP on Monday shared a list of reliability projects it said would be delayed if the temporary rate increase was not approved, citing “mounting financial pressures” affecting the utility.
Those projects include upgrades to substations in Lewiston, Auburn, South Portland, Biddeford and Saco, along with upgrades to one of CMP’s poorest-performing distribution lines in Limington, Baldwin, Sebago and Standish. 
“For more than a year, we have continued investing in reliability and system improvements while managing rising costs and awaiting the necessary regulatory approval to align rates with the cost of providing service,” CMP President Linda Ball said in the Monday statement. “That approach is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain due to inflation, rising costs and other factors.”
In a statement Tuesday, Rebecca Schultz with the Natural Resources Council of Maine called CMP’s statement on delayed projects “unacceptable” and said the company was threatening Maine residents with cutting union jobs and delaying important work. 
Schultz applauded the commission for denying the temporary rate increase.
Public Utilities Commission staff recommends denying CMP temporary rate hike

“No Mainer thinks utilities should be able to make higher profits without accountability while families and local businesses struggle with the escalating cost of everything,” Schultz said. “Today’s decision by the PUC demonstrates that they agree with the hundreds of Mainers who have asked for a thorough and thoughtful review of CMP’s rate increase request.”
At Tuesday’s meeting, Bartlett said he was “mindful” of CMP’s financial considerations, but pointed to the staff analysis and comments from the Office of Public Advocate, which noted that CMP’s capital spending from 2022 to 2025 significantly exceeded its forecast.
“So to some extent, this is a problem of CMP’s own making,” Bartlett said. 
Scully said that it is “likely” that the final decision in the case will result in a rate increase, if only because of the investments CMP has already made and the rising business costs that the utility faces. 
“We will do our best to find a reasonable outcome that balances the needs of the utility to allow it to provide safe and reliable electric delivery service, with the serious affordability concerns facing customers,” Scully said. 
The Fight the Hike Coalition, a consumer defense group, praised the commission’s decision but said there is still work to be done.
“The PUC’s decision is a temporary reprieve for young Mainers grappling with an affordability crisis,” Jackson Chadwick with Maine Youth for Climate Justice said in a statement. “But this fight isn’t over. We continue urging young Mainers to speak out against utility profiteering at the expense of our hard-working communities, who are simply trying to make a living.”

title: Food bank to open volunteer center in former Charleston grocery store
description: Mountaineer Food Bank plans to open a volunteer center in a former grocery store on Charleston, West Virginia’s West Side.  Charleston City Council on Monday approved the transfer of the old Save a Lot building at 748 Virginia Street West to the organization, based in Gassaway.  “We are deeply excited about this opportunity to better […]
text:
The former Save a Lot building at 748 Virginia Street West in Charleston. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)Mountaineer Food Bank plans to open a volunteer center in a former grocery store on Charleston, West Virginia’s West Side. 
Charleston City Council on Monday approved the transfer of the old Save a Lot building at 748 Virginia Street West to the organization, based in Gassaway. 
“We are deeply excited about this opportunity to better serve the Kanawha Valley and become part of Charleston’s West Side community,” Mountaineer Food Bank CEO Chad Morrison said in a news release from the city of Charleston. 
“For 45 years, Mountaineer Food Bank has fought food insecurity in Kanawha County and now we have a chance to call part of it home. We look forward to transforming the building into a space for exceptional volunteer experiences as well as co-creating the rest of the space with community members to ensure community needs are at the heart of what we are making and no one goes to bed hungry.”
Mountaineer Food Bank plans to relocate its volunteer operations to Charleston from its current location in Poca. 
The new building would offer more space and access for volunteers to prepare and pack food, Caitlyn Johnson, a spokeswoman for the organization, said in an email to West Virginia Watch. 
“Longer term, we are exploring how the property could become a broader neighborhood resource, with future uses shaped by conversations with the community,” Johnson wrote. “The goal is not to replace or duplicate services already being provided by food pantries or other community organizations, but to identify gaps and look for ways to complement and strengthen the work already happening in the neighborhood.”
The food bank works with approximately 35–40 partner agencies in Kanawha County, including Covenant House, Step by Step,and A More Excellent Way, the city said in a news release. Opening the volunteer center would be an expansion of the foodbank’s operations, not a relocation, the city said. The foodbank serves 48 counties.
The Partnership for African American Churches had previously planned to develop the building into a community health center. The city awarded PAAC $440,000 in federal money through the American Rescue Plan to purchase the building. PAAC is no longer in a position to complete the project within federal requirements and timelines, the city said in a news release. 
Monday’s agreement allows the food bank to take over the ARPA-funded project. Mountaineer Food Bank will be required to demonstrate progress toward rehabbing the building by the end of the year, the city said. The immediate focus will be on cleaning it out and beginning necessary building improvements so the organization can use the property, the city said.  
“We have the opportunity to put this property to use in a way that can benefit the West Side and our broader community,” Charleston Mayor Amy Shuler Goodwin said in the news release. “Mountaineer Food Bank brings decades of experience and resources to that work. Their volunteer center gives this facility an immediate purpose, while their commitment to listening to the neighborhood and working alongside organizations already serving the West Side will help shape what comes next.”

title: Oklahoma transportation czar to retire, capping long state career
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma Department of Transportation Executive Director Tim Gatz is retiring at the end of October. Gatz announced his retirement Monday during a meeting of the Oklahoma Transportation Commission, which oversees the agency. His retirement comes after 37 years of state service. “I’ve grown up at this agency and it’s incredibly important to […[...]
text:
Transportation Secretary Tim Gatz in 2024 participates in an Oklahoma Turnpike Authority meeting. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma Department of Transportation Executive Director Tim Gatz is retiring at the end of October.
Gatz announced his retirement Monday during a meeting of the Oklahoma Transportation Commission, which oversees the agency.
His retirement comes after 37 years of state service.
“I’ve grown up at this agency and it’s incredibly important to me,” Gatz said. “The men and women that I’ve had the opportunity to get to know and work with are unlike any that I’ve ever encountered. I loved every one of them.”
Gatz was appointed ODOT executive director in 2019 and reappointed. He began his career with the agency in 1990 as a drafting technician and held various other positions.
He said his decision had nothing to do with politics.
“Service to the citizens of the state of Oklahoma has absolutely been the honor of my lifetime,” Gatz said.
Gatz was instrumental in getting a $8.2 billion, 15-year turnpike improvement and expansion project off of the ground.
He is the former director of the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority and serves as Gov. Kevin Stitt’s Transportation Secretary.
Transportation Commissioner Michael Junk called Gatz the “gold standard for public service.”
“We are indebted to you,” he said.
Gatz, of El Reno, earned a bachelor’s in landscape architecture from Oklahoma State University in 1989 and is a registered professional landscape architect.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas attorney general nominees Kris Kobach, Chris Mann tussle in campaign debate
description: Democrat Chris Mann and Republican Kris Kobach debate legal issues ahead of the Nov. 3 rematch of the 2022 election narrowly won by Kobach.
text:
Republican Attorney General Kris Kobach, left, chats with Democratic Party nominee Chris Mann prior to a campaign debate sponsored by the Johnson County Bar Association. The candidates, who faced off in the 2022 election, will learn their fate on Nov. 3. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)OVERLAND PARK — Republican Kris Kobach and Democrat Chris Mann clashed Tuesday in a debate on their top priority as Kansas attorney general, their perspectives on capital punishment and even what they considered their opponents’ greatest attribute.
Mann and Kobach were on stage for a one-hour debate sponsored by the Johnson County Bar Association that broadly tackled issues of law enforcement, the legal system and the judicial branch. They rarely agreed but shared wariness of potential abuse of AI-powered video surveillance systems and endorsed rigorous enforcement of state open meetings and records law.
The 2026 campaign for attorney general represents a repeat of the 2022 race narrowly won by Kobach, who edged Mann by 15,800 votes, or about 1.6 percentage points.
Mann, a Lawrence attorney who had his law enforcement career ended when a drunk driver struck him during a traffic stop, said he was motivated to bring the office of attorney general “back to Kansans.” He said the office was turned into a vehicle to promote Kobach’s personal political agenda. He said the role of a state attorney general was to enforce law rather than dive into partisan conflict.
“I spent my entire life running towards the problem, and I’m not done with that yet. From police officer to prosecutor, I’ve continue to work to keep our community safe,” Mann said. “My opponent has never worn a badge. He’s never stood toe to toe with violent criminals on the street or in a courtroom. Instead, that man has run for almost every office in the state of Kansas, and he’s done it because he wanted to push his political agenda.”
Mann, who announced he was endorsed by the Kansas State Fraternal Order of Police, said a focus of an attorney general must be the support of Kansas law enforcement agencies in the investigation and prosecution of criminals. He asserted Kobach hadn’t done enough to aid local agencies.
Kobach, a resident of rural Lecompton who served as Kansas secretary of state before being elected as attorney general in 2022, said his reelection was endorsed by 50 sheriffs in Kansas. He said his top second-term priority would be continuation of an “extremely effective” crackdown on the scourge of fentanyl abuse. He said four years of emphasis on hindering trafficking of the powerful drug had reduced fatalities in Kansas.
Overall, he said, the Kansas crime rate had fallen to a 57-year low through reprioritization of work by the Kansas Bureau of Investigation and promotion of collaboration among local and federal agencies. He said the Kansas office of attorney general was doing more to assist county prosecutors than any other in state history.
“The bottom line is crime is plummeting in the state of Kansas,” Kobach said. “A lot of it has to do with how we’ve used the KBI and also how we’ve removed violent illegal aliens who are allowed to remain in Kansas.”
Kobach said he was committed to persuading more cities and counties to enter agreements with federal agencies to enforce immigration law.
He said he was among only two state attorneys general in the country who personally argued cases in court. He said he had tackled nine such cases in state or federal courts and won seven. The state’s interests were successfully defended in lawsuits filed against the administrations of President Donald Trump and President Joe Biden, he said.
“I will sue the Trump administration again if they do anything to violate the Constitution,” Kobach said. “I love this job. I love being able to say to say to a judge, ‘Your Honor, I’m here representing the state of Kansas.'”
 
Death penalty
Kobach said the botched lethal injection in Tennessee of convicted killer Christa Pike on Sept. 30 shouldn’t prompt Kansas to consider repeal of capital punishment. Kansas hasn’t executed anyone since 1965.
If anything, Kobach said, Kansas should adjust state law to speed appeals of people sentenced to die. The state should accept his recommendation to reduce reliance on injection of drugs for executions and use gas to suffocate the condemned instead, he said. He also said no person, including Pike, who was involved in a failed execution should be exempted from that ultimate punishment.
“Kansas should still be in the execution business,” Kobach said. “When you delay 20 or 30 years, in actually carrying out the execution, then you deny justice to the family.”
Mann, who operates a private legal practice focused on defending victims of drunk driving, said it wasn’t the job of the attorney general to drive policy on capital punishment. He said that was the domain of the Kansas Legislature. He did say the death penalty hadn’t been shown to deter violent crime and the failed execution in Tennessee illustrated a challenge that state lawmakers should address.
“The rule of law in Kansas right now is the death penalty,” Mann said. “If a case like that comes across my desk, I’ll prosecute it, plain and simple.”
Moderator Nick Haines, executive producer of Kansas City’s PBS television station, asked the candidates about potential abuse of automated license plate readers that create searchable logs of vehicle traffic.
Mann and Kobach agreed the camera systems had been used to help law enforcement solve crimes, but both said privacy rights and abuse of personal information by rogue police officers should be dealt with by state governments. They said private companies operating the systems need to be held accountable.
“What rights does storing and transferring that data implicate?” Mann said. “I think those are important questions that need answers. That’s up to our Legislature to put up guardrails.”
Kobach said storage of information on motorists by government without probable cause should be viewed as a constitutional infringement. He said state law ought to restrict retention of data to license plates that were part of investigations. In addition, he said, the state ought to impose heavy penalties on law enforcement officers who abused access to the records. That should include financial fines, loss of employment and potential jail time, he said.
Haines lightened the mood by asking the political rivals to articulate what they admired of their opponent. Mann said he appreciated Kobach’s public speaking skills, while Kobach praised Mann’s experience as an officer in the Lawrence Police Department.
“I will say that my opponent is a great adversary on the debate stage,” Mann said. “I’d never actually debated before I jumped into running for office. So, I appreciate his adversarial skills.”
In reply, Kobach said Mann’s experience of serving on the front line of law enforcement offered important insight that would be beneficial to anyone serving as the state’s top law enforcement officer.
“I think that’s admirable,” Kobach said. “I thank him for his service when he was a law enforcement officer. And, I think, he’s also a nice guy.”

title: New ad targets Byron Donalds in the counties he lost in the GOP primary
description: With Democrat David Jolly being out-fundraised by more than $100 million in his bid to defeat Republican Byron Donalds and become Florida’s next governor, his campaign will take any support it can get. Some arrived this week in the form of a campaign ad airing in selected Florida markets bashing Donalds for not being able to […]
text:
J.C. Planas is a former Republican state legislator who flipped to the Democrats in 2019.
(Photo via Florida House of Representatives)With Democrat David Jolly being out-fundraised by more than $100 million in his bid to defeat Republican Byron Donalds and become Florida’s next governor, his campaign will take any support it can get.
Some arrived this week in the form of a campaign ad airing in selected Florida markets bashing Donalds for not being able to tell the difference between “right and wrong.”
The ad is paid for by a group calling itself Conservatives for Ethical Leadership, chaired by former Republican state lawmaker-turned-Democrat J.C. Planas and is affiliated with the Lincoln Project, led by famed “Never Trumper” Rick Wilson, a former Republican strategist based in Tallahassee.
The group says the ad is airing on cable in the Tallahassee media market and running digitally in all of the 17 counties Donalds lost in the GOP primary election in August to Lt. Gov. Jay Collins. It’s also airing in the Villages.
“Every conservative in Florida was raised to know right from wrong. Byron Donalds’ record shows he can’t tell the difference,” Planas said in a written statement. “This is not about party. It is about character. The voters in these counties took a hard look at him in August and said no, and nothing he has done since should change their minds.”
Conservatives for Ethical Leadership was created in June and is primarily funded by another political committee called Affordable Florida. It ran a digital ad earlier this summer calling out Donalds for his support for AI data centers.
Meanwhile, the Donalds campaign released two ads Tuesday aimed at raising his support within the GOP base, featuring the endorsements that he’s received from President Trump and Ron DeSantis.
“Byron Donalds will continue Governor DeSantis’ leadership and work to cut taxes, lower insurance bills, and make Florida more affordable,” said Ryan Smith, chief campaign strategist for Donalds. “Byron Donalds is proud to have the endorsement of former President Trump and Governor DeSantis, and he will fight side by side with them to keep the Left’s radical and costly agenda out of Florida.”
The most recent campaign funding reports show Donalds having raised more than $134 million, while Jolly has raised less than $17 million.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont colleges chart a path forward against demographic and financial headwinds
description:
“We cannot lose more colleges in Vermont if we're going to try to address Vermont's demographic issue,” said a leader of Middlebury College.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont colleges chart a path forward against demographic and financial headwinds.
text:
The Champlain College campus in Burlington on Wednesday, June 25, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Higher education institutions in Vermont are devising ways to stay afloat — from tuition discounts designed to boost enrollment to cutting employee benefits — as they face shifting demographics and financial constraints, college administrators say.   
The Northeast region faces some of the sharpest impacts of the demographic cliff due to plummeting birthrates in the aftermath of the Great Recession starting in 2007, leading to a small pool of potential college students in Vermont in the coming years. 
Only 60% of recent high school graduates in Vermont continue their education through two or four year degree programs, according to data from Advance Vermont, a nonprofit that seeks to improve career navigation opportunities in the state. Meanwhile, the specter of the seven colleges across the state that shuttered in less than a decade looms large. 
Many Vermont colleges face the same challenges that higher education institutions across the nation face, including “the demographic enrollment cliff and increased student price sensibility, rising operation costs, growing concerns about student debt and return on investment,” said Kimberly Jessup, president of Association of Vermont Independent Colleges.
One college that is working to remain above water is St. Michael’s College, which received notice from the New England Commission of Higher Education this past summer that it could lose accreditation if operating deficits and dropping enrollments continue. 
St. Michael’s College deficit sat at $2.6 million in 2025, and its projected balance at the end of the 2026 fiscal year left it “little runway” for its financial future, according to a joint statement released by the commission and college. In August, the college received probate court permission to access $30 million worth of the principle from its restricted endowment if needed, said Ellen Kane, vice president of Advancement and Communications for St. Michael’s College.
“That money is not in our bank account; it’s still invested under the purpose of an endowment,” Kane said. “We will only access it if we need it, and the way you can look at it is a safety net or line of credit.”
Kane maintains that things are looking up for the college, which has stabilized enrollment numbers, she said, while it looks for ways to increase enrollment going forward. The college saw a 145% increase in donations in fiscal year 2026, totalling $13.6 million, according to Kane and it is half way through a 5-year plan to improve the school’s resources, educational program and finances. 
New majors and match programs
Among the steps it has taken is creating an emergency services major, which includes emergency medical services and wilderness rescue training, in response to a local workforce gap, hopefully offering ready employment opportunities to students in the program. 
St. Michael’s hopes to boost enrollment with the launch of a flagship match program last year, which sets the cost of tuition equal to the cost of in-state tuition at a student’s home state public university. 
“We may be facing challenges right now, but we’re working on strategies to overcome them,” said Kane.
Tuition discounts are emerging as a popular strategy among higher education institutions across the state, including the University of Vermont and Middlebury College.  
Middlebury College is cushioned from some of the demographic and financial headwinds facing higher education as it has the largest endowment in Vermont, said David Provost, executive vice president of finance and administration. 
Still, Middlebury College has sought out financial sustainability strategies by reducing employee benefits under a budget stabilization plan last year that saved an excess of $15 million annually, said Provost. Middlebury College also sold the satellite graduate campus called Middlebury Institute of International Studies at Monterey to Soka University this year.
Provost said Middlebury College is focused on building out community partnerships in Addison County to try and persuade graduates to stay in Vermont, join the workforce and raise families in the state.  
“We cannot lose more colleges in Vermont if we’re going to try to address Vermont’s demographic issue,” Provost said. 
Lego block curriculum
Champlain College has faced declining enrollment and financial deficits in recent years, while facing backlash for layoffs and phasing out five majors. 
President Alex Hernandez said he recognizes that students are questioning the value of higher education, and Champlain College is allowing students to use more credits for internships and other career-building opportunities. The college hopes to attract people seeking to further their education, training and credentials through a broad selection of online classes. 
Champlain College “redesigned a curriculum that looked a little bit like Lego blocks that you can snap together in lots of different ways to give students lots of different paths into the workforce,”  Hernandez said. 
Hernandez said that Champlain College is looking for ways to invest in financial stability, including by selling off distant buildings in order to build dormitories closer to campus.
Champlain College has also launched a tuition discount beginning in the next school year that would match the tuition for the University of Vermont for a Vermont student’s first year, and cap out-of-state tuition and fees for first year students at $30,000.  
Small colleges lean into their niche
Bennington College, which has faced operating deficits and laid off staff in recent years, created a taskforce to spot inefficiencies and ways to better use resources and engage the college community so it can make smart budget decisions, according to President Danielle Egan. She said the college hopes to close its deficit in the next three to five years. 
It hopes to pump up its revenue with programs like a mental health counseling program, an educational licensure program, non-certificate-bearing summer programs and artistic residencies, Egan said. 
“How do we make sure what we’re doing for our students makes the most sense and really targets back to what we think is most critical for a Bennington education?” Egan questioned. “We’re choosing a strategy that allows us to live into our distinction and live into our niche kind of place in the market.”
Jim Dlugos, president of Landmark College, with enrollment of roughly 600, teaches neurodiverse students and has escaped some of the financial pressures and demographic challenges because of its size and unique educational model. Three quarters of its endowment is unrestricted, giving it more leeway to use funds for various initiatives, he said.
Landmark is working to make the school more affordable for students through scholarships and aid, Dlugos said. Landmark College also has dual enrollment courses for high schoolers and is looking to expand into satellite campuses in other states with the same educational model. Students and alumni of Landmark College also have access to lifelong academic and career advisors, with career planning starting in the first semester, Dlugos said. 
Flexible education helps close the gap
Vermont State University completed its formal merger process of three colleges into one system with five satellite campuses this year. The merger took three years and involved cutting programs. The university is working on closing the remaining $5 million gap of its structural deficit it inherited through the merger, said the Vermont State College System Chancellor Beth Mauch.
Older and working adults and students who need flexible education have helped enrollment at both Vermont State University and Community College of Vermont stay steady amid challenges faced by the industry, said Mauch, who oversees both institutions in her role. 
Vermont Student Assistance Corporation President Scott Giles said he believes that Vermont colleges across the state should respond to growing return on investment concerns raised by students by reducing costs, clearly communicating value and creating shorter-term certificate programs, stackable credits and other workforce development opportunities that bring a more immediate payoff. 
Thomas Cheney, executive director of Advance Vermont, said that it is important that the Vermont school system prioritizes career and education exploration and creates support systems for students so they are prepared after high school graduation. 
“It’s not just that we have fewer young people in Vermont, but that fewer of those who are here are interested in continuing their education,” Cheney wrote in an email, adding that the job for education leaders is to show them a path toward that in Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont colleges chart a path forward against demographic and financial headwinds.

name: Missouri Independent
title: St. Louis jury awards $10 million in sprawling Missouri cannabis ownership fight
description: A St. Louis jury awarded $10 million Tuesday to three plaintiffs in a sprawling ownership battle over six Missouri cannabis licenses involving more than 20 businesses and individuals. Over a week of testimony, jurors heard about a tangled series of business agreements and allegations that partners went behind one another’s backs to secure competing deals. […[...]
text:
Mel Carnahan Courthouse in St. Louis (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).A St. Louis jury awarded $10 million Tuesday to three plaintiffs in a sprawling ownership battle over six Missouri cannabis licenses involving more than 20 businesses and individuals.
Over a week of testimony, jurors heard about a tangled series of business agreements and allegations that partners went behind one another’s backs to secure competing deals.
The case hinged on whether the plaintiffs in the case —  AJO MO LLC, Hi-Rise LLC and DMS Facility Management LLC — lawfully acquired a company through a transaction that would have made them majority owners of a cannabis cultivation and manufacturing facility in Waynesville that also included 40% stake in four Heya dispensaries.
Missouri cannabis regulators recognized AJO and Hi-Rise as the owners of the Waynesville facility licenses in May 2024. However, the state hasn’t approved the disputed ownership changes involving the four Heya dispensaries while a series of lawsuits played out. 
The jurors sided with plaintiffs on counts of breach of contract and tortuous interference, awarding them a total of $10 million.
“We’re pleased the jury decided in our favor and awarded appropriate damages,” Peter Barden, spokesman for the plaintiffs, told The Independent after the verdict.
The decision may not end the company’s struggles for AJO and Hi-Rise. As jurors deliberated inside the Mel Carnahan Courthouse in St. Louis last week, Missouri cannabis regulators filed proposed rules that would change how the state handles the kinds of complicated ownership arrangements exposed during the trial. 
The proposed rules would give regulators new authority when someone with a history of specified violations is found to be “exercising a controlling influence” over a facility. It would lead to a fine of up to $100,000 or suspension or revocation of a license, according to the rules.
That could be significant for AJO, which owns 50% of Delta Extraction, a marijuana manufacturing company whose license the state revoked in November 2023 after it became the center of a massive product recall.
AJO LLC told The Independent last year it was only a passive investor in Delta Extraction, where it owns 50%. However, court documents and testimony in that case contradict that characterization. 
St. Louis Judge Michael Noble barred defense attorneys from telling jurors about Delta Extraction’s license revocation and AJO’s connection to the company. 
The proposed state rules include a detailed list of offenses that include selling or distributing unregulated THC, fraudulently using an agent identification card, tampering with or falsifying video recordings and refusing to cooperate with a department investigation.
Amy Moore, director of the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation, which oversees the marijuana program, explained earlier this year the aim of the rules. 
“What we are saying in the rule is if a year from now [if the rules are approved] we look at your ownership,” Moore told The Independent at the time, “and we see you have someone exercising a controlling influence that you know has done these things, then that is a violation.”
With regards to the proposed regulations, Barden said: “We’re reviewing the proposed regulations to determine how they may impact our ownership structure if implemented.”
 The Case

The case grew out of a partnership between Eric Kirberg and Scott Sterling, who began working together around 2018 on Missouri medical marijuana license applications. When they didn’t win licenses of their own, they did what many others did at the time: they offered to build and run facilities for license winners in exchange for equity.
Kirberg, a contractor, built out a cultivation and manufacturing facility in Waynesville, and Sterling, a cannabis executive, ran operations as CEO. In return, their company got 9.9% of the entity holding the licenses and an option to buy the rest from its owner, 1913 Holdings. They did the same with four Heya dispensaries and secured 40% equity. The two set up three companies, called the Delphi entities, to hold the ownership stakes, the management contracts and the Waynesville property.
Sterling resigned in October 2021 as CEO but retained his equity in the parent company. Soon after, Delphi defaulted on a loan Kirberg had personally guaranteed. 
In May 2022, AJO and Hi-Rise paid about $6.9 million to the lender and acquired the Delphi company that owned the Waynesville facility and property, plus an option to buy 95% of the Delphi company that held everything else. That included the 9.9% stake in the Waynesville license and the 40% share of the Heya dispensaries. Sterling was not a party to the deal and says he never consented to it. 
Just before closing arguments, Noble ruled that the option to purchase agreement — which was a major part of the plaintiffs’ case — was never executed. AJO and Hi-Rise instead ultimately obtained control of the Waynesville licenses through a separate deal with 1913 Holdings to secure 90.1% of the Waynesville licenses, while Kirberg retained 6.9% and Sterling 3% of the licenses.
“They couldn’t sue for breach of contract,” defense attorney Jeffrey Lowe told The Independent. “It’s not until it was exercised was it going to be an enforceable contract, so they didn’t have that.”
(Amanda Watford/Stateline)
In March 2023, Kirberg and Sterling sold their Delphi interests to one of the defendants, TMSKirk, whose principals were then running Heya. The defendants argue Heya had a right of first refusal over Delphi’s dispensary stake that took priority over the AJO and Hi-Rise option, which defendants argued was never executed. 
“We are here trying to get back the business that they stole from us,” Lowe said in his closing statement. 
The plaintiffs successfully argued they were harmed by the defendants.
“This has been a saga for four years now,” Ampleman said in his closing arguments. “You have the opportunity to make a definitive statement on who was in the right and who was in the wrong.” 
Lowe said the defense plans to file a post-trial motion arguing, among other things, that Noble’s ruling removing the option agreement from the case immediately before closing arguments created confusion about what remained for jurors to decide.
 ‘Own the car’

The trial also highlighted a broader issue Missouri regulators are attempting to address: The companies recognized by the state as owners of a cannabis license are not always the same people or companies effectively controlling the business.
One of the defendants, Tim Schlesinger, an owner of TMSKirk, testified last week that he believes under Missouri law, people can buy a cannabis company and operate it without the state’s approval. 
“So you can own the car before you get it licensed at the DMV,” he said. 
He explained how while state regulators may have an owner down on paper, another company could be filing tax returns, taking all the revenue and acting as the owner. And this occurs with many cannabis companies, Schlesinger said, including Good Day Farm cannabis company who purchased one of the Heya dispensaries involved in the case. 
“They are managing it; they’re running it; they’re branded with it,” he said. “The bank accounts are in their names.” 
The Division of Cannabis Regulation did not respond to a request for comment on Schlesinger’s characterization.
Amy Moore, director of the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation, speaks with a microbusiness owner at the National Cannabis Industry Association’s summit in St. Louis (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).
 
AJO and Hi-Rise also operated the Waynesville facility before the state approved their ownership change. These dealings make it difficult for the public and even employees to understand who owns certain dispensaries. 
The new rules won’t necessarily make those relationships more transparent, but they will make it easier for companies to change ownership by streamlining the approval process.
Currently when a cannabis facility wants to make a change in ownership that’s more than 50%, it has to submit a business-change application and get pre-approval to do so. 
That process can drag on anywhere from six months to a year, Moore said earlier this year.
Instead, every licensee would submit a report annually that outlines the ownership percentage for each entity or individual. Licensees must still seek pre-approval if they’re adding a new owner or an individual who has 10% or more interest, or they’re fully transferring their licenses to another entity. 
A state audit released earlier this year found that the division took an average of 165 days to approve or deny business ownership change requests from submission to final action, based on data the auditor reviewed from 2020 through 2023.
The annual review requirement will also offer an opportunity for regulators to catch rule-breakers in ownership or management positions.
Under the proposed rules, regulators can deny ownership applications if “any owner or manager of the applicant entity who exercises a controlling influence over the license’s management, policies, or decision-making” had previously broken specific rules. 
That provision could create additional scrutiny for companies connected to previously revoked licenses.
When the state approved the license change for AJO and Hi-Rise in May 2024, Delta’s appeal of its license revocation was still pending. The final verdict didn’t come down until nine months later. 
“The totality of the circumstances at the time, including the nature of the ownership change, was not sufficient cause to deny the change,” division spokeswoman Lisa Cox said.
Cox also said the state’s administrative rules currently do not prohibit individuals who have had a license revoked from acquiring another license. 
The proposed rules would give regulators greater authority to consider that history.
The proposed amendments will be published in the Nov. 2 issue of the Missouri Register, which can be found on the Missouri Secretary of State’s website. Public comments will be accepted from Nov. 2 through Dec. 2.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Supreme Court denies latest challenge to Indian Child Welfare Act
description: Reprinted with permission from The Imprint.  The U.S. Supreme Court will not take up the most recent attempt to dismantle the 1978 Indian Child Welfare Act, according to the docket posted Monday, leaving in place a Minnesota lower court’s ruling. The case involves Red Lake Nation twins who were placed in a temporary foster placement […]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Reprinted with permission from The Imprint. 
The U.S. Supreme Court will not take up the most recent attempt to dismantle the 1978 Indian Child Welfare Act, according to the docket posted Monday, leaving in place a Minnesota lower court’s ruling.
The case involves Red Lake Nation twins who were placed in a temporary foster placement four years ago. The white couple who cared for the siblings for more than a year sought to regain custody after the children were placed with relatives. Under ICWA, tribal children’s kin and community members are prioritized for foster care placements over non-Native caregivers.
“My clients are deeply disappointed,” Mark Fiddler, who served as co-counsel for the foster couple, said in a statement sent to The Imprint.
Fiddler, a member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians, vowed to continue his yearslong effort to overturn the federal law, which he says “creates a separate and unequal system for Indian children.”
“The fight for equality for Indian children will go on,” Fiddler wrote.
Three years ago, the Supreme Court overturned a similar constitutional challenge to ICWA brought by Fiddler and his legal team in Brackeen v. Haaland.
The latest Supreme Court petition was filed May 4 on behalf of foster parents Kellie and Nathan Reyelts. Local attorneys teamed up on the case with the Goldwater Institute, an Arizona-based conservative think tank. They sought to overturn ICWA and the local version of the federal law, the Minnesota Indian Family Preservation Act. Both require heightened efforts before tribal children and their families can be separated in child welfare cases.
The legal challenge alleged that the laws protecting Indigenous children, families and tribes racially discriminate against white foster parents such as the Reyelts.
“Each day, children like those involved in this case are denied the possibility of safe, loving homes, solely because of the color of their skin,” the plaintiff’s May petition reads.
Minnesota’s state Supreme Court rejected that argument in March, ruling that the Reyelts do not have standing in the case. Indigenous legal scholars maintain that ICWA is not a race-based law, because it hinges on the government-to-government relationship between tribes and the U.S.
The Protect ICWA Campaign, which includes several Indigenous rights groups, praised the high court’s rejection of the plaintiff’s petition, calling ICWA the “gold standard in child welfare policy.”
“We are pleased that the Court rejected another unwarranted attack on ICWA,” said the group in a press statement. Monday’s denial “supports the best interests of Native children, families, and communities.”

title: Voting rights advocates organize volunteers to track potential intimidation at the polls
text: As President Donald Trump refuses to rule out taking extreme action in the midterm elections, voting rights advocates and civil rights leaders are bolstering their voter protection efforts in anticipation of possible federal interference.The focus by activists comes amid uncertainty among advocates and election officials over what Trump may do before, during and after Election Day. Some organizations are preparing to deploy volunteers to the polls to help assure voters in places where fear of federal intimidation may run high.On Tuesday, several groups — including the Save America Movement, the American Federation of Teachers labor union and the National Action Network — launched Vote Safe, an initiative that will put local volunteers at polling locations in areas where they say pressure on Black, Latino and Asian voters is highest. The program will include Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio. The volunteers will document any intimidation and serve as a reassuring presence for voters, organizers said.“The fear is the point and we must do something about it,” Mary Corcoran, executive director of the Save America Movement, a nonpartisan pro-democracy group, said on a call with reporters. “Left unaddressed, fear does the work of keeping people home without a single agent setting foot at a polling place.”Volunteers will include clergy members, veterans, teachers and others trained to provide clear answers on voters’ rights, Corcoran said.In Ohio, where Vote Safe will launch on the first day of early voting, Republican Sen. Jon Husted is facing former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country. Springfield, Ohio, also has a large Haitian immigrant population that has been repeatedly attacked by Trump, who is seeking to deport them.The Rev. Al Sharpton, a civil rights leader who founded the National Action Network, suggested on Tuesday’s press call that some Americans in Ohio fear they could also be detained or even deported by ICE because of their skin color.“‘You don’t understand, any Black looks like a Haitian in Ohio,’” Sharpton said, recalling a previous conversation with a journalist in Ohio. “You’ve got to prove you were from Alabama, not Port-au-Prince, after you’re deported.”ProPublica reported on Tuesday that more than 500 U.S. citizens have been detained by immigration agents during the second Trump administration. About a dozen citizens, mostly children, have been deported.What Trump has saidTrump, who has long made false claims about stolen elections and voter fraud, has maintained ambiguity surrounding what election-related actions he may take after the U.S. Supreme Court blocked his plan to use the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail ballots. Congress also didn’t pass the SAVE America Act, a measure he championed that would require voters to offer documentary proof of citizenship.In a recent TIME magazine interview, Trump said he hadn’t thought of deploying Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, agents to the polls. But he also left open the possibility of declaring a national emergency, which legal experts say would give him no power over elections. Under the Constitution, states administer elections, not the federal government.Earlier this year, Trump told reporters he would “do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.”Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said ICE agents can serve warrants at election sites, despite a ban on armed federal personnel at polling places. At the same time, DHS has denied any plans to target polling places.DOJ election monitorsThe Department of Justice’s plans to deploy 1,000 election monitors at polling places has also fueled concern among Democrats and voting rights advocates — and some Republicans. While the DOJ regularly dispatches monitors each election cycle, the scope of the effort and Trump’s history of pressuring election officials has led to unease about how the monitors will behave. Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, earlier this year expressed reservations about Justice Department monitors, calling their actions “very odd” after DOJ personnel watched voting in the state’s primary election. On Monday, the NAACP sued the Justice Department for records about its election monitor program, alleging the DOJ didn’t comply with Freedom of Information Act timelines.“Americans deserve to know whether the Justice Department is abusing its law enforcement powers to the detriment of voters and the election officials tasked with running our elections,” Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel, said in a statement.Justice Department spokesperson ​​Kiersten Pels wrote in an email to States Newsroom that monitors comply with all legal and ethical requirements. Pels added that they don’t interfere with the voting process and that their work “is consistent with longstanding Department practice of monitoring elections for compliance with federal law."U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche dismissed concerns about the monitors in an interview on “Fox News Sunday.” While confirming plans for about 1,000 monitors, he emphasized that the department sends out monitors every federal election.“They’re not going to Republican states, they’re not going to Democrat states. They’re going to every state to make sure that our elections are carried out legally, fairly and appropriately,” Blanche said.After Election DayThe preparations by civic groups also include post-election planning for potential disruptions to vote counting or attempts to overturn losses.The FBI seized ballots from the 2020 election in Fulton County, Georgia, in January. The then-director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, was present at the raid at Trump’s request, underscoring its importance to the president. The Justice Department also spent months seeking information on election workers in Fulton County during the 2020 election before a federal judge quashed the subpoena in July.The raid raised questions among activists and election experts about whether federal law enforcement would seek search warrants to obtain ballots after Election Day.Ballot seizures are a point of concern, said Andrew Walchuk, senior policy director and counsel for voting and fair representation at Common Cause, a voting rights group. The raid was “an alert” to election offices that a seizure is something they need to prepare for, Walchuk said.“It is definitely something that groups across the country are ready for, that we’re watching,” Walchuk told reporters last week.Like other groups, Common Cause’s election preparations include training a network of volunteers who can help voters and identify potential problems. In Texas alone, more than 400 volunteers are already, said Marliza Marin, Common Cause’s Texas program manager. “It’s kind of unheard of to have this many volunteers already trained,” Marin said.

name: WyoFile
title: Teton County opposes Grand Teton pathway project revived by Trump administration
description:
“We are particularly disappointed by the process,” board of commissioners writes to Burgum.
The post Teton County opposes Grand Teton pathway project revived by Trump administration appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Teton County officials are unhappy with the Trump administration’s reversal of a 2016 management plan directive that paves the way for a pathway in a wildlife-rich Grand Teton National Park corridor. 
The board of county commissioners approved a letter Monday to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum underscoring the body’s dismay at being excluded from the process that resulted in an August amendment to a 2016 management plan. The amendment calls for construction of a multi-use pathway along roughly 7 miles of the Moose-Wilson Road in the park.
“We ask the Department to reconsider the corridor-length pathway decision and include Teton County’s input as a cooperating agency before proceeding,” the letter states. 





This map illustrates the 2026 amended Moose-Wilson Corridor Final Comprehensive Management Plan. (National Park Service)

The letter signifies a win for Friends of the Moose-Wilson Corridor. The volunteer group reformed this year in explicit response to the pathway’s revival. The Friends organization previously opposed the pathway during the public process that resulted in the 2016 Moose-Wilson Corridor Comprehensive Management Plan record of decision. 
“We remain hopeful that the NPS will be allowed to press pause on this destructive project and seek other ways to manage visitation in the Moose-Wilson Corridor in Grand Teton National Park,” group member Joan Anzelmo told WyoFile in an email. 
Teton area residents are not uniformly against the pathway’s revival. Transportation advocate Tim Young, who has long championed the pathway as an important safety upgrade for the congested corridor, told WyoFile he thought the development was “outstanding.”
A road much-traveled
The road is the main artery through what’s known as the Moose-Wilson Corridor — a swath of roughly 10,300 acres that provides access to destinations like the Death Canyon trailhead, Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve and Murie Ranch historic district. 
Located between Teton Village and park destinations, it’s a major starting point for visitors eager to spot wildlife, including bears and moose. Area locals also use it as a shortcut to bypass the town of Jackson, and it’s popular with cyclists. 
In 2016, the park service estimated that roughly 400,000 visitors traveled the Moose-Wilson corridor annually. The narrow roadway is closed to RVs and mostly signed for 25 miles per hour. 
Tim Young walks his bike past a gate leading to an alternative bike route in Grand Teton National Park in August 2026. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
In the late 2000s, Young led an effort to develop an extensive network of bike pathways around Jackson — including Moose to Jenny Lake and Jackson to Moose. His advocacy followed high-profile cycling deaths. 
In 2013, the National Park Service initiated the Moose-Wilson Corridor Comprehensive Management Plan process, proposing four ways, or alternatives, to manage the corridor. During the ensuing public process, stakeholders litigated the concept of a separate pathway. Advocates argued that it would create safer access to the park for the vehicles and bikes traveling the winding roadway at various speeds, while opponents claimed a pathway would unduly harm the corridor’s rich wildlife habitat and archaeological sites.
In its 2016 record of decision, the park service selected alternative C, which generally restricted development within the corridor to the existing footprint. Notably left out of that alternative was the separate pathway proposal. 
“The emphasis of the selected action is to balance preservation and public use and enjoyment by exemplifying conservation legacies within the corridor,” the agency’s record of decision read.
When the federal agency announced in June that it was revisiting the pathway portion of the 2016 decision, it cited a 2025 executive order that “calls for improving visitor services, enhancing access, and reviewing policies that may unnecessarily restrict recreation in national parks.” Recreational opportunities, newly stipulated by President Donald Trump’s order, were not considered during the previous scoping process, the draft stated.
The park service identified additional scoping work related in part to pathway construction and opened a 15-day public comment period. 
With the amendment calling for the path’s construction in August, the park service reopened those old rifts over its obligation to balance multiple concerns, including wildlife protection, archeological preservation, recreation and safe visitor access.
Not so fast
Anzelmo, who worked for the park service for 35 years, was dismayed when she heard of the plan’s amendment. Friends of the Moose-Wilson Corridor had already participated in a robust public process, arguing that a separate paved pathway would damage rich wildlife habitat at a ridiculous cost to taxpayers, she said.
The Friends group supports bike paths in certain places, Anzelmo said. “But there are places in national parks that are not appropriate or compatible with bike paths, most especially in grizzly bear habitat.”
Of particular concern to the group was the absence of a supplemental environmental impact statement or meaningful public involvement in the new reversal. 
In the wake of the amendment, the Friends group reorganized and began its campaign anew, teaming up with the Jackson Hole Conservation Alliance and lobbying local, state and federal officials in an attempt to slow the process. That included the Teton County Board of Commissioners. 
In the letter it approved Monday, the board asked the Interior Department to “conduct further analysis of alternatives that support recreational access other than a separate pathway” and requested that it and other local stakeholders be engaged in the process as cooperating agencies.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Republicans are making a campaign issue out of the projected budget gap
description: As Mainers begin casting votes to determine who will control state government next, a $1 billion projected budget gap has become political fodder.  The Maine Department of Administrative and Financial Services’ Bureau of the Budget last week projected a structural gap in the general fund of $1.085 billion for the 2028-2029 biennium, the first two-year […]
text:
Lawmakers gather for session in the Maine House of Representatives in Augusta on March 12, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)As Mainers begin casting votes to determine who will control state government next, a $1 billion projected budget gap has become political fodder. 
The Maine Department of Administrative and Financial Services’ Bureau of the Budget last week projected a structural gap in the general fund of $1.085 billion for the 2028-2029 biennium, the first two-year budget the next governor and Legislature will be tasked to craft. Maine also has a separate highway fund, for which the bureau projected a $256.7 million gap.
It is not uncommon for these reports to predict structural gaps, said Sharon Huntley, communications director for DAFS. Aside from 2022, after federal relief from the COVID-19 pandemic, every report from the past decade has projected a structural gap, Huntley said. 
The latest gap projection is about the same average rate as the structural gaps over those eight other bienniums. However, the number itself is larger, corresponding with how Maine’s budget has grown during Gov. Janet Mills’ two terms in office. 
“They’ve grown the budget from $7 billion dollars to $12 billion, so it’s easy to see how you can spend ahead of your means,” said House Minority Leader Billy Bob Faulkingham (R-Winter Harbor) during a press conference in Augusta Tuesday. 
Democrats have pushed back, noting that budget growth has corresponded with the state finally meeting its statutory obligations. Under Mills, the state met its responsibilities for municipal revenue sharing to lower tax rates and funding 55% of education, as well as reduced the number of uninsured people at record levels — all growing expenses. Inflation has been another factor. 
“I’m seeing a lot of ridiculous, dishonest, politically opportunistic posts from Maine Republicans who frankly seem desperate as Election Day approaches,” Rep. Drew Gattine (D-Westbrook), who co-chairs the Legislature’s budget committee, wrote in a lengthy rebuttal on Facebook. 
Legislative Republicans are hoping the gap leads Mainers to elect them into office on Nov. 3. During the Tuesday press conference, several raised concern about the growing cost of MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, and broad goals to cut waste and fraud. 
“Unless we change how these programs are managed, we’ll be standing here again with another shortfall, another emergency,” said Assistant Senate Minority Leader Matthew Harrington (R-York), standing behind a podium with a sign that read, “No new taxes. Period.”
Two years ago, when the state faced a MaineCare budget gap, the minority party refused to fund the cost increase without structural changes to the program. 
The next governor, and Legislature, could opt to adjust program spending or raise taxes in light of the latest projections, which are how much revenue is estimated to fall short of what current law requires the state to spend. State revenue projections in December could also alter estimates. 
The three gubernatorial candidates have proposed various plans to lower property taxes and the cost of housing — costs not accounted for in the projections. 
In the end, Maine’s constitution requires a balanced budget. 
“Budgets are balanced when Republicans have control and budgets are balanced when Democrats have control,” Gattine wrote. “The distinction lies in how they are balanced.”
